News.title: Teacher accused of having sex with pupil, 14, tells court she found it hard to ‘say no’ and wanted to be liked
News.content:
'PAEDO' MISS CLAIMS Teacher accused of having sex with pupil, 14, tells court she found it hard to ‘say no’ and wanted to be liked

A TEACHER accused of having sex with a pupil has told a court she wanted to be liked and found it hard saying “no”.

Bronwen James, 30, allegedly had sex with the 16-year-old up to four times after they began messaging on Snapchat.



Winchester Crown Court heard she was teaching PE at Bitterne Park School in Southampton, Hants, at the time of the alleged offences.

Giving evidence, James told a jury she felt she was immature, easily influenced and very lenient with pupils.



But she denied flirting with the teen and having sex with him – claiming the boy made up the allegations to look “cool” in front of his mates.

James also said she began teaching aged just 21 and described herself as “immature” and conceded she did not think she was a good teacher.

She said: “I just don’t think I was ready for it. As my career progressed, I realised maybe I was seeking validation from the wrong people.

“I think I was a very lenient teacher, I was not strict, there were behaviour policies I would not necessarily follow, such as using mobile phones in lessons.

“But I did not want to upset them, I did not want to anger them. I wanted them to like me.”

James suggested leaving her phone on her desk while she was teaching in class may have given the teenager an opportunity to get access to her Snapchat account and they exchanged some messages.



But she told the jury it was only “brief” conversations and not constant exchanges.

Heather Stangoe, defending, asked James why she had communicated with a student when she knew this was against the rules as a teacher.

James said: “I think I wanted to be liked. I did not want to let people down. I was easily influenced.



“I found it hard to say ‘no’ to people I wanted to please.”

The defendant admitted there was “banter” with pupils in her class, but said it was never of a sexual nature.

And she denied “flirting” with the teenager or supplying him vapes and said an occasion when he allegedly slapped her bottom never happened.

But she admitted later lying to police, claiming he had never visited her home in Fareham as she did not want the situation to “blow up”.

She told the jury she was out walking her dog and the teenager messaged her asking for a lift home.



James said she agreed as it was on the way to her home and picked the youngster up in her car.

But she said she drove to her house first to drop the dog off and use the toilet, before taking him home and dropping him off.

She maintained no sex took place and he remained downstairs.

Edward Culver, prosecuting, suggested she gave the boy a lift because she had flirted with him and said he was able to provide police with an accurate sketch plan of her home upstairs because they had sex there.

He continued: “I suggest there’s a lot of mysteries in this case. It’s wholly implausible he was able to provide that plan unless he had been in your bedroom a number of times.



“It’s all explained by you having a relationship with him, having sexual activity with him. There’s no other plausible explanation.”

James replied: “It did not happen.”

The court previously heard James “flirted” with the boy before accepting his request to add her on Snapchat.

After exchanging messages, she drove him to Weston Shore, Southampton, where they parked and kissed in her car, it was said.

The pair then allegedly went back to James’ house where they had sex, which happened on three or four occasions.



Mr Culver said: “The tennis was on at Wimbledon. They began watching TV before kissing and touching each other.

“She took her clothes off and then he took his clothes off.”

Mr Culver said that the pair performed sex acts on each other before they had unprotected sex.

Jurors heard James allegedly told the boy she “loved him” and “wanted to move away” with him in daily messages.

The school was made aware of the apparent relationship when a student showed a teacher some messages between James and the boy.



Mr Culver said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship, he was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover, him being the eighth man she had slept with.

“Her photo was visible on the phone screen.”

After the alleged offences were exposed, James was later spoken to by police whilst under caution.

She prepared a statement claiming she had received communication from an unknown number, which turned out to be him, and suggested he was “being put up” to make these allegations by another student.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

James, of Chippenham, Wiltshire, denies four charges of sexual activity with the boy.



The trial continues.

News.title: Four paintings worth £8million stolen from Renoir Museum in France after thieves ‘cut pictures out of frames’
News.content:
BRAZEN RAID Four paintings worth £8million stolen from Renoir Museum in France after thieves ‘cut pictures out of frames’

FOUR works of art worth some £8million have been stolen from a Renoir museum in the south of France.

Thieves were filmed breaking into the building in Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, on Tuesday morning.



The individuals were allegedly caught on camera cutting paintings from their frames, to more easily get them out of the museum.

But the bungling burglars dropped one of the artworks as they fled, according to mayor Bryan Masson.



Bryan Masson said: “Spotted thanks to the town’s video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran.”

His office estimated the value of the stolen art at 9million euros (£7.7million).

“Two hooded individuals were recorded on CCTV”, according to an investigating source.

At least four paintings were taken, but one was recovered after it was found abandoned, reportedly in the garden, afterwards.

Masson added: “The museum alarm went off at 5:48 am. At 5:53 am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene.”

“Since this morning, both the municipal and national police have been deployed to the site.



“The perpetrators are being actively sought, and the investigation is ongoing.

“Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-Sur-Mer. These events are particularly serious.”

Other popular Renoir works displayed in the Cagnes museum include La Ferme des Collettes, The Farm at Les Collettes in English.



The oil on canvas piece was completed in 1915 and depicts the home Renoir moved to in 1908, which now houses the Renoir Museum.

The painting is displayed in what was once Renoir’s bedroom.

It comes less than a year after thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in broad daylight, lifting £76 million worth of jewellery stolen in just four minutes.

Renoir’s full name was Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Born in Limoges, France, in 1841,he became one of the world’s greatest ever painters.

Many of his greatest works are held in England, including at the National Gallery in London.



His Dans les roses (In the Roses) was sold by Sotheby’s in May 2003 for $23million, while Les Deux Souers (The Two Sisters) went for almost $7million in 2007.

News.title: Huge shake-up of major councils scrapped by Angela Rayner after legal hurdles in ‘humiliation’ for No10
News.content:
CONTROVERSIAL plans to shake up councils across England have been scrapped after legal hurdles in a “humiliation” for No10.

Labour’s local government secretary Angela Rayner yesterday confirmed a scheme to reorganise Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk into unitary councils has been put on ice.



Other changes to 14 areas have also been pulled – with the sudden U-turn coming after what ministers reportedly described as “updated legal advice” as part of a judicial review process brought by some of the affected councils.

The biggest shake-up in more than 50 years would’ve seen England’s smallest county – Rutland – abolished and replaced by a larger authority stretching around Leicester.



Unearthed evidence revealed Ms Rayner’s predecessor Steve Reed had rejected civil servants’ advice on the rejig and allegedly, according to critics, simply selected options that would favour Labour elections.

The government’s plan to scrap the two-tier system of county above district councils, arguing it is inefficient, would have seen unitary authorities created across the country.

Essex, for example, would’ve seen five unitary authorities in place of the current 15 district, borough, town, city and county councils – overseeing 1.9million people, as per Mr Reed’s plan.

However, a letter sent by lawyers to Essex county council showed the ex-local government secretary had been advised against the five-council proposal, with it described as not “financially viable within five years”.

They added it would risk forming councils that are at a “significant disadvantage” and said health officials had “low confidence” of making savings as a result.

The Department for Health and Social Care, meanwhile, had a “strong preference” for four councils, and the Department for Education favoured three – with both raising concerns about plans for five.



However, Mr Reed pushed ahead regardless, arguing it would increase housebuilding around cities.

His critics said it essentially created councils in urban areas the party was most likely to win votes – with similar criticisms arising from similar overhaul plans in Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

As part of the judicial review process, ministers faced having to hand over all internal docs about the decision.

One local government source told The Times “it is a monumental climbdown”, adding: “There is no way they are going to be able to do this before the next election now as they will have to entirely re-run the process for Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.”

Ms Rayner assured MPs there was “no suggestion of wrongdoing” – though ex-Tory minister Steve Barclay said it was “gerrymandering”.



Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a “humiliation” for the government.

He told the BBC: “Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out.”

A spokesperson for Mr Reed denied he had ignored legal advice, stating it had been “followed at every stage”.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called the reorganisation an “unmitigated disaster”, while Sean Matthews, chair-elect of the County Councils Network, welcomed the U-turn.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Essex county council leader said: “This unwanted, unnecessary and financially unhinged reorganisation of Essex’s councils is over.



“Now we’ve succeeded in curtailing the government’s plans, we can now get back to what residents elected us to do — reforming Essex, providing the best possible services at the lowest possible cost.”

News.title: Plane vanishes without a trace in Bahamas carrying pilot, 80, his wife & their two grandchildren sparking frantic search
News.content:
'BRING THEM HOME' Plane vanishes without a trace in Bahamas carrying pilot, 80, his wife & their two grandchildren sparking frantic search

A PLANE carrying an 80-year-old pilot, his wife and their two grandchildren has disappeared without a trace in the Bahamas.

Bahamian and US forces have launched a frantic search to find pilot Mario Lamar, 80, his wife Lili Lamar, 79, and two of their grandchildren, Sofia Sosa, 28, and Christian Sosa, 22.



Their Florida family are begging for all the help they can get to find their loved ones who vanished on the flight from Great Harbour Cay to Miami.

The family had spent Labor Day weekend at their home on Great Harbour Cay before Mario flew them home on a small private plane, the Miami Herald reported.





Mario and Lili’s niece Silvia Larrieu said: “They’ve spent their whole life going there. That’s like their second home.”

The PA-34 Piper plane disappeared from the radar after its speed rapidly fluctuated and its altitude took a sudden drop, FlightAware data suggests.

In the space of just three minutes, it dropped from 10,000ft to 3,700ft.

Authorities received a report that a PA-34 Piper aircraft flying to Opa-locka had plunged into the water 13miles west of Andros Island at 2.20pm on Monday, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.



Niece Silvia said in a video statement: “I ask anybody out there, if you can help with search and rescue efforts, we would greatly appreciate it.

“We need to bring them home.”

The plane passed through rough weather, she said, which hampered authorities’ efforts to search for the wreckage.

The U.S. Coast Guard said it was assisting the Royal Bahamas Defence Force “following a report of a downed aircraft with four souls onboard approx 15 mi off Andros Island”.



It added that a Coast Guard “HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane is supporting the search”, which is ongoing.

News.title: Putin pounds Kyiv with brutal barrage of missile and drone strikes after three-day halt as Trump’s envoys leave
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin has bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missile and drone strikes, killing at least two people and bringing an end to a fragile three-day truce.

The brutal overnight onslaught came as Donald Trump‘s peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner left the Ukrainian capital after holding talks with Volodymyr Zelensky.



Putin’s pounding of Kyiv has cast doubt on Trump’s startling claims that the Russian dictator was “ready to negotiate” and “discuss” avenues to restart peace talks.

Drones and fearsome Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers targeted civilians in the latest barrage, striking the upper floors of a 26-story tower block.



At least ten residents had to be rescued after they were trapped in a five-story that was engulfed in flames.

Kyiv resident Iryna Barisenkova, 61, said she heard explosions while traveling on public transport and was told there was a large fire in the capital.



She said: “Everything was thundering on the left bank. It was just brutal.”

Barisenkova said she slept well during the previous two nights while Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Kyiv and then stayed in the city.

“We got some rest, thanks to them,” she said.

“Let them come more often so they don’t shell us.”



A major fire ignited at a multinational food packaging and processing factory in the city’s north after Iskander-M/Kn-23 ballistic missile strikes.

Ukrainian forces said they shot down and suppressed two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles and 142 drones.

The Kremlin claimed today that it hit stores of cruise missiles and drones in Kyiv and Kyiv region, as well as Chornomorsk Port.



Zelensky said: “The attack was complex, and the Russians deliberately planned it to cause as much damage as possible to people’s lives, using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, and Shahed drones.

“There is significant damage to residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure in the capital.”

Poland meanwhile scrambled fighter jets in a “preventive” measure due to the powerful strikes.

“Due to the activity of long-range Russian air forces conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory, military aviation has begun operating in Polish airspace,” said Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces.

“Ground-based air defence and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness.”



Nato has been forced by Russian actions to scramble warplanes 700 times in two years.

In retaliation, Ukraine blitzed a strategic oil refinery in Saratov region, igniting it in flames, near the Engels-2 base of Tu-95Ms bombers used to attack Kyiv.

Ten people were injured, including three children, in the attack on Saratov, said regional governor Roman Busargin.



An electrical station was also destroyed in a spectacular explosion by a Ukrainian drone in Russian-occupied Melitopol.

Russia said it had “intercepted and destroyed” almost 400 Ukrainian attack drones over its territory and occupied Crimea.

The strikes came as Zelensky revealed he was told by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that Putin was now more open to US-brokered talks.

He remained sceptical due to Russia’s battlefield actions and escalation of air strikes on Kyiv which do not show a readiness to compromise, he told Axios.

Zelensky was speaking before the overnight assault on Kyiv.



The Ukrainian leader said “my feeling is that Putin needs Trump” and “doesn’t want to upset him”, and may want to give the US president a diplomatic win ahead of the November presidential elections.

A part of a new peace process could be de-escalation in strikes by both sides.

Zelensky said: “There are ideas around energy, grain, electricity and oil and gas [exports]. We have different interests, Russia and we.”

It is possible that Ukraine’s recent attacks on Russia – including the crippling of its oil supplies – have put pressure on Putin.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has warned that the West is on the brink of a “real war” with Russia.



He claimed that German had effectively tried to start a war after they blamed Moscow for an explosive drone plot on Leipzig Airport last month.

News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted on slip way’ by shopping centre car park as cops release CCTV of man
News.content:
HORROR 'ATTACK' Woman ‘sexually assaulted on slip way’ by shopping centre car park as cops release CCTV of man

A WOMAN was sexually assaulted by a shopping centre car park in the early hours – with cops releasing CCTV images as part of an urgent manhunt.

The victim was touched by the stranger in Hereford at around 4.30am on Saturday (September 5).



The incident occurred on Blueschool Street on a slip way to the rear of Sensory and Rye, close to the entrance of the car park for Maylord Orchards shopping centre.

CCTV images show a man who was seen at Hereford Train Station around 6am – before boarding the 6.18am train to London Paddington.



The man was seen wearing a black top, jeans and a black cap, and carrying a black Puma rucksack.

In an earlier CCTV image, taken at around 2.15am on the same date, at the Soho Shop on Commercial Road in Hereford, he was seen wearing a coat.



Detective Sergeant Tracy Robinson said: “We are conducting a full investigation and the woman is being supported by specialist officers.

“We are urging anyone who recognises the man pictured, or who may have any information to support our investigation to please get in touch.

“Please call DC Cathryn Blake on 01905 716730 or email cathryn.blake@westmercia.police.uk if you can assist.”

News.title: Businessman, 56, and daughter, 23, killed in horror plane crash minutes after take-off as cops probe cause of smash
News.content:
A DAIRY businessman and his daughter have been killed after their plane crashed into a field minutes after take-off, sparking a major grass fire.

Ian Campbell, 56, and Hannah, 23, were found dead inside the wreckage of their six-seater light aircraft on a rural property just south of Brisbane.



Cops have launched a probe into the cause of the horror crash, with experts analysing the plane’s shattered parts.

The Beechcraft A36 Bonanza took off from an airport in south Brisbane shortly before 11am on Monday.



Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) chief Colin McNamara said: “The aircraft collided with terrain in open ground at Stockleigh at about 11.05am.”

Queensland Police Chief Superintendent Mel Adams said the site was “confronting” for emergency responders.

Eight fire crews rushed to extinguish a large grass fire sparked by the crash.

The plane came down near several houses, but no one on the ground was injured and no other property was damaged.

One horrified local said he witnessed the plane cutting through trees before hearing a “big boom”, followed by a “huge plume of smoke”.

They commented that the plane was flying unusually low and “was just not sounding very healthy at all”.



Three ATSB specialists were deployed to the scene to gather evidence and examine the wreckage.

Investigators have also been recovering equipment, such as avionics and GPS units, to help determine the cause of the crash.

The bureau said that several witnesses described the sound of the engine as “running rough or spluttering” before it came down.



A preliminary report into the circumstances of the crash is expected in eight weeks.

Ian, a fourth-generation farmer, founded the popular dairy company Barambah Organics with his wife, Jane.

The Campbell family have been farmers for several generations and were based in South Burnett, a Queensland region just north of Brisbane, for more than 100 years.

They had recently founded Mañana Pastoral in the Goondiwindi region, producing extra virgin olive oil, as well as grass-fed beef and lamb.

Goondiwindi mayor Lawrence Springborg said: “This tragedy is unfathomable for so many people in the community and is very raw.



“Ian and his daughter will be greatly missed. Our thoughts are with the family as they grieve.”

He added that the family had the “support, prayers and goodwill” of the community.

Springborg said the family raised more than $70,000 (£37,000) for the Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS) and invested in local agriculture.

RFDS Queensland section chief executive Meredith Staib said: “The Campbell family have been treasured ambassadors of the RFDS.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Their connection to supporting the delivery of world-class healthcare to regional Queenslanders ran far deeper than any title.



“Ian and Hannah will be dearly missed, and their contribution to the RFDS and to regional Queenslanders shall not be forgotten.”

News.title: Ship of sex-starved US sailors turns Thai party city into ‘Porno Disneyland’…with 50k prostitute army ready for orders
News.content:
WHEN the USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Thailand last week after 286 days at sea, the 5,000 exhausted sailors on board could not have been happier.

And gearing up to welcome them as they filed ashore after their record-breaking deployment were the 50,000 sex workers based in the nearby resort of Pattaya.



The Marines were expected to splurge an estimated £2.2m during their five-day shore leave – which ended on Sunday – and a large chunk of that will have been spent in the resort’s sprawling Red Light district.

Known as Sin City, Pattaya is like nowhere else on Earth, as The Sun discovered when we visited the coastal city 90 minutes south of Bangkok when the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier was preparing to dock.

Prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand but to say it is tolerated would be an understatement – and nowhere is that more evident than in Pattaya, especially on Soi 6.



The narrow alleyway runs for just 370 yards from the main thoroughfare of Sai Song Road down to the beach but contains a staggering 97 go go bars.

They include Wicked, Sexy in the City and Love Weapon as well as ones with much more explicit, literal names.

Hundreds of women begin to gather through the afternoon and by night it is a noisy, chaotic tourist attraction where the sex workers clad only in tiny bikinis grab men who pass by.

Some hang on for dear life in the hope of dragging a customer into their bar where they will plead for them to buy a drink before quickly turning the conversation into a sex sales pitch.

Most Thai women are quite small so it will be relatively easy for the muscle-bound Marines to prise them off, but a few more steps and they will find another one clinging on.



Down on nearby Beach Road the atmosphere is calmer but no less busy with sex workers positioning themselves every couple of yards along the promenade.

The women here are less aggressive and are more likely to wait to be approached or simply ask: “Where you from?” as you pass by.

The road leads into Walking Street, the most popular tourist spot in the resort.

It is open to vehicles through the day but barriers are erected at 7pm every evening turning it into a 1,000-yard-long pedestrianised High Street from Hell, a migraine-inducing cacophony of deafening beats and neon glare.

There are scores of go go bars along the street including one called Legacy which the US Marines were likely to boycott – the neon sign outside advertises the fact that it offers “Russian Girls”.



The street itself is crowded with touts who thrust laminated menus into tourists’ faces as they hawk tickets for “Ping Pong Shows” while dealers offer ecstasy for 1000 baht (£22) a pill, the same price that the street walkers sell sex for.

The Lincoln arrived in the port of Laem Chabang, 15 miles north of Pattaya, on Wednesday with its deck packed with helicopters and war planes including the latest F-35 fighter jets and its hull streaked with rust after nine months at sea.

It set sail last November and later played a crucial role in the war with Iran.

By the time it docked it had set a modern day record for the number of days at sea.

But that lengthy deployment has brought a host of serious problems with reports of suicide attempts, food shortages and blocked toilets.



The first sailors who disembarked wearing civilian clothes certainly looked delighted to be on dry land again as they headed off to book into a local hotel.

The commander of Carrier Strike Group 3, Rear Admiral Robert E. Loughran, said: “Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved ⁠opportunity for our Sailors and Marines to rest and recharge.

“What this strike group has accomplished is truly historic. I could not be prouder of the exceptional professionalism and expertise demonstrated by every member of this team during our operations.”



Some family members flew in from America to spend time with their loved ones for the first time in nearly a year before the Lincoln began its long journey home on Sunday.

Those left to their own devices had plenty to occupy them in a resort that is well used to entertaining troops.

The US Navy has been visiting this stretch of coast since the Vietnam War.

Pattaya was just a sleepy beach town back then but a nearby naval base and an airfield used by American bombers brought thousands of service personnel to the region and changed the resort’s nightlife for ever.

The city’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said restrictions had been placed on the crew’s activities during the Lincoln’s stay, including visiting certain entertainment zones after sunset which he said could present a negative image.



He said: “We have to be frank, the city has a reputation for bar girls. We can’t stop that.

“What we can do is to show that Pattaya has changed, that we now have other things, such as sports, seminars, wellness and family-friendly activities. It’s a mixture of everything.”

Whatever the sailors who have not set foot on dry land in nine months decided to get up to, local traders were hoping for a bumper payday.

One bar had a sign outside saying: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”



And food seller Saroch, 45, said military port visits were good for business, adding: “They’re here for drinks, having fun, and letting loose.”

One aspect of “letting loose” is still technically illegal – the Prevention and Suppression of Prostitution Act 1996 makes that clear.

But it is rarely enforced, one reason being that prostitution is such an important part of the Thai economy – it is estimated to generate £4.4bn every year.

If any sailors made it north to Bangkok in their brief time on shore they would have found that the picture there is much the same.

The notorious Nana Plaza on Soi 4, off Sukhumvit Road, is effectively a three-story shopping complex where the only things for sale are sex and overpriced drinks.



Each floor has a balcony running around the central area with a series of bars such as Red Dragon, Angel and Witch.

That central area is festooned with Premiership Club pendants although they are yet to update them from last season – those from relegated West Ham, Burnley and Wolves are still on display.

The bars have a curtain instead of a door with a helpful member of staff holding it to one side to usher punters in.



Once inside potential customers are greeted by a small stage with a pole surrounded by two or three rows of seating.

A woman will occasionally put on a pole dancing show but for the most part they crowd onto the stage to dance lazily in the hope that a punter will pick them, using the number pinned to their bikini or mini skirt to let staff know which one they are interested in.

In some bars a couple of naked women covered in soap suds cavort in oversized baths as they encourage men to place Thai banknotes between their breasts.

Prostitution is such an accepted part of the night-time economy that the Plaza employs its own security guards just like any regular night club might.

Wearing body cams and with walkie talkies strapped to their belts, they use metal detectors to scan customers, check bags and ID anyone who appears under the age limit of 20.



Outside the plaza, the nearby streets and Sois (alleyways) are packed with street sex workers.

Joy, 36, said: “It is 2000 baht (£44) for one hour or 5000 (£112) for the whole night.

“I go to men’s hotels or if they don’t want to do that there are two guesthouses near here which I can use. One charges 250 baht (£5.60) for one hour. The other charges 300 baht (£6.72).



“They are both very safe and clean and both provide condoms.”

Back in Pattaya, even if the American sailors were prevented from visiting the city’s hotspots, as the mayor claims, they still had access to hundreds of massage parlours that are often a front for brothels.

On Beach Road, Mint was one of the many sex workers hoping that the arrival of the Lincoln might provide a welcome boost to business, regardless of any official restrictions.

Dressed in a black top and sparkly white miniskirt, she was keen to chat to any passing man in the hope of persuading him to take her back to his hotel or to a room she uses nearby.

But she did make it clear that there was one thing she would not let any American sailor do, no matter how long they had been at sea.



She said: “It’s 1000 baht (£22) for one hour.

“I will do everything but kiss – I want to save that for when I get a boyfriend.”

News.title: Watch: Pupils return to West Bank school behind barbed wire to protect against settlers
News.content:
A school in the occupied West Bank has been surrounded by barbed-wire fencing as Palestinian parents fear for their children's safety due to the rise of Israeli settler attacks in the area.

The isolated village of al-Mughayyir, north-east of Ramallah, has been increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.

Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.

News.title: A&E did not get the basics right - my son's life was ruined at 32
News.content:
In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness.

He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, before going home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now lives in almost complete paralysis.

Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in emergency departments.

Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history.

Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time.

Stephen says the whole family â including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him.

News.title: Prince George set for first day at Eton College
News.content:
Prince George is taking another step in growing up with his first day at Eton College.

He is following in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, who also attended the historic school in Berkshire.

The 13-year-old prince will become a boarder at the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around Â£65,000 a year.

As the oldest child of Prince William and Catherine, George is second in line of succession to the throne.

News.title: Drought and hosepipe bans remain despite wettest week since early February
News.content:
In the last few days of August and start of September, more rain fell than any other week since early February, according to the Environment Agency.

Despite the change to more unsettled and wetter conditions, all of Wales and most of England remains in drought.

And water companies are reminding customers that temporary hosepipe bans are still in force despite the rainfall and decreased demand with the cooler weather.

More rain is in the forecast this week and while that will be welcome, sustained rainfall is needed to reverse drought conditions.

While we had a brief return of summer heat over the weekend for some, the weather since the start of September - and meteorological autumn - has been more unsettled.

According to figures from the Environment Agency (EA), in the week from 28 August to 3 September, rainfall totals ranged from 26mm in south-east England to 48mm in central England.

However, the National Drought Group said that water storage "continued to decline at most reservoirs".

There has been no change to the EA drought status or the temporary use bans in force across ten water company areas.

While there has been less demand for water due to the cooler and wetter weather, "further significant rainfall is needed" to return to normal conditions the EA suggests.

News.title: UK pupils rank highly again in international reading, maths and science tests
News.content:
UK pupils have performed well again in international science, reading and maths tests sat every three years by hundreds of thousands of teenagers around the world.

The UK's performance in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) remained steady, ranking below the highest-performing countries like Singapore, Estonia and parts of China, but ahead of the US, Australia and other major European nations.

But the Pisa report also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills.

England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy".

The Pisa tests, run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire.

Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

News.title: 'Good to have choice': Australians on opting out of social media algorithms
News.content:
Australia is set to force social media companies to allow users to easily opt in or out of content recommended by algorithms when they log in.

The BBC spoke to people in Sydney about how they feel about social media algorithms, and the Australian government's planned legislation.

Read more on the Australian government's plans here.

News.title: AI will cure cancer in our lifetime, claims boss of UK chip giant
News.content:
The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.

Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.

Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.

However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.

Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe.

Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.

Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.

"Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.

"However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.

Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.

He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples.

"It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements.

"That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."

News.title: Police forces failing investigation basics, says inspectorate report
News.content:
Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to His Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary (HMIC).

In her annual report, Michelle Skeer also said too many victims were not receiving the quality of service they should expect.

Forces continue to struggle when it comes to gathering evidence, identifying and progressing lines of inquiry, and keeping victims updated on their cases, she added.

There was progress in neighbourhood policing and in some of the work carried out by regional organised crime units that focus on offenders across multiple local police force boundaries, the report said.

The report continued that the greatest strength of policing is its workforce, with the vast majority of officers showing professionalism and courage.

HMIC inspects all 43 police forces in England and Wales on a two-year cycle.

Out of 13 forces assessed in the current cycle, including Merseyside, Cumbria, and Devon & Cornwall, none received a good or outstanding rating for investigating crime or providing a safe and lawful custody environment.

The other forces assessed were Suffolk, Staffordshire, Thames Valley, West Yorkshire, Northamptonshire, Surrey, Wiltshire, North Yorkshire, Humberside and Kent.

The report says "too many forces still weren't getting the basics right or providing the public with a consistently good service in the areas that matter most to victims".

Beyond weaknesses in investigations, the report highlights gaps in how forces respond to the public, including delays in handling emergency and non-emergency calls, and in response times to incidents.

It also raises concerns about the safeguarding of victims, noting inconsistencies in recognising vulnerability and failure to properly deploy resources appropriately when people are reported missing.

News.title: Minister condemns disorder at Portsmouth anti-migrant protest after police officers hurt
News.content:
Council leader Steve Pitt said the decision had caused "needless disruption".

Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear after they descended on the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were landed.

Police protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. A dispersal order was put in place, meaning anyone failing to comply with police could be arrested.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a handful of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.

It said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

"No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched."

Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: "I've seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I've seen pictures of police vehicles damaged. It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest."

Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo - an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson - was livestreaming from the scene - where he called for his supporters to "get down to Eastney" and stop the migrants being transported.

The coaches carrying the migrants were able to leave in the early hours of Monday and the Border Force confirmed "individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing".

News.title: Police hunt after driver killed in hit-and-run near Edinburgh Airport
News.content:
Police are searching for two women and a man who fled on foot from the scene of a fatal hit-and-run crash on the A8 near Edinburgh Airport.

Officers were called to reports of a crash involving a grey Mercedes A250, a black Renault Captur, a grey Skoda Karoq and a grey Hyundai i30 between the Newbridge and Gogar roundabouts at around 09:25 on Monday.

Emergency services attended, however, the 58-year-old driver of the Hyundai i30 was pronounced dead at the scene.

A police helicopter and dog unit have been used to hunt for the three people who left the scene.

Four others were taken to hospital for treatment following the crash but they were later released.

Insp Thomas Mallinson said: "My thoughts are with the family of the person who died at this incredibly difficult time.

"Our inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances of this crash, and it is vital we trace the three people who left the area before police arrived."

He asked anyone with information to contact Police Scotland, external.

The Scottish Ambulance Service (SAS) dispatched three ambulances, two special operations response teams, a paramedic response unit and a critical care paramedic.

The road was closed for a number of hours to allow an investigation to take place but reopened at 19:05.

News.title: New mums 'left to get on with it' as C-section numbers hit record high
News.content:
Latest figures show 42% of babies in Wales were born by C-section in 2025, with just over half of those operations being emergencies.

Carys' first baby was born in 2022.

After needing an emergency C-section, Carys, a content creator, said she had many unanswered questions about her recovery.

"I think I was thrown in at the deep end and I really didn't know how to deal with it," she said.

It was almost three weeks before the 29-year-old said she felt physically able to leave the house.

"And even then, I only walked up to the top of the street and back," she added.

Carys has since had two more caesareans and said each experience was very different.

Both times, she said the care she received in hospital and from her community midwife was good. But after getting home, she was left with questions about how her body should be recovering.

"You're thrown so into the deep end and there's no sort of, 'Oh, this is how your scar should look. This is quite normal for this sort of time'."

She recalled taking the dressing off her wound and fainting in the shower.

"I didn't know - should my scar be recovering in a certain way, should I really be feeling like this?

"There's just no support around the fact that after it, you're looking after a baby and recovering from major surgery, and everyone's recovery looks totally different."

She has shared her own experiences online in the hopes of helping other women, and said expectant mums often contact her for advice.

"I wish I'd had more stories that I could read to be a bit more informed before I gave birth that way."

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
News.content:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.

The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.

JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.

Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.

"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.

JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.

The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save Â£1.7bn over the next two years.

JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.

He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack.

"It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.

Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.

In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.

In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to Â£22.9bn from Â£29bn in the previous two years.

Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.

"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.

He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party" in terms of electric vehicles.

Jaguar launched the I-PACE, a fully-electric SUV, in 2018. But the electric Range Rover announced last week will be its first electric vehicle launch since then.

Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".

News.title: Chancellor calls for 'confidence about Britain' despite 'historic high' borrowing costs
News.content:
Asked about the impact of higher borrowing costs, which have surged this month, the Chancellor said that the government was responding to "extreme pressures in the wider market," and reiterated that he wanted to "bring down welfare costs."

Earlier, in his first major speech as chancellor, Healey said his mission was to "make Great Britain growth Britain" again.

Speaking at the Manufacturing Technology Centre (MTC) in Coventry, he said,

"My defining mission as chancellor is growth, good growth in every postcode. And I've set out today the way this government will set about it: more devolution, more public leadership and control, more investment, more innovation, more jobs."

Healey said he is in "lockstep" with Prime Minister Andy Burnham about the need for fiscal discipline and having a buffer in the government's spending plans "against the sort of uncertainty that the JLR decision locally has shown".

It came as Healey offered an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of the Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.

Speaking in Coventry, he set out a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas".

With seven weeks until the Budget, Healey said the government will stick to Labour's manifesto pledge, made under Sir Keir Starmer and former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, to not "increase taxes on working people".

He repeatedly refused to comment on possible tax rises or spending cuts ahead of 28 October, stating only: "Staying true to our values means being honest about the need to control government spending."

Conservative Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith, said: "Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises."

He added that Healey "sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves".

In his speech from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in the Midlands, Healey described the UK as "turning the corner" and said greater devolution would spread economic growth more evenly across the UK.

But recent ructions in government debt markets have piled fresh pressure on already-stretched public finances, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs and the need to fund higher defence spending.

News.title: Murder arrest after two people found dead at house
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after two people were found dead in a house in Blackburn.

Lancashire Police said the bodies of a man and woman were found at the home in Hardman Street in the town at about 08:20 BST, and a man aged in his 40s had been arrested.

The man and woman, who have not been named, were both pronounced dead at the scene.

Police said they were unable to confirm the victims' ages but local residents told the BBC they were elderly.

Police said a dedicated team of officers had been assigned to the case, and were carrying out CCTV, house-to-house and forensic inquiries.

News.title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
News.content:
Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.

Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.

Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.

Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.

The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.

Confirming the review in Parliament, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner told MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".

She added: "And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations."

Rayner acknowledged the announcement was "disappointing" but insisted the government was "determined more than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent" - a key priority of new PM Andy Burnham.

The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.

The government was already facing legal challenges over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

In June, Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk launched judicial reviews against the plans, while the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire did the same.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Reform UK not only argued that this government's plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is."

He added: "Thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the government has backed down on their plans yet again."

Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a "humiliation" for the government.

He said: "Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out in the face of relentless Conservative opposition to their gerrymandering."

Liberal Democrat local government spokeswoman ZÃ¶e Franklin said: "This is an embarrassing and chaotic climbdown, which has resulted in already cash-strapped councils wasting huge sums on plans the government told them were legally watertight."

Sean Matthews, from the County Councils Network, welcomed the move, adding: "Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed."

A spokesperson for the Local Government Association, which represents councils, said that while local authorities hold different views on the reorganisation plans "there is no excuse for the government's mishandling of this process".

The spokesperson added that Rayner's announcement "will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours" in the reorganisation programme.

Local government in England is currently covered by a complicated patchwork of arrangements.

In some places, responsibility for local services is shared between county councils, which manage areas including social care and education; and district councils, which cover smaller areas and are responsible for services such as bin collections.

Some areas, particularly larger towns and some cities, have "unitary" authorities responsible for both - while the regions surrounding big cities are increasingly covered by regional mayors and multi-council "combined" authorities, with greater powers in areas such as transport policy, planning and housing.

In late 2024, as local government secretary, Rayner announced plans to move towards unitary councils across all of England, with council boundaries redrawn and smaller district councils abolished.

The government argued the proposals would make the system simpler and produce savings by making the delivery of services more efficient, while also handing new powers from Westminster to regions across the country.

However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.

Under Sir Keir, the government had been pushing ahead with the proposals.

In July â just days before Burnham became prime minister â Rayner's successor as secretary of state, Reed, had announced plans for new councils in 14 areas.

News.title: King makes clear Harry and Meghan remain non-working royals
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will not be working royals allowed to carry out official engagements now they have returned to the UK, a letter sent on behalf of King Charles spells out.

The letter is intended to clarify the status of Prince Harry and Meghan, who moved back from California with children Archie and Lilibet last month.

They will still not be able to use titles of "His and Her Royal Highness", and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.

It comes as Prince Harry appears to have been pictured for the first time since his return, with a photo on social media showing him at a London TV and podcast studio.

A manhunt is underway after thieves broke into the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera early on Tuesday and stole several paintings worth an estimated €9 million, the local mayor said.

Two people broke into the museum shortly before 6am ​and took ⁠four works of art, dropping one as they left, Cagnes-sur-Mer mayor Bryan Masson announced on social media.

"Attacking the Renoir museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer. These actions are particularly serious," Masson said in his message.

The heist comes just months after a raid on Paris’ famed Le Louvre art museum, making off with €88 million ($102.3 million) worth of jewels, including Empress Eugenie's tiara.

open image in gallery A police officer stands in front of the entrance of the Musee Renoir after four paintings were stolen on Tuesday morning ( AFP/Getty )

Masson did not identify the paintings that were stolen. Renoir's most valuable works have fetched dozens of millions of dollars at auctions in the past.

The museum was created in 1960 in the mansion of the impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir on a hill in Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, where he died in 1919.

The collection on display in the museum includes 13 paintings from the master and some 40 sculptures, furniture and photographs.

Art thieves in Europe are committing more violent robberies and specialist gangs have been replaced by ad hoc ​opportunists recruited through social media, pan-European police body Europol said last month.

Line of Duty star Adrian Dunbar has given fans a hint at what to expect from the new series – and it’s an update many are sure to be happy about.

The Irish actor has played police superintendent Ted Hastings in all six series of the hit crime drama, with his character becoming known for his quaint and idiosyncratic turns of phrase.

Previous years have seen Hastings utter such phrases as “Now we’re sucking diesel”, “I didn’t float up the Lagan in a bubble”, and “Jesus, Mary and Joseph and the wee donkey”, with some of his expression entering the lexicon of Line of Duty fanatics.

open image in gallery Adrian Dunbar, Vicky McClure and Martin Compston in 'Line of Duty' ( CREDIT LINE:BBC/World Productions/Steffan Hill )

Speaking on the BBC’s Red Lines podcast during an interview at Belfast's Lyric Theatre, Dunbar said that there were more such phrases being lined up for the show’s forthcoming return.

“I’ve got a couple coming along this time in this series,” he said.

“I say something like, ‘Come on, guys, don’t stall the digger’. ‘Don’t stall the digger’ is going to be my new one.”

Alluding to the way that his past quotes have been merchandised – with fans buying items such as shirts and mugs with Hasting’s phrases on – Dunbar quipped: “There’ll be a mug for that, too.”

The actor also explained that his character’s distinctive idiolect also had roots in his own upbringing.

“‘Mother of God’ was something my father used to say all the time,” he stated. “So I kind of stuck that in a couple of times and it worked.”

Line of Duty is expected to return to the airwaves next year, having formerly suggested that the 2022 series six finale would be the show’s final episode.

open image in gallery Martin Compston, Robert Carlyle, Vicky McClure and Adrian Dunbar at a read-through for series 7 of 'Line of Duty' ( CREDIT LINE:BBC/World Productions )

After years of speculation, it was announced in November that Line of Duty was indeed returning for another series, with Dunbar set to reprise his role alongside fellow series leads Martin Compston and Vicky McClure.

Last week, McClure offered fans an update on the new series, confirming that it had already finished filming.

In an interview with The i Paper, McClure said: “I’m fresh out of Belfast; we only finished filming two weeks ago. I feel like I’ve bagged the best gigs over the years – I was unsure if I’d ever get a job at one point.

“You just can’t predict this industry at all. So, to be able to continually go back to a series and work with good friends like Martin [Compston] and Adrian [Dunbar], who are like family. It was a real pleasure.”

News.title: This £10 perfume reminds me of Chanel Coco mademoiselle – but it’s £70 cheaper
News.content:
An affordable Chanel Coco mademoiselle alternative is one of the most sought-after finds among fragrance fans, with olfactory obsessives hoping to capture the same citrus-floral character without the luxury price tag. As high-street designer-inspired perfumes continue to grow in popularity, retailers such as M&S, Zara and Next are demonstrating that it’s not always necessary to empty your wallet in order to enjoy an elegant, long-lasting scent.

Having tested hundreds of women's perfumes over the years, from luxury launches to supermarket bargains, I've learnt that price isn't always the best indicator of quality. Some affordable fragrances disappear within an hour or miss the mark entirely, while others have carved out a permanent spot on my dressing table.

Among my affordable favourites is Next's eau nude (£10, Next.com). After wearing it alongside Chanel’s Coco mademoiselle (£99.45, Sephora.co.uk) – which I’ve found to be the best long-lasting perfume – I was surprised by just how closely the two fragrances aligned. Scroll on for my honest thoughts and to find out whether it's worth swapping into your fragrance library (for £70 less).



Eau nude eau de parfum After testing Next's eau nude, I named it the best designer perfume alternative for its unmistakable similarity to Coco mademoiselle (£80, Chanel.com). While I’d expected the £10 scent to capture a few recognisable notes from the Chanel perfume, I hadn’t anticipated such excellent mimicry of the fragrance’s overall sophisticated character. In my review of the original Coco mademoiselle eau de parfum, I found it offered a lighter, more delicate take on a floral fragrance than the brand’s more divisive no. 5 scent. It balances bright orange, fresh rose and earthy vetiver in a way that gave it both daytime and evening wearability. Eau nude takes a slightly sweeter approach, blending raspberry, mandarin, jasmine, rose, patchouli and vanilla, but after wearing both fragrances, I found they shared the same bright citrus opening and soft rose heart. My initial scepticism (and, honestly, snobbery) was unfounded. While the opening develops a little differently, eau nude settles into something that comes surprisingly close to Chanel's fragrance, and I found its sillage would fool passers-by, myself included. Considering the roughly £70 price difference between the 30ml Next fragrance and Chanel's 35ml bottle, I can't recommend this high-street alternative highly enough for anyone who enjoys Coco mademoiselle's citrus-floral style but doesn't want to spend luxury-fragrance money. Hawaii Governor Josh Green has closed schools and government offices on Oahu and the westernmost islands of Kauai and Niihau for Tuesday.

The measures came as Hurricane Lowell was expected to pass nearby, threatening damaging winds, mudslides, possible tornadoes, dangerous rip currents and up to 24 inches of rain in parts of Kauai.

The closures, covering community colleges alongside state and county offices, were put into effect across Oahu and Kauai County, which was under a National Hurricane Center warning.

The county encompasses Kauai, which has a population of over 73,000, and Niihau, home to fewer than 100 residents.

A portion of the vast Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument was also included in the warning.

open image in gallery This satellite image released by NOAA shows Hurricane Lowell approaching Hawaii, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026 ( (NOAA via AP) )

The weather agency also warned late Monday of the possibility of “several tornadoes” near Kauai and Niihau in the evening and overnight, with tornadoes also possible on other Hawaiian Islands.

A tropical storm warning was in effect for Oahu, which has close to 1 million residents.

The National Hurricane Center said the core of the storm was expected to pass near or just west of Niihau late Monday and early Tuesday.

While the winds — which were strong enough to make Lowell a Category 2 hurricane as of Monday afternoon — were expected to weaken, the storm was expected to remain a hurricane at its closest approach to the islands.

“Closing offices, schools and courts will help keep people off the roads during dangerous conditions and allow emergency crews to focus on protecting our communities,” Green said in a news release. “I urge everyone in Kaua'i County to remain indoors, avoid unnecessary travel and follow all official emergency instructions.”

open image in gallery Palm trees bend from strong winds as an CH-47 Chinook helicopter flies over Barbers Point in Kapolei, Hawaii ( AFP/Getty )

He also urged residents to stay away from shorelines, avoid driving through floodwaters, prepare for power outages and monitor for updates.

Isolated rainfall totals of up to 10 inches (25 centimeters) were expected in Oahu and Maui, and 12 inches (30 centimeters) was expected in portions of the Big Island of Hawaii, the farthest east of the state's major islands.

Last month, the state had a brush with Tropical Storm Lala. While it did not make landfall, it hit Hawaii — and especially the Big Island — hard, leaving behind landslides, washing away about 100 homes and causing widespread power outages.

A nationwide Cyclospora outbreak tied to contaminated lettuce has raised food safety fears and highlighted a key trend: American regulators conduct fewer foreign inspections to catch tainted produce before it reaches consumer plates.

Food and Drug Administration audits at international food operations — including the Mexican farm linked to the outbreak — have fallen nearly 35% since 2019, according to agency records. The pandemic triggered an ongoing wave of inspector retirements and departures.

Prior to COVID-19, the agency routinely failed to meet congressional mandates for overseas checks. Recent staff cuts, restructurings, and changes under President Donald Trump could lead to even fewer inspections, according to former senior FDA officials.

open image in gallery This undated photo taken through a microscope and provided by the CDC shows Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts found in a fresh stool sample which had been prepared with a formalin solution and stained with safranin ( CDC )

"When you look at the numbers of inspections balanced against the responsibility of the FDA — in terms of all the firms domestically and internationally under its oversight — the agency just can’t achieve what is required," said Michael Rogers, who spent nearly 35 years in various inspection roles within the agency. He added that the FDA still operates "very well with limited resources."

The Trump administration suggested new ideas to stretch resources — including a pilot program for one-day checks. Rogers and others argue brief visits cannot match standard inspections, which take a week or longer to record major issues.

FDA officials maintain that site visits are only one component of food safety oversight.

open image in gallery Taylor Farms, which supplies shredded iceberg lettuce to Taco Bell, has been identified as a possible source of contamination in the cyclosporiasis outbreak that causes episodes of explosive diarrhea, according to a new report ( AFP via Getty Images )

"Inspections will never be the only way to ensure the safety of imported products given the massive volume coming into the country," said Susan Mayne, FDA's former food director who is now at Yale University. "That’s why FDA uses border inspections, importer inspections, sampling and other tools."

But the iceberg lettuce situation has exposed potential weaknesses in that strategy.

In July, officials retracted an erroneous test result that purportedly found cyclospora in a border sample of Taylor Farms lettuce. Despite the mistake, the FDA remains confident the farm is the source of the parasite, while Mexican officials report finding no positive samples or red flags.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which supervises the FDA, said the inquiry continues. Regulators are currently evaluating how many foreign inspections are needed annually "to ensure oversight comparable" to domestic standards.

FDA took four weeks to inspect Mexican plant after massive salad recall, report says

Approximately four weeks after a July 17 recall notice, Food and Drug Administration inspectors reached a Taylor Farms facility in Guanajuato, Mexico, in mid-August.

The visit marked the agency’s first visit to the location since 2019, when foreign food audits hit an all-time high before the pandemic-era withdrawal of field personnel.

Global food safety monitoring—alongside checks on pharmaceuticals and medical devices—has not rebounded. International food audits dropped an additional 17 percent to 1,140 in fiscal year 2025 compared to the previous year.

open image in gallery A drone view shows Taylor Farms Mexico's facilities after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said on Monday that the basis for linking Taylor Farms lettuce from central Mexico to the largest U.S. foodborne illness outbreak in recent years remains unchanged ( Reuters )

Though inspectors were spared from the 3,500 job cuts enacted by the Trump administration, over half of the travel support staff was eliminated, forcing field agents to manage their own flights, lodging, and logistical needs.

Food safety experts noted that the one-month gap before arriving in Mexico was excessive given the extent of the outbreak and the volume of people affected.

"It took us too long to get boots on the ground," said Frank Yiannas, the former top food safety official at FDA. "When these outbreaks happen in fresh produce, you have to respond quickly because these are very complex and changing ecosystems."

open image in gallery Upheavals under President Donald Trump could mean even fewer inspections in the years ahead, according to former senior FDA officials ( AP )

The Taylor Farms incident involved thousands of pre-packaged salad items blending iceberg lettuce and other produce. These units were distributed to major American restaurant operators, including Yum Brands, the parent company of Taco Bell, Pizza Hut, and KFC.

FDA records show that businesses have reported more than 480 food recalls during the current fiscal year, already topping four of the last five years.

Chronic staffing vacancies cripple FDA’s ability to inspect foreign food facilities

Efforts to overhaul the US food safety framework in Washington are not new. Following fatal contamination outbreaks involving produce like spinach and cantaloupe, Congress passed the Food Safety Modernization Act of 2011. The law mandated enhanced farm hygiene, training, and testing, while setting ambitious overseas inspection targets that the Food and Drug Administration has consistently failed to meet.

Under the statute, the FDA must audit more than 19,000 foreign food sites annually. Yet Government Accountability Office data shows the agency peaked at just 1,700 inspections in 2019—less than a tenth of its legal target.

Former FDA regulators argue that the 19,000-site mandate was unattainable from the start, citing years of stagnant congressional funding for the food division. Even so, the GAO noted that the agency "has not identified an appropriate annual target," leaving oversight goals uncertain.

open image in gallery The Trump administration has proposed new approaches to stretch agency resources — including a pilot program of one-day inspections ( Getty/iStock )

Staff recruitment and retention remain the main barriers to expanding these evaluations. The agency's food inspection division includes over 420 roles, but 10 to 15 percent of those positions are chronically vacant, according to former personnel and the GAO.

Inspectors assigned to international duties spend 50 percent or more of their time traveling, a demanding workflow driving continuous turnover.

"Until you can better incentivize people to stay in those positions, I think the agency is going to continue to see high attrition, younger and less experienced investigators," said Rogers. "That ultimately may impact FDA’s ability to enhance and increase inspections."

Industry specialists suggest emerging tools, such as machine learning and remote monitoring of supplier operations, could reduce reliance on physical visits.

open image in gallery Food orders at a Chipotle restaurant on April 01, 2024 in San Rafael, California ( Getty )

"We have to rethink how we oversee the safety of foreign producers," Yiannas said. "We can’t use the same approaches and limited tools that we’ve used for the past 30 years."

The 2011 legislation also required producers to attach bar codes to every batch of produce, enabling rapid tracing during contamination incidents. Slated to take effect in January after years of industry consultation, the FDA delayed implementation once again following pushback from food companies.

"There’s widespread acknowledgment that these are complex issues, but when you have 17 years to prepare for a final exam you should be able to pass it," said Brian Ronholm, a former Department of Agriculture official who is now with Consumer Reports.

When Patrick Sullivan heard a car horn blaring nonstop at 3 am while up feeding his infant son one night this summer, he was convinced a "crazy neighbor" was responsible.

It turned out to be a neighbor of a different kind. A black bear had opened the door of a Toyota SUV and gotten trapped inside the vehicle in Gold Hill, Colorado, northwest of Denver.

As the animal desperately attempted to escape, it repeatedly bumped the horn while ripping apart the interior—one of hundreds of instances of bears causing unusual trouble across the parched Rocky Mountains this summer.

"It’s totaled. It’s unfit to drive," Sullivan said of the car.

open image in gallery A bear sits in a car after getting stuck inside of it in Gold Hill, Colorado

Millions of people live in or near bear habitat across the Rockies, where widespread drought has reduced supplies of nuts, berries, and plants that bears eat. This is prompting the animals to roam far and wide for food.

Sullivan's brother-in-law eventually freed the trapped bear. But such encounters can prove fatal for the animals. One bear recently stuck in a car in Colorado Springs died from the heat, and wildlife officials have killed dozens of others that could endanger people.

Unsecured garbage bins have become the leading driver behind a recent spike in bear encounters, according to figures from Colorado Parks and Wildlife. Beyond waste, residential areas offer other lures, including open garages with pet food, yard bird feeders, and grease collection traps beneath barbecue grills.

open image in gallery A black bear was found dead in a car in Colorado after lying inside the vehicle for days in August, authorities say ( Colorado Parks and Wildlife )

While officers often sedate and relocate animals that wander into populated zones, bears that learn to associate humans with a meal risk being euthanized.

Wildlife authorities repeatedly emphasize their core warning: "A fed bear is a dead bear." They strongly advise residents to safely store any potential food sources out of reach.

Although black bears usually avoid human contact and are considered far less hazardous than the larger grizzly bears found across the Northern Rockies, conflict can still turn violent.

In June, a black bear trailed, attacked, and scratched a hiker in Golden, Colorado. State officials have recorded at least four additional encounters since then, such as an incident near Vail on Aug. 17 where a man was scratched outside his apartment complex laundry room.

Just five days afterward, a young bear tackled and bit an angler in the mountain region southwest of Denver. Officers subsequently tracked the animal down and killed it.

Property owners in New Mexico and Utah have set records for bear killings this year

More than 36 bears have been killed in Utah this year—surpassing the total from the previous three years combined, according to data from the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources. In New Mexico, wildlife officials and permitted property owners have killed 187 bears, marking the highest toll since 2011.

open image in gallery A half-blind, 12-year-old dog fought off a bear that broke into her owner’s New Mexico home, leaving her with severe injuries in March ( Española Humane )

The increase in bear deaths coincides with the worst snowpack on record across the Upper Colorado River Basin, which spans Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, and New Mexico. Scientists indicate that human-caused global warming significantly increased the likelihood of these low snowpack levels.

"Human-animal conflicts in the context of climate change haven’t really been fully researched yet. And we’re still starting to kind of tease out what this means for us and what this means for all the species that we share the ecosystem with," said Samantha Miller, senior carnivore campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity.

Record wildfires have also destroyed expansive areas of bear habitat, compounding the environmental pressures.

open image in gallery A few bear-trouble stories are heartwarming, like orphaned cubs successfully released into the wild after time in a rescue facility, where they learned to live on their own without raiding ( Getty )

Not all encounters with bears end poorly; some prove heartwarming, like orphaned cubs returned to the wild after rescue facilities teach them to live independently without raiding human property.

"We’ve got to rescue a lot of bear cubs out of trees, including standing on some pretty shaky ladders to pull a bear cub that’s sleeping in a tree," said Sauder.

While working on a deck in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, this summer, Andy Kerrigan found a cub inside his truck after it entered through a window. He banged on the vehicle to scare it away.

"But it had found my lunch in the seat. And it was like, ‘I’m not going anywhere,’" said Kerrigan, who eventually chased it away with a piece of wood trim.

In Gold Hill, Sullivan's brother-in-law freed a bear trapped in a Toyota by pulling a rope tied to a door handle, letting it bolt for the woods.

"It was just sitting there waiting for someone to help him, basically," Sullivan said. "So I’m glad we could have done that for him."
