Emery often takes time to integrate signings. Youri Tielemans had to wait four months for his first Villa start before embedding himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. He demands a lot of his players and even more of himself. “In football, if you are expecting transition, maybe you are not in the right way,” he said last month.

“We have to rebuild the team as fast as possible. I don’t know if we need time or not. We are progressing – still not enough because we are not getting good results – but tomorrow is a new test in Europe.”

Sports.title: Newcastle admit they started planning for Eddie Howe’s exit at start of year
Sports.content:
Newcastle’s sporting director, Ross Wilson, has revealed he began planning at the start of this year for Eddie Howe’s departure. Howe stepped down as manager in late July and the club turned to Matthias Jaissle, who had been identified as the preferred successor.

“Eddie leaving didn’t feel chaotic and it didn’t feel painful,” said Wilson, who arrived on Tyneside from Nottingham Forest. “Eddie would be the first to tell you that. I came here 10 or 11 months ago and I’ve been planning in the background for a managerial change over eight or nine of those months. That doesn’t mean we were always going to go to Matthias, but he was always part of our planning.”

When Wilson began making contingency plans, Howe seemed more likely to be poached than to resign or be dismissed. Yet Newcastle’s 12th-placed finish last season raised questions about his future and, after the sales of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, Howe decided he wanted out.

“Big respect to Eddie for the job he did for us over a long period of time,” Wilson said. “He did a wonderful job bringing that trophy [the 2025 Carabao Cup]. He’s a club legend, for sure.”

No one had envisaged parting with Howe three weeks before the season. “Clearly the timing wasn’t planned,” Wilson said. “But the reason we could move so quickly was because we’d been preparing for a number of months.

“Eddie’s an exceptionally talented coach and that meant he was probably going to do something else at some point. We had to be prepared for that.”

With Newcastle having entered a settlement agreement with Uefa after breaching European spending rules last season, selling Gordon and Tonali for almost £170m proved essential but Wilson admitted that offloading Bruno Guimarães to Arsenal for £75m was one sale he never wanted to complete.

“There’s no point pretending otherwise: we did not want to lose Bruno Guimarães,” he said. “That was really disappointing. But everything else that happened during the window was planned. That doesn’t mean every single player [who signed] was the number one name on our list. Clearly we were disappointed a couple of times but that’s normal. No club reaches the end of a window getting every target they wanted.”

View image in fullscreen Bruno Guimarães’ move to Arsenal was ‘really disappointing’ for Newcastle, Ross Wilson has admitted. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA

Wilson has presided over the acquisition of eight players aged 24 and under this summer including Guimarães’s replacement, the £52m midfielder Nico González, signed from Manchester City. They have in common a suitability for the high-intensity pressing game choreographed, in different forms, by Howe and Jaissle.

“I cannot imagine Newcastle United playing a style of football that isn’t aggressive, vertical and attacking,” said Wilson. “For this club to be successful we have to play an attacking, high-press, proactive style and we had to find a coach to do that.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Ultimately, all roads led to Jaissle, for whom Newcastle paid £10m to Al-Ahli. “We used our [data] models to identify those coaches who played the type of football we wanted,” said Wilson. “Matthias was the No 1 choice. It was really, really clear.”

Cue what Wilson described as a “busy” summer. “We had the situation with the manager which we dealt with in complete secrecy for two weeks as well as trying to run a transfer window,” he said. “So it was really, really busy. But good fun as well.”

Until this summer Newcastle had resisted selling established players but that stance has changed. “If you want to be successful in the Premier League you have to trade players,” said Wilson. “If you don’t trade you’re going to get stuck.”

Although Jaissle has not been set targets this season, Newcastle’s chief executive, David Hopkinson, remains confident they can disrupt the dominance of the traditional “big six” by 2030. “We’re going to be consistently and credibly competing for those top prizes,” Hopkinson said. “If we’re compliant with the regulatory regime [spending rules] we can compete consistently.”

Sports.title: Joey Barton to remain in custody until trial after bail application turned down
Sports.content:
The former footballer Joey Barton will remain in custody until his trial next year after a bail application was refused.

The 44-year-old had been due to stand trial at Liverpool crown court last week accused of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to Kevin Lynch, 51, at Fairway, Huyton, on 8 March. But on Wednesday the case was adjourned and put back to March next year.

Barton, wearing a grey zip-up fleece, appeared over video link from HMP Liverpool at a hearing on Monday, when the judge David Potter refused a renewed bail application. Barton nodded as the judge remanded him in custody in advance of a pre-trial hearing on 11 December.

His trial will take place exactly a year after the alleged assault, meaning the defendant, who was arrested shortly after the incident, will have spent 12 months on remand.

Barton is accused of carrying out the attack on Lynch after they had been drinking together at Huyton and Prescot golf club. Lynch, a former non-league football manager and founder of the special education school NexGen Academy, was said to have sustained serious injuries to an eye.

Barton, the former Manchester City and QPR midfielder, of Widnes, Cheshire, won one England cap and also played for Newcastle, Rangers, Burnley and Marseille. After stopping playing he moved into coaching and had managerial spells at Fleetwood and Bristol Rovers.

Sports.title: Chelsea’s midfield a headache for Alonso after Arsenal press advantage | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
There have been seasons when Chelsea have turned up at the Emirates Stadium and parked the bus. “You know, I think 10 years without a title is boring,” José Mourinho said in response to criticism from Arsenal fans after a stultifying 0-0 draw in April 2015. On Sunday, though, there was no holding back from Chelsea. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” Xabi Alonso said after seeing his new side edged out by Arsenal in a breathless encounter. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute. We wanted to be active.”

The plan worked at times. Chelsea maintained their habit of scoring early goals, going ahead through Morgan Rogers, and created further openings. But they were facing the champions and do not have Arsenal’s completeness. Shortcomings were exploited, particularly in midfield. Declan Rice romped through the middle at one point and the winning goal owed much to Reece James losing track of Martin Ødegaard as Arsenal’s captain strode through to fire past Emiliano Martínez.

It was expected to be a key battleground, and the way Arsenal went 2-1 up was felt keenly by Chelsea given their difficulties on deadline day, when Enzo Fernández got his £125m move to Manchester City and no one was signed to replace the Argentinian. However, it is worth remembering Chelsea were short not only of Fernández’s offensive skills as they fell to their first defeat under Alonso. It was also significant that Moisés Caicedo was out again, an unspecified issue proving a nuisance, and it is a concern that Alonso lacks a suitable stand‑in for the Ecuador international whose ability to cover ground, snap into challenges and shield his defence would have come in handy against a midfield as powerful as Arsenal’s.

There is much to like about Alonso’s vision. Chelsea are not obsessed with possession and are speeding forward on the counterattack. Yet while they look menacing with every attack there is a cost to the chaos. Alonso has found balance elusive. Chelsea have conceded seven goals in three games, are without a clean sheet in the league since January and need the oomph provided by Caicedo if they are to make this full-throttle style work.

Caicedo, such an important presence since joining for £115m in 2023, is yet to start this season. He missed the 3-2 win against Fulham and was replaced 14 minutes after coming on during the 4-3 victory against Brighton. Alonso is erring on the side of caution. He stressed there was no long-term problem after the Arsenal game and admitted Caicedo was rushed back against Brighton. “I don’t want to make the same mistake again,” Alonso said, keeping the wider picture in mind. It is a long season, even with no European football, and the physical demands of the league means there is no point Caicedo playing through pain when doing so would surely cause more problems down the line.

View image in fullscreen Romeo Lavia and Cole Palmer (right) of Chelsea try to dispossess Myles Lewis-Skelly of Arsenal. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

As it stands, though, Chelsea are too open and cannot strengthen until January. Compromises are necessary but the jury is out on some fixes.Alonso is a believer in James, whose shift from right‑back to central midfielder started under Enzo Maresca, but the captain is learning the role and his lack of feel for the position was exposed by Ødegaard.

Arsenal found the gaps. Roméo Lavia started alongside James but is yet to complete 90 minutes since joining Chelsea three years ago. The Belgian has struggled with injuries and ran out of steam against Arsenal after an hour, at which point Alonso looked to his bench and replaced Lavia with Malo Gusto, leaving his expensively assembled side to play out the closing stages with two repurposed right-backs in the middle.

This was never the plan. Chelsea looked at replacements for Fernández. They wanted Alex Scott but Bournemouth would not sell. Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton has admirers, there was interest in Roma’s Manu Koné, whilea move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara, which collapsed as the summer window closed, left Chelsea fuming.

In January Chelsea will hope to find a player more suited to Alonso’s system than Fernández, who is not the most mobile. They are not missing him in an attacking sense. Chelsea are scoring and the bigger headache is what to do out of possession. They do not have another player with Caicedo’s skillset.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Dário Essugo was billed as Caicedo’s deputy when he joined last year but does not have Alonso’s trust and has been loaned to Strasbourg. Jordan Henderson is recovering from a broken wrist and is 36, and sending on Gusto over Valentín Barco was an early pointer. Barco, signed from Strasbourg this summer, is promising but the 22-year-old is inexperienced and, in any case, is more passer than destroyer.

Quick Guide Play our football trivia game, On the ball Show The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues? Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Arsenal started with Rice, Ødegaard and Myles Lewis‑Skelly in midfield. They kept the £75m Bruno Guimarães in reserve and brought on two Spanish World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi, another player wanted by Chelsea.

The gulf in midfield resources told and it was the absence of Caicedo that mattered most for Chelsea. Perhaps Alonso could have adjusted and fallen back. If Chelsea continue to look so vulnerable at the back in the big games the tactics will be called naive. Yet Alonso will trust that sticking to his ideals will be rewarded in the long run. This is the start of a process. He is introducing a new system and accepts it comes with risks. The problem is that he does not have a midfielder to put out fires if Caicedo is out.

Sports.title: Fitter, happier, more productive: Arsenal could hardly have started better | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Three league games played, three games won. For Arsenal this season could only have started better if Manchester City, who look like being one of their two most serious challengers, had dropped points. But it’s not just about results: Arsenal have been comfortably the better side in each of those three games, approaching each of them in very different ways.

After the controlled victory over Coventry City and the tight game against Aston Villa that was won thanks to ratcheting up the pressure in the 15 minutes after half-time, came success in a far more open game in which they conceded for the first time this season. Chelsea tested Arsenal on Sunday, went ahead, and yet Mikel Arteta’s side still always looked like they would win – even if it did take a superb late save from David Raya to keep out an Estevão shot. But the goalkeeper too is part of their strength; even if an opposing team can work a shooting opportunity, Raya has the capacity for spectacular saves that can dispirit opponents.

Arsenal threatened from set-pieces but also from open play; they can beat opponents in multiple different ways, even when Declan Rice, probably their player of the season last year, has an off day (his unpunished late trip on Morgan Rogers was cynical and nasty, one of those deliberate offences miles from the ball that the game would benefit from treating as a red card offence).

The uplift may simply be confidence, the pressure of not having won the title, of those three successive second-place finishes, now lifted. But there are also individuals who look sharper, livelier, fresher than they did at any point last season. Martin Ødegaard is perhaps the most obvious. He struggled with injuries last season and scored only one goal; already this season he has two in the league and one in the Community Shield. Some players return from the World Cup and look exhausted or find the readaptation to the grind of the domestic game difficult; Ødegaard seems reinvigorated.

There is an imagination to his play, a lightness, and he took his goal against Chelsea superbly. His link-ups with Kai Havertz, another at times mercurial presence, were often delightful, conjuring space and angles where none seemed to exist and bringing the winner. In a team that last season developed a reputation for uncompromising physicality, there is something almost otherworldly about seeing two such ephemeral talents combining, sprites glimmering on a castle wall.

But it’s not just Ødegaard. For Bukayo Saka, last season felt like chickens coming home to roost. He is only 25 but Sunday brought what was already his 205th league start, while playing regularly for England as well. Fatigue had been stored up, which is always a worry for players who emerge as early as he did. Thomas Tuchel didn’t use him in the World Cup semi-final for reasons of tiredness or injury that remain opaque (the situation was promptly confused when he scored a hat-trick in the third-place game). But he seems back to something like his best in the early weeks of this season, fizzing in from the right-hand side and delivering dangerous corners on demand.

The other standout in the early weeks of the season is Riccardo Calafiori, who has already developed a very promising relationship going forward with Christos Tzolis, even if a few issues remain to be resolved defensively on that flank. The Italian, who scored Arsenal’s opener in the Community Shield, is not only a threat from set-plays but is very good at breaking through the lines, making him a real weapon against low blocks.

Chelsea are improving. Xabi Alonso’s side were far less open through midfield than they had been against Fulham and Brighton – easier as that can sometimes be to manage against sides who don’t instinctively cede possession. It may be, especially as the attrition of European fixtures strikes others later in the season, that they emerge as a very serious force. Arsenal, though, are very, very good now, and that means they could be several points clear by the time that putative Chelsea challenge emerges.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta’s side are not merely playing with great authority; the fixtures have also fallen well for them, getting Villa away and Chelsea at home while both sides are still finding their patterns of play. It’s still very early. We haven’t even got to the first international break yet. Pitfalls are always waiting, and football is not a sport that reacts well to being taken for granted. But for Arsenal, their title defence could hardly have started better. Things could change but, at this moment, it seems more likely that they’ll have it won with several games still to play than that their grasp on the title will have slipped.

Sports.title: Champions League supercomputer: PSG are FIFTH favourites for a third consecutive crown and Man United are given almost the same chance of winning as Real Madrid - but which of Arsenal and Man City top the list?
Sports.content:
Champions League supercomputer: PSG are FIFTH favourites for a third consecutive crown and Man United are given almost the same chance of winning as Real Madrid - but which of Arsenal and Man City top the list?

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Two-time defending champions Paris Saint-Germain have been deemed fifth favourites to win this year's tournament, with a supercomputer viewing Arsenal as the team to beat.

PSG became just the second team after Real Madrid to go back-to-back in the tournament in the Champions League era when the French giants overcame Arsenal in May.

Luis Enrique's side overcame the Gunners in a penalty shoot-out in Budapest following a 1-1 draw.

Ahead of the league phase of this season's competition beginning on Tuesday, Opta's supercomputer has deemed PSG have just a 7.1 per cent chance of clinching a third successive title.

It follows PSG having endured their worst start to a season in 19 years after losing to Lens in the French Super Cup, as well as drawing against Rennes and Lille in Ligue 1 before a 2-1 loss to Monaco on the weekend.

PSG are ranked behind Arsenal, Bayern Munich, Man City and Barcelona in the supercomputers list of favourites.

Two-time reigning champions PSG are deemed by Opta to be the fifth favourites to win this season's Champions League

Arsenal are backed as favourites as they bid to bounce back from losing last season's final to win the tournament for the first time

The favourites have been devised after the supercomputer ran 10,000 simulations of the Champions League season.

Arsenal have come out on top following the simulations, with Mikel Arteta's side backed to win Europe's elite club competition for the first time.

The reigning Premier League champions finished as runners-up in the Champions League for the second time last season, having also made the final back in 2006.

OPTA'S CHAMPIONS LEAGUE PREDICTIONS Winner: Arsenal - 20.9 per cent (chance of winning) Second: Bayern Munich - 19.4 per cent Third: Man City - 12.3 per cent Fourth: Barcelona - 8.2 per cent Fifth: PSG - 7.1 per cent Sixth: Liverpool - 6.1 per cent Seventh: Real Madrid - 4.4 per cent Eighth: Man United - 3.8 per cent Ninth: Inter Milan - 3.6 per cent Tenth: Aston Villa - 2 per cent

Arsenal have been given a 20.9 per cent chance of glory.

The Gunners are seen as having a 50 per cent chance of reaching the semi-finals and are 34.8 per cent to make the final.

Bayern Munich are narrowly behind Arsenal, with the German champions given a 19.4 per cent chance to win the Champions League for the first time since 2020.

Man City follow at 12.3 per cent in their first season under Enzo Maresca, while Barcelona are fourth at 8.2 per cent.

The Spanish giants last reached the Champions League final back in 2015, when they were crowned winners for the fifth time.

Barcelona's best showings since have been two semi-finals, achieved in 2019 and 2025.

Liverpool are ranked as sixth favourites at 6.1 per cent, with Andoni Iraola set to experience his first Champions League campaign in charge of the Reds.

Record champions Real Madrid are ranked down in seventh place, with Jose Mourinho's side given just a 4.4 per cent chance.

Their prospects are only marginally better off than Manchester United, who are given an outsiders chance at 3.8 per cent on their return to the competition.

The top ten is completed by 2025 runners-up Inter Milan and Europa League winners Aston Villa.

Sports.title: INSIDE NEWCASTLE 2.0: Ross Wilson and the men running the show reveal the truth about summer of upheaval - from secret Eddie Howe succession plan to Bruno Guimaraes shock and the deal that had to happen to sign Matias Fernandez-Pardo
Sports.content:
INSIDE NEWCASTLE 2.0: Ross Wilson and the men running the show reveal the truth about summer of upheaval - from secret Eddie Howe succession plan to Bruno Guimaraes shock and the deal that had to happen to sign Matias Fernandez-Pardo

For much of this summer, Newcastle’s transfer window was viewed from the outside as one of chaos and crisis.

Eddie Howe left, Bruno Guimaraes, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali were sold and early deals for the likes of Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi were hijacked by Premier League rivals.

But now, in a revealing sit-down with sporting director Ross Wilson, chief executive David Hopkinson and chief financial officer Simon Capper, they lift the lid on how the club emerged from that summer in a stronger position than many had anticipated – in the dugout, and on the pitch and balance sheet.

Our chief football reporter, Craig Hope, was in the room on Newcastle's Quayside as the hierarchy explained the thinking behind Newcastle 2.0, why trading stars will remain part of their model and the truth of Howe’s succession plan…

In a revealing sit-down with Ross Wilson (left), David Hopkinson (right) and Simon Capper, they lift the lid on how the club emerged from the summer in a stronger position than many thought

Newcastle are unbeaten to start the season and have been hugely entertaining going forward

‘IT NEVER FELT CHAOTIC… BUT LOSING BRUNO WAS NOT PART OF THE PLAN!’

Q: And breathe… the window is closed! But from the outside, it looked like there were moments when it was chaotic and stressful?

WILSON: 'Genuinely, no. It never felt chaotic on the inside. We did not want to lose Bruno Guimaraes and that was not part of our plan. It was really disappointing that we did, albeit we were happy with the numbers (a £75million sale to Arsenal). But everything else that happened during the window was part of the plan. That does not mean every single player (who signed) was the No1 name on our list, but that is never the case. Clearly, we were disappointed a couple of times. But that’s normal.'

Q: So, how do you reflect on the transfer window on the whole?

WILSON: ‘It was almost like running two transfer windows, because we also had the situation with the manager to deal with. We dealt with that with complete secrecy for just under two weeks, as well as trying to run a transfer window for players at the same time.

‘I had a clear idea, identity-wise, of what I wanted Newcastle United to look like, which we (points to Hopkinson) absolutely shared and our ownership share. The key for us was getting to the end of the window, not to the start or halfway through it, and really feeling that identity. That doesn't mean it's perfect, it doesn't mean that we are over the moon with it, but we're happy where we've got to.

‘We're not patting ourselves on the back or saying any more than that. We have to move forward bravely and strongly with our new coach, with our new players and with the players that were here before. There’s lots of work still to be done to get the whole club to where we want to get it to.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: To be in a position to praise the work Newcastle have done did not feel likely as recently as three weeks ago. Since then, the new manager, Matthias Jaissle, has made a very good first impression, while the last three signings – Amar Dedic, Nico Gonzalez and Matias Fernandez-Pardo – have added strength, pedigree and excitement.

It’s early days, but I think it’s fair to say Newcastle have managed to salvage their summer. Saying that, I also think it was fair to look at the situation in early August and believe they were teetering on crisis. The work since has avoided such a scenario, and credit must go to those involved.

Amar Dedic has made an excellent start to life on Tyneside after joining for £30m from Benfica

Nico Gonzalez, brought in for £50m from Manchester City, has also been a huge boost

‘WE HAD BEEN PLANNING FOR A MANAGERIAL CHANGE FOR EIGHT OR NINE MONTHS’

Q: Did losing Eddie Howe create any chaos or pain?

WILSON: ‘It didn’t feel chaotic and it didn’t feel painful. Eddie would be the first person to tell you – I came to the club 11 months ago, and I’ve been planning in the background for a managerial change for eight or nine of those months. We knew which direction we were going to go.

‘Again, that does not mean we were always going to go to Matthias, but he was always part of our planning.

'Part of our responsibility as leaders of the club is to be prepared. Eddie is an exceptionally talented coach and at some point that meant he was probably going to do something else, and we had to be prepared for that. Clearly the timing was not one we had planned for, but we had a plan in place which is why we could execute it as quickly as we did.

‘There is big respect to Eddie for the job he did for us over a long period of time. He did a wonderful job and is a legend of the club.’

Q: Was Jaissle the only manager that you spoke to?

WILSON: ‘No. He was the No1 choice. We knew the type of coach and the type of football we wanted to play. We had to use our models to identify who those coaches might be. So it was really clear that Matthias was someone who would be really interesting to us.

‘I spoke to him on the phone and it was a really good conversation. Then I met him and when I was on the phone he (Hopkinson) said, “You sound really excited about this one”. I said, “You’re probably right!”.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: The timing of Howe’s departure was a shock, but him going was less of a surprise. It should have happened at the end of last season, when he had doubts about carrying on. Nonetheless, Newcastle have, it appears, found a replacement that shares many of the same principles when it comes to playing style and intensity, but crucially Jaissle brings a fresh energy.

I think they’ve appointed a very good coach who will be around the Premier League for many years, even if this season could yet be a one of transition and ups and downs for Newcastle.

The timing of Eddie Howe’s departure was a shock, but him going was less of a surprise

Newcastle have, it appears, found a replacement that shares many of the same principles when it comes to playing style and intensity, but crucially Jaissle brings a fresh energy

‘AGGRESSIVE, VERTICAL AND ATTACKING’ – THE NEWCASTLE IDENTITY

Q: When Howe went, did you have to change the profile of player you were targeting, or did you keep the same idea?

WILSON: ’I cannot imagine, in the short term, Newcastle United playing a style of football that isn’t aggressive, vertical and attacking. For this club to be successful, we have to play an attacking, high press, high engaging, proactive, vertical style of football – and we had to find a coach to do that for us.’

Q: Has Jaissle got a specific target?

WILSON: ‘No. He's here for four years, I hope. If he is, that’s us all doing well.’

Q: Can you feel the rise in expectation (on the back of an unbeaten start and some big signings)?

WILSON: ‘We want Newcastle United to be a club with anticipation and excitement. Because if we’re not, it probably means we’re doing it wrong. We want to feel excitement and ambition and a rise in anticipation. Of course we have to manage that and be balanced. But we want to be a club that’s got excitement around it.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: On the playing style… while I agree with Wilson’s assessment of the fundamental principles of an aggressive and attacking team, I also believe there needs to be an evolution into control.

We saw on Saturday, during the 2-2 draw with Bournemouth, that Newcastle still struggle to take charge of a football match when it comes to keeping possession and dictating where and how the game is played. When fully fit, Gonzalez and Lewis Miley in midfield need to have a big impact on this improvement. Cohesion must complement the chaos.

When fully fit, Gonzalez and Lewis Miley (right) in midfield need to have a big impact on Newcastle's ability to control games

‘WE HAD TO DO A DEAL LIKE ANTHONY GORDON… AND BRUNO MEANT MORE SIGNINGS!’

Q: What is the club's position now with Squad Cost Ratio rules?

WILSON: ‘It (our SCR position) wasn’t hanging over the whole window, but where the club were previously, strategically and financially, led to the sale of Elliot Anderson (to Nottingham Forest) and Yankuba Minteh (to Brighton) and a UEFA sanction (£5m fine).

‘That's the facts, that's the reality. Nobody wanted to be there again. Going into this transfer window, we had to do a deal like Anthony Gordon (sold to Barcelona for £70m). It might have been another player, but it had to be a deal like that.

‘The window started with a new contract for Lewis Miley, which was a big signal for us in terms of identity and what we wanted to look like. A young player with an unbelievably high ceiling.

‘But until we had certainty over that transaction (sale of Gordon), we had uncertainty. Now, we’re very clear that we're in a positive place.’

CAPPER: ‘Every top-level football club in Europe is managing their budget on every transfer. Sometimes, you have to link transactions together, “So we can do this if that player comes in or goes out”. For example, we were able to sign more players because Bruno left. That gave us more headroom to be able to invest.

‘That's the other point. The club has managed to utilise as much of our headroom as we can strategically afford to lose. You can't use 100 per cent on day one, because there's more than just the squad cost moving. If you finish two places lower, that's £7m off your revenue, for example. So you need to have a bit of a margin of error in your planning, because lots of things can change.’

Anthony Gordon has hit the ground running at Barcelona after his £70m move, providing four assists in his first four LaLiga matches

‘FERNANDEZ-PARDO WAS ONLY POSSIBLE BECAUSE OF WOLTEMADE LOAN’

WILSON: 'Because we try to link things together, the ultimate deal for Matias Fernandez-Pardo was only possible because we did the Nick Woltemade loan to Juventus. That (Pardo) was the ultimate deal. Now, if we didn't do the Woltemade deal, we might have done another, but that's what we mean by linking things together.

CAPPER: ‘So the conversation we were having internally was, “If you want to do that, you're going to have to give me something back, otherwise we'll be in a position we're not comfortable with”. We managed to get that.

‘We have come out of this transfer window, I wouldn't say in an absolutely comfortable place, we have some risk around all of our Financial Fair Play measures, but it's an acceptable amount of risk at this point.

‘Our forecasts are all compliant as of today and we can afford a few little things to go wrong and remain compliant. As an organisation, that's the right place to be. We're not going with £100m headroom, just in case. I'm not going to say what the headroom is, but it's not that.’

WILSON: ‘But there is headroom, and that's the key point.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: Former sporting director Paul Mitchell had some fair ideas when it came to changing Newcastle’s transfer strategy. It was an approach to diplomacy akin to a bull in a china shop that meant it was never going to work.

Wilson has arrived with far more footballing statecraft and, primarily because of the sales of Gordon and Tonali (£100m to Tottenham), he has got the club on a sound footing from an SCR perspective. Internally, they’re calling it ‘ripping off the sticking plaster’, and I get that. It’s better to do the big sales at once as opposed to drip feed over several windows, and it serves to redraw the reality of where the club is at.

I’m still not sure about one or two of the younger players brought in at big fees this summer – they will clearly need time – but the evolution of the model was necessary and has been overseen in a relatively short period. With that, they’ve signed some top players who look ready to impact immediately.

'The ultimate deal for Matias Fernandez-Pardo was only possible because we did the Nick Woltemade loan to Juventus'

‘IF YOU DON'T TRADE PLAYERS, YOU'RE GOING TO GET STUCK’

Q: Do the players you’ve signed fit into the 2030 Vision (of being among the top clubs in the world)?

WILSON: ‘We hope they’re with us on our journey to 2030, but we’ve got a player trading model as well. I’m sure there will be players in the 2030 squad that aren’t in the 2026-27 squad – I hope there are anyway! We want to have players here who are on a journey with us, but equally if some of those players’ journeys go at a rapid speed, they might go somewhere else. That’s part of football.’

Q: Does that (SCR headroom) allow you to spend in further windows, if you’re not so close to the limit?

WILSON: ‘Of course, but we built a squad for the season. That doesn’t mean we might not make further alterations to it in January. If you want to be a successful club in the Premier League, you have to trade players. If you don’t, the chances are you won’t be a successful club, particularly when the revenues of this club are in a phase where David and his team are making those really, really grow. But without that, if you don’t trade players, you are going to get stuck.’

HOPKINSON: ‘We’ve been consistent the whole way through – we are going to be consistently and credibly competing for those top prizes. Part of consistently competing means we’ve got to be compliant with the regulatory regime.

‘We know what our revenues are going to be projected, we can figure that part out. At the end of last season, and we did not have a strong finish, we ended up in 12th. When we started our pre-planning for the window – with each match we lost it got worse, because it meant our ultimate envelope would be smaller. So we came into this window knowing how much we would have to work with and a strong recognition that we have to be compliant.’

THE £60-70MILLION CHAMPIONS LEAGUE QUESTION

Q: Does the financial forecasting mean that you need to get in Europe this season?

CAPPER: ‘We forecast all (the scenarios), and basically we're good for this season now. While we've got different scenarios, the answer is the number is quite different depending on where we are. If we're in the Champions League, we've got a much bigger number to spend next summer than if we're not in Europe at all.

‘The revenue difference is so big. We're talking £60-70million minimum for the Champions League. Probably £30-40million for the Europa League and £20million minimum for the Conference League. So even the Conference League is material.

‘Once you get to the Champions League, it ends up being potentially 20 per cent of your revenue. So of course that affects our budgets. Again, we spend what we've got.’

'If we're in the Champions League, we've got a much bigger number to spend next summer than if we're not in Europe at all'

WILSON: ‘But these are the conversations that every club's got to have. So this isn't a choice. And if you don't do it (trade players), then you just keep the squad you've got and they'll grow old and achieve less and leave for nothing.’

CRAIG HOPE'S VERDICT: I left the room with a clear sense of the direction Newcastle 2.0 will be taking. The thinking behind it is sound – and necessary – and I believe those leading that reboot are well intended.

What I’m less certain of is the likelihood of delivering the 2030 Vision the club has as its stated ambition. For that, there needs to be a big upturn in revenue and, probably, a new stadium for that to be possible. Also, the trading model they talk about cannot afford too many misses, not when margins are so tight. Manchester City can get a couple wrong, the chasing pack cannot.

But this, because of SCR and the like, is how a club outside the established top order must operate now. As is the way at Newcastle, it will be never be dull seeing how it all plays out.

Sports.title: Naomi Osaka brutally trolled by fans after debuting latest 'ludicrous' look... only for star to crash out of US Open in straight-set defeat
Sports.content:
Naomi Osaka has been brutally trolled by tennis fans after debuting her latest bold walkout look, only to get blown off the court by world No. 2 Elena Rybakina in a straight-set US Open exit on Monday afternoon.

The four-time Grand Slam champion has dominated headlines at Flushing Meadows all week with a string of unconventional runway-inspired outfits.

However, her fashion statements came back to bite her during Monday's round of 16 clash, where Rybakina dismantled the Japanese star in a brutal 6-1, 6-4 defeat.

Osaka had initially turned heads before a ball was even hit, arriving on court in an eye-catching, oversized hooded coat lined with thick faux-fur.

While the streetwear look marked a shift from her earlier outfits, viewers quickly took to social media to mock the ensemble after Osaka fell flat on the court.

One critical viewer wrote on X: 'Osaka comes out in a ridiculous coat and gets absolutely smoked in 1st set. Maybe leave the ludicrous bling in the locker room.'

Naomi Osaka debuted yet another bold pre-match outfit at the US Open on Monday afternoon

However, the Japanese star's time in the competition came to an end after a straight-set defeat

Elena Rybakina secured a 6-1, 6-4 win over Osaka to punch her ticket to the quarterfinals

Another fan took aim at the pre-match theatrics, writing: 'Clothes are great, but let's see if she can back it up on the court. Style points don't win matches.'

'What is this, a modeling shoot? The outfits are garish!' another spectator blasted.

'Naomi Osaka latest outfit, looks like an oversized fur coat number? Meanwhile her opponent and fellow elite athlete Elena Rybakina entered in her playing outfit, not seeking any attention just here to play a match of tennis,' another wrote.

The online backlash proved swift as Rybakina wasted no time seizing complete control of the contest, ruthless on serve and blasting groundstrokes past Osaka to snatch the opening set 6-1 in a blistering 22 minutes.

Osaka offered stiffer resistance in the second set, however, Rybakina's relentless power proved decisive once again, breaking through in the crucial stages to seal the set 6-4 and punch her ticket to the quarterfinals in just over an hour.

Speaking after the game, Rybakina said: 'I honestly didn't expect it. I played really well today. Feeling the ball was really good from my side.

'A bit lucky in some moments. I caught some lines. Super happy with the performance. Naomi is a tough opponent.

'I knew no matter the score I needed to focus on each ball. She's also an aggressive player. I'm very glad with the way I played today. Thank you so much for an amazing atmosphere guys.'

The Japanese star was swept aside in just over an hour in the round of 16 clash

Osaka wore an eye-catching, oversized hooded coat lined with thick faux-fur on Monday

Osaka, meanwhile, had been the center of attention throughout the tournament after showing off a range of bold pre-match looks at the US Open.

However, after arriving for her first-round match at Roland Garros in a flowing black skirt and corset, then unveiling a shimmering gold dress, her opponent Laura Siegemund aimed a pointed comment in her direction.

'I came here to play tennis, not to put on a fashion show,' Siegemund had told TNT Sports. 'And if others want to put on a fashion show, then they should go ahead and do it. That's totally fine with me.'

But Donna Vekic, who Osaka faced in the second-round, told critics to 'relax' and embrace Osaka's approach.

'Some people take tennis way too seriously,' she said. 'Relax, it's just an outfit. I think it's good that she's doing different things, expressing herself through fashion.

'Whether it's good or bad, that's a different thing, it's fashion.'

Sports.title: 'I let my country down. People are going to be on our case for a while and rightly so': BEN DUCKETT on England's drinking scandals, how he's making up for it under new captain Joe Root and why he prioritised Test cricket over the IPL
Sports.content:
It’s possible that no English summer has generated as many uses of the phrase ‘the penny has dropped’ than 2026 – but for Ben Duckett it feels like more than a cliche.

When Joe Root spoke to the dressing room about player behaviour two days before the first Test against Pakistan at Lord’s, and two days after Brydon Carse found himself in handcuffs outside a Derby nightclub, Duckett decided to follow his captain by saying a few words himself.

In some ways, this was a natural progression: of the team who will take the field at Edgbaston on Wednesday, Duckett trails only Root in terms of age (he turns 32 next month) and caps (48). He is now, officially, a senior statesman.

But his own role in England’s tapestry of misadventure – the late-night wanderings in Noosa during the Ashes tour, captured on video for posterity by a member of the public – persuaded him to back up his captain’s words. Has the penny dropped? You bet it has.

‘In those situations, anyone can talk,’ Duckett tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘But from someone who’s been in situations like that, who’s let the group down, let the country down, it felt important for me.

‘Rooty can’t speak on behalf of everyone all the time. He’s England captain right now and he’s taking a lot of stick in the media on behalf of England cricket. It’s up to me, Brooky and a few of the other guys to take some of that off his plate and help lead as much as we can.’

It’s possible that no English summer has generated as many uses of the phrase ‘the penny has dropped’ than 2026 – but for Ben Duckett it feels like more than a cliche

'Joe’s taking a lot of stick in the media on behalf of England cricket. It’s up to me, Brooky and a few of the other guys to take some of that off his plate and help lead as much as we can'

What exactly did Duckett say to his team-mates in the Lord’s dressing room? 'Don’t do what I did in Noosa'?

He laughs: ‘No, not at all. You know, I didn’t actually break any rules. It was more that this was the moment where we just need to move forward. It’s about showing what it means for us to play for England.’

If it seems strange after the events of the winter that Root even needed to remind the players of their wider responsibilities, Duckett concedes it was ‘probably necessary’.

But he adds: ‘All this stuff off the field only concerns probably five per cent of the group. It’s the team, the management, everyone involved, who get all the stick, but it’s only been a few different people who have put us in these situations, and I spoke about being one of them.

‘I think we have moved past it. The fans want to see us winning games and series, and that’s the easiest thing to put right. The rest of it’s going to come in time, and people are probably going to be on our case for a little while. Rightly so: we’ve made that very easy for them.’

Duckett believes he confirmed his dedication to the cause by turning down a £200,000 deal with Delhi Capitals in the IPL in March, and committing himself to his red-ball game after a difficult Ashes. His reward was a superb century against New Zealand at Trent Bridge in a summer where everyone has found runs hard to come by.

‘I could very easily have gone to the IPL, earned a bit more money, come back to England pretty tired and not scored that Test hundred,’ he says.

Duckett turned down a £200,000 deal with Delhi Capitals in March to work on his red-ball game and was rewarded with a century against New Zealand at Trent Bridge in June

'My biggest advice for Emilio Gay (right) is don't try to be anyone else. He’s been picked for a reason: the way he bats, the time he bats, the hundreds he scores'

‘Ultimately, those decisions should show people how much it means to play for England. I’ve got zero regrets. I want to play as many games as I can for England, and that’s my priority.’

Duckett should win his 50th cap against South Africa at the Wanderers in Johannesburg on December 17, but the question is whether his opening partner will still be Emilio Gay, whose first five Tests this summer have brought him two gutsy half-centuries but an average of just 23.

‘It’s tough,’ says Duckett, ‘because I certainly wouldn’t want to come in at the start of my career and bat on the pitches we have done this summer.’

Speaking from a seat in Edgbaston’s Hollies Stand, he gestures out to the middle, where groundstaff are putting together the finishing touches on a pitch that is browner than the grassy surfaces which helped England bulldoze Pakistan at Headingley and Lord’s.

‘This could be a big week to go and put a big score on the board and showcase what he can do. My biggest advice for Emilio is don't try to be anyone else. He’s been picked for a reason: the way he bats, the time he bats, the hundreds he scores. So I said to him: “Just play the exact way you got into this team.”’

Duckett says his age and experience have helped him deal with the challenge of forming a new opening relationship after three years with Zak Crawley – just as they helped him move on from the disappointment of an Ashes series in which he averaged only 20 with a top score of 42.

‘I’m batting at the top of the order against the best bowlers every time I go out there,’ he says. ‘Maybe the Ashes would have affected me more if I were younger. I’d have probably lost belief.

‘But I walked out there and faced Mitchell Starc bowling 93mph from the first Test to the last, and if you looked through most of my innings, I was in good positions and I was hitting the ball well. I just didn’t go on to get a big score.’

Duckett was speaking to Daily Mail Sport at a Tyrrells event at Edgbaston. Tyrrells are the official snack partner of the England men's and women's Test teams

The 31-year-old isn’t going to change the methods that have brought him nearly 3,500 Test runs at a tick under 39 and at a strike rate of 86

Above all, he isn’t going to change the methods that have brought him nearly 3,500 Test runs at a tick under 39 and at a strike rate of 86.

‘If I tried to be someone else in… let’s call it a new era, then I don’t think I’d perform as well. I know at the age I am how I’m going to get the best out of myself.’

Ben Duckett was speaking at a Tyrrells event at Edgbaston. Tyrrells Crisps are proud to be Official Snacks Partner of England Cricket. Visit tyrrellscrisps.co.uk.

Sports.title: VOICE OF THE PADDOCK: George Russell will never be Mercedes' golden boy - and despite what he says in public, he knows it. If he ever wants to win a world championship, he MUST demand to leave
Sports.content:
George Russell now has to grab his boss Toto Wolff by the neck to assert himself, and/or seek a way out of Mercedes.

Or to accept that he will be a de facto No2 for the rest of his career.

That is the honest truth, but it was not how it was meant to be for him. He started the season with a leap in his gangly step, the world championship at his mercy in a car that was the tops.

He had every reason to believe in himself. He beat Lewis Hamilton, the legend whom Russell deferred to as the GOAT, in two of their three seasons together, and held the whip hand over his team-mate Kimi Antonelli last year. The high road of history was wide open to him, or so it seemed.

Not now. At 28, he is playing second fiddle to the 20-year-old Antonelli, who produced one of Formula One’s finest drives from the back of the grid, from 19th, after taking on a new engine, to first place in Monza, as he became the first home winner of the Italian Grand Prix for 60 years. Laurels fell at young Kimi’s feet, and rightly so. It was a majestic performance.

Russell started the race second and finished second on the day he needed to prove himself, or to forget it. He is now 66 points behind Antonelli. He has won twice this season. Antonelli has won seven times.

Kimi Antonelli's miracle drive in Monza has extended his championship lead over Mercedes team-mate George Russell to 66 points

Russell, who has lived in the shadow of Lewis Hamilton previously, needs to reassert himself

Of all the motorhomes I have been in, the noise was more exuberant in delight that Antonelli had won than in almost any other celebrating a driver’s success. Even allowing for the fact that many of the guests sipping champagne were Italian, there was no mistaking the tsunami of exultation meant something important in intra-team dynamics.

By contrast had Russell won, there would have been pleasure, for sure, polite celebration, but not the bone-deep joy. That is the strong wind Russell is up against.

He is not the team’s favourite child, and a lot of ego goes into this equation. Wolff picked Antonelli as his career-enhancing superstar. Yes, Russell is also a product of the Mercedes academy, but has never been viewed by Wolff as heir to Hamilton, their biggest race winner and a standout sensation of sport.

That is why Russell should leave Mercedes if he ever wants to achieve his ambition of claiming the title. This season is pretty much finished in that regard. He would need to put together multiple consecutive wins – and then, still, hope for the best.

His mood after the gut-wrenching loss in Monza was perplexing. He was downcast, yes. His sentences at the post-race press conference trailed off, realising, as he could not escape, that his hopes were being eclipsed.

But why did Russell not question why the strategy Mercedes deployed that had favoured Antonelli, a tyre change under the virtual safety car brought about by Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin conking out, was loaded against him?

In his own mind, and I say this without speaking to him privately, he did, deep in his psyche.

That is why he is in a funk. He knows he is not given quite equal treatment. There is no escape from it, and his pretence of the team playing fair is nonsensical. He can’t be stupid enough to think so.

He argues repeatedly that there are 2,500 staff at Mercedes and why would any of them care who wins the drivers’ championship. A fair point – up to a point, Lord Copper! The yeomen factory folk all get bonuses if they win the constructors’ title, and new kitchens for all, et cetera.

But what if by small margins, at crucial moments, at the deciding seconds, one or two people at the top are pulling against him?

The noise was exuberant in delight that Antonelli had won. Had Russell won, there would have been pleasure, for sure, polite celebration, but not the bone-deep joy

Russell is in a funk. He knows he is not given quite equal treatment. There is no escape from it

One senior figure in the sport, someone who has won multiple world championships in one form or another, told me the bias towards Antonelli is obvious, and has been for months.

Why is Russell not railing against it?

Has he seriously bought into the delusion of Wolff’s assertion that there is a level playing field? ‘No,’ I doubt, though he says ‘yes’.

As for options to move elsewhere? They are few and far between for 2027. Practically none. Yet, the 2028 grid may be more fluid and that is when he could move if his contract allows him to do so. He is on some £25million a year and is tied up by Wolff under a binding deal as a Mercedes man, so it will be hard to slip away.

Other drivers have had long and distinguished careers as No2s, remunerative ones, too. Valtteri Bottas to Hamilton, Rubens Barrichello to Michael Schumacher, most pertinently David Coulthard to Mika Hakkinen. The list goes on.

The question is whether Russell wants to spend the rest of his time subservient to Mercedes’ golden child Kimi. It’s a ruthless game.

Sports.title: 'Man City have got away with b****y murder': Lord Sugar makes incendiary claim as he accuses the club of 'frightening' the Premier League with case over 115 charges still unresolved after £450MILLION summer spend
Sports.content:
Former Tottenham chairman Lord Alan Sugar has explosively claimed Manchester City have 'got away with b****y murder' due to their 115 charges case remaining unresolved.

City were charged with 115 alleged breaches of the Premier League's financial rules in February 2023 and a 12-week hearing concluded in December 2024 – but an independent commission is still yet to publish its ruling on the 'hugely complex case'.

The club strenuously deny the allegations. The verdict could see City exonerated or facing historic penalties.

Lord Sugar, who served as Tottenham chairman from 1991 to 2001, became the latest critic of the length of time required for the infamous financial charges case.

'I am waiting to see what is going to happen with Man City, the thing is Man City have got away with b****y murder,' Lord Sugar said in an appearance on Football Uncensored.

'For about three years now there has been talk of them infringing these rules, they have most probably paid about half a billion to lawyers so far to frighten the Premier League.

Lord Sugar explosively claimed Man City have 'got away with murder' due to their long-running 115 charges case remaining unresolved

City’s hearing – over allegations of repeated breaches of the top-flight’s financial controls – ended in December 2024 but a verdict remains outstanding. City deny all wrongdoing

'When are they going to get done or aren't they going to get done.'

Host Piers Morgan, a vocal Arsenal supporter, agreed stating: 'It is a very interesting question, City have just spent an absolute fortune in this transfer window and yet they have got 115 charges hanging over them.

'It seems to have been going on with an interminable amount of time but will have dramatic consequences.

'If they are found guilty, you could see them having Premier League titles stripped from them, maybe three, maybe four - hopefully coming Arsenal's way - you could see them relegated. This has enormous implications, how can they spend all this money with this hanging over them?'

Man City spent £440million in the transfer window and equalled the British transfer record signing £125million Enzo Fernandez.

It was a bumper summer for City after the exit of long-serving manager Pep Guardiola. They also signed Elliot Anderson (£116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£86m), Iliman Ndiaye (£60m), Allan and Geronimo Rulli.

David Bernstein, who served as Man City chairman from 1998 until 2003 and served as Football Association chair 2011-13, on Sunday also attacked the lack of an outcome and questioned the Premier League's handling of the case.

Writing in the Sunday Times, Bernstein said: 'The fact they have done this (transfer spend) against the background of the 115 Premier League charges is extraordinary and makes a mockery of regulation in England's top division, supposedly the best-run league in the world.

'Why the league decided to prosecute all 115 alleged offences is a mystery to me. Surely common sense (often in short supply) would point to simplifying the process by taking a handful of the bigger, clearer issues and pursuing these as specimen cases.

David Bernstein was City chairman from 1998 until 2003 and served as FA chair 2011-13

Premier League boss Richard Masters has claimed that Manchester City’s ongoing 115 charges saga is ‘not necessarily top of the list’ when it comes to his conversations with clubs

'Justice delayed is justice denied, and the longer this process is drawn out, the more the resulting implications and challenges are compounded.'

This is the fourth season to begin under the cloud of the City 115 charges announcement.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters conceded last month that the case was taking 'longer than expected', but said the saga was 'not necessarily top of the list' when it comes to his conversations with clubs.

Four Premier League sides have reserved the right to seek compensation should City be found guilty and it would appear that much of football is desperate for an outcome.

However, Masters suggested that the noise in boardrooms up and down the country is not as loud as one might imagine.

'I obviously speak to clubs all the time,' he said last month. 'It's not necessarily a topic of conversation that is top of the list. (There are) Lots of other things to talk about and do. The Premier League moves on. It's starting (again) on Friday evening.'

Masters has previously admitted to being frustrated by the length of time the independent panel is taking to return its verdict.

'The process is the process,' he said. 'It will resolve itself. But as you know, I literally can't say a thing about it. There's only one available option, which is to allow the process to reach its natural conclusion. I can't talk about the substance of the case. I can't talk about the timing of the case. Our rules are very clear about that. I understand that people are frustrated but it will take as long as it takes.'

Man City are joint top of the Premier League, having taken maximum points from their first three matches under the guidance of Enzo Maresca – including a 1-0 victory over promoted Coventry City on Saturday.

Sports.title: Graeme Souness rips into Declan Rice again - insisting he 'plays too deep' and 'might be a centre-half' - as legend claims Arsenal midfielder wouldn't get into any of Real Madrid, Barcelona or Man City's teams
Sports.content:
Graeme Souness has delivered another scathing assessment of Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice, suggesting he might be better suited to playing in defence because he operates 'too deep'.

Rice has established himself as a key figure for both Arsenal and England since his £105million move to the Emirates in 2023, but Souness remains unconvinced the 27-year-old has the qualities required of an elite central midfielder.

The Gunners star, who played a pivotal role in steering Arsenal to their first Premier League title in 22 years last campaign and helped guide his country to the World Cup semi-finals in the summer, was singled out for criticism and labelled 'limited' by Souness after England's heartbreaking defeat against Argentina.

Appearing on Piers Morgan's new Football Uncensored show on Monday after Arsenal's 2-1 victory over title rivals Chelsea at the weekend, Souness doubled down on his view of Rice.

'How many times do you see him as the last man with the ball,' Souness told Morgan. 'In the build-up, he's last man. He's sitting between two centre-halves or between the centre-half and the full-back. He's last man. A lot of the time, he doesn't play in midfield.

'In my second or third home game (of my career), I went into the back four like all midfield players do today. It's old man's football. It's cheating. An old man's way of playing midfield. You get the ball under no pressure and you play it out to the full-back.'

Graeme Souness has delivered another scathing assessment of Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice

He believes the England star is more of a 'centre-half' and ripped into him for playing 'too deep'

Souness went on to explain how he was eviscerated by team-mates at half-time after he dropped back to pass 10metres between the centre-back and full-back - and from then on was 'told to play in midfield' further up the pitch.

'He (Rice) plays too deep to affect the game,' Souness added. 'I don't think he's got enough football. Let me tell you what he can do. He's the best defensive midfielder in the country right now, he smells danger. But then again, he's back there all the time.

'He's not a midfield player then is he? I think he may be a centre-half. The ball travels faster than you do. I see him run with the ball 30 yards and pass it square. He's a lovely kicker of the ball and opens his body up well, there's nothing to dislike about him. But modern players are a bit precious. Criticism doesn't fall easily on these (players') shoulders. He isn't the complete midfield player.'

Morgan then responded with the claim that Rice is a world-class midfielder, to which Souness added: 'I'm not sure if he gets in Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, Man City. If you want the best in that position, City had two of them - Fernandinho and Rodri. They played in midfield. Next time, please watch him. He goes in and gets it cheap under no pressure, a 10-yard pass off Gabriel, and passes it sideways.'

Souness also again blamed Rice for his role in England's World Cup semi-final collapse against Argentina in July.

'When England went one-nil up against Argentina, they s*** themselves. "Oh, what do we do now?" And I put that down to Declan Rice and (Elliot) Anderson as the central midfield players in the engine room,' he said.

'They didn't get them playing. They went back in held hands with the back four.'

So far this season, Rice has helped Arsenal claim three wins from their opening three matches against Coventry, Aston Villa and Chelsea, sitting second in the Premier League behind title rivals Manchester City on goals scored.

Arsenal have bolstered their ranks in midfield with the £75million acquisition of Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United this summer, who started Sunday's 2-1 victory at the Emirates on the substitutes' bench.

Rice played a key role in helping Arsenal win the Premier League for the first time in 22 years

Rice, one of the most durable players in the Premier League, played 55 games for the Gunners last campaign in a crucial role for Mikel Arteta, who will now have the option of resting him more frequently after the arrival of Guimaraes.

Arsenal take on Napoli in the Champions League on Wednesday before travelling to the Stadium of Light to face Sunderland on Saturday.

Sports.title: US Open star Jelena Ostapenko celebrates in the face of her opponent's 'very disrespectful' coach in trash-talking doubles row
Sports.content:
US Open star Jelena Ostapenko celebrates in the face of her opponent's 'very disrespectful' coach in trash-talking doubles row

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jelena Ostapenko roared in the face of the coach she believed was trash-talking her and doubles partner Hsieh Su-wei as she celebrated their victory over Australian-Taiwanese team Maya Joint and Chan Hao-ching.

The former French Open champion is frequently found at the centre of on-court drama, but on Monday was only keen to defend herself and Hsieh from the behaviour of the Joint-Chan coaching box, who she has claimed were cheering and clapping their mistakes past the threshold of sportsmanship.

The on-court fracas bubbled over during the 6-4, 6-4 clash with Hsieh speaking to the chair umpire during the changeover at 4-1 to Joint and Chan. Ostapenko had previously celebrated in the direction of the opposition's player box after striking a winner for 30-15, but things came to a head during the break, with Hsieh heard asking for the chair umpire to intervene.

Hsieh's conversation with the umpire was muted, with the player, who is also Taiwanese, referencing a breach in 'sportsmanship'. This in turn prompted Ostapenko to throw her support behind her long-time partner.

'No, they cannot do this - it’s very disrespectful,' Ostapenko stressed. 'They do this because they know they cannot beat us, because they’re so much worse than us. They’re doing this on purpose.'

Ostapenko then pointed at the player's box, adding: 'If he's going to do this again, call the supervisor.'

Jelena Ostapenko had a retort after allegedly suffering trash talk and poor sportsmanship

Hsieh implied that they had been subject to comments in Chinese, with Ostapenko doubling down on her partner's translation, telling the umpire: 'He's saying s***, he's not cheering.'

There was back-and-forth between the umpire and the doubles partnership, with Hsieh keen that he intervened, hence why she 'reported the issue.'

'You've got to listen to us,' she added, with Ostapenko stressing the same message.

When the chair umpire finally confirmed that he would be taking matters in hand, Ostapenko urged that the chair umpire find somebody who 'speaks her language' to ensure that the comments from the opposition box were caught.

'Then find someone! There are chair umpires who speak Chinese,' Ostapenko replied, after seemingly learning that this might be a challenge.

After the lengthy break, Ostapenko and Hsieh returned to court and let their tennis do the talking, stopping the rot against the younger partnership and carrying off the match in straight sets - prompting the wild celebrations.

Following the match, Ostapenko clarified to Daily Mail Sport the series of events.

'I felt like it was a little bit too intense from their side,' she shared after the match. 'I understand every player has a team behind them and the team is supporting (them), but I felt like when we were on their side, they were doing this on purpose.

'That's why me and Su-wei spoke with the chair umpire because I felt after every easy mistake we did, they were just like clapping and shouting, which in doubles is not very common.

'I understand you can do this sometimes in singles, when you really want to support your player, but normally in doubles, I think that happened for the first or the second time ever.'

After every mistake, Ostapenko added, the team would comment that they had struck a 'beautiful shot' sarcastically in Chinese, with Hsieh translating for Ostapenko. But the jibes only served as fuel for the team.

'I respect all players and all teams of the players, but I feel like sometimes, these kind of things are done on purpose, and I don't feel like this is something that should be happening,' she continued.

'You should respect each other, and that's why I got so angry, and I started to (yell) "come on!" so much. Because these kind of things, they pump me up even more. Then I'm saying (to myself), "I'm not gonna lose this match. I can die on court, but I'm not gonna lose this match."'

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
