World.title: Avi Lewis's NDP is eyeing Toronto for its rebuild
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As NDP MPs meet in Toronto for their fall caucus retreat, the party is still in rough shape politically and financially.

Federal New Democrats are digging themselves out of their election debt. Their leader still doesn't have a seat in the House of Commons. And their tiny caucus enters the fall Parliamentary sitting even smaller, after one MP joined the Liberals and another left.

But that's the one-sided view of the party held by those in the Ottawa political bubble, as NDP Leader Avi Lewis often likes to say. He and others say the New Democrat movement is ripe for a revival — and they think the city of Toronto offers a path forward.

'We are back,' Lewis says

In a video posted on social media the day after last week's byelections — in which the party won no seats — Lewis admitted the New Democrats were "never expected to win."

Nevertheless, Lewis said the results in Toronto signal the party is showing signs of coming back to life. In that byelection, the NDP saw their vote share triple compared to the 2025 general election in the Toronto riding of Beaches—East York.

"The big headline for me is we are back," Lewis said. "Our rebuild as a party is well underway. Lots of work still to do. But the early signs are really encouraging."

Lewis said New Democrats did better in this "sleepy summer, somewhat cynical byelection," than they have in the past 11 years.

The 2025 general election was devastating for New Democrats with their worst-ever result. Jagmeet Singh resigned as leader on the spot.

In March, New Democrats elected Lewis, who won on the first ballot with 56 per cent of the vote. Six months in, and Lewis has yet to secure a seat in the House of Commons, opting not to run in the recent byelections or the six upcoming.

Lewis could run for a Toronto seat

A senior NDP source tells CBC the party's five-member caucus is going to Toronto because the party believes the path back to official party status is through Toronto seats, especially communities like Davenport and Parkdale.

CBC is not identifying the source as they are not authorized to speak publicly about internal party matters.

The city's downtown core and surrounding areas, the source said, is ground zero for the main issues Lewis has been focusing on — the cost of groceries, housing, opposing another West Coast pipeline and tackling the climate crisis.

The NDP hasn't won a seat in Toronto since 2011. But the party has potential, according to Éric Grenier, polling analyst and publisher of The Writ .

"I do think that the kind of messaging that Avi Lewis has been promoting, his general kind of approach and demeanour and policies are more likely to appeal in a place like Toronto, in urban downtown area kind of ridings."

WATCH | Lewis calls for retaliation against Donald Trump: 'This trade war could and should hurt President Trump,' says NDP Leader Avi Lewis | Duration 11:50 Opposition leaders from the Conservative Party, NDP and Bloc Québécois all met with Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday to discuss the government’s response to the latest 50 per cent U.S. tariffs. Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis says he 'was struck' by the prime minister's tone regarding the likelihood of a deal while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Lewis told the independent news website The Breach he was tempted to run in the Beaches—East York byelection.

And CBC's source did leave open the potential that Lewis could eventually run in Canada's largest city.

"We're keeping our options open," the source said. "There are opportunities to win seats … there is real potential to build upon."

It would have been a gamble, but had Lewis run in Beaches—East York he could have won, said Jordan Leichnitz, a former NDP strategist and frequent panellist on CBC's Power and Politics.

Leichnitz said the votes the NDP were able to pick up likely came from progressive voters who are uncomfortable with Carney changing environmental regulations, building a pipeline and attempting to change the Canada Labour Code, potentially making it harder for some to strike.

"The ground organizing muscle that they were able to demonstrate in Beaches—East York is significant," said Leichnitz, who's also the Canada director for the Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, an international German foundation that's aligned with theSocial Democratic Party of Germany (SPD).

"And the fact that they were able to sort of prove, on the ground, the thesis that there are some progressive voters who voted Liberal who are now willing to come home under Lewis's leadership — that's important."

WATCH | Can Lewis unite his party?: Can new NDP leader Avi Lewis unite the party? | Duration 5:32 Chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton speaks with Avi Lewis, the newly elected leader of the federal NDP, about what his win means for New Democrats moving forward and how he will try to rebuild and unite the party.

Year-round organizing, not just elections

Under Lewis, the NDP is developing a model of permanent organizing where the party is training and connecting with volunteers throughout the year and not just during election time, according to Matthew Green, the party's outgoing national director.

At a time when many people have fewer in person social connections, he said, New Democrats hope NDP riding groups become community hubs where people form lasting relationships instead of just the transactional politics of door knocking and phone calls at election time.

"What we're proposing around building communities is the idea that there is space for joy and fun and socializing and community and food and music and dance and things that typically wouldn't be associated in the modern era with politics, but we're a core part of our CCF [Co-operative Commonwealth Federation; the NDP's political predecessor]."

Other than Beaches—East York, the NDP's byelection results were dismal for the NDP, according to Grenier.

Their vote share shrunk in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord and in North Vancouver—Capilano they earned three per cent of the vote and fell to third place, behind the Green Party of Canada.

"The NDP is still not in great shape. They're in better shape than they were in 2025, but that was the worst shape the party's ever been. So it's a low bar," Grenier said.

World.title: Why thousands are paying to watch people play Dungeons & Dragons live
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There is no script, no fixed ending and no guarantee the heroes will make it out alive.

Onstage, performers build a fantasy world together while dice rolls and split-second choices can send the story to places nobody planned.

On Sept. 10, nearly 2,800 people will fill Vancouver's Queen Elizabeth Theatre for a sold-out performance of Endless Dungeon, led by comedian and game master Brennan Lee Mulligan. The Vancouver date follows a sold-out May performance at Toronto's Coca-Cola Coliseum.

Endless Dungeon is part of the growing world of "actual play" — tabletop role-playing games performed for an audience — a genre combining improvisational theatre, collaborative storytelling and game mechanics, with dice helping determine whether characters succeed or fail.

For performers and scholars, the appeal lies in uncertainty, intimacy and collaboration — and in knowing that no two performances will be exactly alike.

Mulligan told CBC News that part of the attraction is simply "the joy of live theatre."

"It's happening in front of your face," he said, adding that the audience reactions become part of the draw. "You are there, your gasps, your laughs, your groans at a bad D&D pun."

WATCH | CBC Exclusive: Brennan Lee Mulligan on the popularity of live D&D: Why live D&D is drawing thousands — and changing who gets seen | Duration 8:08 Brennan Lee Mulligan on why audiences are filling theatres for live D&D, how performers preserve the intimacy of friends creating stories together, and how the form has made queer, trans and other marginalized players more visible.

A roller coaster with no track

The term "actual play" is recent, but the practice is a longstanding one according to Emily Friedman, a professor of English at Alabama's Auburn University who studies the format.

Online shows such as Critical Role, Mulligan's Dimension 20 and The Adventure Zone helped bring actual play into the mainstream. Live performances are often self-contained, with clearer character goals and story beats designed to reach an ending in a few hours. That makes the action "heightened and brightened and made sharper and quicker and faster," Friedman said.

She compared its appeal to being on a roller coaster where "the track is being laid in front of you at high speed."

Vancouver comedian Jess Lupini, who is joining Endless Dungeon for this stop, compared it to another form of unscripted entertainment.

"Watching actual plays is exciting in many of the same ways that watching hockey is exciting," she said. "You don't know what's going to happen."

Emily Friedman, left, and Brennan Lee Mulligan on an episode of Adventuring Academy, a series on the streaming service Dropout. Friedman says live actual play is like a roller coaster whose track is being laid as the performers race forward. (Submitted by Emily Friedman)

'The feeling of being in the room'

But that unpredictable nature only partly explains why people pay to see a format they can watch online.

Abdul Aziz, a Vancouver comedian joining Mulligan for this Endless Dungeon performance, says the attraction is "probably the feeling of being in the room."

Aziz also performs on the actual-play podcast Spout Lore, which has tried to preserve the atmosphere of friends playing together even as those conversations became entertainment for strangers.

"We sort of are more focused on each other while playing than we are focused on the audience," Aziz said.

Friedman says audiences are watching two things at once: fictional characters and the real people creating them reacting genuinely when another player's choice surprises them.

Mulligan says performers have to make the audience feel included without sacrificing their connection to one another.

"The best part of live theatre is the preservation of authentic connection between performers and feeling totally invisible as an audience member, even as everything has been arranged to include you," he said.

"Whatever you do to delight your players will delight the audience."

Abdul Aziz, a Vancouver comedian and actual-play performer, says tabletop role-playing games let people put parts of themselves into their characters, creating an authentic connection with audiences. (Submitted by Abdul Aziz)

A place to imagine differently

For Aziz, fantasy also offers room to question rules that can seem fixed in the real world.

Aziz, whose parents are from Egypt and who immigrated to Canada as a child, says growing up in a mainly white community gave him an outsider's perspective on cultural conventions.

That carried into Spout Lore. While building his barbarian character's homeland, Aziz drew heavily on Middle Eastern cultures.

"In a very literal sense, the outsider's perspective was immediately useful in our show," he said.

Jess Lupini, centre, a Vancouver comedian and actual-play performer, appears with fellow BlackwaterDnD cast member Sean Depner, left, and game master Tim Carlson. Lupini says role-playing gave her a safe way to explore her gender identity before transitioning. (Submitted by Jess Lupini)

For Lupini, who is also a recurring cast member on BlackwaterDnD, an actual-play show streamed on YouTube and Twitch, taking on different characters became a way to explore herself.

Lupini, who is transgender, says tabletop role-playing games give people a chance to try on different identities, pronouns and personalities.

Before transitioning, she played characters who used she/her pronouns.

"That was really liberating and felt like a safe way of exploring a piece of myself that I had been conditioned to be really afraid of exploring," she said.

Friedman says women, gender-nonconforming people, 2SLGBTQ+ people and disabled people have always been part of tabletop gaming as players and creators, but were not always visible in traditional gaming spaces.

"It's just the shift of the spotlight in a lot of ways," she said.

Mulligan agrees, saying actual play didn't create those experiences, but made them easier to see.

"Actual play provided visibility for a reality that was always there," he said.

Em Carlson, CEO and creative director of the Vancouver-based actual-play show BlackwaterDnD, says audiences want stories that make them feel included in the narrative. (Submitted by Em Carlson)

A safe place to play

That kind of exploration depends on trust, says Em Carlson, CEO and creative director of BlackwaterDnD and another performer joining Vancouver's Endless Dungeon.

Carlson, whose professional background is in mental-health therapy, says the group does extensive preparation around safety and collaboration and notes that "play can't happen if you're not safe."

Tabletop role-playing culture still hasn't fully achieved its ideals of inclusion, Carlson says, but the stories reaching audiences have broadened as people want stories that help them feel included in the narrative.

"They can be a part of that joy that the players experience at the table."

For Carlson, Endless Dungeon offers something increasingly uncommon in an era of endlessly replayable media: a story created once, for the people present.

"It's a one-night experience where a fantastic, amazing audience gets to come in and laugh with us and cry with us and feel big feelings and cheer."

World.title: Far-right victory in German state expected to send shockwaves throughout the world
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt have overwhelmingly chosen the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to run their government. It's a historic victory for a once-fringe populist party that's designated as right-wing extremist by local domestic intelligence agencies in numerous states, including in Saxony-Anhalt, and whose members have come under fire for using Nazi slogans. Some experts say the win Sunday signifies a deep crisis of established politics in Germany and sends a message to right-wing populists around the world, ahead of numerous regional and federal elections in the European Union, that the political tides are in their favour. "I'm feeling so excited and I'm so proud of our team here in Saxony-Anhalt," Alice Weidel, federal co-leader of the AfD, told CBC News at the election media centre in Magdeburg, the state's capital. "We have a huge responsibility, not only in Saxony-Anhalt, but in overall Germany." WATCH | Far-right AfD wins state election in Germany: Far-right party wins German state election, falls short of a majority | Duration 4:03 AfD, or Alternative for Germany, a far-right political party surged to a victory Sunday evening, but fell short of holding a majority. It could become the country’s first far-right state government since the Second World War. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt promises to improve relations with Russia, ban Pride flags in schools and create separate classrooms for refugee children. It calls for "remigration," a term often used in far-right circles to refer to mass deportations of people who come from a migration background. "No one who is honest, and no one who is accepting our laws and no one who is not illegal in Germany has to be scared because of our party," said AfD Saxony-Anhalt chairman Martin Reichardt. Elon Musk, Trump react to election results AfD politicians in Saxony-Anhalt have praised U.S. President Donald Trump as a source of inspiration, even using the catchphrase "Make Saxony-Anhalt Great Again" on the campaign trail, an echo of Trump's MAGA movement. Some in the United States are already responding to Sunday's win with their congratulations. Elon Musk wrote "Gut gemacht!" (which translates to "well done") in response to Weidel's post on X congratulating Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD candidate to lead Saxony-Anhalt, on his win. Musk previously endorsed the party at a rally in Saxony-Anhalt in 2025. Trump also posted a screenshot of the preliminary election results to his Truth Social page on Sunday evening. Gut gemacht! —elonmusk Siegmund said Germany's success hinges on having more “sensible diplomacy” with other countries such as the U.S. and Russia. "Momentum is still on the side of the right-wing populists," said Oliver Schmidtke, former director of the Centre for Global Studies at the University of Victoria in B.C. "I think right-wing populists around the western world, they see it as a sign that the frustration with old parties is very profound." Federal AfD co-leader Alice Weidel in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sunday. (Mona Schulze/CBC) The win is also an unprecedented blow to the established political system in Germany, according to Marcus Böick, a University of Cambridge professor who studies modern German history. Voters in rural areas, of which there are many in Saxony-Anhalt, feel neglected by so-called elites in Berlin, he said. This regional vote is a form of protest. "At the moment it’s quite desperate, the situation," said Böick, who is from Saxony-Anhalt. He said many people living in the former East Germany have grappled with ongoing inequality, unemployment and a lower quality of life compared to states in the west, more than three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall. "How should you get out of the mess?" German chancellor faces widespread unpopularity Voter turnout in Sunday's election was around 78 per cent, according to the state election commissioner, reportedly the highest turnout in Saxony-Anhalt since German reunification in 1990. The AfD more than doubled its support from Saxony-Anhalt's last election in 2021, but it fell just three seats short of securing an absolute majority. That means the party could still face challenges in forming government or electing Siegmund to head the state, since the German political system is usually governed by a coalition of more than one party. At a news conference in Berlin on Monday, Siegmund said the AfD will speak with individual parliamentary groups and lawmakers to see if they would support the party in governing Saxony-Anhalt. "We will, of course, hold discussions to see whether there are — and this is a crucial message today — individual parliamentary groups or individual MPs willing to join us in tackling this historic task," said Siegmund in German. Weidel, Siegmund and Chrupalla celebrate as the preliminary results came in on Sunday for the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. (Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters) The win is also already leading to questions for the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which after 24 years of governing in Saxony-Anhalt suffered major losses on Sunday. The CDU received just 17.2 per cent of the vote, compared to 37.1 per cent last election. The centre-right party also leads Germany federally under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who faces widespread unpopularity. "I predict that the CDU will never again win a federal election," Weidel told reporters in German on Sunday. Merz said at a news conference in Berlin on Monday that the results of Saxony-Anhalt's election have shaken him personally. He said Germany has a special responsibility to protect its constitution because of its past, and he pledged introducing reforms to improve the country's sluggish economy. WATCH | AfD eyes national victory in Germany after state win: AfD victory in Germany sparks protest, celebration | Duration 2:07 A day after the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD) victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, thousands protested in Berlin over the party's stance on LGBTQ rights and immigration. Meanwhile, AfD leaders celebrated the win, saying 'Germany is back.' "We are all deeply shocked," said Merz, standing beside the lead candidate for the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt, Sven Schulze. "We did not expect it to turn out like this. We must, of course, accept it. Those are the rules of our democracy. "But yesterday marked a turning point not only in Saxony-Anhalt, but throughout Germany. And this election result will have consequences." The CDU and other mainstream political parties previously kept the AfD out of state power by forming coalition governments by refusing to work with them. The strategy is known as "the firewall" and is meant to safeguard German democracy against threats to the country's postwar liberal values and constitution. LISTEN | Is Germany's 'firewall' against the far right crumbling?: Front Burner 30:48 Is Germany's firewall against the far right crumbling? But experts say options for the mainstream political parties to form a coalition that will keep the AfD out of power in Saxony-Anhalt are limited, especially with the party's level of public support. The AfD also leads national opinion polls at 27 per cent, according to German election research company Infratest-Dimap, and secured the second-highest number of seats in the 2025 federal election. Siegmund arrives for a news conference in Berlin on Monday, a day after the eastern state's election results. (Liesa Johannssen/Reuters) A feather in Russia's cap The AfD is also pitching major overhauls to Germany's current policy toward Russia. There are also reported concerns about the party's ties to the country, because if the AfD holds state power, it could control state-level domestic intelligence services. Weidel told reporters on Sunday that the AfD party wants to help facilitate peace negotiations amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war, but experts say the party takes a clear pro-Russia stance. Party lawmakers have reportedly praised and visited the country, and called for an end to support for Ukraine; in the Saxony-Anhalt AfD's government manifesto, it states it has a strong interest in good relations with Russia both "economically and culturally." Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of Russia's sovereign wealth fund who is considered a longtime ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, took to X to offer his praise for the AfD party. "AfD will restore Germany and Europe by leading the common-sense approach that migrant-friendly, warmongering Biden-think EU politicians tried to eradicate," wrote Dmitriev, who ended his message depicting shaking hand emojis between the flags for Russia, Germany and the United States. AfD will restore Germany and Europe by leading the common-sense approach that migrant-friendly, warmongering Biden-think EU politicians tried to eradicate. 🇷🇺🤝🇩🇪🤝🇺🇸 https://t.co/CohkKRSxYI —kadmitriev Schmidtke said Putin supports right-wing populist movements throughout the world to sow division and weaken support for democracy. "I'm sure the champagne was opened at the Kremlin to see a party that has very strong pro-Russian links and doesn't want to support Ukraine anymore," said Schmidtke of Sunday’s election results in Saxony-Anhalt. "This is a sign that, in a way, the unified front in Europe in support of Ukraine becomes more difficult to sustain." Merz said the election results wouldn't change the country's continued support for Ukraine, and said there are threats to Germany's internal security. "I want to make this very clear: 2,500 kilometres east of here, people are especially delighted with this election result," said Merz, in reference to Russia. It's unclear when a possible coalition government could be announced for Saxony-Anhalt or whether Siegmund will be able to lead the state. The AfD is also leading the opinion polls in nearby Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, which is having its state election on Sept. 20 alongside Berlin.

World.title: Investigators have recovered voice and data recorders from Amazon plane crash at Miami airport
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An investigation is underway into what caused an Amazon cargo jet to go off the runway at the Miami International Airport and slam into two vehicles, killing five people and injuring five others, including the pilots.

The five people killed when an Amazon cargo jet ran off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday were inside a van carrying seven people from a cleaning company and an SUV hit outside of airport property, the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board's (NTSB) chairperson said on Monday.

Jennifer Homendy didn't detail how many people were in the SUV or where the dead were found, but she called the scene of Sunday's crash "utter devastation."

Homendy told reporters she walked the route the Boeing 767 followed, noting tire marks from the pavement into the grass, the destroyed van carrying the cleaning crew, torn fencing, navigational equipment, and the crushed SUV outside airport property.

"It's pretty extensive. Hard to see and I'm sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well."

Investigators have already been able to recover both the voice and data recorders from the aircraft, she said.

WATCH | Watch the full NTSB briefing: U.S. investigators give update on Amazon cargo plane crash | Duration 25:28 The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board holds a media briefing to share its latest updates on Sunday's deadly Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crash at Miami International Airport. At least five people died and five others were injured when the jet barrelled off the runway and slammed into vehicles.

Van was 'torn apart'

The plane, all told, travelled about 396 metres past the paved surface. Debris was everywhere, she said.

"I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation," Homendy said.

The van with seven people inside was "torn apart," she said. The van was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., an airline cleaning contractor.

Homendy said the NTSB would issue more information on Tuesday, possibly including information on the speed of the plane according to the flight data recorder.

Federal investigators examining the crash spent Monday determining whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.

WATCH | NTSB chair describes the scene of the crash: Scene of Amazon plane crash 'utter devastation': NTSB head | Duration 2:59 At a news conference on Monday, the head of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board outlined the route taken by an Amazon cargo jet that ran off a runway at Miami International Airport and struck two vehicles, killing five people and injuring five others. Chair Jennifer Homendy described the scene of Sunday's crash as 'utter devastation.'

No safety system on Miami runways

Video of Sunday's landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Homendy called on anyone with relevant video or photos from the crash to send their footage to the NTSB via its website.

Investigators will examine the plane's speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft's mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun.

The Miami airport is not equipped with engineered material arresting systems (EMAS) that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports countrywide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway.

Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.

Miami's airport appears to be in compliance and wasn't required to have an arresting system because it has a 304-metre safety buffer at the end of its runways, said Mike O'Donnell, the FAA's former director of airport safety and accident investigations.

The NTSB's Homendy told reporters that the question of whether EMAS should be required at every airport and might have prevented Sunday's tragedy in Miami will be a key part of the NTSB investigation.

The requirement was prompted by American Airlines Flight 1420 overrunning a runway at Little Rock National Airport in Arkansas in 1999, killing nine.

The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.

Investigators say they will focus on the moment of touchdown and why the pilots didn't abandon the landing if they had overshot the runway. (David Fischer/The Associated Press)

Plane appeared to float above runway

The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 914 metres of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

Mary Schiavo, a pilot and former inspector general of the U.S. Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.

It wasn't raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.

"A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you've already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away."

History of aircraft

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.

The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon and continued into Monday.

Miami International Airport said two of its four runways remained closed in the morning and operations would be affected throughout the day because of aircraft and flight crews not arriving there due to Sunday's cancellations.

Amazon said in a statement that it would co-operate with any investigation.

"We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today's incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. "Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss."

Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three people were injured.

World.title: Illinois mother charged with killing toddler 'invested' in Lindsay Clancy case: prosecutors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been closely following the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy and was texting friends about the case just hours before her son was found dead, prosecutors said.

Corie Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after her son, Barrett, was found dead in the basement of the family's suburban Chicago home on Sept. 1, according to court records obtained by NBC Chicago.

Prosecutors said Walsh had become "very invested" in Clancy's nationally watched trial and was discussing it with friends until about 12:30 p.m. that day. A neighbour found Barrett less than four hours later.

Walsh was found elsewhere in the home with injuries that authorities said were self-inflicted. Prosecutors said she later told investigators that she killed her son because she believed he was the "devil" and the "anti-Christ." Her lawyer, Andrea Lyon, told reporters Walsh was experiencing a psychotic episode and called the boy's death a tragedy for the entire family.

Police were called to Walsh's home in Frankfort, about 56 kilometres southwest of Chicago, shortly before 4 p.m. after a neighbour discovered Barrett in the basement, according to prosecutors' petition seeking to keep Walsh jailed before trial.

WATCH | Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy case: Mistrial declared over deadlocked jury in Lindsay Clancy case | Duration 2:50 The murder trial of Lindsay Clancy has been declared a mistrial, with one juror revealed as a holdout. Clancy had been charged with murder in the killing of her three children, which her lawyer blamed on postpartum psychosis, but prosecutors argued the killings were premeditated.

The neighbour found the boy and began CPR while calling 911, prosecutors said. He was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. An autopsy determined that he died from asphyxia caused by ligature compression of the neck.

Police searching the house found Walsh fully dressed in a bathtub containing bloody water, prosecutors said. She had cuts to her wrists and thighs and was taken to a hospital with injuries authorities described as not life-threatening.

The disclosure that Walsh had been following Clancy's trial came days after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in that case on Friday, when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.

Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, was accused of killing her three young children in 2023. Her lawyers argued that she was legally insane and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors maintained that Clancy understood what she was doing and knew it was wrong.

Authorities in Illinois have not alleged that Clancy's trial played a role in the killing of Walsh's son, and no evidence made public so far establishes a connection beyond her discussion of the case.

Frankfort police and prosecutors in Will County did not respond to calls for comment on Monday.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with human rights office over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.
