World.title: Fireworks blast in México state kills 10, injures dozens more
World.content:
At least 10 people were killed and 82 wounded after an unknown quantity of fireworks detonated during a celebration for a patron saint in the town of Santa María Canchesdá, in the municipality of Temascalcingo, México state.

Local authorities said the explosion occurred at around 9:30 p.m. on Saturday night in the vicinity of the Nuestra Señora de la Luz (Our Lady of Light) church. Temascalcingo, a municipality of 66,000 residents, is located around 160 kilometers northwest of Mexico City.

Videos shared online show festival attendees carrying a straw bull, with fireworks shooting from the effigy. Shortly after, additional fireworks being stored next to the church ignited, which caused a roof and a nearby wall to collapse, burying several people in the rubble.

“It is with profound sorrow that I received the news of what happened in Santa María Canchesdá, Temascalcingo,” México state native and president of the Senate, Higinio Martínez Miranda, announced on social media.

“I contacted the mayor to reiterate my full support and offer my assistance… My solidarity and most sincere condolences go out to the families who are facing the loss of their loved ones. To those who were injured, I wish a speedy recovery.” Governor Delfina Gómez also communicated her condolences.

Hundreds of people from over 40 nearby communities were preparing to watch the fireworks display as part of the annual religious festival when the explosion occurred.

Civil Protection authorities, firefighters, state police and paramedics were quickly mobilized and continued recovering bodies from the debris and working to remove the collapsed structures until the early hours of Sunday morning.

Two priests were injured but are expected to survive, according to the diocese of the nearby municipality of Atlacomulco. Of the 82 total people treated, 62 have already been discharged, eight remain hospitalized and 11 have been referred to other medical facilities.

The state Attorney General’s Office has initiated an investigation into the cause of the accident.

This is not the first time that the storage of fireworks has turned deadly in Mexico. In 2016, an explosion at a fireworks warehouse in Tultepec, México state, killed 42 people.

With reports from Al Jazeera, CNN, NMás, Sol de México and Quadratín México

World.title: Mexico’s foreign affairs head seeks common ground with China in Beijing
World.content:
Mexico’s Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Monday, marking Velasco’s first official trip to the Asian country and signaling hope for improved political and economic cooperation amid an ongoing trade dispute.

The visit to China takes place under the shadow of trade tensions stemming from the tariffs Mexico applied in January to imports from countries without a free trade agreement, including China.

The package modified duties for 1,463 tariff lines across 17 sectors — with rates of up to 50%. Beijing has questioned the decision, while Mexican authorities maintain that it is not directed at any particular country.

However, a statement issued by the Foreign Affairs Ministry (SRE) downplayed the trade topic, instead describing the meeting as an opportunity to discuss mechanisms for strengthening political, economic, cultural and academic exchanges between Mexico and China.

Velasco highlighted the Mexican government’s readiness to maintain a constructive relationship with China, based on mutual respect, equal sovereignty and non-interference.

The Mexican official proposed strengthening the political consultation mechanism between the two foreign ministries in order to maintain communication and make progress on concrete agreements.

The areas of cooperation highlighted by Mexico include health, education, scholarships, science, technological innovation, the environment, rural development, and cultural exchanges.

The SRE indicated that both parties examined options to expand ties in these areas and leverage existing opportunities for collaboration.

During the meeting, Velasco highlighted coordination between Mexico and China in multilateral forums, including the Group of 20 (G-20) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. He also acknowledged China’s role as host of the upcoming APEC leaders’ summit, scheduled for November in Shenzhen.

Regarding culture, Velasco noted that artistic exchanges offer valuable opportunities to deepen mutual understanding between the two peoples and highlighted the exhibition “On Top of the World Tree: Ancient Civilizations of the Americas” at the Shanghai Museum, which brings together nearly 3,000 archaeological and artistic pieces from Mexico.

Velasco’s trip to China includes the inauguration of the Mexican Consulate in Chongqing, one of the major cities in the western part of the country.

With reports from La Silla Rota

World.title: Trump says Mexico is only good for ‘tamales and tomatoes.’ Trade data says otherwise
World.content:
Listen to this article

U.S. President Donald Trump reasserted on Friday that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs — apart from “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” — and therefore the U.S. could cease trading with its southern neighbor.

However, Trump said he didn’t want to end trade with Mexico — a country that sent more than US $60 billion worth of exports to the U.S. in July alone — “because we get along very well” with President Claudia Sheinbaum.

🇺🇸🇲🇽 Donald Trump aseguró que México no tiene “nada que ofrecer” a Estados Unidos más allá de “tamales y tomates”, al hablar sobre su política comercial desde el Despacho Oval. Pese a la declaración, el presidente estadounidense descartó por ahora interrumpir el comercio con… — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) September 4, 2026

His remarks from the Oval Office came just hours after he threatened in a social media post to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” among which is Mexico, if the U.S. Federal Reserve doesn’t lower its benchmark interest rate, which is currently set at 3.50%-3.75%.

“The Fed Board, with its great new leader [Kevin Warsh], must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!” Trump wrote on Truth Social ahead of the Fed’s next interest rate decision on Sept. 16.

Later on Friday, the U.S. president told reporters that “we could do tremendous good for ourselves by just not trading with countries.”

“We lose with the European Union $200 billion a year. If I didn’t trade with them, we’d lose nothing — just one swipe of the pen,” Trump said.

“We lose with Mexico $195 billion a year,” he said, referring to the United States’ trade deficit with its southern neighbor in 2025.

“… They have nothing that we have to have — I mean hot tamales, tomatoes, a couple of things,” Trump said.

“But basically they have nothing that we need. We have oil, we have everything,” he said, adding that he didn’t want to end trade with Mexico “because we get along very well with the president.”

“We like the president, [we] respect her a lot, but if we didn’t want to trade with Mexico, if we didn’t want to trade with Canada, we’d save from $60 billion to $90 billion a year, just by not trading with Canada,” Trump said.

The U.S. president has previously asserted that the United States doesn’t need anything from Mexico and Canada, its two largest trade partners.

“With Mexico and Canada we have trade deficits. We should have surpluses with them. We don’t need their cars, we don’t need their lumber, we don’t need their energy, we don’t need anything that they have,” Trump said on June 10, the same day that he declared that he wasn’t seeking to renew the USMCA free trade pact.

Three weeks later, the United States announced that it had declined to renew the trilateral agreement in its “current form,” a move that paved the way for annual reviews of the USMCA, which remains in force.

Trump’s assertion that Mexico has “nothing” that the United States needs collides with the reality that the U.S. and Mexican economies are highly integrated and that Mexico ships huge quantities of goods to its northern neighbor on a daily basis. Among Mexico’s exports to the U.S. are vehicles, auto parts, machinery, medical devices, AI servers, alcoholic beverages and fresh food, including tomatoes.

In July alone, Mexico exported goods worth $60.55 billion to the United States, according to the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in the first seven months of 2026 were worth $358.7 billion, an increase of 16% compared to the same period of last year.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: MND Local: Sheinbaum and Lemus tackle water crisis amid power outages in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week, we have some positive developments to report on the water crisis in Guadalajara, while electrical outages across the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA) are becoming more serious.

Sheinbaum discussed Guadalajara’s water crisis with Lemus on a recent visit to Jalisco

On Aug. 26, the governor of Jalisco, Pablo Lemus, met with President Claudia Sheinbaum on her visit to Zapopan, where she voiced her support for badly needed hydraulic infrastructure projects to solve the GMA’s water crisis. Sheinbaum was visiting Jalisco to speak at a graduation ceremony and welcome new officers at the Air Force College in Zapopan.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pablo Lemus Navarro (@pablolemusn)

It was reported that more than 22 billion pesos will be allocated through a combination of federal and state investment, along with additional funds from private sources. Following the meeting, Lemus thanked President Sheinbaum for supporting “the major infrastructure projects that Jalisco needs, especially those that will help us resolve water issues in the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area.”

Governor Lemus further clarified that the federal government plans to invest roughly 5 billion pesos to overhaul the El Zapotillo system to optimize water flow and enable it to operate at a maximum capacity of up to 3,000 liters per second. At the state level, the Jalisco government will invest 7.5 billion pesos in the modernization of the Miravalle Water Treatment Plant No. 1 and construct a Chapala-Guadalajara replacement aqueduct for an estimated cost of 10 billion pesos, leveraging a public-private partnership scheme called CMRO.

Billions in pesos pledged for infrastructure to ease long-standing shortages

For impatient residents anxious to know when the water coming from their taps will improve, Lemus said that gradual improvements will start to become noticeable by this October, with additional gains by the first quarter of 2027.

Last June, in response to mounting public pressure, state leaders announced a plan with more than 30 separate measures aimed at addressing the city’s water crisis. At the time, state leaders said a definitive solution to the current water challenges would require an infrastructure investment of more than 20 billion pesos and a multiyear time horizon.

Some of these projects have yet to be approved by Jalisco’s state congress. Despite continuing questions as to where the funds will come from, Lemus continues to insist that the state will not take on debt, the municipal water system will not be privatized, and water rates will not be increased.

Building a better relationship

Before last week’s meeting, Lemus and Sheinbaum (who do not share the same political party) spent months trading verbal jabs over who was responsible for the city’s water mess. At one point, Lemus claimed the state wasn’t a high priority in Sheinbaum’s federal budget, noting at the time it had received “Zero pesos, zero cents from the federal government … for any infrastructure project in Jalisco. Not for highways, not for water infrastructure, not for anything.”

In response, Sheinbaum defended federal efforts to clean up the Lerma and Santiago rivers to reduce health impacts to those in the GMA who live nearby. She also urged Lemus to take ownership of the problem.

Fortunately for the residents of Guadalajara, their recent in-person meeting appears to have put the relationship on better footing, which will be essential to solving the city’s water woes.

Multiple GMA neighborhoods suffer power outages of up to 20 hours a day

While most of Guadalajara’s news headlines continue to focus on the city’s serious water problems, electricity has quietly crept up the list of concerns residents have about municipal infrastructure.

Long a favorite neighborhood of foreign residents, Providencia is now suffering from many of the same infrastructure issues that have historically plagued less desirable areas. Providencia encompasses Providencia Norte, Providencia Sur and Colomos Providencia. Residents in these areas report that dozens of blocks have been without power for multiple hours a day nearly every day, on top of the previously reported water issues.

The residents’ association president, Piero Vega, stated that when the power goes out, homes can be without electricity for up to 20 hours, causing damage to appliances and spoiling food, which is taking a toll on residents’ quality of life. In a recent interview with Mural newspaper, Vega noted the hardship these outages have put on the neighborhood’s elderly residents:

“Many of them have oxygen concentrators; many have diabetes medications. We have a serious problem with the products or things stored in refrigerators, and several people have already been affected by power surges and dips in their electronic devices.”

Grid strain and aging infrastructure fuel safety concerns

Electrical outages have also heightened feelings of insecurity in the neighborhood, as robberies and assaults across the city have been on the rise in 2026, even as the homicide rate declines.

“(The residents) are already afraid of everything when there is power; now it’s even worse without it, because when the houses lose power, the streets also go dark, and thieves … take whatever they can,” Vega observed.

A similar pattern has been unfolding in recent weeks to the north of Providencia, in north Zapopan. In Ecología Seattle and Colonia Los Maestros, multiple power outages lasting 15-plus hours at a time have left residents frazzled.

For its part, the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) has claimed the recent spate of outages is due to seasonal heavy rains and strong winds. While the storms have certainly done damage, many residents in the affected neighborhoods suspect other factors are in play, namely an overloading of the grid by new businesses, restaurants and power towers, along with inadequate maintenance on transformers and old equipment.

As a resident of this area myself, it is common to hear transformers blow out immediately preceding a power outage, whether there is a storm or not.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Colombia Inflation Accelerates to 6.24 Percent in August
World.content:
COLOMBIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The number Annual inflation reached 6.24 percent in August, up from 6.03 percent in July.

— The monthly rate Prices rose 0.39 percent in the month, against 0.17 percent in July.

— The miss Analysts polled by the central bank had forecast 0.27 percent for the month.

— The catch This is the highest annual reading since July 2024, and it is running above the target range.

— The rate The Banco de la Republica policy rate stands at 12 percent, held on 31 July.

— The split That decision passed four votes to three, with the minority wanting a half-point rise.

Colombia inflation went the wrong way in August, and by more than anyone forecast. The central bank was already split before this print.

A shopping centre in Bogota. Consumer prices rose 0.39 percent in August alone. (Photo: “Andino Mall in Bogota, Colombia ” by momentcaptured1, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Colombia inflation accelerated in August. The annual rate reached 6.24 percent, up from 6.03 percent in July.

The statistics agency DANE published the figure on Monday 7 September. Monthly inflation was 0.39 percent, more than double July’s 0.17 percent.

It missed forecasts in both dimensions. Analysts polled in the central bank’s monthly expectations survey had averaged 0.27 percent for the month.

It is the highest annual reading since July 2024. Colombia’s inflation target range tops out well below this level.

Why the Colombia Inflation Miss Matters

The most pessimistic forecast in the survey reached 0.47 percent. The actual print sat between the average and that outlier, closer to the pessimists.

Corficolombiana had expected 0.32 percent, implying roughly 6.17 percent annually. Even that proved too low.

A single month is not a trend. But this is a second consecutive acceleration in a year that was supposed to see disinflation.

The Central Bank Was Already Divided

The Banco de la Republica held its policy rate at 12 percent on 31 July. That decision passed by four votes to three.

The three dissenters wanted a half-point increase. They lost, and August’s data will strengthen their case at the next meeting.

Twelve percent is a high nominal rate by regional standards. Real rates in Colombia are among the tightest in Latin America.

One caution for readers checking elsewhere. Some data aggregators still show a Colombian policy rate near nine percent, which is out of date.

What It Means on the Ground

At 6.24 percent, prices are rising faster than most Colombian wage settlements. That is a real income squeeze rather than a statistical one.

For foreign residents holding dollars, the peso side of the equation matters more than the index. The exchange rate has been the larger determinant of purchasing power this year.

Colombia’s minimum wage negotiation runs each December and uses inflation as its anchor. A higher print now feeds directly into that talk.

What to Watch

The first marker is the central bank’s next decision. A four-three hold does not survive many upside surprises.

The second is the composition of the increase. Food and regulated prices behave differently from core services.

The third is December. The minimum wage negotiation turns an inflation number into a wage floor, and from there into next year’s prices.

Colombia has run above target for most of two years now. The credibility question is no longer about a single print.

A currency that has been firm through 2026 has done some of the central bank’s work. That support is not guaranteed to continue.

For businesses setting prices, the practical read is that rate cuts are further away than they looked in July.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Colombia’s August inflation?

6.24 percent in the year to August 2026, up from 6.03 percent in July. Monthly inflation was 0.39 percent against 0.17 percent the previous month. DANE published the figures on 7 September.

Did it beat expectations?

It came in above them. Analysts polled in the central bank’s monthly expectations survey had averaged 0.27 percent for the month, and the most pessimistic forecast was 0.47 percent.

What is the central bank doing?

The Banco de la Republica held its policy rate at 12 percent on 31 July 2026, by four votes to three. The three dissenting board members wanted a half-point increase.

Sources: DANE, Banco de la Republica, Bloomberg Linea, Infobae, Finanzas Digital, Rio Times.

World.title: SouthCom Ecuador: A Fifth Boat Sunk, and Nobody Killed
World.content:
ECUADOR · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened US Southern Command sank a vessel in the Eastern Pacific on Monday 7 September 2026.

— The target SouthCom described it as a floating refuelling station supporting drug trafficking, linked to Los Choneros.

— The catch No deaths were reported. Everyone aboard was removed safely and handed to Ecuadorian authorities.

— The sequence It was the fifth such vessel sunk since around 28 August, following four named boats.

— Ecuador’s position Interior Minister John Reimberg says the operations follow investigations conducted with Washington.

— The wider campaign AP reports at least 227 people killed in at least 68 strikes since the campaign began in 2025.

The SouthCom Ecuador operations look different from the strikes that made the campaign notorious. Nobody died, and the crews were handed over.

United States Southern Command sank another vessel in the Eastern Pacific on Monday. The SouthCom Ecuador operations have now claimed five boats in under two weeks.

SouthCom described the target as a floating refuelling station supporting illicit drug trafficking at sea. It linked the vessel to Los Choneros, the Ecuadorian group Washington designates a foreign terrorist organisation.

One detail separates this from the strikes that made the campaign notorious. Nobody was killed.

The Associated Press reports that everyone aboard was removed safely and handed to Ecuadorian authorities. This was a boarding and scuttling rather than a lethal strike.

Why the SouthCom Ecuador Operations Are Different

The wider American campaign against alleged drug vessels has been lethal. AP puts the toll at at least 227 people killed in at least 68 strikes since it began in 2025.

The Intercept counted 227 deaths across more than 65 attacks over the year to 2 September. Fifty of the sixty-eight took place in the Pacific.

The recent Ecuadorian vessels do not fit that pattern. Four earlier boats were named in coverage as the Maria Candelaria, the OM2, Los Tres Hermanos and the Conquista II.

Crews from those operations were transferred rather than killed. Infobae reports that 28 fishermen were released by an Ecuadorian judge after two of them.

Ecuador Is Not Objecting

Interior Minister John Reimberg said on 5 September that the boardings and sinkings were the product of investigations carried out with Washington. That is a description of joint operations rather than a complaint.

Joint missions with the United States began in March 2026. Ecuador has been the most cooperative partner in the region on maritime interdiction.

Authorities did not immediately comment on Monday’s specific sinking. AP noted the silence.

The Part That Is Contested

Relatives of some detained crews dispute the trafficking allegations. They say the men were fishermen.

Amnesty International has sought investigations into the operations. Eight fishermen remain missing from a January incident involving a boat named the Fiorella.

Twenty-six crew members from the Maria Candelaria were transferred to Manta. The judicial outcomes so far have not matched the seriousness of the accusations.

The Numbers Not to Use

A calendar-2026 count of strikes or deaths is not available from any named outlet. Partial data points exist without a running tally.

NPR reported six killed in a Pacific strike on 9 March. The Intercept records a single strike in January that killed two.

The campaign also paused for 63 days from late June to 23 August. Any annual figure built from those fragments would be an estimate rather than a count.

What to Watch

The first marker is whether the non-lethal pattern holds. Five boardings without deaths is a change of method, not necessarily of policy.

The second is the Ecuadorian courts. Judges have already released detainees from two of these operations.

The third is whether the campaign extends beyond refuelling vessels. Those are logistics targets rather than cargo, which suggests a different objective.

Were people killed in the 7 September sinking?

No. The Associated Press reports that everyone aboard was removed safely and handed to Ecuadorian authorities. It was a boarding and scuttling rather than a lethal strike.

How many Ecuadorian vessels have been sunk?

Five since around 28 August 2026. Four earlier boats were named in coverage as the Maria Candelaria, the OM2, Los Tres Hermanos and the Conquista II.

What is the toll of the wider campaign?

The Associated Press reports at least 227 people killed in at least 68 strikes since the campaign began in 2025. A calendar-2026 figure is not available from any named outlet.

World.title: Argentina Malvinas Push Turns Criminal, and Trips Over Itself
World.content:
ARGENTINA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened The presidency announced on 7 September it will file a criminal complaint over Falklands oil work.

— Who is named Three Navitas Petroleum entities, JHI Associates and Eco (Atlantic) Oil & Gas, plus their directors.

— The law Ley 26.659 bars hydrocarbon work on the Argentine continental shelf without national authorisation.

— The catch It was announced, not confirmed as filed. Official statements use the future tense.

— The separate track On 4 September the foreign ministry opened administrative sanctions against 45 people and companies.

— The embarrassment An opposition deputy says a firm sanctioned in 2013 holds 15 percent of a company granted RIGI benefits.

The Argentina Malvinas policy went criminal this week. Within a day it collided with the government’s own investment regime.

Stanley in the Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas. (Photo: “FAL-2016-Stanley, Falkland Islands–Christ Church Cathedral” by Godot13, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

The Argentina Malvinas dispute moved from administrative penalties to criminal law this week. The presidency announced the step on 7 September.

Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno is behind it, with the backing of the treasury solicitor Sebastian Amerio. The venue would be federal court.

Five companies are named. They are Navitas Petroleum Development and Production, Navitas Petroleum Atlantic United, Navitas Petroleum LP, JHI Associates and Eco (Atlantic) Oil and Gas.

One qualification belongs at the top. The government said it will file, and we found no report confirming the complaint had actually been lodged.

The Argentina Malvinas Case Runs on Two Tracks

On 4 September the foreign ministry opened an administrative sanctions process under Decree 868/2026. That decree made the ministry the enforcement authority.

It covers 45 individuals and companies, including operators, shareholders, investors and service providers. They come from the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada, the United States, Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands and South Africa.

Respondents have ten working days to answer. The process can end in disqualification from operating in Argentina for five to twenty years.

The criminal complaint is a separate and additional route. It seeks personal criminal liability rather than commercial exclusion.

The Law Being Used

Ley 26.659 bars exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons on the Argentine continental shelf without national authorisation. It has been on the books since 2013.

Argentina has used it before. Rockhopper Exploration was banned in 2013 and Navitas Petroleum in 2022.

What is new is the criminal framing and the naming of directors alongside companies. That raises the personal stakes for executives.

The Case That Undercuts It

On the same day, the deputy Maximiliano Ferraro of the Coalicion Civica made an allegation that cuts the other way. It concerns Harbour Energy, formerly Premier Oil.

Harbour was sanctioned in 2013 over unauthorised activity in the Malvinas area, with a ban running to 2028. Ferraro says it holds 15 percent of Southern Energy.

Southern Energy’s adhesion to the RIGI investment regime was approved by the economy ministry through Resolution 559/2025. That grants tax, customs and currency benefits to a gas project in Rio Negro.

The precision matters. Benefits went to Southern Energy rather than to Harbour directly, and Harbour’s exposure is as a minority shareholder.

We found no government response to the allegation. Ferraro argues the law reaches shareholders and not only operators.

The Elsztain Intervention

Separately, the businessman Eduardo Elsztain published a statement on 7 September about his own holding. He owns roughly two percent of the Falkland Islands Company.

He said he built the stake around 2005 and 2006, arguing that closer economic ties through an Argentine company could help the sovereignty claim. He said he tried to take majority control in 2017 and that British authorities blocked it.

He also denounced antisemitic attacks and conspiracy theories against him. Quirno defended him publicly, writing that he was the opposite of a traitor.

What to Watch

The first marker is whether the complaint is actually filed, and in which court. An announcement and a filing are not the same thing.

The second is any government answer on the RIGI question. Silence would leave the opposition framing unchallenged.

The third is the administrative process. Forty-five respondents have ten working days, which puts the first decisions in late September.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Argentina filed the criminal complaint?

It announced on 7 September 2026 that it will file one, naming three Navitas Petroleum entities, JHI Associates and Eco (Atlantic) Oil and Gas. Official statements use the future tense and we found no confirmation that it had been lodged.

What is the Harbour Energy allegation?

Deputy Maximiliano Ferraro says Harbour Energy, sanctioned in 2013 over Malvinas activity with a ban to 2028, holds 15 percent of Southern Energy, whose RIGI adhesion was approved by the economy ministry. The benefits went to Southern Energy rather than to Harbour directly.

What did Eduardo Elsztain say?

He confirmed a stake of roughly two percent in the Falkland Islands Company, built around 2005 and 2006, and said he had attempted to take majority control in 2017 before British authorities blocked it. Foreign Minister Quirno defended him publicly.

Sources: La Nacion, Infobae, El Litoral, Perfil, Diagonales, Comercio y Justicia, Rio Times.

World.title: Quaest Poll: Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro Tie at 41 Percent
World.content:
BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — The headline Disapproval of Lula’s government is 50 percent against 43 percent approval, with 7 percent undecided.

— The runoff Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are level at 41 percent each, the first numerical tie of the cycle.

— The first round Lula 36, Flavio Bolsonaro 29, Augusto Cury 8, with Renan Santos and Ronaldo Caiado on 3.

— The catch The Northeast is the number that matters. Disapproval there rose from 29 percent in July to 35 percent.

— The method Fieldwork ran 3 to 6 September, 2,004 voters aged 16 and over, margin of error two points.

— The movement On 2 September the same pollster had approval at 45 and disapproval at 48.

The Quaest poll produced the first numerical tie of the race. It also produced a number from the Northeast that will worry the government more.

The Planalto palace in Brasilia. The government’s approval gap widened to seven points in a week. (Photo: “Palacio do Planalto” by Annemariebr at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

A new Quaest poll has produced the first numerical tie of Brazil’s presidential race. Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are level at 41 percent in a hypothetical runoff.

The same survey puts disapproval of Lula’s government at 50 percent against 43 percent approval. Seven percent did not know or did not answer.

Fieldwork ran from 3 to 6 September with 2,004 voters aged sixteen and over. The margin of error is two points at 95 percent confidence.

It was commissioned by Globo and published on Monday 7 September. It is the first Quaest reading taken after the Supreme Court crisis broke.

What the Quaest Poll Actually Shows

In the first round Lula has 36 percent and Flavio Bolsonaro 29. Augusto Cury is on 8, with Renan Santos and Ronaldo Caiado on 3 each.

Romeu Zema takes 2 percent and Pablo Marcal 1. Blank and null votes run at 8 percent, with undecideds near 10.

In other runoff pairings Lula leads. He is on 41 against Caiado’s 38, and 44 against Zema’s 33.

Only the Flavio Bolsonaro matchup is tied. That is the number that moved the political conversation on Monday.

The Week-on-Week Movement

The previous Quaest release, on 2 September, had approval at 45 and disapproval at 48. The gap has gone from three points to seven.

Both individual movements sit at the edge of the margin of error. The direction is consistent, the size is not statistically dramatic.

That earlier poll also had a different runoff reading, with Lula at 42 against Flavio’s 41. The two surveys are close enough that the tie should be read as a trend rather than a verdict.

Quaest co-founder Felipe Nunes said that at this level Lula’s re-election chance falls below fifty percent.

The Northeast Number

Disapproval in the Northeast rose from 29 percent in July to 35 percent now. That is a six-point move in the government’s strongest region.

The Northeast has delivered Lula’s margin in every presidential election he has won. Erosion there is worth more than a national point.

The corresponding approval figure for the region was not published. We flag the gap rather than filling it.

One Discrepancy Worth Knowing

Most outlets report the runoff as 41 to 41. At least one carried it as 42 to 41, unchanged from the previous week.

CNN Brasil, JOTA and Exame all give the tie, against a single outlet reporting otherwise. The registration number filed with the electoral court also differs between outlets.

Neither discrepancy changes the picture. Both are worth noting because poll numbers travel further than their footnotes.

What to Watch

The first marker is the next Quaest wave. One tie inside the margin of error is not a lead change.

The second is whether the Supreme Court crisis keeps feeding the numbers. This was the first reading taken after it broke.

The third is the Northeast. If that erosion continues into October, the arithmetic of the race changes rather than the mood.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the poll say about the runoff?

Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro are tied at 41 percent each, the first numerical tie of the cycle. Lula leads other tested opponents: 41 to 38 against Ronaldo Caiado and 44 to 33 against Romeu Zema.

How was the poll conducted?

Fieldwork ran from 3 to 6 September 2026 with 2,004 voters aged sixteen and over. The margin of error is two percentage points at 95 percent confidence. It was commissioned by Globo.

What changed in the Northeast?

Disapproval of the government in the Northeast rose from 29 percent in July to 35 percent, a six-point move in the region that has delivered Lula’s winning margin in past elections.

Sources: Genial/Quaest, G1, Metropoles, InfoMoney, Exame, CNN Brasil, JOTA, Rio Times.

Today’s Focus Latin American steel shares told a split story on Friday, September 4, 2026. Brazil’s CSN led the downside, while Gerdau and Mexico’s Ternium held firmer ground. The session was defined by how each name sits relative to cheap Chinese imports. CSN’s 3.17% slide to US$1.22 stood out against Gerdau’s 0.40% gain to US$4.97. Tariff barriers remain the key defence. The trade shield is working for most Latin American mills, and CSN’s fall was a pullback from a three-day rally rather than a break with the tariff-protected group.

Steel — the daily wrap.

01 The session in one read

Latin American steel shares diverged on Friday, September 4, 2026. Brazil’s CSN was the clear laggard, while Gerdau and Mexico’s Ternium showed more resilience.

The New York-traded CSN shares dropped 3.17% to US$1.22, a sharp move for a single session. Gerdau’s US-listed stock rose 0.40% to US$4.97, and Ternium added just 0.03% to US$58.00.

The broader SLX steel-producers ETF gave a modest positive read, up 0.13% to US$110.99. That suggests Friday was not a sector-wide sell-off, but rather a CSN-specific stumble.

Assessment — Tariff protection is not enough HIGH CSN’s 3.17% drop to US$1.22 gave back part of a three-day run that had lifted the shares from US$1.13. Even with Brazil’s 25% tariff and anti-dumping duties shielding domestic flat steel, investors trimmed CSN while rewarding Gerdau’s long-steel exposure to construction demand. Ternium’s flat close at US$58.00 suggests the Mexican story of 50% tariffs and 4% consumption growth is priced in but not yet exciting. The variable to watch is whether Chinese export prices fall further, testing whether the tariff walls hold or simply delay the pain for Brazilian and Mexican mills.

02 The board

The price board showed a quiet session for the sector overall. The SLX ETF’s 0.13% rise to US$110.99 was the calmest signal available to foreign investors tracking steel equities.

Gerdau’s 0.40% gain to US$4.97 kept the Brazilian long-steel producer in positive territory. Ternium’s US$58.00 close, up just 0.03%, reflected a Mexican name treading water.

CSN’s US$1.22 close, down 3.17%, was the outlier. That drop stood in contrast to the other names on the board and hinted at company-specific or flat-steel-specific pressure rather than a regional macro shock.

03 What moved it

Cheap Chinese steel remains the main competitive threat facing Latin American mills. Tariff barriers are the primary defence, and Friday’s moves showed investors weighing how well each producer is shielded.

Brazil has kept a 25% tariff on imports of 23 steel products above quota through June 2027. It also retains five-year anti-dumping duties on Chinese cold-rolled, hot-dip galvanised and pre-painted flat steel.

Mexico’s wall is even higher. Tariffs of 5% to 50% apply to 1,463 tariff lines from countries without a free-trade deal, including steel, a permanent regime that replaced the temporary decrees running since August 2023.

Demand drivers split by product and country. Construction demand supports Brazilian long steel, helping Gerdau. Ternium cites a World Steel forecast of about 4% Mexican steel consumption growth in 2026, while Mexican auto output stays roughly flat near 4 million units.

04 The Latin American read

For foreign investors, the key question is whether tariff walls can keep Chinese steel at bay. Brazil’s protection helps Gerdau, CSN and Usiminas by limiting cheap imports in the local market.

Mexico’s tariff regime supports Ternium by curbing non-FTA imports and backing local supply chains. The 50% ceiling on goods from countries without a free-trade deal is among the region’s most aggressive.

Yet CSN’s drop to US$1.22 on Friday shows that tariffs alone do not guarantee share-price strength. The flat-steel producer faces pressure even with anti-dumping duties in place.

The session’s split between Gerdau’s strength and CSN’s weakness points to a market distinguishing between long-steel demand from construction and flat-steel exposure to global overcapacity.

05 The names to watch

Gerdau’s US-listed shares rose 0.40% to US$4.97, the strongest relative move among the named Latin American producers. Its exposure to Brazilian construction demand gives it a domestic cushion.

CSN’s New York shares fell 3.17% to US$1.22, giving back part of a three-day run that had lifted them from US$1.13, including a 7.69% jump on heavy volume on Thursday.

Ternium closed at US$58.00, barely changed. The roughly 4% expected Mexican consumption growth in 2026 offers a steady backdrop, but with auto output flat the market wanted no more Friday.

Usiminas figures were not available for the Friday session, but the company remains protected by Brazil’s same 25% tariff and anti-dumping regime that shields Gerdau and CSN.

06 The outlook

The near-term outlook hinges on whether Chinese export prices stay low enough to test the tariff walls. If they do, Latin American mills may need to lean harder on domestic demand.

Brazilian construction and Mexican steel consumption remain the clearest demand supports. Ternium’s 6% auto output growth call for 2026 applies to Brazil, not Mexico, where production is flat.

For Brazil, the 25% tariff through June 2027 gives mills a long runway. But CSN’s Friday slide to US$1.22 is a reminder that investors want evidence the protection translates into earnings, not just survival.

The SLX ETF’s 0.13% rise to US$110.99 suggests no regional panic yet. The next test is whether Gerdau’s long-steel strength and Ternium’s stability can offset any further weakness in flat steel.

07 What to watch

Chinese export prices: Any further fall in Chinese steel prices would test whether Brazil’s 25% tariff and Mexico’s 50% tariff genuinely hold back imports or merely delay the pressure.

Any further fall in Chinese steel prices would test whether Brazil’s 25% tariff and Mexico’s 50% tariff genuinely hold back imports or merely delay the pressure. CSN earnings signals: After Friday’s 3.17% drop to US$1.22, any company-specific news on costs, volumes or flat-steel pricing could drive the next leg for Brazil’s most volatile steel share.

After Friday’s 3.17% drop to US$1.22, any company-specific news on costs, volumes or flat-steel pricing could drive the next leg for Brazil’s most volatile steel share. Mexican auto output: Ternium sees Mexican auto production flat near 4 million units in 2026, with its 6% growth call applying to Brazil. Monthly Mexican auto data will test that view.

Ternium sees Mexican auto production flat near 4 million units in 2026, with its 6% growth call applying to Brazil. Monthly Mexican auto data will test that view. Brazilian construction activity: Long-steel demand from construction underpins Gerdau’s resilience. Cement and construction employment data offer early reads on whether that support is holding.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did CSN fall while Gerdau rose?

CSN’s New York shares dropped 3.17% to US$1.22, while Gerdau rose 0.40% to US$4.97. The split reflects stronger construction demand for Gerdau’s long steel versus pressure on CSN’s flat-steel exposure.

What is protecting Latin American steel from Chinese imports?

Brazil has a 25% tariff on 23 steel products above quota through June 2027 plus anti-dumping duties on Chinese cold-rolled, galvanised and pre-painted flat steel. Mexico applies tariffs of 5% to 50% on 1,463 tariff lines from countries without free-trade deals.

What does the SLX ETF tell us about Friday’s session?

The SLX steel-producers ETF rose 0.13% to US$110.99. The small gain suggests the sector was broadly steady, with CSN’s 3.17% drop being a company-specific move rather than a regional sell-off.

What are the main demand drivers for Latin American steel?

In Brazil, construction demand supports long-steel producers like Gerdau. In Mexico, Ternium expects steel consumption to grow about 4% in 2026, with automotive output up around 6%.

03 What moved it

The dominant force is China’s steel arithmetic. China buys about 75% of global seaborne iron ore, so its monthly steel production figures effectively set the global benchmark. July’s 3.6% year-on-year decline tells traders that mills are not converting ore into finished steel at last year’s pace.

Yet there is a floor. Chinese mills have been restocking ore, with Dalian iron ore futures closing up 1.04% at 727 yuan per tonne, and port-side spot prices firming by about 1 yuan per tonne. Imported ore prices into China edged up in the week of August 31 to September 4, though mills bought only as needed, with some scheduling maintenance on tight coke supply.

04 The Latin American read

For Brazil, the iron ore market is a macro indicator as much as a commodity story. Vale is the world’s second-largest exporter and the anchor of the B3 exchange, so when its New York shares slip on China steel jitters, Brazilian investors read it as a warning about export earnings and fiscal revenue.

CSN Mineração’s sharper decline on Friday, at -1.05%, reflects its status as a leveraged, single-commodity equity. Rio Tinto’s modest gain shows that diversified miners are less exposed to the day-to-day Chinese steel equation, even though iron ore is their largest profit centre.

05 The names to watch

Vale is the headline name. Its New York listing remains the most liquid vehicle for global investors who want iron ore exposure without trading Dalian futures.

CSN Mineração is the domestic purity play. In reais, it is the cleanest Brazilian listed exposure to seaborne iron ore demand. Rio Tinto, while Australian-listed, still sets the tone for sector valuations and is watched closely by Brazilian fund managers.

06 The outlook

The range is likely to hold in the short term. Cost-driven support from freight and raw materials keeps a floor under prices, while Chinese steel output declines cap the upside near US$100. A genuine construction recovery in China would be needed to break the range.

07 What to watch

Chinese port stockpiles: Confirmation that mill restocking is replacing cargoes rather than building a demand surge would keep prices pinned below US$100.

Confirmation that mill restocking is replacing cargoes rather than building a demand surge would keep prices pinned below US$100. September peak season steel orders: China’s traditional Golden September construction push is the next chance for a demand-led breakout.

China’s traditional Golden September construction push is the next chance for a demand-led breakout. Vale dividend commentary: Any signal from Vale management on cash returns would signal confidence in the ore price holding near current levels.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is China so important for iron ore?

China buys about 75% of global seaborne iron ore, so its monthly steel output and mill restocking behaviour effectively set the international benchmark.

How can investors track iron ore without a spot feed?

Mining shares act as proxies. Vale’s New York listing, CSN Mineração in São Paulo, and Rio Tinto all move with the ore price, though each has company-specific factors.

Why did Vale fall while Rio Tinto rose on the same day?

Brazilian miners are viewed as more leveraged to a weak Chinese steel cycle, while Rio Tinto’s diversified revenue streams cushioned the impact on Friday, September 4, 2026.

What is the near-term price range for iron ore?

The benchmark has traded between roughly US$93 and US$100 per tonne since June, and Friday’s close near US$99.57 sits at the upper edge of that band.

03 What moved it

Concentrate availability remains constrained across major producing regions, keeping the physical zinc market tight.

On the demand side, galvanised steel orders from construction and automotive buyers have stayed firm, giving smelters little reason to discount.

A separate force pressured gold and, by extension, Buenaventura: robust US jobs figures raised expectations that the Federal Reserve could keep rates higher for longer.

04 The Latin American read

Peru supplies about 11% of global zinc concentrate, Mexico around 5–6% and Bolivia about 4%, making the region central to the metal’s supply chain.

Nexa Resources is the purest Latin American zinc proxy because its Peruvian and Brazilian smelters convert regional concentrates into refined metal and galvanising alloys.

Buenaventura offers zinc exposure inside a wider Peruvian mining portfolio, which is why gold’s slide on Friday overshadowed zinc’s gain for that stock.

05 The names to watch

Nexa Resources: its integrated model means the share price often follows zinc plus the health of Brazilian galvanised-steel demand; Friday’s small decline suggests the equity market has not fully priced zinc’s strength.

Buenaventura: with heavier precious-metals exposure, the company responds more to US rate expectations and gold moves than to industrial zinc fundamentals alone.

06 The outlook

The near-term case for zinc rests on whether tight concentrate supply persists while construction and automotive buyers keep ordering galvanised steel.

If gold stabilises, Buenaventura could recover some of Friday’s 2.50% slide, while Nexa may finally track the metal’s gain more closely.

07 What to watch

US rate expectations: Strong payrolls lifted rate-hike bets, hitting gold and diversified miners like Buenaventura; any repricing will ripple through LatAm mining equities.

Strong payrolls lifted rate-hike bets, hitting gold and diversified miners like Buenaventura; any repricing will ripple through LatAm mining equities. Galvanised steel orders: Construction, infrastructure and automotive demand for zinc-coated steel is the demand anchor; signs of slowing orders would weaken the zinc case.

Construction, infrastructure and automotive demand for zinc-coated steel is the demand anchor; signs of slowing orders would weaken the zinc case. Peruvian and Mexican concentrate supply: Any disruption or export change from Peru, Mexico or Bolivia could deepen the tightness supporting zinc prices.

Any disruption or export change from Peru, Mexico or Bolivia could deepen the tightness supporting zinc prices. Nexa smelter margins: As an integrated miner-smelter, Nexa’s profitability reflects both zinc prices and input costs; watch whether the equity catches up with the metal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did zinc rise on Friday?

Tight supply and steady demand for galvanised steel, used in construction, infrastructure and automotive manufacturing, pushed zinc higher; one benchmark settled at US$3,929.55 per metric ton, up 0.97%.

Why did Buenaventura fall while zinc gained?

Buenaventura has heavier gold exposure, and strong US payrolls data boosted rate-hike expectations, sending gold lower and pulling the stock down 2.50% to US$33.90.

Which Latin American countries matter for zinc?

Peru supplies about 11% of global zinc concentrate, Mexico around 5–6% and Bolivia about 4%.

What is Nexa Resources’ role?

Nexa is an integrated miner-smelter focused on Peru and Brazil, turning concentrates into refined metal and galvanising alloys, making it a key zinc proxy for LatAm investors.

World.title: Man charged after neighbour spots stolen washing machine at repair shop; says he sold it for $25
World.content:
Man charged after neighbour spots stolen washing machine at repair shop; says he sold it for $25

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man accused of stealing his neighbour’s $700 washing machine has pleaded not guilty after telling the court that the owner had actually given him the old machine because it was not working and he later sold it for just $25.

Richmond Isaac Roberts, 51, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a charge of theft involving a blue-and-white Acros washing machine belonging to a 63-year-old neighbor.

Roberts initially attempted to plead guilty with an explanation, but after hearing the prosecution’s allegations, he disagreed.

“No, that dah nuh how it happened,” Roberts told the court.

He claimed the man had given him the washing machine because it was no longer working and that he subsequently sold it to another man for $25 for parts.

Based on that explanation, the Magistrate entered an equivocal plea of not guilty on Roberts’ behalf and offered him bail of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

Roberts, however, was unable to immediately secure his release because court records showed he still had outstanding fines from previous matters, including a 2023 controlled-drug possession case, another theft matter and a 2015 bicycle offence for riding without a bell.

The court informed Roberts that the outstanding fines had to be settled before he could process bail. When he was unable to pay them, warrants were prepared for him to serve the default prison terms, leaving him behind bars at the Belize Central Prison.

In the current theft case, Bodden told police that on August 22 he left the washing machine beside the back step of his home before going to work. When he returned that evening, the machine was gone.

The man later spotted what he believed was his washing machine at a business that repairs refrigerators and appliances. He said the person there told him the machine had been obtained from Roberts.

The maintains that he never gave Roberts permission to take or sell the washing machine and told police it had been in working condition.

Roberts is now expected to challenge the theft allegation in court.

World.title: Two men challenge loitering charge after police bust them on Freetown Road; Man says he was working undercover security
World.content:
Two men challenge loitering charge after police bust them on Freetown Road; Man says he was working undercover security

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two Belize City men have pleaded not guilty to loitering after police accused them of remaining on Freetown Road despite being instructed to move along.

Roman Riverol, a security guard, and BTL software specialist Eli Elezor Obando appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, where they were jointly charged with loitering in a public place.

Police allege the men were on Freetown Road and failed to move quietly along when instructed to do so by separate police officers.

Both men challenged the allegation.

Riverol told the court he was not simply hanging around the area but was working undercover security for a Chinese businessman whose store had reportedly been affected by increased criminal activity.

He said he was deliberately not wearing a security uniform so he would not easily be identified as the person guarding the establishment. Riverol claimed he explained the situation to police, but officers did not accept his explanation.

Obando, meanwhile, told the court he had only been speaking with Riverol when police arrived. He said he initially left the area but later returned and was detained when police came back and found him there again.

Both men pleaded not guilty and were granted self-bail of $100 each.

They are due back in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on October 5, 2026.

The Magistrate reportedly warned both men of the consequences of failing to return to court, as self-bail is less commonly granted than bail secured through a surety.

World.title: Corozal businessman slapped with $94,015 in fines after massive illegal seafood bust
World.content:
Corozal businessman slapped with $94,015 in fines after massive illegal seafood bust

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Corozal businessman has been slapped with more than $94,000 in fines after pleading guilty to illegally importing hundreds of pounds of jumbo shrimp and tilapia fillets along with octopus into Belize.

Leslie Lizarraga, 34, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court alongside 51-year-old David Romano Arana of Consejo Village following a Fisheries Department operation on September 3.

Lizarraga pleaded guilty to three counts of illegal importation and was fined a total of $94,015, while Arana pleaded not guilty and the prosecution subsequently withdrew all three charges against him.

The case arose after Fisheries officers, assisted by police, intercepted a silver GMC Sierra pickup along the Hattieville-Boom Road following a brief pursuit.

Authorities say the vehicle initially turned around and sped away from officers before eventually losing control and ending up in a ditch.

A search reportedly uncovered seven boxes containing 335 pounds of jumbo shrimp, another 58 boxes containing 1,566 tilapia fillets weighing approximately 290 pounds, and a bag containing 14 pieces of octopus.

The Fisheries Department had previously confirmed the seizure, saying the seafood was suspected of having been illegally imported and that both the vehicle and products were taken into its custody. The department warned that unauthorized seafood imports can present food safety and phytosanitary risks and undermine legitimate businesses that comply with Belize’s import requirements.

After seeking a sentencing indication from the court, Lizarraga’s attorney, David McKoy, entered guilty pleas on his client’s behalf. The court took into account that Lizarraga was a first-time offender and had saved judicial time by pleading guilty, opting for fines rather than imprisonment.

Lizarraga was fined $5,000 for illegally importing the shrimp, another $5,000 for the tilapia and $5,000 for the octopus, along with court costs.

The heaviest penalty came from the 1,566 tilapia fillets, for which an additional fine of $50 per piece amounted to $78,300. The 14 pieces of octopus attracted a further $700 penalty.

The prosecution also applied for the forfeiture of the GMC Sierra used to transport the seafood. McKoy objected, telling the court that the pickup does not belong to Lizarraga and arguing that its owner must be given an opportunity to oppose its forfeiture.

The Magistrate agreed to adjourn the forfeiture application until the vehicle’s owner can be notified and heard. The pickup remains in Fisheries Department custody.

Fisheries officials have since said their intelligence indicates illegally imported seafood has been moving into Belize regularly and supplying businesses including resorts and supermarkets. The department says investigators are also tracing potential buyers of the illegal products.

World.title: Joseph Vaccaro committed to stand trial for Gaston Barrow murder after challenging witness evidence
World.content:
Joseph Vaccaro committed to stand trial for Gaston Barrow murder after challenging witness evidence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize City taxi operator Joseph Gabourel Vaccaro has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for the 2025 murder of Gaston Barrow, despite telling the Chief Magistrate that three prosecution witnesses did not identify him as the shooter.

Vaccaro, 31, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday for the conclusion of his preliminary inquiry, nearly a year after he was remanded on the murder charge.

During the hearing, the prosecution submitted more than 70 statements and other documentary evidence, including photographs, DVDs, chain-of-custody forms, warrants and a wanted poster.

Vaccaro challenged portions of the prosecution’s evidence, telling the court that three witnesses whose statements were included in the disclosure did not name him as the person who fired the fatal shots. He questioned why he was being prosecuted for murder if those witnesses had not identified him as the shooter.

The Chief Magistrate explained that the Magistrate’s Court was not conducting the murder trial and that Vaccaro would have the opportunity to challenge the prosecution’s evidence when the matter is heard before the High Court.

The matter ended in a paper committal, and Vaccaro was ordered to stand trial during the High Court session beginning October 7, 2026.

Vaccaro was originally arraigned on October 6, 2025 and remanded to the Belize Central Prison. In July, he received 154 pages of disclosure along with five CDs and photographs forming part of the prosecution’s case.

The charge stems from the September 28, 2025 shooting at the Old Belize compound along the George Price Highway.

Police said Barrow was travelling in the front passenger seat of a vehicle driven by Hance Card, with two women in the rear, when a gunman allegedly approached from the vicinity of a taxi and opened fire.

Barrow was fatally wounded, while Card was also shot but survived. Police later said Card declined to provide investigators with a statement.

Investigators reviewed surveillance footage from the Old Belize compound, which police said eventually led them to Vaccaro. Public reporting at the time said police believed the attack was gang-related and possibly connected to retaliatory violence.

Vaccaro remains on remand awaiting his High Court trial.

World.title: Nearly 400 police officers, undercover cops and drones deployed for Carnival; about 12 detained
World.content:
Nearly 400 police officers, undercover cops and drones deployed for Carnival; about 12 detained

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly 400 police officers were deployed for Saturday’s Belize City Carnival Road March as authorities used uniformed officers, undercover personnel, drones and Coast Guard support to police the massive event.

ASP Stacy Smith said major events such as Carnival require advance operational planning because of the large crowds and the possibility that individuals may use those gatherings to target rivals.

Just under 400 officers were strategically deployed, including uniformed personnel, members of specialized operational units and undercover Special Branch officers.

Smith joked that some undercover personnel may even have been dressed in Carnival costumes.

Police also deployed drones along the route, which Smith said allowed officers to identify and intervene in disturbances before they escalated.

About 12 people were detained in connection with various disturbances, but police say the event generally concluded without any major security incident.

The Belize Coast Guard also assisted police because portions of the Carnival activity took place near the seafront.

The 2026 Road March began at Lord Rhaburn Plaza at Memorial Park and ended at the Marion Jones Sporting Complex.

Smith thanked the officers who worked the event as well as members of the public who cooperated with authorities.

World.title: Police say no extra officers deployed to Cayo despite drug tensions; technology and intelligence driving operations
World.content:
Police say no extra officers deployed to Cayo despite drug tensions; technology and intelligence driving operations

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department says it has not deployed additional officers to Western Belize in response to recent drug-related violence, arguing that sustained operations and increased use of technology are already underway in the area.

ASP Stacy Smith said police have been concentrating operational resources in Cayo for some time and believe recent successes are partly the result of investment in technology and intelligence-led policing.

Police have previously linked violence in San Ignacio and Santa Elena to competition over the illegal drug trade and have said cocaine and crack cocaine are increasingly appearing among younger users and street-level dealers.

Last week, police reported that operations in Cayo had removed more than 35,000 grams of cannabis, 2,468 grams of cocaine, 1,253 grams of crack cocaine and 1,043 grams of methamphetamine from the streets. Police said those operations resulted in dozens of people being charged.

Smith said authorities remain interested in targeting major suppliers but stressed that street-level dealers are also part of the trafficking network.

She argued that disrupting retail sellers reduces the local market and, in turn, the incentive for larger quantities of drugs to enter the country.

Smith also noted that drugs do not only enter Belize by illicit aircraft, pointing to Belize’s land borders with Guatemala and Mexico. Police continue to use the Mobile Interdiction Unit in northern and western Belize to target suspected trafficking routes.

Two of five new pickup trucks recently provided to the Police Department have also been assigned to the Cayo District.

World.title: Police identify vehicle type in Brianna Myvett murder but still have no motive or suspects
World.content:
Police identify vehicle type in Brianna Myvett murder but still have no motive or suspects

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say surveillance footage has helped investigators identify the make and model of a vehicle believed to have been involved in the murder of 20-year-old Brianna Myvett, but the vehicle did not carry licence plates and no motive has yet been established.

Myvett was shot and killed on Freetown Road on the night of August 31 while she was inside a Ford Escape with 24-year-old Alexander Carr, who was also shot and injured. Public reports described Myvett as a recent Wesley Junior College graduate, volleyball player and employee of the Belize Central Prison.

ASP Stacy Smith said investigators have retrieved several pieces of video footage and have been tracing the vehicle of interest in an effort to determine who entered or occupied it.

Two persons of interest were detained based on statements investigators received concerning a possible motive, but Smith said that line of investigation has so far yielded nothing concrete.

Police say neither Myvett nor Carr was known to police, and investigators have not determined whether Myvett, Carr or both were the intended targets.

“No motive has been established,” Smith said, adding that police are continuing to commit resources to the investigation.

Myvett was laid to rest on September 2.

World.title: NIP issued to pickup driver after Red Bank motorcycle crash kills 59-year-old man
World.content:
NIP issued to pickup driver after Red Bank motorcycle crash kills 59-year-old man

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have issued a Notice of Intended Prosecution to a female pickup driver following a fatal traffic accident in Red Bank Village that claimed the life of 59-year-old Nerry Campbell.

The collision occurred at about 10:45 a.m. on Saturday, September 5.

Police say Campbell was travelling on a motorcycle and was turning onto the Red Bank Road when a collision occurred with a pickup truck.

Campbell sustained serious injuries and was taken for medical treatment but succumbed shortly after 1:00 p.m.

Public reporting identified Campbell as a Guatemalan labourer living in Red Bank Village and identified the pickup as a Toyota Tundra driven by 30-year-old Deidra Jackson of Silk Grass. The collision reportedly occurred at the junction of Red Bank Road and the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway.

Police have since issued Jackson a Notice of Intended Prosecution as the investigation continues.

World.title: Rough start
World.content:
Grade two students at Holland Primary School seated during their outdoor class under a bamboo structure on Monday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

THE education ministry on Monday reported a generally smooth reopening of schools across the island for the start of the 2026/27 academic year but principals, mostly in hurricane-ravaged western Jamaica, highlighted a raft of difficulties.

Among the complaints were incomplete repairs as well as classes held in heat-trapping tents that turn into sweltering ovens under the tropical sun.

“Based on preliminary data received from all seven educational regions covering approximately 1,000 schools, only three schools did not open today, meaning that approximately 99.7 per cent of the schools captured in the data were able to open on the first day of the new school year,” the ministry said in a news release.

While the ministry said late furniture delivery was among the most frequently reported challenges on Monday, Jamaica Observer journalists received first-hand reports of the rough start to the academic year in the sections of the island that suffered the brunt of Hurricane Melissa’s fury last October.
