World.title: Two traditions, one future
World.content:
Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon (centre), along with former Hydel High Principal Dr Walton Small (right), as well as teachers and students of the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School, release balloons in celebration of the official opening of the merged institution on the first day of the new academic year, Monday. (Photos: Garfield Robinson)

EDUCATION Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon officially unveiled the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School Monday, declaring that the unification wasn’t about erasing either school’s identity, but rather combining the best of their traditions to create a single learning environment better equipped to serve students and make fuller use of existing resources.

“I love to see the new motto: ‘On the wings of excellence, endeavour to soar.’ And that’s a merger of the two mottos of the two schools. So even starting with the name, we merged the two schools. With the motto, we have merged the two schools and their ethos,” Morris Dixon said Monday while delivering greetings at the name unveiling ceremony at the school’s campus in Portmore, St Catherine.

As she helped to officiate both the historic first day of the school and the start of the 2026-2027 academic year, Morris Dixon explained that Cumberland High School had a capacity for 1,200 students but had only been operating with just over 300 students when she visited about a year ago. She added that the infrastructural challenges at Hydel High, coupled with Cumberland’s available space, made the merger a practical option.

“One of the things we had thought about was potentially moving the children in little groups to different schools, putting them all around St Catherine. But I think this is the best option. I think this was quite strategic in nature, and that’s how we’re going to continue to do this restructuring of education in Jamaica — be strategic — because now that we have one institution instead of two, it means we can direct more resources to one… that is our plan,” said Morris Dixon.

Already, significant investment is being made in the new school. The minister announced that $70 million is being spent to improve its electrical system while work is also being done on the home economics laboratory.

She added that the school’s parking lot will be expanded to accommodate the increased number of staff, while upgrades to the sporting facilities are also planned.

“So there’s a lot that will happen here, and Principal [Carlon Pitt] can ask for everything he wants. Principal, we’ve already granted your first wish, which was more students, but your success, the success of this merged institution, is really important to the Ministry of Education. We are very much committed to it. We’re committed to seeing the traditions work together and to achieve so much more,” she said.

Morris Dixon acknowledged, however, that bringing together two established school communities would not be without challenges but promised that her ministry would be strongly supporting the school’s leadership to smoothly navigate any trials that may arise.

“There are understandable emotions when schools merge. I know there is sadness from some who are, you know, leaving a space that they’re used to. There are those who are seeing all these new children come and these new teachers come. There are a lot of emotions involved in this, and so I want to acknowledge those emotions. Change is never easy; it’s always hard. And us adults, we sometimes have a harder time than the children with change,” she said.

“So teachers, I know this is an emotional period for you… I know that you’re great, I know you’re wonderful, I have no doubt that we have the best teachers in this world in Jamaica, so I know we can get through this. The ministry is here to support, in whatever way we can, to the students who may be coming to this new environment. You have a good principal, you have a good team here; you’re going to be okay,” Morris Dixon assured.

Principal Pitt told the Jamaica Observer that as the former head of Cumberland High he was highly receptive to the idea of a school merger.

Welcoming this new chapter in his career, Pitt emphasised that his vision focuses heavily on academics while prioritising students’ holistic development.

Highlighting Cumberland’s status as a leading Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institution in St Catherine, alongside Hydel’s strong culture of sports and academics, the principal noted that the merger offers the perfect opportunity to fulfill his goals.

“Whatever we do in school, it must result in student outcome, the students must be the biggest beneficiary of whatever we do. And so the primary focus is on adding value, value-added education, adding value to the students with respect to their starting point and where they exit. So far we have added more sciences to the curriculum. We have now the traditional sixth form… we have a sports programme to roll out that we are excited about, and so with all of these things it is about the holistic development of the child,” Pitt said.

World.title: Jahshii to embark on islandwide tour; aims to reconnect with his fans
World.content:
JAHSHII...the fanbase a grow and mi just waa continue grow with the fans.

IN a move to reconnect with his fan base, dancehall artiste Jahshii is set to embark on a multi-stop tour across the island in November.

The Born Fighter artiste says the tour will feature performances backed by Tower Band and he’s also bringing along some special guests at each stop.

“The fanbase a grow and mi just waa continue grow with the fans,” he told the Jamaica Observer recently.

“The islandwide tour will kick off in November, and you can expect high-energy performances, special guests at each stop. We’ll be going across the island, and it will be a live music experience like no other,” Jahshii assured.

He added, “We really want to get the fans dem closer, like in an up close and personal vibe, so we have been doing rehearsals while locking in the venues.”

Jahshii, who is best known for songs like Pieces featuring Masicka, Cream of the Crop and

Born Fighter, revealed that it wasn’t an easy journey to get to where he is today.

“Mi a come from nobody naw do nuttin fi mi; a fight wi fight to get up deh. But it is very satisfying to help other emerging talent and see how they develop and make it in the music,” he shared.

Father to a young son, Jahshii says fatherhood has changed his perspective on life.

“It has changed my outlook on life; family comes first and my priorities come first. That’s what we get from being a father,” he shared.

Jahshii’s latest single Auto Pilot, produced by Troublemekka, was released two months ago. He says new music is on the way.

“We definitely have some new music coming especially for the ladies, because we not leaving them out,” he said.

World.title: CPL Hall of Fame award named in honour of Sir Garfield Sobers
World.content:
Garfield Sobers

BRIDGETOWN, Barbados (CMC) — The Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL) has announced that the trophy presented to each year’s player inducted into its hall of fame will be officially named the Sir Garry Sobers Award, in tribute to the man universally recognised as the greatest all-rounder West Indies cricket has ever produced.

The naming follows the recent launch of the CPL Hall of Fame which will honour two inductees annually, one player and one off-field contributor.

Dwayne Bravo and Ian Bishop were confirmed as the inaugural class, and the CPL has now secured the Sobers family’s blessing to attach Sir Garry’s name to the award, marking one of the most significant moments in the league’s history.

As one of the finest cricketers the game has ever seen and a defining figure of West Indies cricket, Sir Garry’s name gives prestige to the Hall of Fame recognition.

The Sir Garry Sobers Award will be presented for the first time at the CPL Hall of Fame Gala Dinner on September 15, 2026 at the Hilton Barbados.

The evening is being held in support of the Sir Clive Lloyd Healthcare Foundation’s prostate cancer awareness, testing, and early detection work across the Caribbean.

With the trophy carrying Sir Garry’s name the gala brings together two of West Indies cricket’s most respected figures for a single showpiece night in support of the region.

Pete Russell, CEO of CPL, said “Sir Garry Sobers was, without question, the greatest all-rounder the game has ever seen, and having his name on this award means a great deal to everyone at CPL. We are enormously grateful to the Sobers family for trusting us with his name and his legacy. It gives this trophy, and this hall of fame, a weight our players will carry with real pride. To present it for the first time at a gala dinner in support of Sir Clive Lloyd’s Healthcare Foundation makes 15 September an even more prestigious night for West Indies cricket.”

World.title: ‘SPOILT KIDS’
World.content:
RICKETTS... FIFA has supported us and I’ll be very ungrateful not to show some regard, and show some respect, and say thanks to a man that has supported Caribbean football (Photo: Observer file)

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts has come to the defence of FIFA President Gianni Infantino, saying he doesn’t deserve the treatment he’s receiving from stakeholders. Ricketts also labeled UEFA “spoilt kids” for its stance against the FIFA boss.

On Sunday, football’s world governing body confirmed that Infantino intends to stand again in next year’s elections for a fourth term, despite mounting criticism over recent months. Infantino proposed selling stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup, to private investors and offered FIFA’s 211 member associations US$40 million ($6.3 billion) each if they backed the plan.

However, the 56-year-old Swiss ultimately scrapped it following widespread opposition, including European football governing body, UEFA, who voted to boycott all World Cups if it went ahead. Concacaf, who governs North America and the Caribbean, also rejected the proposal.

Infantino, though, attempted to smooth things over with several Concacaf members after attending a Caribbean Football Union (CFU) Presidents’ Meeting and the CFU Under-14 series in the Dominican Republic last month, where Jamaica reached the final. Concacaf President and FIFA Vice-President Victor Montagliani had written to Infantino, asking him not to attend.

Reports from England stated many of the Concacaf members were “infuriated” by Infantino’s behaviour.

However, while not providing the details of the meeting, Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that the FIFA boss was treated with the utmost respect.

“That’s how reporting and that’s how media is — some people try to sensationalise certain events to suit their own agenda — but that’s the farthest thing from the truth,” he said. “I think Infantino was warmly, warmly welcomed; he was embraced by almost every single CFU member.”

Ricketts, who has served as JFF boss for nearly a decade, admits that Infantino should have approached the proposal differently, although he had no issue with its premise.

“Infantino might have made a mistake, but the intentions were to help Caribbean countries or help smaller countries. Can you imagine Jamaica getting 40 million US dollars to invest in football? Can you imagine the difference that would make in four or five years?” said Ricketts.

“In my very first utterance, I did say that the gesture would suit me but we thought [there] was [a] lack of communication, lack of discussions, it seemed non-transparent. But I don’t think Infantino meant to hurt anybody or would have tried to make himself a beneficiary of the gesture.”

The fallout from the proposal continues Belgium Football Association, on Monday, the latest to oppose Infantino’s re-election. At least 11 other FIFA member associations have publicly withdrawn their support including major European football nations such as England, Germany, Norway and the Netherlands.

UEFA has led calls for Infantino to step down and is preparing legal action against him, accusing the FIFA president of “criminal mismanagement” over the proposal. FIFA, in return, has accused the Euopean governing body of a “smear campaign against it and its leadership”.

Ricketts believes UEFA are being unreasonable and has no intention of following its stance.

“People will have different views and different opinions for different reasons. But I am not supporting UEFA because I think that they always want to be in opposition and always want to oppose. It doesn’t matter who is president, they are going to have issues. It doesn’t matter how well the president does, they are going to have issues and I think that UEFA is behaving like a set of spoilt kids,” he said.

“From a commercial standpoint, they really don’t need FIFA. They probably have as much money as FIFA does so they can do and say anything. I can’t do that because I need support and FIFA has supported us and I’ll be very ungrateful not to show some regard and show some respect and say thanks to a man that has supported Caribbean football.”

More than 20 FIFA member associations, including 2026 World Cup finalists Argentina, World Cup co-host Mexico and African champions Morocco, have publicly expressed support for Infantino .

Ricketts praised Infantino’s performance but says the decision on Jamaica’s support for rests with the JFF board.

“This is something I probably don’t even have the right to speak on because it’s a decision that the board will have to make. But personally, I think Infantino has done a good job,” he said.

The nominations for FIFA presidential candidates must be submitted by November 18. Infantino is currently the only candidate, though Concacaf President Victor Montagliani is being touted as a potential challenger.

World.title: Wedding, Fashion & Interior Design
World.content:
Inspired by the beautifully curated spaces they encounter worldwide, couples are choosing venues like boutique hotels to evoke those same unforgettable feelings on their wedding day. -

New York Fashion Week is upon us, and it got me thinking about how much fashion and interior design influence the wedding industry. We often look at weddings as their own creative world, but they are actually incredibly responsive to what is happening around us. What we wear, how we decorate our homes, the restaurants and hotels we are drawn to, even the way luxury brands present themselves all eventually find their way into weddings.

And increasingly, I think the most interesting weddings are borrowing ideas rather than following wedding trends.

The Runway Has Always Found Its Way to the Aisle

Fashion is perhaps the most obvious influence. What happens on the runways of New York, Paris, Milan and London eventually changes what brides and grooms want to wear, but its influence goes much further than the dress.

The current fashion conversation is full of personality: sculptural silhouettes, interesting textures, dramatic draping, bows, metallics, sheer fabrics, unexpected colour and a renewed appreciation for beautiful tailoring. Those ideas translate remarkably well into weddings.

A beautifully draped fashion silhouette can inspire the treatment of a tent. A couture floral appliqué can become the starting point for an invitation, cake or tablescape. A runway colour combination can suddenly make traditional wedding palettes feel completely different.

Even bridal fashion itself has become less formulaic. Brides are changing looks throughout the celebration, experimenting with shorter dresses, statement accessories, dramatic veils and fashion-forward reception looks. Grooms, too, are embracing more colour, texture and individuality.

Weddings Are Beginning to Look More Like Beautiful Interiors

Interior design is having an even greater influence on weddings.

For years, wedding décor was largely about flowers, linens and centrepieces. Couples are paying attention to chairs, lamps, rugs, bars, shelving, interesting furniture, textured fabrics and architectural details. The lounge is no longer simply somewhere to put a sofa; it can feel like the living room of an incredibly stylish home. Bars are becoming statement pieces. Dinner spaces are layered with lighting and objects in much the same way an interior designer would style a room.

I particularly love the move towards residential-style lighting. Table lamps, shaded pendants and warm pools of light immediately change the feeling of a wedding. They make large spaces feel intimate and give outdoor celebrations a sense of permanence and warmth.

This is where I think the influence of boutique hotels, restaurants and private members’ clubs has become especially important. Couples travel. They dine out. They experience beautifully designed spaces around the world, and naturally they want their celebrations to evoke some of those same feelings.

They may not say, “I want an interior-designed wedding.” They say, “I want it to feel like this hotel in Paris,” or “I loved this restaurant in New York.” That distinction matters.

The New Luxury Is Atmosphere

I think we will continue to see couples becoming more confident about mixing influences — vintage furniture with contemporary florals, fashion-inspired fabrics with traditional tablescapes, chrome against soft linen, sculptural pieces beside organic greenery.

The objective isn’t necessarily for everything to “match.” It is for everything to belong to the same story.

Fashion Is Also Teaching Weddings to Be More Personal

Perhaps my favourite influence from fashion is individuality. For a long time, weddings came with an unwritten formula of what was considered “bridal”. White, blush, certain flowers, certain chairs, certain stationery, certain photographs. That vocabulary has expanded enormously.

Today’s couple can create a wedding that is minimalist, maximalist, tropical, editorial, romantic, architectural, vintage, fashion-forward or wonderfully difficult to categorise.

Looking Beyond the Wedding Industry

As New York Fashion Week begins, I’ll certainly be watching the clothes, but I’ll also be looking at the sets, colour combinations, fabrics, styling and tiny details that make a collection memorable.

Because inspiration doesn’t always arrive labelled “wedding.”

Sometimes it is a handbag. A hotel lobby. A fashion show. A restaurant in another country. A fabric you can’t stop touching. A beautifully designed room. A colour combination you would never have thought to put together.

The best wedding professionals know how to notice those things, reinterpret them and make them relevant to the couple, the location and the celebration. For me, that is where wedding design becomes most exciting.

The future of weddings isn’t simply about following the next wedding trend. It is about looking at the wider world of design, fashion, travel and culture — and asking: how can we turn that inspiration into something that feels entirely our own?

World.title: Documentary on James Bond creator Ian Fleming to premiere at GoldenEye
World.content:
Portrait taken in the early 1960s of Ian Fleming, a British journalist, secret service agent, writer, whose most famous creation was the superhero James Bond, agent 007. (Photo: AFP)

Ian Fleming and the Curse of James Bond, directed by Adam Low, a new feature documentary exploring the life, imagination and enduring legacy of James Bond creator Ian Fleming, will premiere at GoldenEye, Fleming’s former Jamaican home, during the 80th anniversary year of the villa’s construction.

The documentary explores Fleming beyond the legend of 007, considering the contradictions, pressures and fascinations that shaped both the man and the charged literary world he created, according to a press release by Gross Media, which executive produced the project.

Presented at GoldenEye by Gross Media, the premiere weekend – November 19 to November 22, 2026 – brings together biography, place and mythology in a setting deeply connected to the Bond story.

“GoldenEye’s enduring legacy as a center of Jamaican art and creativity is rare and compelling,” said Gross Media founder David M Gross. “So much new has originated here and radiated outward — through music, painting, literature and the performing arts. Our film invites a new generation to come to Oracabessa, St Mary, to understand that legacy and be inspired by it.”

Built in a uniquely Jamaican architectural style, the iconic villa features whitewashed walls, wooden louvers and has no glass windowpanes.

Upon returning from espionage duties during World War II, Fleming built the villa in 1946 on Jamaica’s famed North Coast. GoldenEye became the creative sanctuary where he wrote each of the 12 James Bond nov els and the stories that introduced one of the most recognizable characters in modern popular culture.

Eight decades later, the property remains a living landmark: part legendary literary site, part cultural myth and an enduring symbol of Jamaica’s oversized place in the Bond story and the wider cultural world.

“Fleming built GoldenEye as a place where he could write, and every James Bond novel was written here. Eighty years later, it remains the spiritual birthplace of Bond. To screen a film that looks so closely at Fleming himself, during GoldenEye’s 80th year, is very special,” said Chris Blackwell, Founder, and Marika Kessler, CEO, Island Outpost.

Adam Low, the film’s director, said he was “determined to put Jamaica at the centre of the story” with the project.

“Even the Bond books not set there are infused with the island’s atmosphere, landscape and history. By including Jamaican voices — from Fleming’s longtime gardener Ramsay Dacosta to novelist Marlon James as well as Minister Olivia ‘Babsy’ Grange whose relative Aunt Violet was Fleming’s house manager — the film shows how deeply Jamaica shaped Fleming’s imagination and the world of Bond,” Low said.

“As Minister Grange says in the film, ‘Jamaica is the star of the Bond films,’ and the documentary makes a compelling case that without Jamaica, there would be no James Bond,” said Low, underlining the Jamaican connection.

The perspective of the film deepens the premiere’s connection to GoldenEye by positioning Jamaica not simply as Fleming’s retreat, but as a defining creative force behind Bond’s settings, sensibility and mythology.

“By weaving together Jamaican voices, landscapes and history, the documentary underscores the island’s central place in both Fleming’s imagination and the continuing cultural life of 007,” said film editor Joanna Crickmay.

According to the release, the film’s opening sequence features a moving benediction in the Rastafari tradition by author, journalist and cultural liaison Barbara Blake-Hannah, while driving the vibrant streets through Oracabessa, St Mary, en route to GoldenEye with Desmond Dekker & The Aces’ legendary rocksteady and reggae track “007 (Shanty Town)” on play.

The premiere film weekend will bring guests from around the world to the place where Fleming’s daily writing ritual helped launch the Bond phenomenon, the release stated, adding that the programme includes a screening at PlayScape, a cocktail party at the GoldenEye villa with a Jamaican jazz band, a classic Jamaican BBQ on Button Beach with members of the film’s crew and Ian Fleming-themed morning breakfasts: scrambled eggs, toast, guava jelly, local fruits and Blue Mountain coffee.

Together, the events offer guests a rare opportunity to experience the film in the setting most closely associated with Fleming’s creative life, according to the press release.

World.title: Stronger schools
World.content:
Education Minster Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon walks with students of Maud McLeod High School in Westmoreland where she filmed her back-to-school message to the nation.

After a school year battered by Hurricane Melissa, particularly in western Jamaica, but capped by improved results in the country’s major examinations, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon is looking to the new school year with optimism, pointing to increased investment, and stronger infrastructure as Jamaica pushes to transform its education system.

The scale of the challenge facing schools remains stark.

According to Morris Dixon’s back-to-school message, more than 688 schools were damaged by Melissa, 313 of them severely, while almost $26 billion is being spent on repairs and reconstruction. As she has repeatedly done in the past few weeks she acknowledged, however, that the work is not advancing as quickly as the Government would like.

Still, she said preparations were being made to get schools open, including contingency arrangements for institutions where repairs have not yet been completed.

“Thanks to the excellent work of our principals, boards, and the ministry team, we are working to have all schools open tomorrow. I have to thank all who have worked so hard over the summer and who have put in place contingency plans to support reopening even where repairs are not completed,” she said.

For Morris Dixon, however, rebuilding after Melissa is only part of the task.

The Government is entering the new school year with more than $835 million in operational support for schools, representing an average 55 per cent increase in funding. The minister said all schools received the first tranche of the increased funding in June, ahead of the reopening.

More than $1 billion is also being invested in educational resources, including workbooks, readers, textbooks, e-books, virtual learning solutions, and supplementary materials.

The increased spending comes against the backdrop of what Morris Dixon described as a strong finish to the last academic year, despite the disruption caused by the Category 5 storm.

“Despite the historic, once-in- a- 100-year devastation caused by the passage of Hurricane Melissa, we ended the last academic year with improved results across our major exams — PEP, CSEC and CAPE. Jamaica’s children did so well despite so much being thrown at them!” she said.

The minister is now betting on that resilience, alongside new investments, to drive further gains. In her speech she reminded the country of plans already in place.

Among the biggest initiatives is a $400-million investment in technical and vocational education at high schools. Technical high schools are to receive state-of-the-art laboratories in areas including autonomous robotics, renewable energy, virtual welding, electrical engineering, industrial controls, and optoelectronics.

The Government is also retooling science laboratories, while more than 150 satellite systems have been distributed to schools to improve Internet access, with additional devices being procured, particularly for rural institutions.

Morris Dixon said the hurricane recovery programme is similarly being used as an opportunity to improve schools beyond simply repairing the damage.

“Our Melissa reconstruction programme has not only presented an opportunity to make our schools more resilient, but it has also provided an opportunity to upgrade and renovate staffrooms for educators across Jamaica. The Staffroom Renovation Programme covers 74 institutions in the first phase, with work concentrated heavily in the parishes hardest hit by Melissa,” she said.

And while buildings, equipment and technology are central to the push, the minister also highlighted the needs of students outside the classroom.

More than 160,000 students are projected to benefit from the traditional cooked lunch programme, while another 69,000 students in the most challenged schools are expected to receive both breakfast and lunch. Meanwhile, 316 school cooks were trained and received range cook certification over the summer.

Psychosocial and psychological support, including trauma-informed services and Psychological First Aid, will also continue into the new academic year, after being intensified during the previous one.

Morris Dixon said the ambition extends beyond simply getting schools reopened and students back into classrooms.

“The ministry’s commitment is to continue transforming education so that every child, regardless of where they live or their circumstances, has a fair opportunity to learn, grow and succeed,” she said.

World.title: Inside Burnham’s big Israel gamble
World.content:
Britain is about to take its toughest stance yet against Israel – but will it make a difference, or will it leave the UK isolated on the international stage?

Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband will unveil a package of sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, putting Britain at the forefront of the G7’s effort to pressure Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine what the move means in practice – and why the government has chosen to act now.

But with tensions rising, will the move impact the UK’s relationship with the United States and Israel?

Plus, after a turbulent conference, has Reform UK seen a bounce in the polls, and could it give an early indication of the direction of travel for the Holborn and St Pancras by-election?

World.title: Kaja Kallas takes another hit
World.content:
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, wanted a group of heavyweight former leaders to come up with fresh ideas to address Europe’s defense gaps. Instead, the initiative was killed before it even launched. Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart look at why some capitals pushed back — and what the episode says about Kallas’ authority and the battle over who drives European defense policy.

Then, European Council President Antonio Costa continues his tour of European capitals as negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget get more concrete.

And finally: could Ukraine and Poland make a joint bid to host the football World Cup?

World.title: Mobilité : l’Europe doit passer des objectifs aux conditions de leur réalisation
World.content:
Premier exemple : le poids lourd. 78 % du fret terrestre européen passe par la route : presque tout ce qui remplit nos rayons a voyagé en camion. Pour électrifier ces flux, la technologie est là, le cadre aussi ; le nœud est économique. Surcoût à l’achat, valeur résiduelle incertaine, bornes de recharge à déployer, raccordements électriques trop lents, attentisme face à une technologie qui progresse vite : aucun acteur ne peut porter seul ces risques. La réponse consiste à mieux les répartir, voire à transformer des risques pour les uns en opportunités pour les autres. Location de la batterie, garantie des valeurs résiduelles, mutualisation de la recharge, sécurisation des volumes par contrat : l’écosystème dispose déjà d’une partie des solutions. L’action publique devient décisive là où le marché ne peut agir seul, ou pas assez vite, notamment sur les raccordements électriques et l’interopérabilité. Elle doit aussi rassurer sur la fermeté du chemin : non pas en généralisant les contraintes, mais en rendant la trajectoire crédible, en facilitant l’amorçage des transformations volontaires, et en accompagnant ceux qui prennent les premiers risques. Ce sont eux qu’il faut aider, avant de laisser les suiveurs rejoindre un marché devenu lisible et désirable. L’Europe ne doit pas revoir sa destination à chaque difficulté d’exécution, car rien ne décourage plus l’investissement que l’instabilité des règles ; elle doit créer les conditions permettant de l’atteindre. Faute de quoi l’incertitude sur le passage à l’échelle nourrit une contestation du cap lui-même. Le choix : répartir le risque pour créer le marché, ou rester trop longtemps prisonniers du diesel.

Deuxième exemple : la petite voiture populaire. L’Europe en a fait des icônes : la 2 CV, la Fiat 500, la Coccinelle. Puis nos voitures ont grossi : certains modèles pèsent désormais deux fois plus que leur ancêtre du même nom, et leur prix a suivi la même pente. Aujourd’hui la voiture électrique européenne reste hors de portée d’une grande partie des ménages. Nous avons commencé par le premium, subventionné les SUV, en espérant que les coûts descendent ensuite ; pendant ce temps, une déferlante de petites voitures électriques asiatiques, abordables et produites à grande échelle, se prépare à occuper l’espace que nous choisissons, par défaut, de laisser ouvert. La Commission a pris le problème de front en proposant une catégorie dédiée aux véhicules électriques compacts, avec des incitations pour ceux produits en Europe. C’est une avancée. Nous pensons qu’il faut aller plus loin, parce que tout s’y joue à la fois : la souveraineté industrielle, le pouvoir d’achat et l’écologie. C’est l’ambition du projet Pop Car, que nous menons avec une coalition d’industriels et d’experts : une voiture mieux dimensionnée dans sa masse, sa batterie et son coût complet d’usage, sobre, abordable, sans rien céder sur la sécurité ni la désirabilité. Là encore, ne pas vouloir contraindre tout le monde à basculer au même rythme, mais sécuriser une offre européenne qui amorcera le marché et laisser l’adoption s’élargir lorsque prix, usage et confiance seront réunis. La question est celle-ci : quelle voiture électrique un ménage européen pourra-t-il s’offrir demain, et où sera-t-elle produite ? Le choix : refaire de l’entrée de gamme un segment stratégique, ou la laisser se jouer ailleurs.

Troisième exemple : l’intelligence artificielle. Elle orchestre une part croissante de nos mobilités. Elle oriente les itinéraires de millions de véhicules, arbitre des flux entiers de circulation, répartit des ressources rares : le temps, l’espace public, les chargements, l’énergie. Depuis le 2 août 2026, l’AI Act impose ses premières obligations de transparence à certains systèmes. Nécessaire, mais cela ne dit pas ce que l’IA doit optimiser. L’IA exécute la consigne. Elle ne décide pas seule de ce qui compte. Faut-il privilégier la vitesse, l’efficience ou l’écologie ? Le coût pour l’opérateur ou l’accessibilité pour tous ? Ces priorités ne s’imposent pas d’elles-mêmes : ce sont des choix collectifs, qui s’écrivent dans le logiciel, et engagent autant nos mobilités qu’une infrastructure physique. Notre conviction : toute IA déployée dans la mobilité devrait démontrer son gain net — carbone, coût pour l’usager, accessibilité — et non le seul temps gagné. Ici aussi, le régulateur a un rôle décisif : fixer la boussole collective sans étouffer l’innovation, donner confiance aux pionniers, puis faciliter la diffusion des solutions utiles. Le choix : écrire la consigne collectivement, ou subir les règles opaques que d’autres auront écrites pour nous.

Trois exemples, un même fil : une transition réussit lorsque ceux qui doivent la rendre réelle ont intérêt et capacité à le faire. Familles, transporteurs, opérateurs, industriels : face au prix, au financement ou à l’investissement, tous pèsent le même type d’arguments. Mais tous ressentent aussi que notre modèle économique épuise la planète. Notre pari européen est de le réinventer par l’alignement volontaire des intérêts, et non par un dirigisme excessif. En démocratie, la puissance publique fixe une destination ; elle ne peut, seule, rendre le trajet possible. Il faut aussi donner à chacun les moyens, l’intérêt et la confiance nécessaires pour s’y engager librement.

Poser les contraintes sur la table, mettre les désaccords au travail, construire des trajectoires communes : c’est ce que nous faisons chez Movin’On, et ce que nous porterons les 8 et 9 octobre à Paris, lors de notre Summit. L’Europe a longtemps débattu de la destination. Elle doit maintenant organiser le voyage. Cela suppose une puissance publique ferme sur le cap, utile dans l’amorçage, attentive aux pionniers, puis confiante dans la capacité des acteurs à suivre lorsque les conditions sont réunies. C’est l’heure des choix.

Gaël Quéinnec

Directeur général de Movin’On

World.title: Draghi Report or Hugging Face: who will win the tech race?
World.content:
When a swarm of AI agents decided to hack the computation company Hugging Face in July, it took them six days. That event became a case study on how, and how fast, artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping both economic and power dynamics worldwide. When Mario Draghi published his report on how to re-establish European competitiveness, it took 729 days for Brussels to realize that only a fraction of his recommendations had been enacted. Tomorrow will mark the second anniversary of the report’s presentation and, according to draghiwatch.eu, only 15.7 percent of his recommendations have been fully implemented so far.

Tech and telecoms policy might have lost the “Draghi spirit”

In digital and tech, the number of fully implemented recommendations is currently even lower: only 6.4 percent. Draghi made a point of putting technology at the core of EU reform, and zoomed in on telecoms as a critical sector to deliver tech sovereignty and growth for future decades to come. Why? Because 5G, fiber and future 6G networks are the backbone of our economies and societies at a time in which economic growth is driven by technology.

As to the connectivity sector, less than half of Draghi’s telecom recommendations have been picked up in ongoing reforms and policy strategies. None has been implemented yet. Worse, the recommendations that have moved forward so far are largely cost-creating for the industry, such as technology bans in 5G or forced phase-outs of copper networks. The measures that would directly boost investment remain limited, for now, mainly to spectrum proposals; more on this below. That implementation gap matters because the technologies now moving fastest are precisely the ones that depend on Europe’s connectivity foundations. AI, cloud, defense tech and satellite connectivity are no longer separate policy files: they are becoming one industrial race.

Four fights reshaping connectivity (and tech leadership) today

Since Draghi’s report was published in 2024, innovation in connectivity has moved fast. The first fight is helping Europe claim its slice of the AI boom. Telecom operators are doing their part: data must move between AI data centers and back to users, and advanced 5G and future 6G networks can help industry turn AI into productivity gains. A German manufacturing plant or an Italian port using 5G and AI applications should be able to compete with Chinese or American peers.

Worse, the recommendations that have moved forward so far are largely cost-creating for the industry, such as technology bans in 5G or forced phase-outs of copper networks.

The second fight is creating a healthy sovereign cloud market. Many telecom operators are already responding to the demand from European businesses and public administration to provide sovereign cloud offers.

Another crucial fight is the one for developing more defense tech capabilities in Europe. Here, the synergies between defense companies and the telecom sector are becoming ever clearer, as keeping Europeans safe now requires advanced and secure communications. Just think of drones: telcos are already deploying services to keep our public spaces safe from malicious drones.

Finally, the fight for tech leadership also takes to space: Europe rightly has the ambition to get into the satellite connectivity game rather than leaving it only to others. Here, a recent positive satellite spectrum decision by the European Commission might help build leadership over time.

Four reforms that will decide whether Europe catches up

The European telecom sector is a regulated one and its health has downstream effects on the whole digital economy. This is why Europe can only win in tech when it completes the deep telecom reforms suggested by Draghi. Our view is that this depends on at least four major policy actions.

First, we need scale. Europe’s telecom markets remain too fragmented, with many operators too small to invest at the scale needed for advanced networks and dramatically improved customer experience. Consolidation therefore becomes a necessary tool, both in-market and across markets, to create stronger operators able to invest, innovate and interact with major global AI, chip and platform companies. The review of the EU Merger Guidelines, and its practical application in telecom cases, will play a crucial role here.

Second, we need a new telecom rulebook. The Digital Networks Act (DNA) is currently being reviewed by the European Parliament and member states. So far, the Commission’s main material improvement for 5G and 6G investment is the proposal to make spectrum licenses unlimited. Yet, troubling signals from co-legislators suggest that even this improvement could be watered down. If that happens, the DNA would lose the one positive measure that analysts and investors have identified so far. Other areas that should be tackled are: deregulating the current heavy-handed access regime, which currently prevents a rush to invest in fiber; removing the introduction of mandated switch-off of copper networks, which might end-up unintendedly harming consumers and removing their freedom of choice; and materially improving the space for telecom innovation, with clearer rules on specialized services and simplified service regulation.

Europe can only win in tech when it completes the deep telecom reforms suggested by Draghi.

Third, we must defend security with better tools than some of those suggested in the Cybersecurity Act (CSA). Unless improved, the current CSA will impose major costs, estimated at €30-40 billion by GSMA Intelligence, on telecom operators and their customers, effectively contradicting other pro-investment policy objectives. De-risking connectivity is worthy, however, we have serious doubts that this can be done simply by imposing an indiscriminate technology ban, while we would need a proportionate and truly risk-based approach. What about compensation, as the U.S. did? What about the investment capacity of the sector? What about unintended effects on consumers? Things are still not well-thought through.

Fourth, we need a Cloud and AI Development Act that strengthens Europe’s sovereignty, competitiveness and resilience in practice. The starting point in the Commission draft is good: the ultimate goal should be to accelerate Europe’s cloud and AI capacity, while creating the right conditions for demand, investment, deployment and scale.

The time that separates the presentation of the Draghi Report from today’s underwhelming implementation is 729 days. In the same timespan, AI agents can generate 120+ Hugging Face hacking scandals. If we are to win the race, Europe needs good quality legislation, bold one. And it needs it faster.

World.title: Nigel Farage exploring Ukraine visit, Reform officials say
World.content:
The imprisonment of Reform’s former Wales leader last year for taking Russian bribes has only added to perceptions that Farage has a “Putin problem.”

Polling carried out by More in Common last year suggests that while every voting group in Britain overwhelmingly backs Ukraine, only 26 percent believe that Farage feels the same. Some 21 percent reckon he sympathizes more with Russia.

But Reform hopes it could go some way to dispelling that perception by arranging for Farage to visit Ukraine.

“I know it’s been discussed,” said a first official, whose comment was backed up by a second official. Both were granted anonymity to discuss plans yet to be finalized.

Neither could say at what level the talks have been held. Reform declined to comment, as did the Ukrainian Embassy.

The first official said they believe a visit could go some way to dispelling the impression Farage has any sympathy for Putin — but warned a visit could “piss off a lot of our members.”

World.title: The least free place on earth: Occupied Ukraine
World.content:
From passportization to deportation

Starting from 2014, Russia has occupied about 20 percent of Ukraine in the country’s south and east — land Moscow calls “new historical territories.” And one of the processes aiding the Russification of these areas is passportization.

By officially designating Ukrainians living in Russia-occupied territories as “foreigners,” occupation authorities compel them to obtain Russian citizenship — which they can do through simplified procedures — in order to access essential rights, such as health care, social services, employment or property ownership.

For Liudmila Chub, it all began with her job. Speaking to POLITICO, Chub said that in 2023, she was told by her employer in Melitopol — located in the occupied Kherson region — that she had to obtain a Russian passport to keep working in his shop, or he would be fined. Chub went to the passport office, where she recorded an angry video about being forced to get a “chicken passport” — a dig at the two-headed Russian eagle emblem. The office’s security guard marched her straight to the occupation police.

A man waits for documentation to apply for new Russian passport at a centre in Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region in August 2022. | AFP via Getty Images

Chub spent the next eight months in detention in Kherson, with the courts regularly extending her arrest, alleging she was breaking military curfew. She was eventually given a statement to read out on camera, saying she did not want to live in Russia, then was allowed 15 minutes to collect items from her apartment and transported under armed guard to Russia’s border with Georgia.

Deported from the home she lived in her whole life, Chub still considers herself fortunate. She said others she encountered in prison had gone through the process of obtaining Russian citizenship only to be charged with spying or treason under Russian law, which carries huge sentences.

“They tie this passport to you, and then with it, they make you traitors to their country,” she said. “Everything in me was opposed to getting that passport, and it’s lucky I didn’t get it. That saved me.”

World.title: Ceuta crisis forces Europe’s migrant-rights groups to rethink their playbook
World.content:
“The conversation around migration and the language used to refer to migrants has changed in many EU countries, even center-left member states,” said Michele LeVoy, director of the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, a network of organizations that advocate for unauthorized migrants across Europe.

In response, migrant-rights groups are changing tactics. As humanitarian appeals lose political traction, they are turning more heavily to the courts, building broader alliances and experimenting with new ways to talk about migration.

“We’re trying to be stronger together by working with organizations from across civil society, working with lawyers to challenge litigation, and really showing that these policies are bad for everyone, not just migrants,” LeVoy added.

From rescue to deterrence

In 2013, the death of hundreds of migrants in a shipwreck off the Italian island of Lampedusa shocked the continent.

Top EU officials, including then-Commission President José Manuel Barroso, traveled to the site to declare that “the European Union cannot accept that thousands of people die at its borders.”

The bloc’s then-Home Affairs Commissioner Cecilia Malmström called for a “change of approach towards migration,” adding that “this restrictive approach is not sustainable and that it is now time to move towards more openness and solidarity.”

World.title: What's in a name? Trump suggests renaming New Mexico state 'New America'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's name-changing spree found an unlikely new target earlier this week when he suggested the state of New Mexico could be renamed "New America."

 

His proposal, which was immediately dismissed by the state's governor, comes days after he signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America" in the middle of a trade war with neighbouring Canada.

"Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico...to NEW AMERICA," the Republican president posted on social media.

"So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!"

The White House reposted an image showing the Mexico part of the state's name crossed out and replaced with "America."

A screenshot of a post on US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account, 8 September, 2026 @realDonaldTrump

Trump’s Truth Social account also posted several such maps showing the name change.

Some US media reports said the idea originated as an internet hoax.

State governor Michelle Lujan Grisham told Fox News that the name "isn't up for debate, it's been ours since before the United States existed."

She said the president wanted to "distract Americans" from issues such as soaring gas prices.

Trump last week suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as "Trump Strait" as the war with Iran continues, then hours later implied he was not serious about the plan.

He renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" on his first day back in the White House in 2025 in a move rejected by Mexico.

Canada has also rejected the attempt to rename Lake Ontario.

World.title: AfD surge in Germany exposes deep divisions on the Italian right
World.content:
As the far right made significant gains in local elections in Germany, divisions have opened up within Italy's political right.

 

The AfD (Alternative for Germany) took 43.8 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, a historic result that has shaken the federal government in Berlin. The shockwave reached Rome, where reaction from Italy's governing parties was sharply divided.

Sunday's election result in Saxony-Anhalt is "a worrying signal", said Forza Italia leader and foreign minister Antonio Tajani. "A negative signal," he added, although there is no need to "overdramatise" it, he told Il Messaggero.

"It was widely expected — it was known that the AfD could score a clear victory. After all, most of their success comes in eastern Germany," said the deputy prime minister. "That region is the poorest part of Germany, and extremism always takes root where there are the greatest economic difficulties."

Transport and infrastructure minister Matteo Salvini took a very different view. "An extraordinary success, which highlights the strong demand for change, security and jobs," the League leader said in a post on X.

"Fear? Terror? Danger? No, it's called DEMOCRACY. Another Europe is possible," he concluded.

Italy's two deputy prime ministers remain split over support for the AfD who is opposed to arming Ukraine and keen to end sanctions on Moscow in return for cheaper energy supplies. Meloni herself chose not to comment directly, leaving Galeazzo Bignami, Brothers of Italy's leader in the Chamber of Deputies, to speak on her behalf.

"This is neither a positive nor a negative assessment," he said. "When the electorate speaks, the outcome of the vote must always be accepted, whatever it is."

"Handing out certificates of democracy or otherwise to a force that has taken part in the democratic game and been democratically elected seems to us a prejudiced judgement," Bignami added.

The Vannacci question and the rise of the pro-Russian right

The election result in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany's poorest state, has made the question of how to handle the rise of former general Roberto Vannacci even more complex for Rome.

The former Folgore Brigade commander — now an MEP and leader of Futuro Nazionale — celebrated the AfD's victory on social media. "Europe is changing," he wrote on Facebook. "Nessun dorma."

Vannacci's platform overlaps closely with the AfD's: both attack the EU, call for forced "remigration", and push for cuts to aid for Ukraine. According to the latest YouTrend polling, his party stands at 7.9 per cent, ahead of Forza Italia (7.1 per cent) and the League (4.4 per cent) — putting Meloni's next election at risk without his support.

Vannacci has repeatedly criticised the governing coalition's approach to migration and aid for Kyiv, earning him the Financial Times label "Russia's Trojan horse". Russia remains one of the sharpest fault lines on the right: the AfD opposes aid to Ukraine, and leader Alice Weidel has proposed scrapping sanctions on Moscow and resuming Russian gas and oil imports.

The result was welcomed in the Kremlin. "The historic AfD victory humiliates the arrogance, narrow-mindedness, warmongering, ineptitude and hypocrisy of the discredited German governing coalition," wrote Kirill Dmitriev, the Kremlin's special envoy and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, in a post on X.

This pro-Russian wave — echoed in Italy by Vannacci — creates headaches for Meloni, who has pledged support for Ukraine, underscored by defence minister Guido Crosetto's appointment of former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as an adviser on military innovation.

Divisions on the right are visible in Europe

Italy's right is split on how to treat the AfD, and the divide is sharpest on foreign policy — particularly Russia.

Forza Italia takes the toughest line. As Italy's member of the European People's Party (EPP), the centre-right group that dominates the European Parliament, it firmly backs NATO unity and supports a "cordon sanitaire" — a deliberate political isolation — to keep the AfD shut out of mainstream EU politics.

Meloni's own party, Brothers of Italy, sits in a different group, the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), but takes a broadly similar view.

Salvini's The League's relationship with the AfD has followed a different path. The two parties were once allies in the European Parliament, first in a group called Europe of Nations and Freedom, then in its successor, Identity and Democracy. That alliance collapsed in May 2024, when the League voted to expel the AfD after its lead candidate, Maximilian Krah, made controversial remarks about the Nazi SS.

Since then, the two parties have gone their separate ways. The League now sits with the Patriots for Europe group, while the AfD leads its own bloc, Europe of Sovereign Nations although Salvini's overtures could pave the way for closer cooperation once again.

World.title: Donald Trump as Green Lantern? Why the Trump administration needs to stop (mis)using pop culture references
World.content:
Another day, another AI slop rampage from Donald Trump, whose latest Truth Social posting spree has left the internet saying one thing in unison: Enough.

 

Trump is no stranger to bulk posting AI-generated imagery as part of what has been referred to as “memetic warfare” - a tactic which sees him and his administration flood the zone when it comes to AI-generated imagery in order to appeal to his base and beyond. But the increasing frequency and quantity of the posts (as well as the very bizarre content) is leading people to seriously wonder about the mental health of the president, the security of the modern world, and the Trump administration's loose grasp on pop culture references.

One social media user argued: “Something is very wrong with the president. And yet, still has the codes to our nuclear arsenal and is the single person who can order their use.” Another pointed out: “The man with the nuclear codes. You'd be concerned if these were being posted by an elderly relative.”

In his latest posting spree, Trump renamed New Mexico as “New America”, shared an image of his silhouette over Iran, proposed new uniforms for the United States Space Force (which gave off Starship Troopers fascist chic), and even declared the Moon as US territory...

Yes, really. He declared the celestial body “is ours”.

It goes without saying that the Moon is in fact not owned by anyone, as stated by Article II of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967. Still, the internet was quick to point out that Trump should have more pressing priorities...

“Maybe get control of the Strait of Hormuz before you start on the moon,” one social media user wrote, while another posted: “Reporter: What do you say to Americans who want affordable food, gas, healthcare, and no war? Trump: The Moon is Ours.”

“WTF? Honestly this dude is losing his mind,” another commented.

One AI-generated image has angered comic book and film fans – and not for the first time.

Trump has previously appropriated several pop culture touchstones, including Superman, Hannibal Lecter, Jedis and Spider-Man, and the references have backfired every time – not only by sparking the ire of the original creators and fans, but also for how these hijacked cultural winks display a lack of appreciation or understanding when it comes to the references themselves.

The latest is an image of Trump as a DC Universe superhero. He could be seen wearing a Green Lantern Ring and appearing to build a green border wall with the ring’s power. Then, there’s a holographic “American manufacturing” cityscape that appears, before green military aircrafts fly over his head.

You couldn’t make this up.

The clip was posted by the official White House account, which captioned the clip by reappropriating the oath spoken by heroes in the Green Lantern Corps: “In brightest day, in blackest night, no evil shall escape my sight. Let those who worship evil's might beware my power... Green Lantern's light!”

Beyond the fact that “America is actually being run by a 12 year old on iPad privileges,” as one person shrewdly commented on X, as well as the very serious real-world issues Americans are facing (“Day 190 of the Iran War,” someone pointed out online, while another argued: “Anything to distract from gas prices”), Trump’s White House shows once again that it has misused the cultural reference and that the ironic implications clearly escape them.

Much like the backfiring Jedi image (red lightsabers are for the baddies, Donald), the glaring irony of Trump portraying himself as Superman (technically an illegal immigrant on Planet Earth) and how Spider-Man would actually be fighting ICE, not supporting them, the Green Lantern reference misfires.

You see, the Green Lantern Corps are an intergalactic peacekeeping force that protects the entire universe without borders. Hijacking this character to symbolize an "America First" agenda and using the ring to build physical border walls is contradictory to the core principles of the fictional character.

Plus, all card-carrying nerds will rush to correct this clip, as Trump would not be a Green Lantern, which imbues hope. A more accurate colour would be Yellow, for the love of chaos, or Orange - chiefly due to his greed and hunger for power.

In addition to the thesis that the Trump administration might be culturally illiterate is the fact that using artificial intelligence to display supreme strength and dominance only highlights imaginary power. Not true might that would decry from real-world policy.

Understand your references, or they risk rebounding and making you look like cosmic embarrassments.

“In brightest day, in blackest night, no backfiring AI shall escape from my device during outrunning iPad privileges.”

Granted, it doesn’t have the same ring to it, but lessons need to be learned.

World.title: EU institution leaders blast Serbia over 'shocking' Ratko Mladić's funeral
World.content:
The heads of the EU's two main institutions have condemned the presence of senior Serbian officials at the funeral of the convicted war criminal, in a joint statement published simultaneously on X on Tuesday morning.

 

"The images from Ratko Mladić's funeral yesterday in Belgrade were shocking. Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal. He was responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa wrote on X.

Ratko Mladić, known as the Butcher of Bosnia, died in late August aged 84 in a UN detention facility in The Hague. The Bosnian Serb had served in the Army of Republika Srpska with the rank of colonel-general during the Yugoslav Wars.

Following his death, his body was flown to Belgrade on a state plane, given an honour guard by the Serbian military and various security forces, and commemorated by the public broadcaster and the Serbian Orthodox Church. His coffin was wrapped in a Serbian flag.

On Friday, the glorification of the war criminal attracted the ire of senior EU officials, national ministers and diplomats, while Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos warned the funeral would be an "important test" for Serbia's accession bid.

"He died while serving a life sentence for the Srebrenica genocide and other crimes. The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable," the post continues.

On Monday, the Commission's chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, caused a public backlash after telling the daily press conference that "we had heard that there was a funeral foreseen with state honours, and that has not been the case."

"Five ministers from the Serbian Government were seated in the front row at the funeral, a convicted war criminal was given military honours, and his body was flown in on a Serbian Government aircraft," the official X account of the Foreign Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina wrote, calling Pinho's statement "a disgrace to the entire European Union."

Von der Leyen and Costa's joint statement appears to cement the EU's institutional condemnation of Mladić's glorification, stressing that Serbia's failure to confront a dark chapter of European history contradicts the values underpinning EU membership. It also marks a sharp escalation from warning to institutional condemnation.

In July, the Commission tried to revive Serbia's accession bid by putting the opening of Cluster 3 back on the table. Eight member states blocked the move, citing rule-of-law concerns and Belgrade's failure to align with EU sanctions against Russia.

"Everyone can see that, following this heinous glorification of Mladić, the opening of Cluster 3 is completely out of the question for now," an EU diplomat told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled her planned visit to Serbia, while a Commission spokesperson denied that von der Leyen had ever had a visit to Serbia planned at all.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić called for snap parliamentary elections to take place in late October.
