World.title: Los pantalones ‘barrel’ de Zara y el “motín” de las mujeres perimenopáusicas: “¿Sería mucho pedir existir?”
World.content:
He aquí la breve historia de la nueva silueta que está en todas partes y el debate que ha despertado en las redes sociales

Zara es un poco como la Coca Cola, todo el mundo conoce la marca, pero nadie más tiene su fórmula. La que sí ha dado en una de las teclas de Zara (al menos en la de ciertas clientas) ha sido la psicóloga afincada en Zaragoza Pilar Cebrián, gracias a un vídeo cómico que publicó en su perfil de Instagram en los últimos días de agosto: “Querida Marta Ortega, tenemos que hablar”, comenzaba.

“Estoy en un punto de mi vida en el que Zara y yo hemos tomado caminos diferentes. Y yo me pregunto, Marta, ¿por qué? ¿Por qué los pantalones barrel?”. Pilar se refiere a esos pantalones “que no quedan bien a las mujeres que [hemos pasado de los 40]”, un diseño que desde hace unos meses inunda la colección de la marca de Inditex (y de todas las demás cadenas de moda asequible, para ser más precisos). “Mujeres perimenopáusicas!! Levantémonos en armas!! Fuimos las primeras en comprar en sus tiendas y en lucir sus prendas! Y ahora vamos a permitir que nos dejen en la cuneta de la moda de Inditex?”, bromeaba en el pie del vídeo.

Historia de los barrel

Primero, una cuestión de nomenclatura. El pantalón balloon fit o barrel fit debe su nombre a la forma de su pernera, que recrea la de un barril o un globo. Al vestirlo, dibuja una silueta ovalada: gana volumen en la zona del muslo, se curva hacia fuera y vuelve a estrecharse en el tobillo.

Su origen está salpicado de referencias. Algunos sitúan sus primeros antecedentes en los uniformes de trabajo franceses de los años 20 y 30, que incorporaban pantalones amplios y estructuras cónicas. Otros los relacionan con los pantalones de los vaqueros de principios del siglo XX, cuya silueta abombada tendría que ver con la posición de las piernas al montar a caballo. Y hay quien sitúa su salto definitivo a la moda en los años 80, de la mano de la cultura hip-hop y el streetwear, cuando las prendas amplias y con movimiento se convirtieron en parte esencial de la estética urbana.

El vaquero de tipo 'barrel', un modelo muy popular en las marcas 'fast fashion'. Moritz Scholz (Getty Images)

Lo que sí sabemos es que la silueta no nació ayer y que su actual reinado tiene bastante que ver con el cansancio colectivo de los skinny. Tras años de pantalones pegados al cuerpo, y al calor de la “nueva comodidad” que llegó tras la pandemia, la moda empezó a ensanchar las perneras: primero llegaron los rectos, después los wide leg, los baggy y, finalmente, esos pantalones que tienen a internet dividido.

Uno de los modelos que contribuyó a popularizar esta silueta fue el Horseshoe de Citizens of Humanity, lanzado en 2021. Sus perneras anchas y curvas, con el bajo ligeramente cónico y corto, resultaron demasiado vanguardistas para muchos consumidores en un primer momento. En redes sociales hubo risas, burlas y referencias a los Looney Tunes. Pero la resistencia fue durando lo que suele durar cuando hablamos de tendencias de moda: hasta que este corte de pantalón dejó de parecer extraño. Y así, el Horseshoe pasó de ser una rareza a convertirse en un modelo de culto de la firma.

Un salto en el tiempo nos lleva hasta aquí: con los barrel ocupando escaparates y catálogos y con la industria de la moda explicándonos que, en realidad, son unos pantalones muy democráticos. Que se ajustan en la cintura, dejan espacio en la cadera y el muslo y se estrechan en el tobillo. Que no ciñen. Que no restringen. Que funcionan para distintos tipos de cuerpo. La teoría es estupenda. La práctica, por lo visto, tiene sus matices.

Invisibles más allá de los 40

Lo que pudo ser una publicación entre tantas acabó convirtiéndose en una pequeña “trama” viral (con giro de guion incluido: tras una serie de críticas muy encendidas, Pilar se grabó probándose unos que, para su sorpresa, al final le quedaban bien) y abriendo un debate entre los miles de comentarios que despertó el tema. Muchos de ellos eran mujeres alrededor de los 40 que siempre consumieron ropa de Zara y que hoy, para su disgusto, no encuentran prendas que se adecúen a sus cuerpos en esta etapa.

Porque quizá el problema no sea exactamente que los barrel sienten mal. Quizá sea que, cuando una mujer llega a los 40, empieza a preguntarse si la ropa que lleva toda la vida comprando sigue estando pensada para ella.

Algo parecido comentó días después, en su perfil de Instagram, Ana Santamarina, experta en dermocosmética y creadora de su marca homónima de cuidado de la piel. “Tengo 48 años y no me siento representada en ninguna de las marcas que yo consumo. Somos casi 50 millones de personas en España y seis de cada diez tiene más de 35 años. Y no solo eso: más de la mitad de las personas que trabajan y están afiliadas a la Seguridad Social tienen más de 45 años. Trabajamos, consumimos, compramos ropa, accesorios, perfume, maquillaje, skincare, de todo… pero somos invisibles. ¿Sería mucho pedir existir en el imaginario de las marcas?”. Y proponía a sus seguidores fijarse en las tiendas de los centros comerciales a ver si alguna de las modelos de los anuncios y escaparates tiene más de 25 años.

La pregunta resulta especialmente pertinente si tenemos en cuenta que las mujeres empiezan a desaparecer de la imagen pública justo cuando empiezan a tener más poder adquisitivo, más criterio y, probablemente, menos paciencia para que le digan qué debería ponerse.

No es que la moda no haya intentado corregirlo. Zara, de hecho, fue noticia precisamente por hacer algo bastante poco habitual en 2017. Aquel año lanzó Timeless, un editorial protagonizado por Malgosia Bela, de 40 años; Yasmin Warsame, de 41; y Kristina de Coninck, de 53. Las tres hablaban, además, del paso del tiempo y de cómo se sentían con respecto a envejecer.

Fue un gesto celebrado porque rompía con la imagen habitual de las modelos veinteañeras que pueblan los e-commerce de moda. Y Zara no fue la primera: Celine había convertido a Joan Didion en una de sus musas, Mango había contado con Lyn Slater, de 63 años, y Desigual había recurrido a mujeres de edades muy superiores a las que solemos ver en una campaña de moda.

El problema es que una campaña puntual no necesariamente cambia el imaginario de una marca y quizá por eso el pequeño motín de los barrel resulta más interesante de lo que parece. Porque no estamos hablando solamente de unos vaqueros difíciles. Estamos hablando de una generación de mujeres que ha crecido comprando en las mismas tiendas que sus hijas y que, de pronto, siente que las prendas ya no están diseñadas para el cuerpo que tiene. El cuerpo cambia, pero la moda parece seguir dibujando el mismo cuerpo de siempre.

En resumen, las mujeres mayores de 40 están pidiendo espacio en el escaparate. Y, ya puestos, en los pantalones.

World.title: Lo que ocurre cuando se deja crecer a la bestia
World.content:
Exposición didáctica de ideas, conjeturas o hipótesis, a partir de unos hechos de actualidad comprobados —no necesariamente del día— que se reflejan en el propio texto. Excluye los juicios de valor y se aproxima más al género de opinión, pero se diferencia de él en que no juzga ni pronostica, sino que sólo formula hipótesis, ofrece explicaciones argumentadas y pone en relación datos dispersos

En la novela 22/11/63, Stephen King juega con la posibilidad de que alguien viaje en el tiempo para impedir el asesinato del presidente John F. Kennedy en Dallas y así cambiar la historia. Pero la llegada de los grandes totalitarismos fascistas al poder en la Europa de los años treinta —primero Mussolini en Italia, luego Hitler en Alemania y, finalmente, Francisco Franco en España, que no hubiese ganado la Guerra Civil sin la ayuda de los otros dos tiranos— no se hubiese podido evitar con una sola acción. Fue un proceso tremendamente complejo, en el que se mezclaron la violencia con la ceguera política de aquellos que creyeron que los monstruos podrían ser controlados. Las grandes potencias democráticas occidentales no supieron ver lo que se les venía encima. Y no se trata solo del desgraciado “no hay nadie que quiera más la paz en Europa que Hitler”, que persiguió para la historia al premier británico Neville Chamberlain.

El historiador británico Frank McDonough está reconstruyendo la historia del nazismo a través de una serie de libros bajo el título genérico de The Hitler Years. El último volumen está dedicado al Holocausto y las fechas en las que enmarca la destrucción de los judíos de Europa son especialmente significativas: 1933-1945. La Shoah no empezó con la II Guerra Mundial, ni con la decisión de Hitler de ordenar el exterminio —que se debió tomar en algún momento del tramo final de 1941, antes de la Conferencia de Wannsee—, ni con las cámaras de gas y los fusilamientos masivos en la antigua URSS. El Holocausto empezó cuando los nazis, nada más llegar al poder, aprobaron las primeras leyes antisemitas desde la emancipación de los judíos en Alemania en 1871.

Charles Chaplin como el dictador Adenoid Hynkel en la sátira del nazismo 'El gran dictador'. Bettmann (Bettmann Archive)

Resulta especialmente incómodo leer lo que ocurrió entonces en el resto del mundo: los grandes periódicos estadounidenses —McDonough cita a The New York Times, el Chicago Times, el Atlanta Constitution y el Washington Post— publicaron 455 artículos y editoriales “sobre la persecución de los judíos en Alemania con informaciones que ofrecían descripciones muy gráficas de la violencia física que sufrían”. El 27 de marzo de 1933 —Hitler llegó al poder el 30 de enero— tuvo lugar un mitin para condenar la violencia nazi que reunió a 20.000 personas en el Madison Square Garden de Nueva York dentro del auditorio y a 35.000 en los alrededores. Estas manifestaciones pidieron el boicot de los productos alemanes. En abril, se convocaron marchas en todo Estados Unidos que reunieron a casi un millón de personas. El boicot no se produjo y Alemania siguió siendo tratada como un país más.

Las protestas masivas fueron recibidas con indignación por la cúpula nazi. Hitler calificó las manifestaciones de “propaganda” y Goebbels aseguró que era una prueba más de que los judíos controlaban los medios de comunicación. Básicamente, ninguna de las grandes potencias hizo nada pese a que la bestia de la represión iba creciendo en Alemania y los judíos —y todos aquellos que se oponían a los nazis— eran destruidos.

Manifestación contra los nazis en Nueva York en mayo de 1933. FPG (Getty Images)

El gran dictador, la gran película de Charles Chaplin, una sátira del nazismo considerada actualmente una obra maestra sobre los totalitarismos, provocó un profundo malestar en Hollywood. Los estudios tenían miedo de que el filme que ridiculizaba a Hitler y denunciaba la persecución de los judíos les cerrase el mercado alemán. Por no hablar de la participación, como si no estuviese ocurriendo nada, en los Juegos Olímpicos de Berlín de 1936, una clara operación de propaganda nazi por mucho que Jesse Owens demostrase que la superioridad racial era una de tantas patrañas supremacistas.

La ignominia alcanzó cotas difícilmente superables cuando numerosos países se reunieron, en junio de 1938, en la Conferencia de Evian para hacer frente al problema de los refugiados judíos, que todavía podían huir de Alemania. Los delegados de 32 países fueron incapaces de adoptar un acuerdo y cerraron las puertas a decenas de miles de personas que hubiesen podido salvar sus vidas. Jaim Weizmann, líder sionista que acabaría por convertirse en el primer presidente de Israel, resumió el encuentro con una frase: “El mundo parece estar dividido en dos partes: una donde los judíos no pueden vivir y la otra donde no pueden entrar”.

El candidato de Afd, Ulrich Siegmund, el pasado domingo en Magdeburg. Matthias Schrader (AP Photo/Matthias Schrader)

Es imposible saber qué hubiese ocurrido si las democracias llegan a adoptar otra actitud ante evidentes violaciones de los derechos humanos, si hubiesen tomado medidas antes contra aquellos tiranos, si no hubiesen mirado hacia otro lado y pensado que se podía llegar a algún tipo de acuerdo con el mal absoluto. Los años treinta del siglo XX están, afortunadamente, muy lejos (aunque la arrolladora victoria del partido ultra AfD en Sajonia-Anhalt arrastra ecos del pasado), pero hay situaciones, no solo en Europa, que recuerdan a lo ocurrido entonces: la estigmatización de pueblos y religiones, la violencia desatada contra población civil indefensa sin consecuencias, los discursos del odio y la deshumanización del otro, la manipulación del pasado, el ensañamiento con los débiles y los refugiados... El racismo y el supremacismo no deberían admitir compromisos. La historia nos enseña claramente que, cuando se deja crecer a la bestia, acaba por destruirlo todo.

World.title: La prueba que detecta la pérdida auditiva que los médicos no pueden diagnosticar
World.content:
Una enfermera realiza una prueba de audición a un estudiante en la Escuela Primaria Oneonta, el miércoles 12 de marzo de 2025, en Imperial Beach, California.

El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

Un grupo de investigadores ha desarrollado un dispositivo compacto y portátil para tratar la sinaptopatía coclear

Imagine que le cuesta seguir las conversaciones en un restaurante ruidoso o en una oficina ajetreada, y que, en cambio, el médico le diga que su audición está bien. Esa es la frustrante realidad a la que se enfrentan las personas que padecen sinaptopatía coclear, o pérdida auditiva oculta.

Según el Foro de Salud Auditiva de la UE , alrededor de 34 millones de adultos de la UE padecen una pérdida auditiva incapacitante. Sin embargo, es probable que la verdadera magnitud del problema sea mucho mayor, ya que las pruebas convencionales no pueden detectar en absoluto la sinaptopatía coclear.

No existe un diagnóstico clínico para esta afección ni ningún tratamiento autorizado, lo que hace que muchas personas sufran dificultades reales y no dispongan de ayuda alguna.

Esta pérdida auditiva oculta puede resultar incapacitante, según explica la catedrática Ingeborg Dhooge, directora del departamento de Otorrinolaringología del Hospital Universitario de Gante, en Bélgica. Dhooge fue asesora clínica en una iniciativa de investigación denominada EarDiTech, que estudió esta afección entre 2022 y 2026.

El proyecto lo financió el Consejo Europeo de Innovación, que ayuda a investigadores e innovadores a convertir ideas científicas audaces en productos del mundo real.

”Vayas donde vayas, siempre hay ruido”, declara Dhooge. ”Cuando vas de compras, hay ruido y suena música. En el trabajo, es común tener un espacio abierto como única oficina. Esto genera mucho ruido de fondo, que afecta a la productividad de estos pacientes”.

Las opciones actuales son limitadas: formar a las personas para que lean los labios y se centren más en los sonidos del habla. Sin embargo, los investigadores de EarDiTech han desarrollado una prueba capaz de detectar la pérdida auditiva oculta y han estado trabajando en un nuevo software para audífonos.

Cómo se altera la audición

En el oído interno, unas diminutas células ciliadas, las receptoras sensoriales clave, captan el sonido y convierten las vibraciones en señales neuronales. Estas se transmiten al cerebro a través de conexiones sinápticas entre las células ciliadas y el nervio auditivo.

Hasta hace poco, se creía que la pérdida auditiva relacionada con la edad se iniciaba debido a daños en las células ciliadas.

”Ahora sabemos que el primer daño que sufren las estructuras auditivas no se produce en las células ciliadas, sino que, en realidad, afecta a estas sinapsis que conectan las células ciliadas con el cerebro”, explica la catedrática Sarah Verhulst, directora del laboratorio de Tecnología Auditiva de la Universidad de Gante.

”Esta distinción es importante”, subraya Verhulst. Como coordinadora del proyecto de investigación EarDiTech, era consciente de lo que estaba en juego: basta con una sola sinapsis por célula ciliada para detectar un sonido, pero se requiere el funcionamiento conjunto de muchas para descodificar el habla en un entorno ruidoso.

La herramienta clínica habitual para evaluar la audición es el audiograma, en el que se reproducen diferentes tonos a diferentes volúmenes a través de unos auriculares y se pide a los pacientes que indiquen si los oyen.

Mide el funcionamiento de las células receptoras, pero no aporta información alguna sobre el número de sinapsis funcionales que tiene el paciente. No puede captar las dificultades a las que se enfrentan las personas con sinaptopatía coclear en el mundo real.

Recuento de sinapsis

La prueba EarDiTech combina electrodos colocados en la frente y en los lóbulos de las orejas con un estímulo especialmente diseñado que fue desarrollado tras años de investigación sobre la modelización del sistema auditivo.

”Hemos creado modelos informáticos de las células ciliadas y las sinapsis”, afirma Verhulst. Podemos simular las respuestas del nervio auditivo o la respuesta de las sinapsis en todo el modelo coclear. Mediante este método computacional, podemos determinar qué estímulo auditivo tiene mayor capacidad de activar todas estas sinapsis al mismo tiempo”.

La prueba está diseñada para dar la respuesta sináptica más potente posible. Cuando una persona con sinapsis sanas percibe el estímulo, los electrodos detectan un fuerte pico de actividad neuronal. En las personas que presentan pérdida de sinapsis, la respuesta es menor.

”Al comparar la intensidad de la respuesta de un paciente con la respuesta auditiva normal, podemos estimar el grado de sinaptopatía coclear”, afirma Verhulst.

Los investigadores han reducido el tamaño de esta tecnología hasta convertirla en un dispositivo compacto y portátil. Los ensayos clínicos realizados en la Universidad de Gante han demostrado que permite identificar la sinaptopatía coclear en diferentes grupos de edad.

La prueba es sencilla y no requiere ninguna intervención quirúrgica, por lo que puede integrarse fácilmente en la práctica clínica diaria, lo que proporciona a los audiólogos y a los otorrinolaringólogos una herramienta de la que actualmente carecen.

El siguiente paso es obtener el marcado CE, a fin de certificar que el producto cumple los requisitos de la UE en materia de equipos de diagnóstico médico. Según Verhulst, una vez que cuenten con la inversión necesaria para financiar este proyecto, el proceso tendrá una duración prevista de 18 meses a dos años. ”Creo que, cuando salga al mercado, los otorrinolaringólogos y los hospitales lo utilizarán”, añadió.

Un audífono más inteligente

Detectar la pérdida auditiva oculta es solo la mitad del reto. La otra mitad consiste en encontrar una solución.

Los audífonos convencionales se limitan principalmente a amplificar el sonido, lo que no ayuda mucho a las personas que tienen dificultades para distinguir el habla del ruido de fondo.

”Hasta cierto punto, los audífonos pueden ayudar, pero es complicado porque con ellos todo suena más alto, aunque no necesariamente más claro”, afirma Dhooge. ”Esto significa que los pacientes pueden seguir teniendo dificultades para captar distintos sonidos en entornos ruidosos”.

Para abordar este problema, el equipo utilizó el aprendizaje automático para entrenar un algoritmo de software a partir de dos modelos computacionales: uno que simulaba la audición normal y otro que simulaba el procesamiento defectuoso del sonido en una persona con sinaptopatía coclear.

El objetivo era crear un algoritmo capaz de modificar el sonido entrante de manera que estimulara al máximo las sinapsis que aún conserva el paciente. Esto mejoraría su capacidad para seguir el habla en entornos ruidosos.

Los ensayos clínicos han demostrado beneficios en pacientes con sinaptopatía coclear. El equipo también ha demostrado que el algoritmo puede funcionar con un bajo consumo de batería y en los chips de procesamiento que se utilizan habitualmente en los audífonos.

En teoría, esto significa que el algoritmo podría funcionar con la próxima generación de audífonos o, incluso, con los auriculares de los consumidores. Verhulst imagina un futuro en el que las personas podrán decirle a su teléfono que quieren oír mejor y este activará el software para la pérdida auditiva oculta en los auriculares.

Por el momento, el equipo de EarDiTech busca activamente fabricantes de hardware, como fabricantes de audífonos y empresas de circuitos integrados auxiliares, que puedan ayudarles a seguir desarrollando su software y convertirlo en productos que los pacientes puedan comprar.

El algoritmo utiliza los resultados de la prueba de CochSyn de cada paciente para ajustar el sonido a su grado específico de daño, algo que actualmente no puede hacer ningún audífono.

Más allá de la consulta

La pérdida auditiva oculta solo se ha identificado adecuadamente en la última década y aún se sabe poco sobre cuántas personas la padecen o cómo evoluciona con la edad.

”Ahora disponemos de una herramienta que podemos utilizar en la consulta para hacernos una idea más clara de la magnitud del problema y del grado de discapacidad que padecen las personas”, afirma Dhooge. ”Podemos realizar estudios a largo plazo haciendo un seguimiento de los pacientes y ver cómo evoluciona”.

Los investigadores esperan que esa base empírica sea lo que convenza a los sistemas sanitarios para que actúen.

World.title: Van de Zandschulp reaches US Open quarter-finals for second time
World.content:
Dutch number one tennis player Botic van de Zandschulp has reached the quarter-finals of the US Open after winning a five-hour marathon against Frenchman Arthur Gea.

The 30-year-old came back from two sets down to win the third and fourth sets on a tie-break before clinching the final set 6-4 in a match that swung back and forth.

Van de Zandschulp was warned by the umpire at one point for smashing a ball out of the stadium in frustration, but regained his composure as he wore down Gea, who only got into the tournament as a lucky loser.

“I’ve had some tough years, but since this year things have gone better,” he said afterwards. “I still need to let it sink in, but tomorrow I’ll probably wake up feeling good.”

Gea took the first set 6-3 after Van de Zandschulp failed to convert two break points at 3-3, while in the second set the Dutchman surrendered a 4-1 lead before losing the tie-break to love.

Van de Zandschulp was on the point of going out in straight sets when Gea served for the match in the third-set tie-break.

But the Dutchman won the point and went on to take the fourth set, also on a tie-break, before making the decisive break at 3-3 in the decider. He served out the match to wrap up the win in five hours, 13 minutes.

His reward is a daunting quarter-final against the top seed, Alexander Zverev, after the German beat Italy’s Luciano Darderi in straight sets. Zverev is aiming for his second Grand Slam title after winning the French Open in June and reaching the final of Wimbledon.

World.title: Nationwide 24-hour transport strike to go ahead as unions rally
World.content:
Thousands of public sector workers are expected to rally in The Hague on Tuesday against the cabinet’s social security cuts, a day before a 24-hour strike halts all trains, buses, trams and metros across the country.

Staff from councils, provinces, ministries, water boards and universities will march to the finance ministry behind a mock golden coach, a week before the real one carries the king on Prinsjesdag.

Union federation FNV said the coach carries a briefcase of alternative plans for the cabinet. Home care and nursing home staff are also taking part, and The Hague’s street cleaners are on strike.

“This cabinet keeps putting the bill on ordinary people,” FNV chairman Hans Spekman said in a statement. “The social safety net we have all paid into for years is being dismantled.”

No trains on Wednesday

The rally is the second of three days of action this week. Dockers in Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Zeeland walked out on Friday, and on Wednesday public transport stops for 24 hours.

NS is running no regular trains at all. The only exception is the airport sprinter between Amsterdam Centraal, Schiphol and Hoofddorp, which will run four times an hour.

International services, including Eurostar, ICE, Eurocity and the NightJet, will not run within the Netherlands, nor will the regional trains to Antwerp and Aachen. It is the first nationwide 24-hour public transport strike since May 2019, when unions walked out over the state pension age.

Back to normal on Thursday

NS expects to run its normal timetable on Thursday but is advising passengers to check the NS app shortly before departure. Its refund scheme for delays applies on strike days, although a separate allowance for alternative transport was scrapped earlier this year.

FNV called the strike in July as part of its campaign against plans to shorten unemployment benefit and cut payments for the long-term sick and disabled.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has since dropped a plan to raise the state pension age faster in line with life expectancy, and the cabinet has scrapped part of the remaining cuts and delayed others, according to the Telegraaf. The unions say most of the savings are still on the table.

World.title: Gridlock around A28 after bridge closed for emergency repairs
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Traffic on one of the main east-to-west routes through the Netherlands ground to a standstill on Tuesday morning after a motorway bridge was closed for emergency repairs.

The A28 has been closed at Nijkerk since Monday afternoon, when the highways agency Rijkswaterstaat closed the Hardenbergerbrug in both directions.

The motoring organisation ANWB reported a 23km tailback on the diversionary route on the A1 at 8.30am on Monday and 4km on the A704. Traffic was also at a standstill through Nijkerk.

The bridge was due to be repaired in November, but during an inspection the agency found that large quantities of sand and gravel around the concrete supports had washed away.

“The pillars are unstable and we can’t guarantee people’s safety,” spokeswoman Marike Broos told NOS.

The cycle bridge beneath the road and the canal below have also been closed to traffic.

Rijkswaterstaat is carrying out emergency repairs to support the bridge with sand and gravel before the strengthening works start in November, but it is not known when the road will reopen.

World.title: Nijmegen streets sealed off over gunfire report after Overasselt
World.content:
Armed police sealed off several streets in eastern Nijmegen on Monday evening after residents reported hearing what sounded like automatic gunfire. It turned out to be a false alarm, a week after the deadly attack in nearby Overasselt.

Officers ordered people around the Hengstdalseweg to stay indoors and out of sight, a police helicopter came in and the DSI special intervention unit of heavily armed police was called in. Police later said they had found no evidence that any shots had actually been fired.

“We are extra alert to reports like this at the moment,” a spokesperson told regional broadcaster Omroep Gelderland. A spokesperson told news agency ANP that the scale of the response was linked to the attack in Overasselt, roughly 10 kilometres to the south, in which two police officers were hit.

Belgian arrest

Police said on Sunday that a 26-year-old Belgian national had been arrested in Amsterdam on Friday in connection with the attack, bringing the total number of arrests to 35. Two people released earlier remain suspects.

Specialist teams backed by riot police are continuing to search Overasselt and the surrounding area for evidence.

Previous convictions

Several of the men being held have previous convictions for firearms offences, kidnapping and fraud, the AD reported on Monday, citing the list of suspects brought before an examining magistrate on Friday. Police declined to comment on the report to broadcaster NOS.

One 23-year-old from Amsterdam was jailed for four years after firing on a house in Antwerp in 2022, the AD said. The intended target was a relative of kickboxer Jamal Ben Saddik, but the gunmen hit the wrong address.

A second Amsterdam man was given 15 months, six of them suspended, for kidnapping and robbing an elderly man at gunpoint in 2024. A third, aged 20, appeared in court over a shooting late that year and is suspected of firing the fatal shots in Overasselt, according to the paper. Prosecutors have not said who they believe pulled the trigger.

World.title: Phone subscriptions for internationals: What you need to know
World.content:
Whether you’ve just moved here or are looking to change your mobile phone provider, finding a phone subscription in the Netherlands can be a daunting task. So many s! So many choices! So many requirements!

Sometimes, it seems as if you’re stuck in a Catch-22 situation: you need a BSN (Dutch social security number) to get a contract, but you often have to pay for it with a Dutch bank card. But to open a Dutch bank account, you will have to provide most banks with a BSN number (four banks in the Netherlands – ING, bunq, ABN Amro and Revolut – let you open an account without it, but you still have to provide them with a BSN number within 90 days).

To avoid this bureaucratic spiral, mobile service provider Simyo offers contracts without the usual required BSN number, giving you the option of moving beyond the prepaid plans most other companies offer to those without a BSN.

You can also use a foreign bank account to pay for your contract (although you must arrange that with customer service).

What’s the deal?

Simyo has been voted Best in Test by the independent Dutch consumer organization Consumentenbond for the second quarter of this year – its 38th time with that distinction.

Launched by telecom giant KPN some 20 years ago as an online-only mobile service provider, the budget Simyo uses KPN’s reliable 5G network, meaning you get excellent quality for a competitive price. (And if you have KPN internet and TV, you’ll get extra data at no charge.)

“Overall satisfaction with Simyo receives a 9.8 in the second quarter,” writes the Consumentenbond, which rates how satisfied customers are with their provider. Overall, Simyo got a rating of 8.2, “making it the Best in Test in during the second quarter of 2026.”

Specifically, says the Consumentenbond, “Customers report few outages regarding mobile internet and calling. They also experience few issues with slow connections. Administrative problems hardly occur. For example, about 1% reports a non-working SIM card, problems logging into the account, or an unjustified debit.”

Simyo’s mobile abonnement beat out Odido, Lebara and Vodafone/Ziggo, among others, in the consumer organization’s ratings.

À la carte pricing

Simyo offers both Sim Only and phone subscriptions that bear out its stellar quality to price ratio, with a Sim Only plan costing as little as €6,50 per month for the first year, increasing to €15 per month after 12 months. (And that includes Dutch taxes!)

For those looking for a subscription, plans offering 40 GB of data and 400 min/sms start for just €6,50 monthly (a temporary offer). You choose your plan à la carte, meaning you can decide how many minutes, gigabytes or months you’re looking for and the price will adjust automatically as you build your plan on Simyo’s website.

Buy a data cap

Don’t forget to take out the data cap for an additional €1 per month to save you from unexpected costs when your bundle runs out; your internet will then stop automatically when it reaches your limit.

Flexibility

Flexibility is another compelling reason to choose Simyo: monthly subscriptions allow you to adjust or cancel according to your needs and budget, doing away with those one- or two-year set contracts that lock you and your bank account in until they expire. That’s a huge advantage for internationals residing in the Netherlands for just a short period.

Data bundle

Simyo offers a data bundle for outside the EU that makes calling and internet surfing affordable while travelling.

eSIM cards

Simyo also offers eSIM (embedded SIM) cards that save you the hassle of inserting plastic chips, as you can download your mobile plan by scanning a code or using an app. You can manage your subscription via the user-friendly Mijn Simyo app.

“I wanted a second mobile number, for distant external contacts, to protect my main number,” wrote user Bert on Trustpilot, who gave Simyo a 5-star rating. “With an e-sim card from Simyo, I fixed that in 15 minutes, and it works fine.”

So if you’re looking for a new mobile phone plan, updating your old one or buying one for your teenage children, Simyo is an easy, affordable and reliable choice.

World.title: Netherlands must double water spending, delta commissioner warns
World.content:
The Netherlands must at least double what it spends on keeping the sea out and fresh water in, and even then it will not be able to prevent all the damage from climate change, delta commissioner Co Verdaas said on Monday.

Spending on flood defences, fresh water and climate-proofing currently amounts to about 1% of GDP, or just over €11 billion a year, and needs to rise to at least 2%, broadcaster NOS reported. His statements come ahead of the national budget day next week.

Verdaas gave a six-yearly review of the national delta programme to infrastructure minister Vincent Karremans. Carrying on as before “is not an option”, the infrastructure ministry said in a statement. The review stressed that the country is in “the next chapter of our water tradition.”

“We are world-renowned for our water management,” Verdaas said. “But this summer’s extremes have once again rubbed our noses in the facts. We are not going to make it with technology alone,” Verdaas said.

Pumps and salt

The review calls for billions of euros in new pumps at IJmuiden and, later, on the Afsluitdijk, so that river water can still be pushed out to sea as levels rise. NOS puts the IJmuiden works alone at around €2 billion. The pumping station protects some 4 million people, as well as Schiphol.

Preparations should also start now on new “Delta Works” to replace the Maeslantkering storm surge barrier near Rotterdam, and the IJsselmeer should be allowed to hold more water so it can keep supplying half the country in dry summers.

But technical fixes will not be enough, Verdaas said. Land use will have to change in the most vulnerable areas, including the bulb-growing Bollenstreek, the sandy soils of the east and south, the Noord-Holland coast and parts of Friesland and Groningen, where salt water is creeping in and farmers may have to change the crops they grow.

Households should expect “wet feet and flooded cellars” more often, the statement says, and hospitals and power installations will need extra protection from cloudbursts.

The findings follow a summer in which the Rhine fell to its lowest level in 80 years and the government formally declared a water shortage. The full Deltaprogramma 2027, with the revised strategy, is published on Prinsjesdag, September 15, alongside the budget.

World.title: Nazi’s daughter gives up looted Goudstikker painting
World.content:
The daughter of a Nazi official has given up all claim to a painting looted from the collection of Amsterdam art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, a year after it was spotted hanging above her sofa in photos on an Argentine estate agent’s website.

A federal judge in Mar del Plata approved a settlement on Friday in which Patricia Kadgien and her husband Juan Carlos Cortegoso can avoid trial for concealing the work, Argentinian media reported.

In return they have to each pay 2.4 million pesos, around €1,400, to a local mother and child hospital.

Portrait of a Lady now passes to Marei von Saher, Goudstikker’s daughter-in-law and sole heir, who has spent decades tracking down works from the collection. Her lawyers said she has agreed to let it go on show in Argentina before it is handed over, AP reported.

Estate agent’s photos

The painting had been missing since the war until August 2025, when AD journalists researching Kadgien’s father recognised it in photos of her house, which was for sale.

Friedrich Kadgien was financial adviser to Hermann Göring and fled to Argentina after the war. He died there in 1978 without ever being charged.

By the time police raided the house, the painting had gone and a tapestry of horses hung in its place. The couple were placed under house arrest and handed the work to prosecutors a week later.

Not a Ghislandi

The portrait of the Contessa Colleoni was catalogued by Goudstikker as the work of Giuseppe Ghislandi, but a court-ordered examination by Argentina’s national academy of fine arts concluded it was painted by Giacomo Ceruti, another 18th-century Italian, according to AP. Experts put its value at around $290,000.

Goudstikker died in May 1940 after falling into the hold of the ship carrying him away from the German invasion. Some 1,100 works from his stock were sold under duress to Göring and other senior Nazis, and the Dutch state returned 202 of them to his heirs in 2006.

World.title: Amsterdam canal swim raises record €3m for ALS research
World.content:
More than 3,300 people swam 2km through Amsterdam’s canals on Sunday and raised a record €3 million for research into the muscle-wasting disease ALS. Last year’s event brought in just under €1.73 million.

Swimmers set off from the Keizersgracht in groups every few minutes and finished at the Marineterrein, next to the maritime museum. A shorter 750-metre swim for children and less experienced swimmers took place earlier in the day.

Among the participants were 12 people who have ALS, some swimming under their own power and others towed through the water by family and friends. Television presenter Beau van Erven Dorens, radio host Marieke Elsinga, actress Monic Hendrickx and singer Maaike Ouboter also took part.

Hellespont origins

The event grew out of a 2011 fundraiser in which a group of friends swam the Hellespont in Turkey in memory of a friend who had died of ALS, raising €90,000.

The first Amsterdam edition followed in 2012, when some 1,100 swimmers, including the then Princess Máxima, raised €740,000.

ALS, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, causes progressive loss of muscle control and has no cure. Most patients die within three to five years of their first symptoms. Around 500 people in the Netherlands are diagnosed every year, according to broadcaster NOS.

Donations remain open until the end of September and the final total will be announced on October 1.

Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus. “This is about depriving people who illegally cross the border in organised groups, using violence or destroying border security measures, of the right to international protection,” Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister who oversees migration policy, told broadcaster RMF. Polska zabiega o to, by Unia Europejska przyjęła jej interpretację przepisów dotyczących ochrony międzynarodowej. „Chodzi o pozbawienie prawa do ochrony międzynarodowej osób, które nielegalnie przekraczają granicę w zorganizowanych grupach, z użyciem przemocy albo niszcząc… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) September 6, 2026 The station reports that, at a meeting of the European Council next month, Poland will propose expanding the interpretation of article 33 of the United Nations’ Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. That section outlines the principle of “refoulement”, under which states are barred from expelling or returning refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened. The article includes a clause saying that the principle does not apply if “there are reasonable grounds for regarding [a refugee] as a danger to the security of the country” in which they have arrived, or if they have a criminal conviction that makes them “a danger to the community of that country”. Poland wants that clause to be applied in situations where someone applies for asylum after being part of an organised and aggressive border crossing. Since last year, Poland has itself banned asylum claims from people who illegally cross the border from Belarus. Since 2021, the Belarusian authorities have encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to irregularly – and often aggressively – enter the EU. Poland’s asylum ban, which has exceptions for certain vulnerable categories of people, was introduced as a temporary measure in March 2025 but has been repeatedly renewed since then. Warsaw now wants a similar interpretation of international refugee law to be applied across the EU Its proposals come in the wake of July’s incident in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands of migrants irregularly entered from Morocco. Soon afterwards, Poland urged the EU to adopt tougher measures, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. Prime Minister Donald Tusk was also one of 22 EU leaders who signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. After last week's migration crisis in Ceuta, Poland has called for tougher EU measures, including an automatic ban on residence for anyone who enters illegally. It pointed to its own experience of dealing with "weaponised" migration from Belarus https://t.co/2VHn5ZUJx7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 5, 2026 Poland has long argued that the situation on the Belarus border is an example of how migration has been “weaponised” by Russia and its allies to sow social discord in EU countries. In response, Poland has invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, has deployed thousands of additional officers there (and granted them expanded rights to use firearms), and has banned asylum claims. In 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, and the figure remained as high as 30,000 in 2025. However, in the first half of this year, only 235 attempted crossings were recorded, which the Polish government has hailed as evidence of the success of its tough measures. However, Poland’s human rights commission recently raised concern at how long the technically “temporary” asylum ban has been in place. Some Polish courts have also ruled that Polish border guards acted unlawfully when forcing migrants back into Belarus. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Has Karol Nawrocki’s first year as Poland’s president been a success?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Poland’s right-wing president has been largely successful at transforming his office into an assertive centre of resistance to the liberal centrist-led government, frustrating its agenda through extensive use of constitutional powers. He has emerged as the leading unifying figure on the fragmented Polish right but faces new challenges moving towards the next election. Scuppering the government’s reform agenda Last month, Polish President Karol Nawrocki marked the first anniversary of his inauguration following a surprise victory in the May-June 2025 presidential election over Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, the candidate of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main governing party since autumn 2023, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. A relatively unknown conservative historian and head of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical research institute, Nawrocki ran formally as an independent but was backed by the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping. The election result represented a significant upset, ushering in a period of tense “cohabitation” between the Tusk government and a hostile president. The Polish presidency is not a day-to-day governing role, and in many respects largely ceremonial, but retains important constitutional powers. Karol Nawrocki has now issued more vetoes than any other president in Polish history Three vetoes on Thursday took his total to 37 in just ten months since taking office, surpassing the 35 issued by Aleksander Kwaśniewski during his ten years as president https://t.co/xf27K8Fyn6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 These include a legislative veto, which the government lacks the required three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, and the ability to suspend a piece of legislation coming into law by referring it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Given that a majority of tribunal members were appointed under previous PiS-dominated parliaments, this also functioned as a de facto veto. As a result, Nawrocki was able to severely complicate the Tusk government’s plans to push through its legislative and elite replacement programme, notably efforts to roll back PiS’s judicial reforms. This, combined with the political authority that stemmed from Nawrocki’s strong electoral mandate, meant that the government faced continued resistance for the remainder of its term of office until the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027. An assertive presidency From the outset, Nawrocki has been a much more assertive president than his predecessor Andrzej Duda, leveraging his mandate to carve out a role as an active centre of resistance to the government. Although both presidents were PiS-aligned, during cohabitation with the Tusk administration, Duda used his powers more selectively and occasionally sought common ground. Nawrocki, by contrast, interpreted his strong electoral mandate as authorising a more confrontational approach. He has surrounded himself with a strong political support base who have helped him to develop and carry forward a blaze of independent initiatives in both the domestic and foreign policy spheres. As well proposing a series of his own draft laws, Nawrocki has used the legislative veto far more frequently than Duda (who issued only 19 across two full five-year terms) or any previous post-1989 president in a comparable period. By mid-2026, he had already surpassed previous records, blocking over 40 government-sponsored laws on issues such as judicial reform, socioeconomic policy and defence financing. In foreign policy, where the president’s formal competencies are more limited, Nawrocki pursued independent initiatives that often diverged from, or complicated, the government’s line. He has, for example, prioritised close personal and strategic ties with the USA, positioning Washington as Warsaw’s primary security guarantor. He cultivated a high-profile relationship with the Trump administration that yielded commitments to ongoing US troop deployments in Poland, sometimes bypassing or challenging the Tusk government. On Ukraine, while supporting continued military and diplomatic aid, Nawrocki has adopted a more transactional and assertive approach, opposing rapid Ukrainian EU and NATO accession until bilateral issues are addressed, and taking symbolic steps such as removing a Polish state honour from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over unresolved historical grievances. Polish President Nawrocki has announced that he will strip @ZelenskyyUa of Poland’s highest honour in response to him naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII Ukraine's foreign minister condemned Nawrocki's "reckless" decision https://t.co/CEqj4aaHYg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 These have drawn criticisms that he is playing into Russian hands by weakening regional unity, but were clearly in line with changing Polish public attitudes towards its eastern neighbour. Uniting the fragmented right? Nawrocki has also emerged as the most important unifying figure on the increasingly fragmented Polish right. PiS, long the hegemonic force on the conservative side, has seen radical-right challengers, the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), gaining ground. In July, PiS also suffered its biggest ever internal split, with a significant group of parliamentarians aligned with former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki breaking away. All of this weakened PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński’s once unquestioned authority as the central broker on the Polish right; he is now one leader among several. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 Alone among leading right-wing politicians, Nawrocki possesses genuine crossover appeal across the fractured conservative landscape. His 2025 presidential victory showed that he could consolidate a broad right-wing coalition and attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists, capturing the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. Although he was the PiS candidate, Nawrocki operates as an independent authority outside of direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative independent figure, which gives him greater moral and symbolic stature than any partisan leader. Nawrocki’s assertive use of his constitutional powers has further reinforced his position as a natural focal point around which the broader right can unite. Many conservatives now look to him as a potential patron or broker ahead of the 2027 election. Nawrocki can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. However, he has no unifying mandate and his ability to bring together the right depends ultimately on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally non-partisan and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, Nawrocki lacks the party organisational levers needed to enforce messy backroom deals. Focus of government attacks The Tusk government knows that Nawrocki’s is now the most potent counterweight to its authority and potential unifier of the fragmented right, which is precisely why he has become the main focus of its attacks on the opposition. An essential element of this has been trying to portray Nawrocki’s more active presidency as destructive and undermining the unity of the Polish state. This forms a principal component of its broader “security” narrative, a calculated strategy to reframe political debate around the ongoing Russian threat. At a time of heightened geopolitical risk with hybrid threats against Poland, the government has portrayed presidential obstruction as undermining the country’s military readiness and ability to co-ordinate with its allies. Karol Nawrocki has sought to redefine Poland's presidency and become the figurehead of the right-wing opposition. So far, it is working, but questions remain over what his end goal is and whether these tactics will get him there, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/TNDRGGv2QT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The Tusk administration cites Nawrocki’s veto of legislation enabling Poland to access its €43.7 billion allocation from the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence procurement initiative as an apparently perfect example of this, although the president argues that the loans saddle future generations with a huge, long-term debt and undermine Polish sovereignty. In fact, Nawrocki is fairly relaxed about the government’s attempts to portray his more active presidency as obstructive. Rather, he feels he needs to be assertive because that is precisely what those who voted for him expect: action and change, not passivity or compromise. Nawrocki’s 2025 presidential victory was based on a sharp critique of the Tusk administration and framed, and widely interpreted, as a vote of no confidence in the government’s performance. The president believes that this gives him a strong mandate to confront the ruling coalition across a wide range of issues and that the greater political risk lies in undermining the political momentum that his win created and appearing weak or inactive, rather than in the government’s counternarrative that he is a “blocking” president. A clash between the right-wing president and more liberal government over Poland's receipt of EU defence loans has sharpened polarisation and turbocharged the ruling coalition’s “Polexit” and security narratives, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/Iu7rcJfj5e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 More broadly, Nawrocki is not too concerned about what the Warsaw opinion-forming elites say about him. His approach stands in stark contrast to earlier presidents, even right-wing ones such as Duda, who, conservative critics argue, paid excessive attention to elite and liberal media criticism and received no meaningful political reward or pay-off for doing so. Instead of seeking to present himself as a “president of all Poles” in the traditional, consensus-seeking sense, Nawrocki has deliberately prioritised appealing directly to his core electoral base: Polish voters living beyond the large urban agglomerations in smaller towns, rural areas, and the provinces. By maintaining an assertive, unapologetic style that resonates with this electorate’s sense of cultural and political marginalisation, Nawrocki has sought to consolidate that support rather than diluting it in pursuit of metropolitan elite approval. Poland’s most popular politician There have obviously been plenty of missteps along the way. One clear risk has been the sheer volume and sometimes seemingly indiscriminate nature of the legislative vetoes. While this has successfully blocked key elements of the government’s agenda and reinforced Nawrocki’s image as an assertive counterweight, it has also handed the Tusk administration a ready-made narrative that the president is simply an obstructive “veto machine”. A number of Nawrocki’s more high-profile vetoes, such as the cryptocurrency regulation law, have proved highly contentious. PM @donaldtusk called a classified meeting of parliament in a bid to persuade opposition MPs to overturn the president's veto of crypto-asset regulation, which Tusk said threatens national security. However, in a subsequent vote, the veto was upheld https://t.co/Vj0Zh9wxpH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 5, 2025 Moreover, some of the other constitutional instruments that he has sought to utilise have not been particularly successful or even proved counterproductive. These include attempts to introduce his own legislation or referendum initiatives that have been stymied in parliament, as well as his original idea of holding the government to account via the so-called “Cabinet Council”, a formal meeting of the Council of Ministers chaired by the president. Nonetheless, in general, Nawrocki’s strategy appears to have delivered political dividends for him. He can, for example, point to a number of foreign policy successes, particularly in cultivating close personal and strategic ties with the USA under the Trump administration and positioning himself as a significant actor on security issues. President @NawrockiKn has recorded the highest ever level of trust (54.8%, up 8.4pp since May) of any politician in the history of regular polling by @IBRiS_PL for @onetpl Foreign minister @sikorskiradek (42.6%) was second and PM @donaldtusk (38.1%) third https://t.co/POuUFR3Khk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 26, 2026 At the same time, Nawrocki has asserted a greater degree of independence from PiS than Duda was ever able to achieve. This has been helped by the simple fact that PiS is now in opposition rather than in government, which reduces the formal and informal constraints that tied his predecessor more closely to the party. As a result, Nawrocki has emerged as Poland’s most popular politician, with consistently high approval ratings that set him apart from both the government and right-wing opposition party leaders. Challenges ahead There are clear challenges ahead for Nawrocki in the run-up to next year’s election and beyond. The first is how to respond to the argument that electing a right-wing government would concentrate excessive power in one side of the political spectrum. This is an awkward point for Nawrocki because he himself used a version of this argument during the 2025 presidential campaign, presenting his candidacy as a necessary check on the Tusk government. Opponents of the right will inevitably turn this logic against the broader conservative camp in the run-up to the 2027 election, claiming that the combination of a sympathetic president and a right-wing parliamentary majority risks the very imbalance Nawrocki once warned against. A second, related strategic challenge arises if a right-wing government does take office, and Nawrocki finds himself cohabiting with an ideologically and programmatically aligned administration rather than a hostile one. In that situation, he would still need to carve out a distinct and independent role for himself. The risk is falling into the trap that afflicted Duda during the years of PiS government: being widely perceived as little more than the government’s “notary” or a passive rubber stamp for its agenda. Maintaining personal authority, visibility, and a sense of autonomy, while avoiding conflict with an ideologically allied government, would demand a different style of presidency from the approach that has defined his first year. The very assertiveness and independence that have served him well in cohabitation with the Tusk government will prove harder to sustain if the political balance shifts after 2027. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” those among the right-wing opposition who have celebrated Sunday’s state election victory by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted. The rise of the AfD has been watched with concern by many in Poland due to the party’s attempts to downplay the significance of Germany’s Nazi history and its sympathy towards Russia. W Polsce tylko idioci albo zdrajcy mogą się cieszyć z tryumfu AfD w Niemczech. Trochę się ich nazbierało w Konfederacjach i PiS. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 6, 2026 The AfD came first by a large margin in Sunday’s election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, with preliminary results giving it around 44% of the vote. The centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz is trailing in second on around 17%. The victory continues a recent rise for the AfD, which also came first in the Thuringian state election in 2024, with 33% of the vote, and second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition party. The AfD’s latest result was welcomed by some figures from Poland’s right-wing and far-right opposition. “Germany is waking up,” tweeted Jacek Wilk, a former member of Poland’s parliament who is part of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party. World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains. World.title: Poland to begin using sewage water to cool power plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will begin using reclaimed sewage water to cool power plants from the start of next year. The measures are intended to reduce the use of fresh water and make the power system more resilient to increasingly frequent droughts. The change comes after some of Poland’s power plants were partially shut down this summer amid a series of heatwaves and lack of rain that led to record-low water levels in many rivers. 💧⚡ Otwieramy sektor energetyczny na wodę odzyskaną. Od 1 stycznia 2027 r. polskie elektrownie i elektrociepłownie będą mogły wykorzystywać wodę odzyskaną ze ścieków komunalnych w systemach chłodzenia. Nowe rozwiązania przedstawiliśmy dziś wspólnie z ministrem energii… pic.twitter.com/qRDOgjcDwb — Dariusz Klimczak (@DariuszKlimczak) September 3, 2026 “This may seem to many like a minor change, but it is of fundamental importance for many power-generating units in Poland,” said energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Thanks to this, we will be even more resilient and even better prepared for crises of all kinds.” The legislation was first proposed by a group of MPs from The Left (Lewica) and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), two members of the current ruling coalition, in May, and was then approved by parliament in July. Last week, President Karol Nawrocki signed it into law. The law, which will come into force at the start of 2027, introduces a definition of water recovered from municipal sewage, which, in turn, will allow its use in the cooling circuits of power stations and combined heat and power plants. Power stations require large amounts of water to help cool and condense steam, which drives the turbines, back into liquid form so that it can be reheated into steam once more. Orlen Termika, a subsidiary of state energy giant Orlen, has announced that it plans to invest more than 1 billion zloty (€230 million) over the next four years to maximise the benefits of the change by connecting sewage treatment plants with three of its power and heat plants around Warsaw. According to Andrzej Gajewski, the CEO of Orlen Termika, one of the plants, Żeran, will be able to save up to 80% of previous water use. Another, Siekierki, will save up to 20%. The company also plans to install heat pumps to extract heat from sewage, which can then be used to help supply heat to residents of Warsaw before the water is then used to cool down the plants. Sewage is relatively warm, typically between 10°C and 20°C, making it a good source of recoverable heat. “From the point of view of security of supply for Warsaw’s residents and from the point of view of efficiency – that is, the price of heating – this is the best and most advantageous solution,” emphasised Gajewski. Poland’s power grid operator has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid a heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced https://t.co/fIDR4SimgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Poland has experienced increasingly hot temperatures in recent years. This summer, the country broke its all-time record, as temperatures reached more than 40°C. That, along with low amounts of rainfall, has seen rivers reach record lows. As a result, Poland’s power grid operator has this summer been forced three times to invoke emergency measures to ensure supply. Previously, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. Last month, state power supplier Enea announced that it had reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants due to the low level of water in the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, just over 1% of Poland’s total, was taken offline. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prime minister’s “right-hand man” elected as Polish constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition. Critics argued that the nomination violated the government’s pledge to “depoliticise” the TK, including by banning recently active politicians from sitting on it. Berek served as a government minister from 2023, when Tusk came to power, until last month, when he stepped down in order to run for the TK. However, it is far from clear what will happen next. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has this year refused to swear in four TK judges chosen by parliament, and he has made clear that he also opposes Berek’s candidacy. ✅Sejm dokonał wyboru Macieja Berka na stanowisko sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. pic.twitter.com/ek0ak9C33v — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 4, 2026 In mid-August, Berek announced that he was leaving the government, where he had served as minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy. Shortly afterwards, Tusk confirmed that Berek would be nominated to fill an upcoming vacancy on the TK. The prime minister argued that, during his time in government, Berek had undertaken a technocratic role that was “apolitical and nonpartisan”. He said that Berek’s extensive experience in constitutional law and the legislative process made him an ideal candidate. However, some MPs from Tusk’s junior coalition partners publicly opposed the nomination. They noted that the government’s parliamentary majority had, in 2024, approved a law banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. The law never went into force as it was effectively blocked by a combination of then-President Andrzej Duda and the TK itself, which were both aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party from 2015 to 2023 and now the largest opposition group. Polish NGOs have urged Tusk's "right-hand man" to withdraw his Constitutional Tribunal candidacy, warning his political ties could undermine efforts to restore the court’s independence. The nomination has also exposed tensions within the ruling coalitionhttps://t.co/jQn0MyuS7G — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 Ahead of today’s vote in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, it remained unclear if Berek’s candidacy would be approved. In the end, he obtained the necessary majority, receiving the support of 226 MPs among the 437 who voted in the 460-seat chamber. Within the ruling coalition, only four MPs voted against Berek’s candidacy, including one from Tusk’s own centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Klaudia Jachira. Another opponent was Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of Tusk’s junior coalition partners, and the speaker of the Sejm. Eleven MPs from the ruling coalition did not take part in the vote. The entire right-wing and far-right opposition voted against Berek’s candidacy. Berek is now meant to join the TK after the next vacancy on its 15-person bench opens up on 18 September, when the nine-year term of an existing judge, Justyn Piskorski, ends. However, under Polish law, a new TK judge must first swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the ruling majority in the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. Nawrocki argued that there were legal doubts over the appointment of the quartet whose oaths he refused to receive. However, the government says that the president does not have the right to assess their candidacies and that the swearing-in is merely a formality. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The four judges instead organised their own swearing-in ceremony in the Sejm before a notary, after which they forwarded their oaths to the president and attempted to take their seats on the TK. However, the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, refused to allow them to serve, citing their failure to swear an oath before the president. Święczkowski previously served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government and is still seen as loyal to the party. In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim order requiring that the four judges be allowed to take up their positions. However, Święczkowski has ignored it, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 It appears likely that Nawrocki will refuse to swear in Berek. “I think the last thing the TK needs is another politician, especially a politician who is a close collaborator of Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” said Nawrocki on Thursday. On Friday morning, ahead of the Sejm vote, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, addressed the chamber to outline the president’s opposition to Berek’s candidacy. He said that, as well as Berek’s political association with the government, there are doubts over whether he even meets the formal requirements to sit on the tribunal, in particular the need to have practised the law for at least 10 years. Berek says he does meet that requirement. Adding to the confusion is the fact that Tusk’s government does not regard the current TK as legitimate because of the presence of judges, including Piskorski, who were unlawfully appointed when PiS and Duda were in office. It ignores all TK rulings. Tusk has emphasised that one of the reasons he wants to appoint Berek to the TK is to help “fix” the tribunal. Berek’s nomination means that there are now eight TK judges chosen by the ruling coalition, giving them a majority on the court. However, with Nawrocki and Święczkowski refusing to accept four of them, and likely to reject Berek too, some kind of drastic action would be required to allow them to begin to serve. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. President Karol Nawrocki has launched a programme allowing Polish companies looking to expand into international markets to apply to join his foreign visits. “Seats on the presidential plane will soon be available to Polish businesses,” Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, announced in a video published on X. “I want Polish companies, including small and medium-sized ones, to be able to establish new contacts, develop existing business relationships and successfully conquer foreign markets alongside the president.” Już niedługo miejsca w prezydenckim samolocie będą dostępne także dla polskiego biznesu. Chcę, żeby polskie firmy, również te małe i średnie, mogły u boku prezydenta nawiązywać nowe kontakty, rozwijać już istniejące relacje biznesowe i z sukcesem podbijać zagraniczne rynki.… pic.twitter.com/kO6L1t1m4D — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) September 3, 2026 To launch the programme, Nawrocki’s office is already accepting applications from business representatives interested in joining the president on his trip to New York later this month to attend the United Nations General Assembly. A one-day Polish-American Economic Summit is also planned during the visit, linked to Poland’s participation in this year’s G20 summit, which is being hosted by the United States. When deciding which businesses to invite on the trip, the presidential chancellery says it would seek “well-established companies with the potential to grow in the US market and seeking new partners and opportunities for collaboration” Those selected will be invited to travel on the presidential flight from Warsaw to New York and back, and will also receive local transportation. However, other costs, such as accommodation, meals and any necessary visas, will have to be paid by the businesses themselves. Nawrocki’s office says that the new programme was launched in response to long-standing calls from businesses for presidential foreign visits to be used to promote the international expansion of Polish companies. Opportunities to join presidential visits will be offered regularly, with details of new application rounds published on the prezydent.pl website. In recent years, a growing number of Polish companies have expanded abroad, helped by the country’s strong economic growth over the past three decades. Polish mobile payments system BLIK has, meanwhile, expanded into Slovakia, while state energy group Orlen has sought to grow its presence in other European markets. Polish companies are less likely to expand beyond Europe, but there are some exceptions. Earlier this year, Polish infrared sensor maker Vigo Photonics acquired a US rival to reduce the impact of tariffs. Some Polish firms have also been looking to expand their presence in Africa.
