Poland has summoned Russia’s ambassador in response to recent hostile actions against Germany. “[We] expressed our strong condemnation of state terrorism perpetrated by Russia – because what is a problem for one ally is a problem for the entire alliance,” said Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Putin’s Russia remains one of the most serious security threats – not just for Europe, but for the entire world order,” he added. “Its goal is to permanently destroy the European security architecture.” 💬 Nie ma zgody na podpalenia, ataki na kolej, morderstwa i inne prowokacje. Polska też wezwała ambasadora Rosji po to, aby wyrazić nasze stanowcze potępienie dla terroryzmu państwowego autorstwa Federacji Rosyjskiej. | wicepremier, minister spraw zagranicznych @sikorskiradek… pic.twitter.com/LChAjwsX8H — Ministerstwo Spraw Zagranicznych RP 🇵🇱 (@MSZ_RP) September 3, 2026 On Tuesday, the German government announced that it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. In response, it ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin. This week also saw attempts to sabotage Germany’s electricity network in two locations. While they are still being investigated, on Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested that they may also be part of “Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region”. On Thursday, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that Russia’s ambassador to Warsaw, Georgy Mikhno, had been summoned to the ministry. Wewiór said that Poland wanted to convey “our firm opposition to the escalation of Russia’s aggressive actions” as well as to show solidarity with Germany. A number of other European leaders have also this week expressed solidarity with Germany, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Poland has itself been a major target for Russia. Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland was the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage. It has also suffered cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, and “weaponised migration” on its eastern border. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates in the country, with Moscow responding by doing the same with Polish consulates operating on its territory. This week, after a fire broke out at a drone factory in Poland, Tusk said that there is “no doubt” it was caused deliberately and suggested it was also likely carried out on behalf of Russia. There is now “no doubt” that a fire this week at a drone factory in Poland was caused deliberately, says Prime Minister @donaldtusk, who also suggested it was carried out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/fLdRcCLkgw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026 Speaking today following a meeting with his German and French counterparts, Sikorski said that, “in these difficult moments, we counted on our allies, and our allies can count on us”. “Poland supports the German government’s reactions and decisions regarding Russia’s aggressive actions in Germany, including decisions similar to ours, such as closing the Russian consulate,” he added. “We do not consent to unpunished testing of our borders or hostile actions on our territories.” Russia has denied responsibility for the drone incident in Leipzig, calling it a “fabricated provocation”. World.title: Prague Bids to Host 2029 European Figure Skating Championships
World.content:
Prague is preparing a bid to host the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships, with the O2 Arena expected to serve as the main venue if the Czech capital wins the right to stage the competition.

Prague City Council approved the candidacy on Monday following an approach from the Czech Figure Skating Union.

The proposal comes several months after Prague hosted the 2026 World Figure Skating Championships in March.



City councilor for education and sports Antonín Klecanda (STAN) said the success of that event helped encourage the city to pursue another major international competition.

“The response was very positive, and other countries asked whether another event of this kind could be held in Prague,” Klecanda said on Monday. “We reached an agreement, and today we approved our candidacy to host the European Figure Skating Championship in 2029.”

The 2026 World Championships attracted a record number of spectators for a figure skating world championship, according to Klecanda. He also said international visitors had responded positively to Prague’s role as host city.

The city has not yet determined when the 2029 championship would take place. The date will be discussed at a later stage, while Prague currently expects the competitions to be staged at the O2 Arena.

The financial impact of hosting the championships has not yet been calculated. The city would have to cover not only the direct costs of organizing the competition but also additional expenses linked to public services, including increased public transport capacity, emergency services and police deployment.

Klecanda said these costs could reach tens of millions of Czech crowns. He argued, however, that part of the expenditure could be offset by additional tax revenue generated by the event, while the championship would also strengthen Prague’s international profile.

The final decision on the host city for the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships has yet to be made.

World.title: Pickles Prague Festival: A Celebration of Pickled and Fermented Vegetables
World.content:
The Pickles Prague Festival will take place on September 19-20 at the Prague Exhibition Grounds, bringing together producers, food enthusiasts and visitors interested in pickled and fermented vegetables.

The festival will run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and will focus on the wide variety of vegetables preserved through pickling and fermentation.

More info here.

Visitors can expect everything from traditional pickled cucumbers, peppers and beets to less familiar varieties from the Czech Republic and abroad.

Alongside tastings and opportunities to buy pickled products, the programme will include workshops and educational talks covering pickling techniques, fermentation, the nutritional aspects of fermented vegetables and the role of preserved foods in different culinary traditions.



The event will also feature live music throughout the day, while a dedicated children’s area will offer activities for younger visitors, making the festival suitable for families as well.

Admission to the Pickles Prague Festival is free.

World.title: Czech Politicians Divided Over AfD Victory in Saxony-Anhalt
World.content:
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has secured a major victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, prompting different reactions from Czech politicians.

While some have congratulated the party and called for dialogue with its leaders, others have warned that the result reflects the growing strength of political extremism.

The result has also renewed debate in the Czech Republic over migration, security and how mainstream parties should respond to the AfD.



Martin Kupka, chairman of the Civic Democratic Party (ODS), described the result as a warning for Europe. He said democratic parties could not counter extremist movements simply by labeling them or ignoring issues that concern voters.

“Democratic parties must offer clear solutions: a tough migration policy, security, less regulation and no populist waste of public money,” Kupka said.

He added that the Czech Republic should avoid following the same political path.

Vít Rakušan, leader of the Mayors and Independents (STAN), similarly said the election should serve as a lesson for Czech politicians.

According to Rakušan, mainstream democratic parties risk losing voters when they leave issues such as migration and social problems to populist movements.

Rather than focusing solely on the AfD’s success, he said, democratic parties should develop practical and sustainable responses to issues that voters consider important.

Former Prime Minister Petr Fiala offered one of the strongest warnings. In a post on social media, the ODS politician called the result a “political earthquake” and said the AfD’s success could not be explained solely by the failure of mainstream democratic parties to address voters’ concerns.

Fiala argued that the reasons were more complex than economic dissatisfaction alone. “The causes are deeper and far from just economic,” he wrote.

The response from the Czech government’s current Foreign Minister Petr Macinka was more cautious. Macinka said the next steps by the AfD and Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) would be particularly significant.

He said it would be important to see how the winning party uses its strong mandate and how the CDU responds to the result.

Tomio Okamura, chairman of the Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party and speaker of the Czech Chamber of Deputies, took a more positive view of the AfD’s performance.

He congratulated the party and said the election showed that voters were dissatisfied with the policies of Germany’s established parties, particularly the CDU.

“The people of the former East Germany have made it clear that they no longer want this policy to continue,” Okamura said in an interview with Czech Television.

Okamura also rejected criticism based on the AfD’s classification as a far-right party. He questioned the credibility of reports concerning extremism and pointed to similar accusations involving his own SPD.

Radek Vondráček of the ANO movement also called for a different approach to the AfD. Speaking to Czech Television, the chairman of the Chamber of Deputies’ foreign affairs committee said the election had given the party a clear mandate and expressed hope that it would be able to form a stable government.

“I hope that the time for dialogue is coming, when citizens will receive some appropriate result for what they have chosen,” Vondráček said.

World.title: Boris Brejcha Brings his High-Tech Minimal Show to Prague in October
World.content:
One of the world’s most sought-after producers and the king of the high-tech minimal genre, German DJ Boris Brejcha, is returning to the Czech Republic.

As part of his Reflections world tour, he will perform at Prague’s O2 Arena on Friday, October 2, 2026. For electronic music fans, one of the highlights of the season.

Boris Brejcha, whose identity is inextricably linked to a mysterious Venetian mask, promises a show full of spectacular lighting and a breathtaking visual spectacle.

He is recognized worldwide as a creator and pioneer of the “high-tech minimal” genre. The concert will be the artist’s only performance in the Czech Republic.

Official ticket sales have already begun. Tickets are available exclusively through the official Ticketmaster and Ticketportal sales networks.

Where did the iconic mask come from?

At the age of six, Brejcha suffered serious injuries in a plane crash. He sustained severe burns to his face and body. Music became his escape, and he began producing it on his own at the age of twelve.

He launched his official career in 2006. He made his debut at the Universo Paralello festival in Brazil, where he was inspired by the local carnival and chose his iconic Joker mask, which has become an integral part of his image.

Brejcha is best known as a creator and pioneer of high-tech minimal—a musical genre that combines electronic music with elements of techno, house, and trance, featuring distinctive melodies. He plays exclusively his own original music.

“Hello, Prague! Returning to your beautiful city is always a special experience for me. This time, I’m bringing the ‘Reflections’ show to the O2 Arena, which will feature a unique visual stage and my exclusive extended set. I’m already looking forward to the amazing atmosphere we’ll create together in the arena. It’ll be a night we’ll never forget. See you there,” says Boris Brejcha.

The unique atmosphere will be further enhanced by artistic support from Brejcha’s own label, FCKNG SERIOUS.

World.title: Langdon Appears in Prague! Netflix Presents New Series Based on Dan Brown
World.content:
Netflix has begun filming its new series based on Dan Brown’s The Secret of Secrets, bringing Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon back to Prague.

The production officially started in the Czech capital this week, with Netflix releasing a first look at Morgan Spector as Langdon and Rebecca Hall as scientist Katherine Solomon. The series is currently untitled and does not yet have a release date.



Netflix has now added five more actors to the production. Mamoudou Athie will appear as Michael Harris, Ben Levi Ross as Alex Conan, Anamaria Marinca as Dr. Gessner, Richard Sammel as Karl Muller and Elena Saurel as Susan Housemore.

The series is being developed by Carlton Cuse, who co-created Lost and later worked on Jack Ryan, Locke & Key, Bates Motel and Five Days at Memorial. Cuse serves as co-creator, showrunner, writer and executive producer. Emma Forman is also an executive producer for Genre Arts, alongside Cuse and Brown.

Brown is involved in the project as a co-writer and executive producer.

The novel takes Langdon through several recognizable parts of Prague, including Charles Bridge and the Klementinum, as he searches for answers following Solomon’s disappearance. Netflix says the television adaptation will combine scientific ideas, historical mysteries and mystical elements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dan Brown (@authordanbrown)

The Secret of Secrets was published in September 2025 and became the latest installment in Brown’s Robert Langdon series. The book was released simultaneously in multiple countries, including the Czech Republic, and Prague is closely tied to its plot.

The Czech Republic is expected to play a significant role in the new television production. Prague has previously served as a filming location for a wide range of international productions, making the city a familiar setting for foreign film and television crews.

The arrival of the Netflix series could also have an impact beyond the production industry. Czech travel companies and Argo, the publisher of Brown’s books in Czech, have previously pointed to the potential for two waves of tourism connected with the project: first from readers discovering the novel and later from viewers of the television adaptation.

World.title: Prague Planetarium to Become a Concert Venue Under the Stars
World.content:
The Prague Planetarium in Stromovka will host a new series of chamber concerts combining live music with projections of the universe from September 2026.

Called Niche Nites, the series will feature 10 concerts between September 2026 and June 2027. Each performance will be accompanied by visuals projected across the planetarium’s 22-metre-wide dome, with the imagery responding to the music in real time.



The programme will take place on the final weekend of each month. Rather than staging repeated performances, each musician or group will appear at the planetarium only once, giving every concert its own programme and visual design.

The series will open on September 25 with cellist Terezie Kovalová, whose work combines classical music with pop, alternative and electronic influences.

Other performers confirmed for the programme include guitarist and composer Michal Pavlíček, who will appear with singer Bára Basiková, pianist and composer Beata Hlavenková, and singer-songwriter Lenka Dusilová. Further names will be announced by the organisers in the coming months.

Producer and dramaturg Michala Komrsková said the project is intended to present established Czech musicians in a more intimate setting than the large concert halls where they usually perform.

The planetarium’s technology will play a central role. Its dome is fitted with an LED system containing millions of diodes, allowing large-scale visual sequences to accompany the performances. The imagery will be prepared specifically for each concert rather than using a single projection throughout the series.

More recently, the planetarium was used during this year’s Spectaculare festival, which combined music by composer Rafael Anton Irisarri with visual work by Czech artists Dalibor Cée and Alex J. Jindrák.

World.title: Gipsy Kings by André Reyes to Perform in Prague This November
World.content:
The legendary Gipsy Kings by André Reyes will perform in Prague this November, bringing their distinctive mix of flamenco guitar, rumba and Latin rhythms to Lucerna Great Hall on November 29, 2026.

Led by founding member André Reyes, the group will perform some of the songs that made the Gipsy Kings famous around the world, including “Bamboleo,” “Djobi Djoba” and “Volare,” alongside newer material.



The concert is being presented by Gotobeat and will begin at 7 p.m. Tickets are online here.

From southern France to the world

The Gipsy Kings’ story began with the Reyes family and their musical roots in the south of France. André Reyes was one of the founding members of the group, which went on to combine traditional flamenco with rumba, Latin rhythms and pop influences.

Their energetic guitar playing and Spanish-language songs helped turn rumba flamenca into an international sound. Tracks such as “Bamboleo” and “Djobi Djoba” became global hits, while their version of “Volare” introduced the group to an even wider audience.

Music associated with the Gipsy Kings has sold more than 60 million records worldwide, making the group one of the most successful international acts to emerge from the flamenco-rumba tradition.

Their music has also appeared in popular culture, including their version of “Hotel California,” which featured in The Big Lebowski.

A new generation of the Reyes family

André Reyes continues the tradition today with Gipsy Kings by André Reyes, performing alongside younger members of the Reyes family.

The current show combines the group’s best-known classics with newer music, including material connected to Nací Gitano, the band’s latest project. The group is also touring internationally in 2026 as part of its Viva el Arte Tour.

For audiences, the concert offers a mix of familiar songs and new material, with the performance centred on the fast-paced guitar playing, percussion and vocals that have defined the Gipsy Kings sound for decades.

Date: Sunday, November 29, 2026

Time: 7 p.m.

Venue: Lucerna Great Hall, Štěpánská 61, Prague 1

Promoter: Gotobeat

World.title: No Tickets Needed: Six Free Events in Prague This September
World.content:
Prague is offering a packed lineup of free events this September, from an air show and science festivals to a rare public viewing of the Czech Crown Jewels and a celebration marking a local brewery’s 15th anniversary.

Here are some of the best events taking place across the Czech capital this month.



Free Sightseeing at Historic Sites

The National Heritage Institute will open selected state-owned castles, chateaux, monasteries and other historic sites to visitors for free on Sunday, September 27.

Most of the properties managed by the institute will take part, although the tours and routes available will vary by location. Free admission will cover standard tours and selected additional routes. Capacity is limited, so visitors must book a free ticket online in advance for a specific time.

The Prague 10 Science Festival returns to Gutovka on Saturday, September 12.

From 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., 25 stations will offer visitors the chance to take part in chemistry experiments, explore LEGO robotics, play math games and learn more about nature, technology and the human body.

The program will also include workshops, a competition, a toy and plant swap, and a science show by Michael Londesborough. DJ SÂN will perform from 6 p.m., with the festival continuing until 8 p.m.

Dokola Festival

The Dokola Festival will take place on September 10 and 11, focusing on creative ways to reuse items rather than throw them away.

Visitors can repair broken electronics, make furniture from leftover wood, upcycle old clothes or try making kimchi. The program will also feature talks, a clothes swap, an upcycled fashion show and stand-up comedy. Most of the program is free, although some workshops charge a nominal fee.

Břevnov Brewery Celebrates 15 Years

Břevnov Brewery will mark its 15th anniversary on Saturday, September 12, with a day of beer, live music and family activities.

From 11 a.m. to 9 p.m., the meadow beside Břevnov Monastery will feature beer from the local brewery, along with special brews from other monastic breweries from across the Czech Republic.

Live performances by HUGO, Funk Corporation and JAKSI TAKSI will accompany guided brewery tours, barrel-throwing and timed barrel-rolling competitions, as well as activities for children.

There will also be a workshop for visitors interested in learning how to brew beer at home.

Czech Crown Jewels on Display

One of Prague’s most prestigious treasures will go on public display this month, when the Czech Crown Jewels are exhibited in Vladislav Hall at Prague Castle from September 19 to 28. Admission is free.

The exhibition marks 500 years since Ferdinand I of Habsburg became King of Bohemia. Alongside the famous St. Wenceslas Crown, the display will feature the royal sceptre and orb, a coronation robe dating from 1653 and historic keys once used by guardians of the Crown Archive.

Visitors will enter through the South Gardens and Bull Staircase from Hradčanské Square. Everyone must pass through a security check, and organizers advise against bringing prams.

Letňany Airport Day

After a two-year break, Letňany Airport will once again open its doors to the public on Saturday, September 5.

This year’s event will focus on legendary training aircraft and pilot training during World War II and the postwar years.

The program will feature historic aircraft from the Czech Republic and abroad, demonstrations by the Czech Army and police, model aircraft and a chance to see the airport’s current operations.

Events will take place in half-hour blocks between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m.

World.title: Video: Two 14-year-olds arrested after fire-setting and vandalism at Hungarian school
World.content:
Two teenagers have been identified and detained after setting fire to rubbish, damaging trees and throwing stones at a surveillance camera outside a secondary school in Polgár, eastern Hungary. Police reportedly identified the suspects within just 24 hours.

The incident caused widespread outrage in the town after security camera footage captured the youths vandalising the public space in front of the local secondary school.

Camera footage captured the vandalism

Polgár Mayor József Tóth first reported the incident on social media in an unusually angry post, expressing his frustration over the destruction of trees, shrubs and flowers that had been carefully maintained throughout the hot and unusually dry summer.

The town’s surveillance cameras recorded two young people tearing out newly planted trees before apparently setting fire to rubbish in the public area. They also threw stones at one of the cameras, according to the footage released by the mayor. The damage came despite the municipality’s efforts to keep the area in good condition throughout the summer heat and lack of rainfall.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Police identified the suspects within a day

The vandalism prompted an immediate police investigation. According to HAON, officers in Hajdú-Bihar County identified the suspected perpetrators within 24 hours. The suspects are reportedly two 14-year-old boys.

The mayor subsequently shared a photograph of one of the minors on social media, describing the youths as having disregarded the basic rules of community life and calling for them to face the legal consequences of their actions. “In addition to legal accountability, his actions should result in public condemnation and contempt,” he added.

At the same time, his comments prompted a discussion about how communities should respond to serious vandalism committed by minors, particularly when public property and potentially dangerous acts such as fire-setting are involved.

The case has attracted considerable attention locally, with residents expressing anger over the destruction of public greenery and the apparent attempt to damage the town’s surveillance system. The investigation will determine the exact circumstances of the incident and what legal consequences the two teenagers may face.

World.title: PM Magyar: “Hungarians turned against Hungarians” in the past 16 years
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar told Parliament on Monday that over the past 16 years Hungarians had turned against Hungarians and “those who took an oath to serve the Hungarian people plundered the country”.

“The previous regime unleashed destruction”

He said the previous regime had unleashed such destruction that it left behind parched land, hospital wards at 40°C, trains with flaming wheels, and humiliated teachers, “as if a foreign army had marched through the country”.

While Hungarian families fought for survival, he said, the former political “mafia” leader, Viktor Orbán, had built “a private estate out of our labour and our tax forints”.

Magyar began his speech by thanking Speaker of Parliament Agnes Forsthoffer for assuming the responsibilities of the president of the republic in the interim.

He also thanked the viewers of public news channel M1, noting that after more than a decade, parliamentary proceedings had returned to public media airwaves. “Viewers can now hear the truth firsthand,” he said.

Magyar said the Hungarian people had often experienced devastation from external forces throughout their history. “That is why the betrayal committed by the governments of Viktor Orbán against Hungary over the past decades is unforgivable, because they did not attack us as a foreign army under foreign flags,” he declared.

He said the previous regime had unleashed such destruction that it left behind parched land, hospital wards at 40°C, trains with flaming wheels, and humiliated teachers, “as if a foreign army had marched through the country”. While Hungarian families fought for survival, he said, the former political “mafia” leader, Viktor Orbán, had built “a private estate out of our labour and our tax forints”.

Photo: MTI

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

“Denying responsibility amounts to complicity with the past”

Regarding the responsibility of previous governments, Magyar warned that denying responsibility amounted to complicity with the past, and that delivering justice was the most fundamental moral condition for laying new foundations. “And we will not be complicit,” he declared.

Referring to the former ruling parties, Fidesz and the Christian Democrats, Magyar said that a “solid future” could not be built as long as the “perpetrators” sitting in parliament tried to evade responsibility.

He thanked voters for the mandate they gave him on 12 April and said people had begun turning to each other again, with less hatred and more joy, with families no longer turning away from each other because of partisan politics. “Once again, we are thinking and acting as one united nation for Hungary,” Magyar said.

If you missed it: Magyar government targets thousands of billions in Orbán-era private equity deals

The prime minister said that by the spring of 2026, the state had “basically ceased to function” in areas such as railway services, hospitals, water management and schools. “The state gave up its most fundamental tasks: protecting its citizens and their dignity,” he added.

Magyar thanked nurses, teachers, police officers, firefighters, social workers, child protection and water management staff, as well as government officials, who, “despite the Orbán regime’s destructiveness, carried the country on their shoulders for years, trying to ease the consequences of the previous government’s ineptitude”.

Photo: MTI

Normal state operations “cannot be built on exploitation of public employees”

He pledged to build a state in which those people “do not need to take a daily exam of heroism and self-sacrifice”, arguing that the operations of a normal state “cannot be built on the exploitation of those working in the public sector”.

However, Magyar asked public sector workers for patience, citing the “extremely difficult” budget situation caused by “emptied coffers and amassed debt”. He said the government’s room for manoeuvre was severely restricted. “We have to fight for each forint, and we will do so,” he added.

Magyar said that there was no more uplifting mission than “restoring Hungary from the ruins,” while calling it “infinitely sad how little our predecessors loved the country”. “Anyone who truly loves their nation would never, not for a single moment, allow rural hospitals to fall into disrepair, leave Hungarian soil parched, or view their own people as mere subjects to be exploited while stuffing private estates with wealth stolen from the nation,” he added.

He said the government’s determination to act stemmed from this deep outrage, driving them to pull the country back from the “edge of the abyss” and begin “laying the foundations of a new fortress system”.

Magyar noted that the Tisza government had ended rule by decree and removed “the puppets of the Orbán regime” from their positions. He accused the former ruling parties of planning to lose the election while ensuring they never truly lost power. “We did not come here to assist those who covered up the plundering of the nation in any way, no matter where the political mafia placed them. We have no business with them,” he said.

The prime minister said they had negotiated the “historic” agreement with the European Union in just three weeks, whereas their predecessors “spent years merely blackmailing, vetoing and fighting a pointless battle on the international stage”, while denying Hungarian families access to their own lawfully due funds.

Photo: MTI

The government fully meets all conditions required to unlock EU funds

By 31 August, the government had fully met all the conditions it had committed to — despite every attempt to prevent it — thanks to thousands of well-prepared diplomats, lawyers and government officials working day and night, who showed the world what Hungarian expertise and professional dedication are capable of when they are finally given a clear goal and genuine appreciation by their government, he said.

Magyar said funds recovered would be used to renew public transport, develop the electricity grid and energy storage, modernise hospitals and primary care, support home renovations, Hungarian SMEs, research, innovation, digitalisation in education, and water management and environmental projects.

He noted the government had cut ministers’ and state secretaries’ pay and party group allowances and was now discussing a radical cut in the prime minister’s salary. Magyar noted that in July, the Hungarian budget had produced a surplus unseen for decades.

A National Asset Recovery and Protection Office has been set up “so that the fate of every stolen forint can be revealed”, he said, adding that the dissolution of 16 public-interest asset management foundations had returned over one trillion forints in public assets to the state. This included 845 billion forints in corporate stakes, 162 billion forints in cash, nearly 90 billion forints in securities and about 88 billion forints in real estate, he said.

Photo: MTI

Public media “freed” from “party propaganda”

The prime minister said the public media had been freed from “party propaganda” and expressed his satisfaction that parliamentary sessions could again be followed on the M1 news channel.

Magyar said the minimum old-age pension would be raised to 120,000 forints, benefits for people with changed work capacity would be restored, a 100,000-forint school-start allowance would be introduced, the price of firewood would be cut by 5 percent and resources for social firewood frameworks would be doubled, and VAT on prescription drugs scrapped.

He said there had been critical weeks this summer when the country had had to fight for its sheer physical functioning, in reference to problems at the Paks nuclear power plant, and he thanked Hungarian families and businesses for curbing their consumption. He outlined measures taken to protect the plant and said that in the coming weeks, permanent technical protection would be built at Paks.

“For us, this is what a functioning Hungary means,” he said, adding: “We do not shirk responsibility, we do not paralyse ourselves, we do not make excuses, we assess the situation, we decide and we act.”

The government was building a functioning rule-of-law state with clear steps, and would review and transform concessions, Magyar said.

“We will take back what we can”

He stressed that they faced a historic task: laying new, rock-solid institutional foundations. They would start where money had been flowing unchecked into private pockets for years, and in the coming weeks, they would review and likely completely transform the tobacco, casino, waste and motorway concessions, he said, adding that the billions in profits would then enrich the community, the budget and Hungarian taxpayers instead of “private oligarchs”.

“From what the Orbán regime cynically siphoned off over the decades, we will take back what we can, renegotiate where necessary, while filling the state administration with qualified experts,” he said.

Regarding the protection of natural treasures, the prime minister spoke of tightening environmental fines, setting up the National Environmental Inspectorate, submitting a new climate law to parliament and launching a national afforestation programme.

In health care, Magyar highlighted the publication of hospital infection data hidden for years, reducing waiting lists, launching a hospital cooling programme, renewing the financing of GP practices and restoring the dignity of the midwife network.

New budget to begin wage adjustments

He said the new budget to be submitted in mid-October would begin wage adjustments for those in education, social and child protection work, law enforcement and national defence. A stricter child protection law would be adopted and a national drug strategy launched, he added.

The prime minister said they would put a roof over the heads of those guaranteed affordable housing by the housing law, launch the “Your homeland awaits” programme to bring back talent forced abroad, restore freedom in research and develop a modern higher education strategy. A large-scale main and secondary road renovation programme would be launched, railways would be developed and “stolen” local government autonomy would be returned to settlements, he said.

Magyar said order would also be restored in the world of bailiffs, notaries and liquidators.

World.title: FM Anita Orbán reports progress on minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine
World.content:
Hungary says progress has been made in securing minority rights for the Hungarian community in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region, with Kyiv beginning preparations for the legislation needed to implement previous commitments.

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said on Monday that the latest developments marked a step forward in efforts to protect the rights of ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia. She said she had spoken three times with Hungary’s consul general in Uzhhorod over the previous 48 hours, as Ukraine’s education ministry had begun preparing the necessary legislation.

Hungary and Ukraine resume minority talks

Orbán recalled that minority rights consultations between Hungary and Ukraine resumed on 20 May. Since then, she said, the two sides had secured concrete commitments from Kyiv. Under the agreement, Ukraine has pledged to incorporate the minority rights discussed during the negotiations into national legislation.

According to Orbán, the first tangible result has already emerged. Following a decision by the Ukrainian government on 15 July, the network of small educational institutions will be preserved from 1 September, while their state funding will also continue.

The issue is particularly significant for Hungary’s community in Transcarpathia, where access to education in the Hungarian language has been a long-standing concern.

EU also links minority plan to talks

Hungary has also sought to ensure that Ukraine’s obligations are reflected at EU level. At Hungary’s initiative, the European Union has stipulated that Ukraine’s minority action plan must be brought into line with the results of the Hungarian-Ukrainian negotiations, Orbán said.

“This is now about implementation, and both sides are working on it,” the minister wrote.

Hungary and Ukraine have recently been putting effort into addressing longstanding disputes over the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. Budapest has repeatedly called for guarantees concerning education, language use and other minority rights, while Kyiv has been seeking closer integration with the European Union.

World.title: Orbán’s Fidesz demands EU ‘immediately release’ all funds owed to Hungary
World.content:
Fidesz MEPs are demanding the European Union immediately and unconditionally release billions of euros in funding for Hungary, while also calling for more money for border protection and agriculture.

The Fidesz-KDNP group in the European Parliament has called for the immediate and unconditional payment of all EU funds allocated to Hungary, arguing that money negotiated by Viktor Orbán’s government has been withheld for political reasons.

In a statement sent to Hungary’s state news agency MTI on Monday, the group said it wanted the EU’s 2027 budget increased by EUR 11 billion. Tamás Deutsch, a Fidesz MEP and member of the European Parliament’s Budget Committee, submitted the proposal on behalf of the Hungarian delegation.

Fidesz demands billions in frozen EU funds

According to Fidesz, around 55% of the funding under three Hungarian operational programmes – approximately EUR 6.3 billion – was frozen in 2022 for political reasons. The party is now demanding that not only the post-pandemic recovery funds but also Hungary’s entire cohesion funding allocation be paid without conditions.

Fidesz stressed that an Orbán-led delegation negotiated EUR 22 billion in cohesion funding for Hungary in December 2020, in addition to the EU’s recovery fund. The party claims that part of this money has subsequently been withheld by the European Commission and what it called the European Parliament’s “liberal majority”.

The statement also called for a EUR 2.5 billion increase in the Common Agricultural Policy budget, with additional support for young farmers, the wine sector and beekeepers.

If you missed it: Here comes the twist: could Fidesz and Mi Hazánk be heading for a merger?

More EU money for border protection

The Hungarian delegation within the European Parliament’s Patriots group is also seeking major changes to EU spending on migration. It wants EUR 1 billion removed from what it describes as the EU’s “failed” migration policy and EUR 2 billion more allocated to border protection. The group is specifically demanding reimbursement for Hungary’s border-protection costs.

“We demand that the illegally forced-through migration pact be reviewed and withdrawn,” Fidesz-KDNP said.

The group is also seeking to double the EU’s agricultural crisis fund from EUR 450 million to EUR 900 million, citing the damage caused by drought. It said recent dry conditions had reduced cereal and maize yields by 20–30%, while livestock farmers have also been struggling with damaged pastures and soaring feed prices.

Fidesz also targets Erasmus funding

Fidesz-KDNP has once again proposed placing Erasmus funding for Hungary’s foundation-run universities into reserve until the European Commission releases the money.

The issue has already begun to change, however. Education Minister Judit Lannert announced last week that Erasmus will return to Hungary’s universities from the 2026/2027 academic year, with students at all 21 universities previously affected by restrictions once again able to participate.

If you missed it: Erasmus returns to Hungary – Hungarian university students can once again study abroad!

Fidesz nevertheless accused the Tisza government of failing to resolve the dispute and called for the Commission to immediately lift the restrictions.

The group also proposed cutting EUR 250 million from EU funding programmes supporting what it described as “left-wing” civil society organisations, arguing that member states should not face politically motivated pressure from EU institutions.

World.title: Hungarian Ferencváros fans face police complaint after ‘We’ll beat you to death’ banner
World.content:
Police are examining a complaint over a threatening banner displayed by Ferencváros supporters during Sunday’s derby against Újpest, while the club says it “basically condemns all threats”.

The Ferencváros–Újpest derby ended in a 2-2 draw on Sunday, but the football result was overshadowed by a bitter exchange between the two fanbases in the stands. Among the banners displayed by Ferencváros (Fradi) supporters was a particularly disturbing message directed at anyone who might “hurt” the club:

“Love Fradi and you’ll be happy. If you hurt Fradi, you’ll be dead. Love Fradi and support them with us; if you hurt Fradi, we’ll beat you to death.”

The message has now resulted in a police complaint. According to Magyar Hang, the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) has received a report concerning the banner and is currently examining its contents. A criminal investigation has not yet been formally launched over the threat.

Fradi asked to condemn threats

Telex contacted Ferencváros to ask whether the club condemned the message and how it viewed a separate incident in which a critic of club president Gábor Kubatov was allegedly attacked by masked men after a men’s handball match.

The club initially declined to comment on the attack, saying that a police investigation was under way and that it would not discuss the case until that process was completed. After repeated questions, however, Ferencváros gave a brief response concerning the threatening banner:

“The FTC basically condemns all threats.”

The club’s press office repeatedly shifted attention to a banner displayed by Újpest supporters reading “Gábor Kubatov, start worrying”, asking whether the media intended to comment on what it considered a threat against its president.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The controversy surrounding Fradiváros

The increasingly hostile atmosphere is linked partly to the long-running Fradiváros controversy, which concerns billions of forints in state funding awarded to Ferencváros for the development of its Népliget sports complex.

Ferencváros received almost HUF 25 billion (about EUR 63 million) in state support in 2016 and 2017 for the project. However, little of the planned development materialised. According to the club’s accounts, much of the money was reported as operating and material expenditure, while HUF 11.2 billion was spent on signing professional footballers.

The Hungarian Interior Ministry has filed a criminal complaint over the matter, and an investigation is under way. Journalists investigating the spending have subsequently become targets of threats from sections of the club’s fanbase. A banner recently appeared referring to journalist János Kele, who reported extensively on the Fradiváros case, while another message targeted journalist András Murányi.

If you missed it: Ferencváros narrowly beaten by Real Madrid at packed Groupama Arena

From threats to an alleged attack

The controversy has also moved beyond banners and online messages. Last week, four masked individuals allegedly attacked Zoltán Lajos Németh, who runs the C-Közép supporters’ blog and has long been critical of Kubatov. He was reportedly sprayed with pepper spray and called a “traitorous lackey” following the Ferencváros–Dabas handball match.

World.title: FlixBus launches domestic services in Hungary: 14 cities now connected, including direct airport routes!
World.content:
FlixBus has officially launched domestic ticket sales in Hungary, allowing passengers to travel between Hungarian cities on its existing international routes without needing an international ticket. The service currently covers 41 domestic connections across 16 international routes, linking 14 Hungarian cities.

FlixBus finally enters Hungary’s domestic travel market

Hungary has been one of the few European countries where FlixBus had not yet established a domestic network, despite already operating domestic services across most European markets and several neighbouring countries.

Now, as FlixBus celebrates the 10th anniversary of its presence in Hungary in 2026, the company is changing this, immediately expanding domestic mobility options for both local residents and tourists visiting the country.

By 2026, FlixBus had built an extensive international network connecting Hungary with almost every part of Europe. A total of 65 international routes link Hungary with 267 cities in 21 countries. These routes have long included stops in Hungarian cities, but passengers can now also purchase tickets for journeys between those domestic stops.

Direct buses from Budapest Airport to major Hungarian cities

One of the most significant additions is the introduction of direct connections between Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport and major cities outside the capital – a service that has so far been largely missing from Hungary’s transport offering.

Passengers can now travel directly from the airport to Szeged, Győr, Miskolc, Siófok, Debrecen, Kecskemét and Szolnok, covering seven major Hungarian cities outside Budapest.

The longest airport connection currently operates between Budapest Airport and Debrecen, taking around 2 hours and 45 minutes. All other destinations can be reached in less time.

The airport routes operate in both directions, meaning passengers travelling from Hungary’s major cities can reach the airport directly, while international visitors arriving in Budapest can continue straight to their final destination without changing buses.

“Connecting Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport directly with Hungary’s major cities creates a travel option that simply did not exist before: passengers can now get from the airport to Miskolc, Szeged or even Siófok easily and affordably by bus – without a taxi, transfer or car hire,” said Michal Leman, Vice President of FlixBus’ Eastern European region.

“For Hungarian passengers living outside the capital, this is a genuine new option: once they land at the airport, they can arrange their journey home with just a few clicks by booking through the FlixBus app. We believe this type of convenient, accessible and sustainable mobility will benefit not only passengers, but Hungarian tourism as a whole – and this is only the beginning.”

FlixBus services in Hungary. Photo: FlixBus

14 cities and 41 domestic connections already available

Beyond the airport links, FlixBus’ domestic network already covers many of Hungary’s largest cities.

The 41 currently available domestic connections serve 13 Hungarian cities outside Budapest:

Győr

Siófok

Szeged

Kecskemét

Debrecen

Miskolc

Szolnok

Hévíz

Keszthely

Sárvár

Sopron

Nagykanizsa

Székesfehérvár

Within Budapest, passengers can access domestic connections from several major stops, including Népliget, Kelenföld, Keleti railway station and Mexikói út, making the service accessible from different parts of the capital.

Another notable connection is the international route running between Sopron, Sárvár, Hévíz and Keszthely. Passengers can now purchase tickets between the Hungarian stops on the route connecting Brno and Zagreb, opening up another domestic travel option.

These are currently the most popular routes

Since domestic ticket sales began, passengers have already made their preferences clear. Based on booking data so far, the five most popular domestic connections are:

Budapest Népliget – Budapest Airport Budapest – Siófok Budapest – Kecskemét Budapest – Győr Budapest – Miskolc

The current 16 routes are expected to be joined by additional services in the near future, with FlixBus saying its network for domestic travellers will continue to expand.

If you missed it: New Budapest Airport FlixBus service launches in days as Wizz Air rolls out in-flight perk

How much do FlixBus domestic tickets cost?

FlixBus domestic tickets are available through the company’s website and mobile app. The ticket price includes the transport of one smaller and one larger piece of luggage, onboard Wi-Fi and travel in an air-conditioned coach.

However, travellers should be aware that ticket prices are dynamic rather than fixed, meaning they change depending on demand.

Some starting fares currently include:

Budapest Airport – Kecskemét: from HUF 1,599 (EUR 4.4)

from HUF 1,599 (EUR 4.4) Budapest Airport – Szeged: from HUF 2,249 (EUR 6.2)

from HUF 2,249 (EUR 6.2) Budapest – Siófok: from HUF 2,349 (EUR 6.5)

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

FlixBus points to neighbouring countries as proof of demand

Based on its ten years of experience in Hungary, FlixBus says it wants to see greater competition in Hungary’s long-distance public transport market.

The company argues that opening up the market would not only make transport more competitive, but could also improve mobility across the country and make smaller cities easier to reach.

The first step came in March 2026, when FlixBus began selling tickets between Budapest Keleti railway station and Budapest Airport. This was the company’s first domestic cabotage service in Hungary.

Although it was a relatively modest beginning, the company says it demonstrated that FlixBus is ready to gradually build a domestic network in Hungary.

Examples from neighbouring countries suggest that demand could be substantial if the Hungarian market is opened further.

In Romania, passengers responded strongly to liberalisation. Between July 2025 and February 2026, just eight months, FlixBus carried 300,000 passengers on domestic routes, accounting for almost half of all FlixBus passengers in Romania during the period.

In Croatia, FlixBus’ domestic expansion added 2.7 million kilometres of new annual capacity to the network, creating connections that either did not previously exist or had been difficult to access.

Improved connections between Croatia’s Adriatic coast and inland regions have also had a direct impact on both tourism and local mobility.

With its first domestic services now available in Hungary, FlixBus appears keen to follow a similar path – potentially giving travellers a new alternative for getting around the country without relying on cars, taxis or multiple connections.

World.title: 5 children’s remains found in unmarked grave in Hungary: They may have died together – Photos
World.content:
The remains of five unidentified children, including a baby, have been discovered in an unmarked grave in Kerepes, near Budapest. The children are believed to have died at least 80–100 years ago, and may have been victims of an epidemic or other devastating illness.

Remains discovered during cemetery works

The discovery was made by chance during landscaping work at the local cemetery in Kerepes. Workers came across an unmarked grave that did not appear in any official records. Neither cemetery staff nor local historians were aware that the grave existed, Blikk reports.

Although burials have taken place in Kerepes for centuries, there are no surviving records identifying the five children or explaining how they came to be buried together.

The size of the bones immediately indicated that they belonged to children. Their condition suggests that the burial dates back at least eight to ten decades, and possibly even longer. Apart from the bones, nothing else survived in the soil, not even traces of coffins or clothing.

May have died at the same time

The way the children were buried may offer a clue about what happened to them. Rather than being hastily buried or thrown together, the remains were found carefully arranged next to one another. This suggests that the children may have died around the same time. One possible explanation is that they were victims of a serious disease or epidemic that swept through the community many decades ago.

Local officials also believe the discovery does not point to a recent crime. The extensive deterioration of the remains is consistent with a burial dating back many decades, if not a century or more.

If you missed it: Was the weather completely different 500 years ago? This is what was recorded in the days before the Battle of Mohács

A final resting place at last

With no names or records available, the identities of the children are likely to remain unknown. However, Kerepes Municipality decided that the remains should not be left forgotten. The five children were given a proper reburial in the local cemetery, with an officially registered and maintained resting place marked by an unnamed grave cross.

Kerepes Mayor László Gyuricza described the ceremony as the saddest duty of his time in office, saying the five forgotten children had finally been given a dignified final resting place.

The ceremony was attended by a local cantor and staff involved in arranging the reburial. After decades (and perhaps a full century) of lying forgotten beneath the ground, the five unidentified children can now rest in peace.

World.title: Former Slovak police chief warns Hungary’s asset recovery office: ‘2 years should be enough for accountability’
World.content:
Former Slovak police chief István Hamran has criticised the head of Hungary’s newly established National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH), saying it is unacceptable to suggest that no legally final corruption convictions can be expected for six years.

Hamran, who led Slovakia’s police force between 2021 and 2023, discussed Hungary’s new anti-corruption institution, accountability and the challenges facing investigators in an interview with Slovak-Hungarian news outlet Bumm.sk.

He said he was initially somewhat sceptical about the idea of creating a dedicated authority to recover assets allegedly diverted through public procurement and other schemes. However, he acknowledged that the NVVH has been given strong formal powers, its own budget and staff.

“On paper, the conditions are good,” Hamran said.

‘Six years without results is unacceptable’

Hamran was particularly critical of Anna Róza Unger, the political scientist chosen by Hungary’s parliament to lead the NVVH for six years. Unger has no previous experience as an investigator, prosecutor or judge, although Hamran said she should be given an opportunity to prove herself.

What he found unacceptable, however, was Unger’s suggestion that expecting final court convictions within six years would be unrealistic.

“I understand that Hungarian courts work slowly, but even as the head of a new authority, you cannot say this in advance,” Hamran said. “It discourages those who are waiting for accountability.”

He pointed to Slovakia’s experience after 2020, when investigations reached senior politicians, police chiefs, prosecutors and business figures. According to Hamran, more than 40, approaching 50 people, received final convictions within two years.

“If a country invests money, energy, experts and six years into an authority specifically created for this purpose, but it cannot produce a single result backed by a final conviction, I would immediately dissolve it,” he said.

‘It’s the people, not the organisational chart’

Hamran argued that the success of an anti-corruption authority ultimately depends less on its formal powers than on the people working inside it.

During his time as Slovakia’s police chief, he said he replaced investigators he considered untrustworthy with experienced officers and younger recruits. This, he claimed, helped dramatically improve public confidence in the police and enabled investigations into previously untouchable figures.

He also warned that investigators need political independence and personal courage.

“You need professionals who cannot be bought, who do not want to serve politicians, oligarchs or influential businessmen, but the public interest,” he said.

If you missed it: PM Magyar vows to tighten asset recovery rules and refuses to bow to political pressure

A warning from Slovakia

Hamran believes Hungary faces another challenge: ensuring that institutional reforms survive future changes of government. He pointed to Slovakia, where Robert Fico’s return to power was followed by the abolition of the National Criminal Agency (NAKA) and the Special Prosecutor’s Office.

For Hungary, he said, this should be a warning that simply establishing a powerful new institution is not enough. Strong legal and social safeguards are needed to make it harder for a future government to dismantle it.

Hamran also believes Péter Magyar’s government must avoid turning accountability into political revenge.

“Politicians cannot decide who should be handcuffed or imprisoned,” he said. Investigators should examine well-founded suspicions regardless of who is involved, while courts must ultimately decide guilt.

The former police chief also warned that Viktor Orbán could eventually return to power if the new government fails to meet voters’ expectations. For Magyar, he said, creating the NVVH is therefore only the beginning. The authority must quickly demonstrate lawful, credible results, or risk disappointing the very voters who demanded accountability.

World.title: Falling Profits Cloud Horizons for Turkey’s Booming Tourist Industry
World.content:
Turkey continues to draw millions of holidaymakers to its beaches, resorts and historic sites, but beneath the headline visitor numbers, the country’s tourism industry is showing signs of strain.

After a record year, Turkey entered 2026 with high hopes, having hosted nearly 64 million visitors and generated 65.23 billion US dollars in tourism revenue in 2025, up 2.7 and 6.8 per cent respectively compared to 2024, and ranking fourth globally for international tourist arrivals.

However, official figures show that visitor numbers actually fell 5.1 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, while tourism revenue dropped 2.6 per cent to 15.87 billion US dollars.

Meanwhile, industry data cited by Turizm News showed average hotel occupancy falling from 40.17 per cent in the first half of 2025 to 36.80 per cent in the same period this year.

World.title: BIRN Fact-Check: Has Romania Made a Success of Post-Pandemic EU Funding?
World.content:
In the final two weeks of August, Romania was suddenly awash with positive news. Almost every day brought reports of a renovated hospital or school, new stretches of motorways or railway lines, completed water and sewage networks, or newly rehabilitated public buildings.

Authorities announced new green hydrogen production facilities, reforestation projects covering large areas of land and other investments, all presented as evidence of Romania’s rapid modernisation.

The wave of announcements was driven mainly by the August 31 deadline for it to complete numerous projects financed through the European Union’s post-pandemic recovery programme, the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, PNRR.

Authorities rushed to showcase projects launched, completed, or brought close to completion, often presenting them as tangible proof that Romania had successfully used the unprecedented EU funding made available after the pandemic.

World.title: Czech PM’s Balkan Schengen Illusion Is a Security Risk for Europe
World.content:
A geopolitical trap

In the case of the Western Balkan states, the issue of Schengen accession carries a strong geopolitical dimension. While even the harshest EU sceptics did not question Croatia or Romania’s pro-Western orientation, fundamental questions remain about the true foreign policy orientation of some Western Balkan states and their willingness to align their policies with Europe.

This issue is particularly evident in Serbia, which has maintained close ties with Russia and China as part of a foreign policy that seeks to balance competing geopolitical interests, while remaining reluctant to bring its policies fully into line with those of Europe.

Certain recent gestures by President Vucic, such as hosting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky or rearming the country’s air force by replacing Russian MiGs with French Rafale fighters, do not signal a Serbian turn away from Russia, but are merely a reflection of his long-standing policy of geopolitical balancing, which is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain as geopolitical tensions between Europe and Russia escalate.

A key problem with Babis’s proposed accelerated Schengen accession is Serbian visa policy, which precisely reflects the country’s geopolitical balancing act. Serbia is one of the last European states to maintain a visa-free regime with Russia, despite EU pressure to terminate it and align its visa policy with that of the EU.

In Serbia’s case, this is no minor unfulfilled task. Beyond its considerable symbolic significance, the open-door policy for Russians carries a strong economic and security dimension. Over the last four years of Russia’s war against Ukraine, Belgrade has become a major hub for Russians traveling to Europe for various reasons. Serbian state airlines operate regular direct flights to five destinations in the European part of Russia. Belgrade Airport is the only one on the European continent offering such connections, making it a key transit hub on this route.

A significant number of Russians have also settled permanently or temporarily in Serbia, which is not only easily accessible to them but also culturally relatively close. While the Serbian border police registered nearly a million single entries by Russians between 2022 and 2024, estimates put the number of Russians residing in Serbia long term at around 100,000. The Serbian government has accommodated this trend with generous residence permits and citizenship grants, in some cases through accelerated procedures “in the state interest” or even to Russians under sanctions.

What statistics fail to capture is the political profile of this new Russian diaspora. It is presumed to be a mix of pragmatically minded Russians, many of whom are successfully building businesses in Serbia; anti-Putin exiles; and prominent figures directly linked to Putin. The proportion of these individual groups remains unknown, and judging by recorded intelligence activities targeting the Russian opposition in Belgrade, Moscow is seeking that answer as well.

Furthermore, Serbia is not merely a venue for Russian intelligence services to monitor their own opposition, but also a safe staging ground for operations elsewhere in Europe. For instance, BIRN recently documented the Russian recruitment of volunteers in Serbia for the war against Ukraine, as well as training centres for hybrid operations in Moldova. As-yet unconfirmed reports of a Serbian citizen’s involvement in a hybrid attack in Leipzig and the use of Serbia for the transit of Russian operatives provide further evidence of Serbia’s role in Russian activities on European soil.

It is precisely Russia’s ongoing intelligence links with Serbia that expose the main flaw in Babis’s statements on Serbia’s rapid Schengen accession. While the prime minister defends such a plan as a means of combating illegal migration, he completely overlooks another risk that cannot be ignored during a period of escalating Russian operations against Europe. Czechia’s European allies are well aware of this risk and for this reason won’t permit any hasty expansion of the Schengen Area.

Serbia may have its place in the EU and Schengen someday, provided it genuinely desires membership and meets at least the basic political and security conditions. Ending its visa-free policy with Russia certainly ranks among them, regardless of the Czech prime minister’s disregard for the issue.

Petr Čermák is a Research Fellow at the Association for International Affairs focusing on Western Balkan politics.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Ratko Mladic Buried with Military Honours in Serbia, Thousands Attend Funeral
World.content:
Large crowds of mourners, including Serbian ministers, gathered in Belgrade on Monday for the funeral of Ratko Mladic, who died in detention while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Troops lined the road and police saluted the coffin, which was draped with the flags of Serbia and Republika Srpska, as it was transported to Topcider Cemetery from the Church of St. Luke, where the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, led a funeral service.

The Patriarch declared that Mladic’s name will “remain deeply woven into the memory and prayers of the vast majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and cultivate deep gratitude toward him”.

A Serbian Army honour guard gave a three-volley salute as Mladic’s coffin was lowered into the grave, and mourners shouted “Long live Ratko Mladic” and “Glory to the hero”. He was buried next to his daughter Ana, who committed suicide in 1994.

Serbian Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic, Minister without Portfolio Nenad Popovic and Minister for Labour, Employment, Veterans and Social Affairs Milica Djurdjevic Stamenkovski attended the funeral, as did war veterans in military uniforms.

From Republika Srpska came Milorad Dodik, the head of the ruling coalition in the Serb-dominated entity, and Zeljka Cvijanovic, the Serb member of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s tripartite presidency. The Russian ambassador to Serbia Aleksandar Bocan-Harchenko came to pay condolences to the Mladic family.

But European Union officials, the foreign ministers of neighbouring Croatia and Bosnia, and survivors of wartime crimes committed by Mladic’s forces strongly criticised the commemoration of the genocide convict.

The EU warned that the glorification of war criminals and genocide denial “contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries”.

T-shirts celebrate Mladic’s wartime actions

From early on Monday, hundreds of mourners streamed towards the Church of St. Luke, some walking several kilometres to pay tribute to the war criminal they consider a Serbian hero, despite his convictions by the Hague Tribunal.

Many carried flags and wore T-shirts depicting Mladic or symbols of Republika Srpska and its army, which he led during the war. One T-shirt slogan read: “Ratko Mladic – Is it a crime to defend the Serbian people?”

“Now even the [football] supporters are together, now we’re all together,” said one man, referring to the fact that both fans of Red Star and Partizan, Belgrade’s main football clubs, had paid tribute to Ratko Mladic during their weekend derby.

A younger Mladic supporter standing next to him was in tears. “He tried to protect us, and now we are here to see him off,” he said.

At noon, the Patriarch Porfirije led the funeral service, saying that Mladic “stood at the head of the army of his people and carried a great responsibility and burden, made a sacrifice, and laid down his life for the freedom, defence and survival of his people”.

Following the service, members of the Serbian Armed Forces carried the coffin from the church to the funeral procession heading towards Topcider Cemetery.

In the procession, Mladic’s son Darko carried a sabre, while other family members carried Mladic’s military decorations and a photograph of him. Mladic’s wife, Bosiljka, walked behind the coffin.

Along the route between the church and the cemetery, water tankers and temporary public toilets had been installed for those attending. The city of Belgrade deployed significant resources, providing the water supplies, electric transport vehicles and city-run security services.

Free transport was offered from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects, Reuters news agency and media outlets in Serbia and Montenegro reported. Dozens of buses travelled from Republika Srpska, while organised bus transport was also arranged from Montenegro.

At the ceremony, flags bearing the deceased general’s image were flown and a sound system had been set up so mourners could hear Mladic’s son Darko speak.

Darko Mladic thanked the mourners for what he called a “magnificent farewell.”

“Thank you, my brothers, for coming to decide whether my father is a hero or a criminal,” he said.

Mladic was then buried with a ceremonial volley, an honour traditionally reserved for senior military officials. Mladic held the rank of general in the Yugoslav People’s Army, JNA, during the early 1990s but legal experts in Serbia are divided on whether there is any basis for a funeral with state or army honours, given that he was convicted of genocide

Anger in Bosnia and Croatia

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic condemned Monday’s commemoration of Mladic, accusing Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic of “leading Serbia towards complete isolation in the region”.

“We saw a war criminal being given the highest military honours. We saw a large number of Serbian government officials attending the funeral and commemoration,” Konakovic told reporters.

Konakovic said Vucic had been “cowardly” to stay away from the funeral, but claimed that “we all know very well that he is the organiser, implementer and personally the most responsible person”. Vucic avoided the issue of attendance at the funeral by saying he was busy on Monday meeting Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.

Konakovic said draft letters had been prepared for the US, EU and UK, adding that Bosnia will ask the EU “whether it truly respects its own principles”. He added that he will seek to reduce contact with Serbia and withdraw personnel from Bosnia’s embassy in Belgrade. “There will be no more talks on economic cooperation with Serbia while I am here,” he added.

Croatia’s Foreign Minister Gordan Grlic Radman also slammed Monday’s commemorations in Belgrade – and warned that they could affect Serbia’s EU accession process.

“Glorifying this war criminal is truly incompatible with European values,” Grlic Radman declared.

He noted the glorification of Mladic not only in Serbia, but also in Montenegro. “This is above all an insult to the victims, survivors and their families,” he said.

He called for action to be taken over threats to European values in countries that are candidates for EU membership, which include Serbia and Montenegro.

Mladic was found guilty of some of the worst atrocities in Europe since World War II by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia in The Hague.

He was convicted of genocide of Bosniaks in Srebrenica in 1995, the persecution and extermination of Bosniaks and Croats across the country, terrorising the population of Sarajevo with a campaign of shelling and sniper attacks, and taking UN peacekeepers hostage.

World.title: Kosovo Man Pleads Not Guilty to Spying for Serbia
World.content:
Fatmir Sheholli at the Pristina Basic Court on Monday, September 7, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Former political commentator Fatmir Sheholli pleaded not guilty to carrying out espionage and blackmail for the Serbian intelligence agency, BIA, on Monday in a pre-trial hearing at the Pristina Basic Court.

Sheholli, former head of the Pristina-based Institute for Advancing Interethnic Relations, was arrested in October 2025 and has been in detention ever since.

He is accused of acting on instructions from the BIA to collect and pass on information about Kosovo’s institutions, political activities, and security situation.

Judge Avni Syla informed the accused and his counsel that they had the right to challenge the evidence and request the dismissal of the indictment within a 30-day period. However, Sheholli’s lawyer, Mentor Neziri, said his client had waived this right and requested that the court proceed immediately to the trial phase.

According to the indictment, seen by BIRN, Sheholli worked for the BIA until his arrest in October 2025, “collecting and passing on information about Kosovo’s political activities, security situation, and state institutions”.

It alleges that Sheholli carried out the orders of Bojan Dimic, who the prosecution claims is a senior BIA official. Some of the material Sheholli shared, according to the prosecution, concerned Serb-owned properties in Kosovo, business activities, and the functioning of Kosovo’s institutions.

According to the indictment, on August 5, 2025, Sheholli sent a document labelled “Top Secret 2” to a person identified as Viktor Makedonija, outlining a covert political and strategic plan involving influential figures in Kosovo in fields such as sports, music, media and politics, that the prosecution claims aimed to assist Islamic radicalisation in Kosovo and the region and destabilize the country.

They allegedly aimed to portray Kosovo as a radicalised and extremist state, damaging its international standing and influencing Western countries’ positions towards it.

The prosecution further alleges that in September 2025, Sheholli gave material obtained from Dimic to journalist Milaim Zeka for publication through his “Pa Rrotulla” TV programme, including the timing of publication, for which Zeka allegedly received 1,000 euros.

Sheholli denied that Zeka knew about his direct communication with Dimic. He also told the prosecution that Zeka had requested 3,000 to 4,000 euros for translating, editing, and publishing the material.

The prosecution claims that one month after his arrest, Sheholli told his visitors at the Gjilan/Gnilanje Detention Centre “that he received a USB drive, transcripts, and 5,000 euros from a person in North Mitrovica, materials which, according to him, contained intercepted communications and information concerning abuse of office and corruption.

‘He stated that he had handed the materials to journalist Milaim Zeka for publication, giving him 1,000 for publishing them,” it added.

Zeka has not responded to BIRN’s request for comment.

In another allegation, based on a photograph of a document found on Sheholli’s phone, the prosecution alleges that he was involved in a plan to discredit Kosovo’s acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti.

The document found on Sheholli’s phone relates to the time when Kurti was a political prisoner in Nis, Serbia from 1999 to 2001. The prosecution claims that the document, which Sheholli allegedly planned to use against Kurti, was allegedly drawn up by Serbia’s state security structures in 2001 and was signed by the head of the third sector of Serbia’s state security service.

Sheholli is also charged with blackmailing a Kosovo Albanian businessman, Arben Jetullahu, between 2022 and December 2025, demanding more than 13,000 euros, threatening that video recordings and other information damaging to the businessman would be made public if he refused.

In December 2021, a BIRN investigation found that RAD, a company owned by Radule Stevic, a Kosovo Serb businessman blacklisted by the US for alleged corruption, had been winning government tenders in Kosovo’s Serb-dominated north and then subcontracting construction work to ethnic Albanian-owned firms, including one owned by Jetullahu.

In October 2025, BIRN reported that former KIA director Driton Gashi spent more than 1 million euros from the Special Operational Fund, including 500,000 euros for which the recipient could not be identified. However, the agency’s chief inspector, Kujtim Shala, confirmed that the other 500,000 had been received by Sheholli.

This is the sixth case at the Pristina Basic Court related to charges of espionage for Serbian intelligence agency in the past two years.

In August, the Pristina Basic Court ordered 30 days of detention for Fehim Sali, who has reportedly admitted working for Serbia’s BIA, which allegedly paid him to identify other potential recruits.

In June, the same court sentenced a Kosovo Albanian man, Hysri Selimi, a former Islamic State member, to six years in prison for espionage. In May, the court sentenced Kosovo Police lieutenant Bojan Jevtic to six years’ imprisonment for espionage. Jevtic was found guilty of leaking information about the Kosovo police to the BIA.

In April, the court sentenced Jelena Djukanovic, an employee of the OSCE Mission in Kosovo, to six years’ imprisonment for spying for Serbia by providing internal OSCE information related to the situation mainly in the Serb-majority municipalities in the north of Kosovo.

In June 2025, the court sentenced Aleksandar Vlajic to five years’ imprisonment for espionage as the BIA’s resident agent.

World.title: Belgrade Pride March Marks 25 Years with Call for Tolerance
World.content:
Serbia’s annual LGBTQ+ Pride March took to the streets of the capital Belgrade on Saturday, with participants waving rainbow flags as they walked through the city centre.

The march – held 25 years after the first Belgrade Pride was attacked by homophobic thugs – was held under police protection and passed off without incident. Part of Belgrade Pride Week, it had the slogan “There Is Room for All of Us” – the same as the first march in 2001.

Participants carried banners reading “Visibility is not propaganda”, “God loves everyone” and “Queer students are winning too” – a refence to the slogan used by students who have led anti-government protests since 2024.
