World.title: Former Croatian PM Seeks Suspension of Serbian EU Accession Talks
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – Former Croatian PM Jadranka Kosor is seeking total suspension of all Serbian EU accession talks, calling on Ursula von der Leyen to take action.

Former Croatian Prime Minister Jadranka Kosor has called on the European Commission to completely suspend Serbia’s EU accession negotiations following today’s mass farewell for Ratko Mladić in Belgrade, which was held with the highest state and military honours. “After today’s funeral, involving the anti-civilisational bowing of Serbia to a war criminal convicted of genocide, I expect the incompetent European Commission and its incompetent leader Ursula von der Leyen to fully suspend Serbia’s accession negotiations for entry into the EU. That is the minimum,” Kosor wrote on X.

a serbian state funeral for a genocidal maniac

Index reports that thousands of people gathered in Belgrade to bid a final farewell to the former commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Disgraced Ratko Mladić was buried at Topčider Cemetery with state honours, in the presence of members of the Serbian Army and an honour guard. Numerous Serbian officials, the political leadership of Republika Srpska, and the Russian ambassador to Serbia attended the funeral. Before the burial, his coffin was displayed in the Church of St. Luke, where the service was led by Patriarch Porfirije. On the coffin were his officer’s cap and sabre, and members of the army and veterans of the former Army of Republika Srpska stood beside it. The Serbian Government had previously sent a state aircraft to collect Mladić’s remains from The Hague, and soldiers carried his coffin, covered with the Serbian flag, out of the plane. A commemoration was also held for him on Saturday in an official facility of the Serbian Army.

serbia honours one of the worst monsters of the 20th century

Mladić died on the 27th of August at the age of 84 in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence. He had suffered several quite serious strokes and his health had been declining rapidly for some time. He was finally convicted of committing genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity, and war crimes during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. His forces were responsible, among other things, for the massacre of more than 8,000 innocent Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995, as well as for the multi-year, dreadful siege of Sarajevo.

the eu’s position is clear – no glorification of war crimes and war criminals

The European Union has already very clearly warned Serbia over the glorification of the vile Ratko Mladić. European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos cancelled a planned visit to Serbia after a state aircraft brought his body to Belgrade. The European External Action Service stated that the glorification of war criminals, denial of genocide, and revisionism have no place either in the European Union or in candidate countries. Serbia has otherwise held candidate status for EU membership and has been conducting accession negotiations since 2014.

World.title: Osijek Company to Develop Unmanned Systems & More in Vukovar
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – An Osijek company is set to develop unmanned systems in Vukovar and more as part of a five million euro project.

A new production facility is being built in the Vukovar Business Zone by the Osijek-based company GAUSS d.o.o., which focuses on the development of digital and high-tech solutions. Poslovni reports that last week, representatives of the investors, together with Deputy Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Ivan Penava, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries David Vlajčić, and State Secretary Dario Tišov, toured the investment worth slightly less than five million euros.

The new facility is expected to start operating during the second quarter of next year. It will develop and produce unmanned systems using artificial intelligence, smart software and other advanced tech. Hrvoje Sagrak, Director of Business Development and Sales at the Osijek company, emphasised that coming to Vukovar is an opportunity to transfer the experience gained through cooperation with international partners, especially in the United Arab Emirates.

“It is truly a great honour for us to be here in Vukovar because we have a unique opportunity to transfer the business experience and know-how that we have acquired through cooperation with partners abroad, primarily in the United Arab Emirates, to Croatia. Right here we want to build a point that will be a centre of excellence and a centre of knowledge about high technologies,” said Sagrak.

ai, unmanned systems and more

The future facility will not deal only with the production of aircraft. It will develop systems that include smart software, artificial intelligence and other devices, and the applications could range from surveillance and protection to fire prevention, protection of critical infrastructure and border monitoring. Special emphasis will be placed on the rapid development of new products and turning ideas into prototypes. Industry 4.0 technologies and 3D printers will be used so that new solutions can be designed, tested and verified more quickly and cheaply.

In the initial phase, around ten experts with multidisciplinary knowledge in electrical engineering and other modern fields are expected to work at the facility. “It isn’t about the number of employees itself, but about what will be developed through such a venture and spread throughout the entire ecosystem,” Sagrak said, adding that the facility has the possibility of further expansion.

the future has (finally) arrived in vukovar, a town scarred by the past

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister David Vlajčić recalled that the story of this investment has been ongoing since the time when he was assistant director of the Vukovar Business Zone. “The investor then took a plot and began developing something that combines hardware and software, i.e. solutions that we do not have in Croatia today. Such investments require a trained workforce, but at the same time they open up the potential for smart technologies from all over the world to come right here, to Croatia and Vukovar, and for us to have something special on the territory of the European Union,” said Vlajčić.

The importance of the investment was also highlighted by Deputy Speaker of the Croatian Parliament Ivan Penava, who believes that the project places Vukovar alongside modern technological environments. “The future has arrived in Vukovar,” Penava said, emphasising that artificial intelligence, 3D printers and unmanned aerial vehicles represent high-tech industry, and by connecting them integrated production is created.

“When we talk about artificial intelligence, 3D printers or unmanned aerial vehicles, each of these technologies on its own already represents high-tech industry. However, here we’re talking about integrated production and connecting all of that through one product. All of this has today, on a symbolic level, arrived in Vukovar,” said Penava. He added that talks with the investors lasted about two years and emphasised that their arrival is important because, despite economic logic, they are choosing Croatia and Vukovar also because of their connection with this area.

The investment worth slightly less than five million euros represents a new step in the development of the Vukovar Business Zone, as well as in the effort to position Vukovar as a place for the development and production of advanced technological solutions for the domestic and global market.

World.title: 3% More Vehicles on Croatian Motorways Than This Time in 2025
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – There have been 3% more vehicles recorded on Croatian motorways this year than back during this period in 2025.

From the beginning of the year until the end of August, 56.5 million cars passed along Croatian motorways, which is an increase of 1.6 million, or three percent, compared with the same period last year, HRT reports. “Croatia as a tourist country is recognised not only for its natural beauty, but above all for the safety it offers to all tourists, and this increase in traffic is a result of that,” said Ivan Ribičić, Director of the Toll Collection Sector.

Poslovni reports that the busiest periods, according to Ribičić, are the end of July and the beginning of August. “All three summer months were very successful. Compared with last year, that is 300,000 more vehicles. These are excellent results, he said. In the last three to four years, large traffic jams on Mondays have become increasingly frequent. This weekend also exceeded expectations. On Sunday by 18:00, 100,000 vehicles were recorded at the Lučko entrance alone, which is more than last year.

In the autumn, works on the Zagreb bypass are finally due to begin, which should make passage between Zagreb East and Zagreb West easier, as well as access to the Lučko toll booth.

World.title: New Poll Lays Bare Worst Result for HDZ in the Last Two Years
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – A brand new poll has showcased the absolute worst result for HDZ in the last two years, with Prime Minister Andrej Plenković personally scoring very poorly.

Public dissatisfaction over the hazardous waste affair in Lika has been reflected on the political scene, as shown by the latest monthly CRO Demoskop survey. Index reports that according to the poll conducted for RTL this month, both HDZ and SDP recorded a significant drop in support, with the ruling party, being HDZ, falling to its lowest level in the past two years.

If parliamentary elections had been held at the beginning of the month, HDZ would still have been the relative winner. Index reports that the CRO Demoskop survey was conducted by the agency Promocija plus from 1 to 3 September using a telephone survey (CATI) on a representative sample of 1,000 respondents. The sample was stratified by counties and settlement size, with control of socio-demographic characteristics. The standard sampling error is ±3.04% at a 95% confidence level.

most and Možemo! outperform hdz and sdp

According to the latest poll, HDZ has the support of 25.3% of voters, a drop from 27% seen in July. This is also the party’s weakest result since April 2024. SDP is in second place with 20.5% support, also recording a decline from 21.5% in July and its lowest rating in the current term. Možemo! ranked third with 12.9% support, a slight increase from 12.2% in July. The biggest rise was recorded by Most, which jumped from 7.7% to 9.5%. It is followed by the party Drito with 1.8% and Domovinski pokret with 1.6%. Both parties have slightly lower support than in July. Most thus recorded a rise of 1.8 percentage points, and Možemo! of 0.7. HDZ is down by 1.7 percentage points, SDP by 1.0, and Drito and DP by 0.5 percentage points each.

Other parties have support below 1.5%. Above one percent are Domino (1.4%), Centar (1.1%), Pravo i pravda (1.1%), IDS (1.0%) and Nezavisna platforma Sjever (1.0%). Below that threshold are HNS (0.9%), Hrvatski suverenisti (0.8%), HSU (0.8%), HSS (0.7%), HSLS (0.4%) and Fokus (0.3%). All other parties together have two percent support, while undecided voters stand at 16.9%.

president milanović receives the most positive rating among politicians, while pm plenković receives the worst

The most positively perceived politicians are as follows:

Zoran Milanović – 23%

Andrej Plenković – 15.6%

Tomislav Tomašević – 4.1%

Marin Miletić – 3.8%

Ivana Kekin – 2.9%

Dalija Orešković – 2.7%

Nikola Grmoja – 2.5%

Ivan Anušić – 2.2%

Sandra Benčić – 1.6%

Biljana Borzan – 1.5%

The most negatively perceived politicians are as follows:

Andrej Plenković – 37.3%

Zoran Milanović – 12.3%

Tomislav Tomašević – 5.6%

Sandra Benčić – 2.5%

Ivan Penava – 2.3%

Milorad Pupovac – 2.1%

Dalija Orešković – 1.8%

Hrvoje Zekanović – 1.6%

Siniša Hajdaš Dončić – 1.4%

Andrija Mikulić – 1.4%

most believe the country is heading in the wrong direction

This September, only 17.5% of citizens believe that Croatia is moving in a good direction, a drop from 20.2% in July. At the same time, the share of those who think the direction is wrong rose from 70% to 74.6%. Undecided stand at 7.9%. Among HDZ voters optimism prevails and 55.4% of them consider the direction good. Voters of opposition parties are considerably more critical.

President Zoran Milanović received an average grade of 3.08 for his work. He received the highest grade from SDP voters (3.97) and the lowest from HDZ voters (2.32). The work of the Croatian Parliament was rated 2.16. It received the highest grade from HDZ voters (3.0) and the lowest from Možemo! platform voters (1.69). The Government received a grade of 2.23 for its work, the lowest grade in the past year. HDZ voters rated the Government’s work at 3.81, while voters of other parties were considerably stricter. Support for the Government’s policy fell to 25.7%, compared with 27.6% in July.

the appalling lika hazardous waste affair is the hot topic

The hazardous waste affair in Lika and other parts of the country was the most important topic of the past month for as many as 40.4% of respondents. This is one of the highest results for a single event since measurements began in 2004. In second place in importance is the fire in Omiš and the surrounding area, which 27.9% of citizens singled out as a key event. These are followed by the heatwave (5.4%), inflation (3.5%), the extraordinary session of Parliament (3.0%) and the rise in fuel prices (2.9%). Among the more important topics are also sporting successes, Thompson’s concert in Vukovar and arrests related to arson.

World.title: Slaven Bilić Surprises with New Names in Croatia’s Nations League Squad
World.content:
Croatia head coach Slaven Bilić announced the squad list he’s counting on for the upcoming Nations League fixtures in September and October.

Croatia have four competitive matches in the space of 11 days ahead of them, and head coach Bilić will be relying on the following players for this “campaign”:

“Summer has passed, that period where I did a lot of thinking, a lot of talking. The time to gather has come, and I think we’re ready now. I talked a lot with the players, watched, thought it over, and arrived at the final list. This is a specific situation — it’s the first time we’ve had four Nations League matches in around ten days. I don’t want this to disrupt my work. We’ve gone with 23 + 3.”

Player list

GOALKEEPERS: Dominik Livaković (Barcelona), Dominik Kotarski (Dinamo), Ivor Pandur (Rangers)

DEFENDERS: Joško Gvardiol (Manchester City), Josip Juranović (Union Berlin), Josip Šutalo (Lazio), Luka Vušković (Brighton), Ivan Smolčić (Como), Josip Stanišić (Bayern), Martin Erlić (Midtjylland)

MIDFIELDERS: Luka Modrić (Milan), Mateo Kovačić (Manchester City), Mario Pašalić (Atalanta), Nikola Vlašić (Torino), Petar Sučić (Inter), Luka Sučić (Real Sociedad), Josip Mišić (Dinamo), Martin Baturina (Como)

FORWARDS: Ivan Perišić (PSV), Andrej Kramarić (Hoffenheim), Ante Budimir (Osasuna), Igor Matanović (Freiburg), Franjo Ivanović (Lens), Dion Drena Beljo (Dinamo), Marco Pašalić (Orlando City), Petar Musa (Dallas FC)

ON STANDBY: Karlo Letica (Luzern), Marin Pongračić (Fiorentina), Kristijan Jakić (Augsburg), Nikola Moro (Bologna), Lovro Majer (AEK), Toni Fruk (Rijeka)

Bilić’s debut on September 26th

The big news of the weekend just gone is that Luka Modrić has confirmed he will continue playing for Croatia.

Luka Modrić has made 202 appearances for Croatia to date, and will now work with Slaven Bilić again after 14 years.

The squad list also features some new names, while some players will lose the place they held in the national team’s previous campaigns.

As for the Nations League schedule, what lies ahead for Croatia is anything but easy.

Bilić’s side travel to Czechia on September 26th, then to Spain three days later.

Two home matches follow: against England on October 3rd and Spain on October 6th.

Croatia’s fixture schedule in Nations League Group A3:

26 September, 20:45: Czechia – Croatia

29 September, 20:45: Spain – Croatia

3 October, 18:00: Croatia – England (Rujevica Stadium, Rijeka)

6 October, 20:45: Croatia – Spain (Poljud Stadium, Split)

World.title: Nikola Šubić Zrinski – The Croat Who Stopped 100,000 Ottomans
World.content:
September the 7th, 2026 – Turning the clock all the way back to the 7th of September 1566, and we meet the famed Nikola Šubić Zrinski, the Croat who stopped 100,000 Ottomans, but lost his life during the final charge.

Nikola Šubić Zrinski was a Croatian nobleman, ban (viceroy) and soldier who lived during the 16th century and is remembered as a defender of Christianity throughout Europe. Index writes that he is best known for the Battle of Szigetvár, in which the sultan himself also lost his life. In Croatia, he holds additional importance because he elevated the Zrinski noble family to the status of the most powerful Croatian family of all.

he never shied away from battling the fearsome ottoman forces

He was born sometime during 1508. We don’t know exactly where he entered the world, but we know he had five brothers and sisters. His father was Nikola Šubić and his mother Jelena Karlović. Nikola’s political activity did not come only from the fact that he was a nobleman; the Karlović family had a long tradition of state functions. Nikola’s uncle Ivan Karlović later served as ban. The brave Zrinski was primarily a soldier. After finishing military school, Šubić joined the ongoing war and defended Vienna in 1529, at which time he was noticed by many nobles and military officials. After the siege he was rewarded with a golden chain and received a horse.

The conflict with the Ottomans only continued. When he inherited the estate in the Una valley in 1534, he also inherited the obligation to pay tribute to the Ottomans. Nikola truly did not want to pay tribute to the enemy, so he provoked a conflict over the fortress of Dubica in order to justify not paying the taxes.

habsburg or zapolya?

At the same time the Kingdom of Hungary was very unstable. After the death of Vladislav II Jagiellon at Mohács, the whole country split into two camps: one favoured the Habsburgs and wanted to bring them to power in Hungary and Croatia, while the other favoured the local Hungarian nobleman John Zápolya. Nikola Šubić Zrinski considered Ferdinand Habsburg the better and wiser choice, and he had already become acquainted with the Habsburgs during the siege of Vienna. That is why, on his own initiative, he decided to kill the nobleman Johann Katzianer, who had rejected the Habsburgs and sworn loyalty to Zápolya. He captured Katzianer’s fortress of Kostajnica, but soon handed it over to the Ottomans, from whom he expected retaliation for refusing to pay tribute.

the zrinskis head north…

From the 1540s on, he was given administration of the whole of Međimurje. He soon moved there, renovated the castle in Čakovec, and after a few years received the right to collect taxes himself and to settle serfs in the area. At the same time he became Ban of Croatia, a title he held until 1556. He left the “office” of ban because he was dissatisfied that he had failed to raise more funds for the fight against the Ottomans. He wanted someone more capable to take the position while he continued to wage war against the enemy. He immediately received the position of treasurer in Hungary (Hungarian nobles were inclined to give him whatever he wanted because he was highly respected even before Szigetvár) and fought the Ottomans twice. He believed he already knew their strategies well and rushed into war with them whenever possible.

the famous battle of Szigetvár

The next opportunity presented itself in 1566 when he was staying in the fortress of Szigetvár. Szigetvár is located in Hungary on the shortest route to Vienna. Suleiman the Magnificent led 100,000 men to capture Szigetvár and begin a new siege of Vienna. To them Szigetvár was just another miserable Christian fortress; the Ottomans conquered such places every other day. However, Suleiman the Magnificent was not prepared for what was about to happen. Around 2,000 men, mostly ethnic Croats, decided that the Ottomans would not pass here. As soon as Ottoman infantry approached the gates of Szigetvár, the defenders threw everything they could at them and the enemy withdrew. Szigetvár was constantly bombarded with cannonballs for a full month, and one did not walk in the inner courtyard because of the arrows that fell into the fortress without stopping.

The defenders ate all the food they had, then began to eat their own horses. They maintained their morale largely thanks to Nikola Šubić, who in his classic style still saw only victory. Then came 7 September 1566, and it was clear that that morning the Ottomans would break into the town. Nikola put on a hat and noble attire, left his knight’s armour aside, took his father’s sabre and bravely led his men into the final episode of that nightmare. All the defenders died that morning, and the Ottomans achieved their goal.

an extremely costly goal

But the goal was achieved at too great a cost. The Ottoman army should not have lost a fifth of its force on some stupid and unimportant fortress, nor should it have been delayed there for half the summer. To make matters worse, during the siege Suleiman the Magnificent died, so the army’s morale was weak and worthless. The army was soon recalled and headed home. Nothing came of a new siege of Vienna. The heroic defence of Szigetvár was the main topic of conversation throughout Europe in the following months. Everyone spoke about Nikola Šubić: from Roman and Spanish diplomats who claimed that God had sent him to save Vienna from the Muslims, to the French Cardinal Richelieu who called him “the saviour of Europe and the Christian world.”

His descendants continued to act politically and hold various positions in the new state, the Habsburg Monarchy. Nikola elevated the Zrinskis from an ordinary noble family to the most important family in Croatia. Their influence would mark the following period, right up to the Zrinski-Frankopan conspiracy of 1671.

Nikola Šubić Zrinski remains incredibly relevant to this very day. Legends of his defence of Szigetvár were retold to children in the following centuries, and when the awakening of nationalism began in the 19th century, Nikola became even more popular. Then the 1880 earthquake struck Zagreb and the city had to be rebuilt. About a hundred metres southeast of Zagreb’s main square, construction began on the most beautiful park in the city centre. The park would be named Zrinjevac, or Nikola Šubić Zrinski Square, further immortalising him.

World.title: Much More Than Tourism: Croatia’s New Zagreb-Beijing Connection
World.content:
September the 7th, 2026 – Croatia’s brand new Zagreb-Beijing connection by Air China means much more than just more tourism from Asia, with business and cultural ties implied.

On Friday at 09:47, fire engines stood ready as the “giant” Air China aircraft touched down on the runway of Zagreb’s Franjo Tuđman Airport. The majestic plane of the Chinese carrier completed the first, inaugural flight between Beijing, Bucharest and Zagreb. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that the aircraft was welcomed with a water salute upon landing, while passengers and crew were greeted by a number of high-ranking officials. This flight marked the start of year-round services between the mentioned cities.

a bridge of friendship

Air China’s aircraft landed in Zagreb for the first time and thus began regular operations to Croatia, opening many doors for cooperation and travel. The new route will operate three times a week (Monday, Wednesday and Friday), and flights will continue year-round, including throughout winter. “Good day, welcome (Dobar dan, dobrodosli,” Qi Qianjin, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Croatia, briefly addressed everyone in Croatian. He added that the new route represents much more than an air link between China and Croatia: “It’s a bridge of friendship that connects our peoples and develops potential for further bilateral cooperation in culture, tourism, trade… It will also reduce logistics costs and improve delivery efficiency.”

He emphasised that this is the first such flight in the history of the two countries, while recalling that, despite this, we have a long history of cultural exchanges and economic and trade ties dating back to the time of Marco Polo.

The new route connects Beijing and Zagreb via Bucharest, the capital of Romania. Operations will work as follows: passengers, for example, board in Zagreb and fly to Bucharest as they would to other Schengen countries. There is a three-hour stopover during which border formalities and passport checks are carried out, after which the journey continues to China. The procedure is the same for return flights, while luggage remains on the aircraft. The total flight time is around 14 hours and practically connects two ends of the world.

more opportunities for cooperation

“Today we’re celebrating not only a new air route, but also a new opportunity for cooperation between the two countries in the fields of tourism, business and culture. We look forward to the development of this partnership in the years to come. This new route expands our connections and links Croatia with one of the most dynamic markets,” said Nicolas Duthilleul, CEO and Member of the Board of Zagreb International Airport (MZLZ). He added that more than 4.7 million passengers passed through the airport last year and that he is convinced that with this new route China and Croatia gain more opportunities to grow even closer.

He also noted that travel opportunities have now expanded and that the airport has prepared additional information and signage in Chinese throughout the terminal for Chinese passengers so they can navigate more easily and feel more comfortable.

Air China is using wide-body Airbus A330-200 aircraft on the route. This first arrival brings yet another major global carrier to Zagreb and further expands the flight offer. The A330-200 has a capacity of 265 seats, while around 120 passengers arrived on this inaugural flight from Beijing via Bucharest to Zagreb. The arrival time suits everyone, as morning disembarkation allows them to continue their day normally with other flights or to head into the city very early.

In any case, this is a good foundation for the coming tourist years, and Monika Udovičić, State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, also sees potential in it.

great results for croatian tourism

“Croatian tourism will again finish this year with very good results, but what is more important is that we are significantly investing efforts in sustainable tourism, and I think this is something that will resonate well on the Chinese market. They come to see our natural beauty and cultural landmarks. The main motive is not only sun and sea, but our natural beauty,” she said, adding that Croatia has never been closer to China and that this is not just a route, but a better connection between the two countries that is moving towards strengthening relations, friendship and business.

“On distant markets, presence is built continuously through better transport connectivity, promotion and long-term partnerships, and this route represents an important step in that direction. I believe this route will contribute to an even stronger positioning of Croatia on the Chinese market.”

After the official part and the welcome of the crew and passengers, a cake was cut and champagne was poured, because big and new things need to be celebrated. Six journalists from China also attended the ceremony, as well as representatives of tourist boards. Among the speakers were also State Secretary at the Ministry of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure Tomislav Mihotić, Director of the Croatian National Tourist Board Kristjan Staničić, and many others.

World.title: The Guardian Names Cres Europe’s Best Hidden Gem
World.content:
September the 7th, 2026 – The Guardian has spotlighted gorgeous Cres, referring to it as Europe’s best hidden gem.

The influential Guardian was well and truly won over by the wilderness of the beautiful island of Cres and its crystal-clear sea, which we must protect if we want it to remain that way.

Morski reports that the very widely read British newspaper The Guardian published a selection of lesser-known European islands worth visiting. Among suggestions from numerous countries, Cres in the Kvarner archipelago took first place. Reader Rhiannon, whose recommendation was chosen as the best, particularly highlighted the island’s nature and its impressive griffon vultures.

The Guardian describes Cres as the least populated of the four large Kvarner islands. The island features a mix of the Tramuntana forests, rocky terrain, olive groves, lavender and hidden coves – all of which clearly left a strong impression on the British. The island is known for its hiking and cycling trails, as well as traditional gastronomy and, of course, Cres lamb.

A particularly special attraction are the rare griffon vultures, which nest on the cliffs above the sea. In the settlement of Beli, there is also a visitor centre and recovery centre for these special natural “hygienists” that we must carefully protect.

World.title: Estonian firm buys Lithuanian agricultural group Litagra
World.content:
Infortar's subsidiary Infortar Agro is expanding into Lithuania by buying agricultural group UAB Litagra, which operates in milk and crop production, poultry farming, feed manufacturing and other farming activities.

Litagra is a Lithuanian agricultural group that began operations in 1991. The Litagra group includes UAB Joniškio Grūdai, UAB Litagros Žemės Ūkio Centras and Agrohold Estonia OÜ, whose shares belong 100 percent to UAB Litagra. In total, in addition to the parent company, the Litagra group includes 34 companies.

The transaction expands Infortar's agricultural operations into Lithuania and complements Infortar's existing investments in this field in Estonia. Once the transaction is completed, the farms owned by the group will have a total of 16,600 animals, annual milk production will reach 93,000 tonnes and the total area of farmland will increase to 23,000 hectares. Poultry farming, including turkey and broiler farms, will become a new area of activity.

"Estonia and Lithuania have historically been agricultural countries. Our latitude and climate are well suited to milk production, our cows are among the highest-yielding in Europe, and our farms are among the most modern. Milk is one of our most important natural resources. By increasing production, it could become an important export product and strengthen our position in international markets," said Ain Hanschmidt, CEO of Infortar.

Martti Talgre. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Infortar's managing director Martti Talgre added that they have operated in Lithuania for eight years, experienced an investor‑friendly environment and taken part in economic growth.

"Agriculture is highly valued in Lithuania, and both performance and productivity are strong. This is why we decided to make one of Estonia's largest foreign investments in Lithuanian agriculture and acquire a well-established company with a long history," said Talgre.

According to Invalda INVL, which has been a Litagra shareholder since 2011, the transaction confirms the value created in the company and marks the end of a successful investment cycle.

"Fifteen years ago, we invested in Litagra with the ambition of building a competitive company operating in high-value, profitable segments of the food and agriculture industry. Over the years, we consistently invested in dairy and poultry production, expanded into new businesses and exited activities that no longer fit our strategy," said Invalda INVL's CEO Darius Šulnis.

Litagra's current management will continue to run the company's daily operations, and Infortar does not plan significant changes to the company's existing activities as a result of the transaction. To complete the transaction, permits and approvals from authorities must be obtained and other additional conditions fulfilled.

The Litagra Group employs almost 400 people. As of the end of last year, the group's consolidated turnover was €69 million and EBITDA €14.5 million. The group has a total of 10,500 hectares of arable land.

Litagra's subsidiary UAB Sūduvos Ūkis, which is wholly owned by UAB Joniškio Grūdai, is the largest turkey farming company in the Baltic States. The company operates six production sites comprising a total of 29 modern barns with a total of 160,000 turkeys.

In addition, the group operates broiler production facilities with capacity for approximately 360,000 broilers per production cycle. The poultry operations are supported by the group company UAB Joniškio Grūdai, which produced 69,000 tonnes of compound feed and related products in 2025, including protein, vitamin and mineral supplements, premixes, baits and pet food. The company also supplies compound feed to Litagra Group's poultry farming companies.

Kõrtsi Dairy Farm, a member of OÜ Estonia Farmid. Source: Olev Kenk/ERR

Litagra's subsidiary UAB Litagros Žemės Ūkio Centras (LŽŪC) is the third-largest dairy farming company in Lithuania by herd size. The company operates eight farms and focuses on dairy production and crop farming. The company's dairy herd comprises approximately 8,300 cows and young cattle, and it produces an average of 35,000 tonnes of raw milk per year.

Infortar operates in seven countries; the company's main fields of activity are maritime transport, energy and real estate. The group includes 107 companies, and excluding associated companies, Infortar employs 6 890 people.

World.title: 'Death to the fascist snake' Soviet-era poster prompts police action
World.content:
Misdemeanor proceedings have been opened following the appearance of a large World War Two-era Soviet propaganda poster outside a residence near Tallinn, Postimees reported .

At the end of last month, TV3 reported a Russian‑language poster had been hanging on the external wall of a private home and in clear view from the road, which had caused concern among residents of Vääna‑Jõesuu, west of Tallinn.

The poster bore the Russian‑language slogan "Death to the fascist snake" and depicts a Red Army soldier piercing a swastika‑shaped snake with a bayonet.

Triin Škubel, head of the general crime investigation group at the Lääne‑Harju Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) station, told Postimees' Russian‑language edition that misdemeanor proceedings had been launched over the appearance of the poster, under the section of the Penal Code dealing with incitement to hatred.

"The details of the incident will be established in the course of the proceedings," Škubel said, adding: "Publicly displaying a banner with such content and imagery is not consistent with the legal norms and general values prevailing in Estonia."

The poster had been hung from the outside wall of this residence of Vääna-Jõesuu, near Tallinn. Source: Screenshot.

"We understand that this situation undermines the sense of security of the Vääna‑Jõesuu community," she went on, and said the PPA is looking for a "fair and swift solution to the incident," meaning the removal of the "provocative" poster.

Both the owner of the residence, on Napsiku tee, who was outside the country when Postimees spoke to them, and his son, who the paper also reached, initially denied knowledge of the placard, while the father subsequently added that perhaps it had, and asked what difference that would make, also suggesting phone footage of the offending item might have been doctored.

The image reported on was originally created by Soviet graphic artist Alexei Kokorekin, who produced many propaganda posters for the Soviet Union, and was published on June 24, 1941 – two days after Nazi Germany launched its invasion of the Soviet Union.

Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine starting in 2022, greater scrutiny has been placed on both displays, slogans, placards and other items, and on more concrete installations, monuments etc. which appear to glorify military aggression. In April 2022, the Riigikogu adopted a law banning hate symbols, and the PPA has reiterated that the use of symbols that justify or support military aggression are prohibited by law in Estonia. The present‑day Russian Federation states in its own constitution that it is a successor state to the Soviet Union.

World.title: SDE chair: Herem defense minister nomination a Reform reputation play
World.content:
The Reform Party's invite to former Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) commander General Martin Herem to be the next defense minister may be an effort by the party to shore up its reputation, opposition Social Democratic Party leader Lauri Läänemets said.

Herem is seen as the most likely candidate to replace Hanno Pevkur, who resigned last week.

Under the coalition agreement with Eesti 200, the post of defense minister belongs to Reform, and the party may name the next defense minister tomorrow, Wednesday.

"I would imagine he has to weigh up the fact that he would be coming directly from a vital defense industry company into a ministerial position. There are conflicts of interest there. The fact that he himself was in office at the time and people close to him held positions in the institutions where all these problems emerged — would all this action and the restoration of trust be credible? That is something he has to consider," Läänemets said.

SDE chairman Lauri Läänemets. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

MP Peeter Tali (Eesti 200) said whoever the new defense minister is should quickly take charge of the sector; alleged mismanagement of procurement and leaving unknown the whereabouts of several million euros meant to go to an Indian company producing shells for Ukraine was what triggered Pevkur's resignation last Wednesday.

According to Tali, Herem has both advantages and disadvantages. "Herem is focused on developing national defense and on getting things done in a short period of time, within six months. The risk is that we must not come to a standstill and lose time," Tali said.

Reform Party secretary general Kristo Enn Vaga said the new minister can take the oath of office before the Riigikogu next week, when the Riigikogu convenes for its autumn session, adding the party is "screening people both from within and outside the party," with the party board to discuss the issue Wednesday of this week.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) discussed the post of defense minister with Herem last week, though no formal offer has been made. Herem is "certainly one of Estonia's strongest, if not the strongest, experts on security and defense issues, and he would be very well suited to hold the defense minister portfolio," Vaga added.

Herem was EDF commander until summer 2024 and is currently an adviser with private sector defense firm Milrem Robotics.

Pevkur had been defense minister since July 2022 and said while he was unaware of the issues with the procurement involving the Indian firm Datasel, he would take political responsibility for oversights.

Tali may also become new chair of the Riigikogu's National Defense Committee, which has been vacant since Kalev Stoicescu left Eesti 200 last month.

World.title: Estonian MP: US administration has no idea how deep the roots of the Ukraine war go
World.content:
Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Marko Mihkelson said Moscow sees no need for a breakthrough in peace efforts and believes it can intensify attacks on Ukraine's infrastructure as winter approaches.

The latest meeting between Vladimir Putin and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also failed to deliver any breakthrough because Putin has no need for one.

"Russia senses that as winter approaches, it has an opportunity to destroy Ukraine's economic infrastructure to the greatest possible extent. Ukraine's air defense problem is growing and serious," said Marko Mihkelson, chair of the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee.

"Dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to Moscow. The situation we have to deal with today is, of course, complicated," Putin said.

"The Russian side gave a clear and comprehensive assessment of the situation that has developed in the course of the special operation. In particular, the tangible successes of the Russian army in the combat zone were noted, confidence was expressed that the objectives that had been set would be achieved and, naturally, the need to address the root causes of the conflict was emphasized," Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said.

"The Trump administration certainly does not have a good understanding of just how deep the roots of this war really go. In Moscow, Putin once again reminded Witkoff and Kushner that this war cannot be ended until the root causes are addressed. We know that the root cause has not been some desire by NATO to expand, but rather the desire to restore the Russian Empire and shift borders through force and violence, as Russia does every day against Ukraine," Mihkelson said.

The meeting in Moscow also explored opportunities for doing business with Russia.

"Economic issues were also discussed in considerable detail, as were potential major Russian-American projects that would benefit both sides," Ushakov said.

"Kushner and Witkoff are not ordinary diplomats. Above all, they also represent interests that extend beyond conventional diplomacy and by that I mean economic interests in particular. The desire to restore some kind of normal interaction between the United States and Russia unfortunately gives Putin confidence that he can manipulate anyone who comes to talk to him," Mihkelson said.

One tangible benefit, however, may be that Kyiv was not bombed while the U.S. envoys were in Ukraine.

"When I arrived at Kyiv's train station in the morning, a good colleague from the Verkhovna Rada was there to greet me cheerfully and said, 'You know how wonderful it is? We got to sleep last night.' For the past 10 days or so, Russian airstrikes have been taking place here without interruption," Mihkelson said. (Air strikes on Kyiv resumed in the early hours of Tuesday — ed.).

What was actually discussed in Moscow and what was agreed upon, however, is something we will probably only find out later, when the memoirs are written.

"We were just sitting on the terrace — me, Jared and Kirill — and then Yuri joined us, and we talked about how, when we eventually retire, we'll have all these incredible stories and memories to tell, and these are the most extraordinary ones of all," Witkoff said.

World.title: Estonian agency fails to demonstrate how €70 million unsuccessful ammo contract reached
World.content:
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) is unable to provide documentation showing how it selected Datasel S.R.L., the company with which it signed an approximately €70 million contract to purchase ammunition.

It is now known that in 2024 and throughout the procurement projects involving Datasel established procedures for conducting procurement processes were not followed. RKIK Director General Elmar Vaher said he does not know how the initial negotiations with Datasel were conducted. "I wasn't working here at the time and neither was my team. So what we can talk about now is how we operate today," he said.

Media reports have said that Datasel copied images of artillery shells from other websites and even used cover art from a computer game. RKIK does not know how the decision was made that Datasel was an appropriate company to work with. There is also no documented account of how contact with the company was established or how RKIK came across the company in the first place.

Nor has RKIK subsequently determined how Datasel's background check was conducted and there is no summary of that check. This is important because procurement procedures generally involve checking first and foremost whether a company actually possesses the technology it is offering and how it can demonstrate its ability to supply that technology. The company's financial capacity is also assessed, including whether it has investors, bank guarantees and other financing options.

Elmar Vaher. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Former RKIK head: I do not have the documents

Magnus-Valdemar Saar, who headed RKIK when the contracts were signed, told ERR's "Aktuaalne kaamera" news program in response to an inquiry that the agency's contact with Datasel came through high-level international cooperation.

"Such direct contacts are generally neither documented nor made public. There are normally various ways of conducting background checks on bidders. In Datasel's case, it was demonstrably an affiliate of a publicly traded company and that company was involved in the preparation and execution of the contract at RKIK from the outset. Documents to that effect exist," he said.

Saar said that before the contract was signed, several inspection trips were made to India where Datasel's connections and production capacity were verified. RKIK representatives also made visits to Italy and to manufacturers and assemblers of components.

"All of this took place before the contract was signed and continued while the contract was being carried out," he said.

Saar confirmed that RKIK took possession of the goods following a visual inspection, but that this did not constitute the transfer of ownership under the contract. "A separate expert assessment was carried out to check the quality and ownership has not been transferred," he said.

Saar added that he is, of course, prepared to provide the European Commission's investigative team with background information and explanations, but that he no longer has the documentation in his possession.

"Detailed review meetings with European Commission contacts also took place previously, including when problems emerged during the performance of the contract," Saar added.

Datasel counsel: RKIK verified production and quality

According to Datasel's attorney, RKIK verified both the company's production capacity and the quality of the goods delivered.

"RKIK thoroughly verified that Datasel had the necessary production capacity. Even before the contracts were signed, during a process and discussions that lasted several months, several RKIK employees visited the production facilities in person to conduct inspections," said Veiko Viisileht, an attorney at law with LINKLaw.

"Every batch delivered was thoroughly inspected and handed over to RKIK only after all quality-control requirements under the contracts had been met. It is important to note that RKIK did not raise a single complaint regarding quality before terminating the contracts," he said.

Viisileht said he could not comment on the substance or value of Datasel's counterclaims. RKIK's attorney considers the counterclaim likely to be a tactical move.

Investigative team to travel to Estonia

Speaking at a Monday meeting of the Riigikogu State Budget Control Select Committee, Vaher said the European Commission will send an investigative team to Estonia for three days at the end of September to examine how well RKIK fulfilled its due diligence obligations.

According to Vaher, RKIK is continuing to search for documents related to what happened in 2024 and is speaking with former managers to obtain as complete a picture as possible of how the Datasel contracts came about.

The initial claim made publicly that only one contract had gone wrong has since changed. According to RKIK, seven contracts have been terminated.

Five of them are currently the subject of court or arbitration proceedings, while two contracts have been terminated but remain under negotiation, with preparations underway for possible litigation. RKIK cannot currently comment in greater detail on the latter two contracts because the negotiations are confidential.

The contracts currently before the courts or in arbitration are connected to Datasel.

Datasel, in turn, has filed a counterclaim against RKIK, although its exact contents are not currently being disclosed. RKIK has also not seen the documents on which the claim is based. As the disputes are ongoing, RKIK did not rule out the possibility that the counterclaim could be a tactical move. The center declined to disclose the monetary value of the counterclaim at this time.

Money from the European Peace Facility

Funding for the approximately €70 million procurement involving Datasel did not come from Estonian taxpayers but from the European Peace Facility (EPF). The funding was provided at the European level and includes, among other sources, proceeds generated by frozen Russian assets.

According to Vaher, RKIK currently has around 200 procurement projects underway, handled by approximately 80 people. They include lawyers, project managers and specialists who prepare technical specifications. Procurement decisions are made by RKIK and contracts are signed by RKIK's director general. "That means RKIK is responsible for its own actions," Vaher said.

Asko Kivinuk, RKIK's deputy director general for procurement, said RKIK becomes involved in procurements as early as the planning and pricing stage. Infrastructure and procurement plans are drawn up based on the Ministry of Defense's development plan and procurement plans are then prepared on that basis.

Maria Pihlak, an attorney at law with Sorainen who advises RKIK, stressed that court and arbitration proceedings are closed and that the parties cannot publicly comment on all the circumstances or evidence involved in the proceedings.

In addition, the contracts contain confidentiality clauses that may carry contractual penalties. RKIK must therefore be cautious about what information it discloses regarding ongoing disputes.

Contracts fail to arrive

Vaher also rejected the claim that RKIK had withheld information from the National Audit Office. He said the organization's employees cooperated fully, but a technical problem occurred when the contract materials were sent. The necessary documents were first sent to the National Audit Office on May 21 and again on June 5, but initially failed to reach the recipient.

Vaher said that, as director general, he takes responsibility for the failure to verify that the materials had been received.

According to RKIK's management, one of the main lessons from the Datasel case is that the reasoning behind procurement decisions, background checks and documentation must in the future be recorded in a way that makes it possible, even years later, to clearly establish how and why a particular contract came to be signed.

In RKIK's lawsuit against Datasel S.R.L. before Harju County Court, RKIK — and, in effect, the Estonian state — is represented by Raul Kartsep, Maria Pihlak and Kaupo Lepasepp of law firm Sorainen. Datasel is represented by Maksim Kozlov, Veiko Viisileht and Liina Rekand of law firm LINKLaw.

It emerged last Wednesday that Estonia sought to buy shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to Indian businessmen who had reportedly never sold a single shell before. RKIK terminated the contract after the company only delivered an incomplete shipment of low-quality components.

The article was updated on September 8 to add details and comments by former RKIK head Magnus-Valdemar Saar and the defense counsel of Datasel.

World.title: Silvia Urgas: Monoculture is dead, long live the monoculture
World.content:
The death of monoculture is not entirely bad, but the number of cultural references understood across groups and age brackets is shrinking, Silvia Urgas says in a culture column.

This summer's theme in the music world seems to be the final death of monoculture. When looking for a global summer hit, there are two undeniably strong candidates. The duet "Rein Me In" by English singers Sam Fender and Olivia Dean has topped the United Kingdom singles chart for twenty‑three weeks. That breaks a record set in 1953, when Frankie Laine's "I Believe" managed to stay in first place for eighteen weeks.

This week, the English duo lost the top spot in the UK chart to Ella Langley, a country singer from Alabama whose song "Choosin' Texas" has been at the top of the U.S. Billboard chart for twenty weeks. Three more weeks and it will break the record held by Mariah Carey's Christmas song "All I Want for Christmas Is You."

A person who claims they have never heard Mariah's Christmas song is likely mistaken or lying, yet both "Rein Me In" and "Choosin' Texas" are unfamiliar tracks to many music listeners. People say they first heard about "Rein Me In" only when reading about its historic chart achievement. It seems unbelievable that something can be so popular and yet so unknown at the same time.

What should we conclude from this? That charts lie? Probably not, but it is becoming increasingly clear that culture no longer reaches people through the same TV and radio channels, or even the same playlists. Some songs are still a bit more popular than others and break through several social bubbles, but creating a summer hit that unites the public or a cross‑generational favorite is becoming harder. Maybe the search for a summer hit should be retired for good. Everyone has their own summer hit, whether someone generated theirs with AI or another listens to songs from the 1970s regardless of their birth year.

Looking at Estonia's Spotify chart, it is still dominated by Nublu and Sadu, with a bit of Säm and Triibupasta in between. The Estonian‑language pop music world is simply so small that artists known to everyone from preschoolers to retirees are still possible. Nublu's "Kesselaid" got an excellent jump start on the path to becoming Estonia's summer hit thanks to the Eesti Laul program. Eesti Laul and Eurovision seem to be the last breaths of monoculture in this region, but it is already clear that Eurovision can no longer unite an entire continent the way it once did.

It is possible that the only major cultural event that truly unites the world is the soccer World Cup. Only young men from selected countries make it onto the field, but the audience and fans are much broader. Music charts hint at this through the continued presence of Shakira and Burna Boy's song "Dai Dai," made for the tournament. Still, "Dai Dai" is only a pale shadow of Shakira's 2010 World Cup song "Waka Waka," and it is doubtful that anyone will remember "Dai Dai" sixteen years from now, unlike the latter. In Estonia, Villemdrillem and Triibupasta jumped quite successfully onto this year's soccer excitement train with their song "Mr. Atškoo."

The death of monoculture is not entirely bad, but the number of cultural references understood across groups and age brackets is shrinking. People who do not share a common cultural space are easier to pit against one another and easier to manipulate into distrusting those who are different. An annoyingly popular pop hit is silly and simple, but it is an effective way to create the feeling that we are all similar people under the same sky.

World.title: School psychologist: Signs of school avoidance manifesting increasingly early in life
World.content:
Kiili High School psychologist Kristi Feldman says she is seeing more children and young people develop school avoidance each year and that it is occurring at increasingly younger ages.

How often do you encounter young people in your work who, at some point, lose the desire to learn?

It seems to me that there are more and more of these young people every year. In fact, perhaps we are no longer even talking about young people, but about children. School avoidance is increasingly affecting younger children and we are also hearing that even children in preschool do not want to go. In other words, avoidance can sometimes begin before children even reach school age.

What causes this avoidance?

I think of school avoidance as a concept in which a child's needs and their environment are not well aligned. In other words, there is something in the environment that makes the child feel they do not want to be there. There can be many different reasons for this.

When we talk about young people, we often see school avoidance and mental health disorders become most prominent when puberty begins — when hormones kick in and a young person starts asking questions such as: Who am I and what am I doing in this world? There is also anxiety about graduating from school and what to do next.

School avoidance is most common in the third stage of basic school, but the signs are usually visible earlier. Today, there are also children in primary school who do not want to go to school. Some children entering first grade have difficulty adjusting.

We also see straight-A students who one day simply stop coming to school. They no longer have the energy to go. They cannot get themselves up in the morning. They simply do not have the energy to go to school.

We live in a highly information-saturated and achievement-oriented society. A great deal is expected of children and they are not given the time to develop at an age-appropriate pace and as individuals because expectations are so high.

This kind of achievement-oriented society creates the expectation that you always have to be exceptional. You constantly have to do everything as well as possible. You cannot just participate in a sport for the sake of it — you have to compete and win. At school, you have to get good grades, be talented at something and stand out.

Children grow up in this environment and internalize these expectations and they begin expecting a great deal of themselves. Children are extremely self-critical. As the saying goes, sometimes a person is their own worst enemy and the same is true of children.

When we talk about young people who have already developed school avoidance, we can usually also talk about burnout. If an adult burns out, they can take sick leave for several months and nothing particularly drastic happens. But a young person is constantly falling further behind. Young people themselves say they cannot stay home sick for a week because afterward they will have so much schoolwork to catch up on.

How can young people who have developed school avoidance be helped?

First, it is essential that we notice them. Schools and families can work closely together on this. If a parent notices that something is different about their child, they should first try talking to their child at home and asking what has happened. They should also feel comfortable contacting the school and asking whether something has changed there that has led to the child no longer wanting to go to school.

On the one hand, it may have to do with relationships. On the other, changes may need to be made to the child's curriculum because the child is unable to cope with the program they are currently expected to follow.

There can be many different causes that create such severe stress that it leads to mental health disorders. This, in turn, can leave a child unable to attend school or study and unable to find enjoyment in what they are doing.

That young person definitely needs support to keep them from falling into that hole, to keep them from slipping. Once they start slipping, it is very difficult to come back. And if they do not come back, the longer a child remains at home, the harder it becomes for them to return to the school environment.

Young people who drop out of the education system are often described as coming from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds. From what you're saying, it sounds like that is no longer necessarily the case.

Yes, I also feel that we cannot really say that anymore. Of course, it varies by region, but I think the support system is what ultimately makes it possible either to bring a young person back to school or to prevent them from dropping out.

The thing about prevention is that we probably do not have statistics showing how many people it has saved who might otherwise have ended up on the brink of dropping out.

What we do know, however, is that among young people who need this support, a very large proportion can be brought back to school if they are given that support. And it needs to be done in cooperation with their families.

Schools can do quite a lot to create an environment that suits the child. For example, if a child has fallen behind or developed excessive anxiety or mood disorders, we know that their capacity is reduced at that point and that needs to be taken into account. They can be supported through an individualized curriculum, including studying temporarily at home.

The most difficult situations are actually those in which it is not school avoidance but learning avoidance that develops. In other words, the child is at home but does not do even the bare minimum there because they simply do not have the energy. They also blame themselves a great deal. They often say themselves, "Oh, I'm just lazy." But in reality, they are confused too and do not know what would help.

Do we have sufficient resources to work with students individually?

Our children have to be number one. Our priority across the country must be to support the mental health of our children and young people. At present, about half of schools have a school psychologist. Quite a few schools have a social pedagogue. What is important here is identifying and making use of the support systems available at school. Another important point is that a student's homeroom teacher plays a central role at school and can communicate with the family and provide support.

Municipalities have child welfare specialists and today they also have youth welfare specialists who work to prevent young people from dropping out of school and to encourage them to continue their education. I think support is available, but coverage is not equal across Estonia and these services are not accessible to every child. It is important to point out that these services are, in fact, required to be provided under the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act.

If a child has to obtain this support outside school for a fee — for example, by seeing a psychologist because that option is not available at school — the local government is required to reimburse the family. Support must be provided to children, but I suspect many parents do not know that.

Several years ago, we also launched a school psychologists' advice line that any parent, child, young person, teacher or support specialist can call to ask questions and receive initial advice from a qualified school psychologist. It is open on weekdays from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. at 1226. It is free and anonymous.

How does a child's motivation to learn develop in the first place?

Children arrive at school curious and eager to learn. My question is actually how that motivation disappears. But perhaps societal expectations are again partly to blame: We are expected to do everything with enormous motivation. Sometimes a particular subject is simply boring or part of a subject is boring and that is when the teacher needs to explain why it is necessary to learn it.

At our school, we have now drawn up a new development plan and made developing self-directed learners our main goal. In other words, we are training our teachers in how to develop self-directed learners. When students are self-directed, they understand why they are learning, what they are learning, how they learn and how they could learn better. We place autonomy and responsibility in the child's hands.

If people do not understand why they are learning something or what they are learning, no one wants to learn that way. We need to understand things; that is part of human nature. Young children are extremely curious. They ask a lot of questions and if they do not get answers, if they do not understand why something is necessary, their motivation disappears.

There is quite a lot we can already do at home. During that difficult and sometimes slightly tiresome "why?" phase, parents can answer a great many of their child's questions, helping preserve the child's curiosity about the world.

World.title: Minister: Ukraine was discussed at Tallinn dinner with Donald Trump Jr.
World.content:
Ukraine was high on the agenda in a meeting between Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) and Donald Trump Jr., the minister said.

Trump Jr. was in Tallinn recently, departing Monday morning according to Delfi.He was in town discuss security and economic policy at the same time high-level U.S. negotiators were in Ukraine, while he also attended functions organized by the casino industry.

While US peace negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were in Moscow and in Kyiv, Donald Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., was in Tallinn. Please, tell us what was he doing here?

He had some meeting of his own, but I also got the opportunity to attend a dinner, at the invitation of the U.S. side. Frankly, it was very interesting to meet someone who is not an active politician but who is nevertheless a very influential individual, to get a view of his attitude towards us, plus there was also an opportunity to talk about our own views on both security and economic policy. Perhaps contacts like these, with unconventional people close to the U.S. presidential administration, may prove handy one day.

Delfi has written about this expensive invite party held by casino company Studioworks at the Euroopa Liidu Maja in quite colorful terms, pointing out that it brought together a rather motley crew. Are you sure that conducting business in this kind of company is now the direction of our foreign policy?

It is not my place to comment on what Delfi writes, but those are two different events: One was a dinner with 13 people and the other was some other event. I had the opportunity to speak with Donald Trump Jr. at considerable length, and about important issues.

Did you also ask for any kind of support for Ukraine, and did you get any positive response?

Ukraine was discussed quite actively at the table.

And how was it discussed at the table?

I'll leave the details to one side.

Then you should also know what took place in Moscow, as you happened to have an excellent contact at hand to ask about it.

Speaking seriously, I had a call with the Ukrainian foreign minister today, and he gave me an overview of what was talked about. In his assessment, there was no major breakthrough between Ukraine and Russia or on the peace process as a whole. But I will get an opportunity this week to find out more precisely through direct discussions.

However, I am still interested in this: When you did speak with Donald Trump Jr. about Ukraine, what was his attitude? How could it be that we have a freedom of the media in which Estonia ranks second and America is quite some way far behind – I understand all that – but how can it be that the son of such an influential president comes here yet we do not know what he was doing here?

We do know what he was doing, but those questions need to be put to those people who organized his visit here. The issues I discussed were related to security and economic policy.

Come on, you posed for a photo with an American rapper. I don't know whether that was related to security or economic policy, but what was that rapper's name? I've already forgotten.

I genuinely don't know the rapper's name. There were a lot of people there.

Margus Tsahkna with the unnamed US rapper. Source: Screenshot.

The one you posed for a photo with and who wrote in his social media post that he had taken a photo with the 'prime minister'?

You'll have to ask him about what he writes on his social media.

BOLD: Among the people you were there with were also – at least according to Delfi – was a New York mafia boss, I don't know whether former or current, some casino people and some beauty queens. The whole thing had a bit of a 1990s vibe to it, I have to say.

You are now conflating two different events.

Then explain exactly what went on. Am I right in understanding that Donald Trump Jr. was here conducting casino business?

You will have to ask him and the people who organized his visit here. I attended a dinner where neither the casino business nor any business activities were discussed.

You didn't ask why he was here either? Do you know why he came here?

My understanding was that he had business meetings here, so that is for him or his team to comment on.

When I think about it, it still could have been on casino business, as it was a casino company's party that you were invited to. Were you there primarily as foreign minister, or were you carrying out Eesti 200 politics?

I was there at the invitation of the U.S. side, we held talks, and I think it would be pointless not to make use of a contact like that when a person like that comes to Estonia and is willing to discuss issues that are of interest to us, and that is what actually happened. There was no party at the dinner table where the 13 of us were seated.

So what did go on there?

There was a discussion on various topics, as I already said.

Who else from the government was invited?

No one else from the government was invited. It was a personal invitation for me.

Donald Trump Jr. Source: Gage Skidmore / Wikimedia Commons.

All right, let's change track. In the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, the far right achieved a historic election result, winning nearly 44 percent of the vote. Can you imagine that one day you could be Estonia's foreign minister at a time when the far right is in power in Germany?

Anything can happen. We saw the elections in that state and unfortunately the rise of extremist forces is indeed a reality not only in Germany but across Europe more broadly. I had thought that Germany's extraordinary step of publicly attributing the Leipzig terror attack to Russia may also be an attempt to make its people understand that Russia genuinely poses a direct threat to them. Russia really is carrying out attacks against Germany and the German people.

But it seems to be having the opposite effect. When we watched Epp Ehand's report from Germany, a great many people there seemed to feel that Russia is a much more normal country than Ukraine. It seems to be some kind of trend. What is the point of us making all this effort to help Ukraine if Germany itself starts leaning towards Russia?

We have to make the effort. It is in our own security interests, it is in Europe's interests, and we should not draw definitive conclusions from the election result in a single state.

But as Epp Ehand said, that is actually the trend.

All of that is there, and I talk to Germans quite a lot and they are highly concerned. Voter turnout was also very high. The question is whether the majority of Germany can somehow consolidate itself, also looking at the results of this particular state election. Will there be a debate about what is genuinely in the security interests of Germany and Europe, or will we indeed at some point see a Germany whose government says that relations with Russia are normal and that we want the good old days back? That would certainly not be in Estonia's interests.

What will happen to the EU if the far right comes to power in Germany?

We saw what happened in Hungary, under Viktor Orbán. I would not get ahead of events, though the issue is actually very serious, because the current model, in which 27 member states try to reach a consensus on security and foreign policy, would turn into something entirely different. I would also remind you that France has elections coming up next year and the far‑right presidential candidate there is also getting increasingly popular. Europe is facing some very serious and important questions.

One of the things we are also facing up to is climate change. Of course, you are the foreign minister, not the climate minister, although perhaps you could still become one. Do you also think about the possibility that climate change around the world could at some point put Estonia in a completely different foreign‑policy position from the one it is in today?

Foreign‑policy problems arising from climate change already exist in Europe, for example when we talk about migratory pressure from Africa. That is a reality. I remember that when I was social security minister in 2015, it directly affected Estonia's domestic politics too, even though climate refugees did not actually want to come here. EKRE also emerged around that time, and one of its platforms was immigration, which may now also be helping AfD come to power in Germany, for instance.

Those direct links stemming from climate change, such as migration pressure or changes in the economic situation, will certainly be reflected in the domestic politics of democratic countries. Domestic politics, in turn, shapes foreign policy to a very large extent, so we certainly think about it. But if you ask whether we are prepared for it, or whether Europe, for example, has some well‑thought‑out strategy, I can say that in reality it does not, and the problems are dealt with one by one. The root causes of these problems are very often not purely scientific; they are also a matter of belief, and we see conflicts and divisions in different societies, not only in Europe.

Finally, I would ask this: When I usually interview a foreign minister, there is at least some hope that I will meet them again the following year. What do you think will have become of you six months from now? Will you still be in politics, or will you have left?

It is very hard to say. According to my original plans, I took the job of foreign minister for about a year, yet I am now already in my fourth year. I think the elections are in March, then forming a new government usually takes a couple of weeks or a month, and ultimately the voters will decide. Whether I am still in politics then or not, the good thing about foreign and security policy, at least, is that fortunately it is not a matter of day‑to‑day politics. We have agreed on certain fundamental principles, and in that sense I am not worried in terms of the elections, as Estonia's foreign and security policy will certainly continue on the same trajectory.
