World.title: In a league of her own: A Japanese F-15 pilot guarding the northern skies
World.content:
In Hollywood, the archetype of the fast-jet aviator is Tom Cruise’s Maverick in “Top Gun” — a reckless, rules-defying hotshot. At Chitose Air Base, that job belongs to 31-year-old Capt. Momoka Fujii, call sign “Jasmine.”

As one of a tiny minority of female pilots flying front-line combat jets in the Air Self-Defense Force (ASDF) , Fujii spends her days in the cockpit of an F-15 Eagle guarding Japan’s northern flank, where split-second decisions carry international consequences.

Yet when asked if the high-flying Hollywood image matches her daily reality, she quickly sets the record straight.

World.title: Japan tightens measures against private jet pilots with three-strikes rule
World.content:
Japan is tightening measures against private jet pilots who fail to follow instructions from air traffic control, with three strikes resulting in a ban from Haneda Airport.

The move comes as the government tries to lure business jets and other private jets to airports nationwide. But as the number of private jet flights increase, so too have pilots who fail to comply with traffic controls, which could lead to large-scale accidents.

Last year, there were five instances of foreign-owned private jets not following instructions from air traffic control, according to the transport ministry.

World.title: Key ministers, LDP leaders expected to keep positions amid personnel changes
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi appears to be opting for continuity and stability ahead of the autumn session of parliament, as key members of her Cabinet and the Liberal Democratic Party’s leadership are expected to remain when personnel changes are announced next week.

Takaichi secured a mandate Tuesday morning during a party officials meeting to carry out party executive appointments as early as Sept. 16. Those will be followed by a Cabinet reshuffle, but major changes may not be coming, especially in the party leadership where it appears policy chief Takayuki Kobayashi could remain.

Liberal Democratic Party policy chief Takayuki Kobayashi (left) hands a policy proposal to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Tokyo on Aug. 26. | JIJI

LDP Vice President Taro Aso, the party’s powerful behind-the-scenes kingmaker who turns 86 on Sept. 20 and whose support was crucial for Takaichi winning the LDP presidency last year, is likely to remain in his position. Aso’s brother-in-law — LDP Secretary-General Shunichi Suzuki — and Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, a close ally of Takaichi, are also expected to stay on.

Kobayashi appears likely to stay put or, possibly, receive a Cabinet post. As policy chief, he played a key role in getting controversial legislation — including that to revise the Imperial House Law, one establishing a secondary capital concept and another that punished acts of vandalizing the national flag — passed in parliament.

Kobayashi maintaining his current position means he would take the lead on the party’s parliamentary legislation this autumn, particularly on a bill to reduce the food consumption tax from 8% to 1% that has many LDP members concerned about how the Takaichi administration plans to cover the lost tax revenue.

Remaining policy chief or having a Cabinet position could also make it more difficult for Kobayashi to challenge Takaichi in next year’s presidential election. He ran against her in last year’s contest and is considered a potential rival next year.

The prime minister may keep Shinjiro Koizumi as defense minister for similar reasons as with Kobayashi — to have an experienced hand at the post and to keep Koizumi, a potential rival who lost the presidency to Takaichi in a run-off last year, at bay.

Other key LDP members who could be part of a reshuffle include Minister of Internal Affairs Yoshimasa Hayashi and Koichi Hagiuda, a powerful senior LDP executive. Hayashi also ran against Takaichi last year and may do so again.

Hagiuda was caught up in a slush fund scandal and received a one-year suspension from the party in 2024. Though on good terms with Takaichi, there is some concern within the LDP that appointing him to a Cabinet position could create public backlash that hurts the party.

World.title: South Korea’s power demand set to soar on AI boom
World.content:
South Korea’s demand for power in the coming years is set to surge on plans by chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix to expand production and the building of new artificial intelligence data centers, according to the country’s energy minister.

Those AI-driven power needs alone will lift South Korea’s demand for power by 25 to 30 gigawatts, the Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Sung-whan said in an interview this month.

On top of that, the country will also need to contend with increased power demand due to the shift to electric vehicles from gasoline-engine cars and to heating via electricity rather than gas, he added.

World.title: The tiny island where the U.S. and Canada could mend their rift
World.content:
We picked a helluva time to go RVing in Canada. My wife and I crossed the border in Maine as recent trade talks in Washington were collapsing, and we awoke to news of a major escalation in tariffs and even talk of war. It made for some awkward moments in the days that followed.

“I shouldn’t say this because you’re Americans,” a man on Cape Breton told us, “but most Canadians want nothing to do with the U.S. anymore.”

He was genial but not joking. Even if he was exaggerating, his words stung, because we knew there was more than a grain of truth in them. A friend of ours in Maine, who is from Ontario, told us that her family has stopped coming to the U.S., even for family reunions.

World.title: Tokyo’s Taito Ward, long popular with tourists, looks to ban minpaku in certain areas
World.content:
Tokyo’s Taito Ward, home to popular tourist spots such as Asakusa and Ueno, is moving to ban minpaku in certain parts of the ward beginning next year, as local governments across Japan begin restricting the short-term private-residence lodging system.

An ordinance was submitted to the ward assembly Tuesday that proposes effectively ending the program for new minpaku in residential areas and locations where traditional hotels and inns are restricted. It will do so by limiting the number of days that such minpaku can operate to zero.

The ward cited increasing reports of bad behavior such as improper trash disposal and loud noises as being behind the new ordinance.

Both the number of minpaku in Taito and the number of complaints stemming from them have risen dramatically in recent years. The number of new minpaku applications tripled in 2025 compared with the year prior, hitting nearly 1,400, while the number of complaints accordingly increased fourfold to 257 cases.

In addition to the proposed policy on new minpaku, Taito Ward will begin enforcing fresh restrictions on all minpaku later this year. While the ward currently allows them to operate on any given day up to the nationwide legal limit of 180 days a year, beginning in October they will only be able to accommodate guests on weekends and holidays.

The minpaku program allows approved operators to provide lodging in their private residences. Since starting in June 2018 as a way to meet higher tourist demand and fill houses vacated by Japan’s diminishing population, the system’s popularity has rapidly grown, especially in recent years.

Taito’s potential ban comes as other municipalities around the country are introducing restrictions. Since July, when the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism notified local governments that they had the authority to limit minpaku operations, Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward as well as the city of Kyoto have moved to implement bans, both referencing an increasing number of local complaints.

World.title: Japan not confident that U.S. relations will improve after Trump, survey finds
World.content:
Japan views the United States as a necessary partner, but has low confidence it will become “a better ally” after U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term ends, according to a new study .

Just 26% of Japanese surveyed said that the U.S. will improve as an ally post-Trump, compared with 45% of Australians and 46% of Americans, according to the study by the University of Sydney’s United States Studies Center.

The researchers polled more than 1,000 people from countries that make up “the Quad” security grouping — Japan, the U.S., Australia and India.

“Japanese respondents are much less confident,” the study noted, referring to their views of Tokyo’s security ally once the U.S. president leaves office.

Trump’s transactional approach to U.S. alliances and his freewheeling use of tariffs or the threat of them has tested diplomatic ties.

Around 53% of Japanese surveyed said Trump’s second term has been a negative for Japan, with just 8% viewing it positively for the country.

Despite this, the countries surveyed still characterize their relations with the U.S. overall as very important, with 36% of Japanese respondents feeling that the alliance with the U.S. is more necessary than ever. The same sentiment was voiced by 44% of Indians and 49% of Australians.

But while the U.S. relationship is viewed as vital, in Japan, confidence in the country as a protective force has been dented.

While in 2023, 77% of Japanese surveyed felt confident that the United States would come to their country’s aid if they were attacked by China, that figure sank to 60% in this year’s survey.

Tokyo’s ties with Beijing have deteriorated since November, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi publicly commented about Japan intervening militarily in the event of an attack on Taiwan by China. Despite this, there was a slight decline in the belief among Japanese that an armed conflict with China will occur within the next 10 years.

A majority in Japan, 66%, view China as a danger while 28% see it as an economic partner, with a similar picture among Americans (55% danger, 43% economic partner), and Indians (59% danger, 43% economic partner). Australia, however, stands in stark contrast, with 64% viewing China more as an economic partner, while 47% consider it a threat.

Americans were also more critical of their government’s “handling” of China, being the largest Quad member to characterize it as “too aggressive,” with 20% responding in this way. Only 4% of Australians and 7% of Japanese felt the same way about their respective governments’ approaches.

World.title: Japanese carmakers brace for profit hit after yen strengthens
World.content:
Toyota Motor and other Japanese carmakers risk taking a hit to their bottom lines after the yen strengthened to its highest level in more than six months.

The currency traded just above ¥153 against the dollar on Tuesday, its strongest level since February. That’s squeezing many of Japan’s export-focused automakers, which have partly based their earnings forecasts on weaker yen assumptions.

At ¥160 yen to the dollar, Toyota has the most bearish projection. The world’s biggest automaker said in August its annual operating income falls by about ¥50 billion ($326 million) each time the yen appreciates by ¥1.

The swings are a source of uncertainty for Japanese automakers, highlighting the economic cost of a volatile currency. A stronger yen erodes the value of overseas earnings when they’re brought back to Japan, hurting companies that generate much of their sales in the U.S. and Europe.

The yen is currently outperforming the assumptions of all Japanese carmakers except Nissan Motor, which projects it at ¥150 against the dollar for the fiscal year through March 2027. Toyota and Suzuki Motor revised their projections upward in August from May.

Japan’s automakers have long embraced conservative currency assumptions, helping them to meet or exceed forecasts when posting results. Many of them produce cars and even parts closer to final sales markets, creating a natural hedge because production expenses can be paid in the same currency.

Toyota is better equipped to tolerate the risks that come with adopting a weaker-yen assumption. Its earnings are among the most global in the industry and are spread across financial services and other businesses, giving it additional operational flexibility to offset adverse swings.

While the weak yen has threatened to drive up inflation and import prices in Japan, it had offered the island nation’s largest exporters a much-needed respite from U.S. tariffs, soaring oil prices and supply chain snags.

In late June, the yen was trading at its lowest since 1986, prompting the U.S. and Japan to make their first joint intervention in 15 years.

World.title: Hong Kong’s MTR Corp wins bid as part of group to build new Sydney station, properties
World.content:
Hong Kong rail giant the MTR Corporation has won a bid as part of a consortium to design and build a metro station and develop property in Sydney’s second central business district in Australia.

The corporation said on Tuesday that it and its two partners – both subsidiaries of Malaysian engineering firm and developer Gamuda Berhad – won the bid as the joint-venture Riverside Link Consortium, with Australian media reporting the deal was worth A$880 million (HK$4.99 billion).

The deal is a major part of the Sydney Metro West project in the state of New South Wales.

It will be key to the growth and development of Parramatta, a commercial and financial centre located 24km (15 miles) west of Sydney and regarded as the city’s second central business district.

“The project provides an opportunity for the MTR to apply our experience in integrating transport infrastructure with residential, commercial and community development opportunities to create well-connected, vibrant and people-focused urban precincts,” the MTR Corp’s managing director for property and international business, David Tang Chi-fai, said.

The joint venture will be responsible for designing and building the Parramatta metro station by 2032. The facility is expected to cut train travel times from Parramatta to Sydney’s city centre to about 20 minutes.

World.title: Beijing recommends 16 Hong Kong civil servants to UN roles, highest number to date
World.content:
Beijing has recommended the largest-ever cohort of civil servants from Hong Kong to take on roles in United Nations agencies this year, expecting the deployments to broaden their global perspective and strengthen the city’s position as a bridge between China and the international community.

The batch of 16 officers sent under the UN Junior Professional Officer (JPO) scheme came from 13 grades and departments, including customs, police and the city’s anti-corruption agency. The number surpassed the five deployed in 2019 and 12 in 2023.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Tuesday said previous officers had excelled across fields spanning anti-drug operations, climate and resource co-ordination, trade and transport, and intellectual property protection.

“Previous batches contributed across fields, from drug enforcement to climate coordination. They earned high praise from the UN, with nearly half seeing their tenures extended at the organisation’s request,” he said.

“This affirms Hong Kong youth and strengthens our resolve to contribute to the international community.”

Lee said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, set to be unveiled next Wednesday, would align with the national 15th five-year plan, and that dispatching young civil servants to the UN was part of the city’s effort to serve national diplomacy and meet global commitments by leveraging its professional strengths.

The UN JPO Programme provides young professionals with hands-on experience in international development and multilateral cooperation through positions funded directly by sponsoring member governments.

World.title: Hong Kong families hit as volcanic ash strands up to 200 helpers in Indonesia
World.content:
Up to 200 Hong Kong-bound domestic helpers remain stranded in Indonesia despite the reopening of several affected airports, as the city’s employment agencies association braces for possible further closures due to volcanic ash.

The Indonesian transport ministry said Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport resumed operations on Tuesday after being shut for several days, following the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatoa on Saturday, which affected thousands of travellers.

Among those stranded are 150 to 200 helpers heading to Hong Kong, including both new recruits and workers who had returned home for holidays, Cheung Kit-man, chairman of the Hong Kong Employment Agencies Association, said.

Some were expected to fly out on Wednesday as operations resumed, Cheung said, but agencies remained concerned flights could be suspended again if further eruptions occurred.

“Of course we are worried, because it is a natural phenomenon and [the volcano] can erupt at any time. No one can predict it,” Cheung said. “If it does erupt again, we already have contingency plans in place.”

Eight airports in Indonesia halted operations over the weekend, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights. Photo: AFP

He said some workers had been diverted to depart from Surabaya, Indonesia’s second-largest city, located east of Jakarta and currently unaffected by the eruptions.

World.title: Hong Kong a boon to Kazakhstan’s advanced manufacturing ambitions, ties to Europe: expert
World.content:
Hong Kong firms could look to Kazakhstan as a base for advanced manufacturing and as a gateway to Europe, while the city’s robust capital markets could attract businesses in the Central Asian country, a diplomat and business adviser has said.

Sabr Yessimbekov, adviser to the chairman of the presidium of the National Chamber of Entrepreneurs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the inaugural China Conference: Central Asia 2026 that some projects in MOUs signed during Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s trip to Kazakhstan in June had already got under way.

“We are talking about processing of raw materials and industrial production. There are some companies from Hong Kong and they have already started investing,” he said on Monday.

The firms included tungsten miner Jiaxin International Resources, which became the first company to be dual-listed on Hong Kong and Astana’s bourses last year.

In June, Lee led a 70-strong business and professional delegation from Hong Kong and mainland China to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to establish new trade corridors amid global geopolitical tensions, resulting in 96 deals worth US$1.65 billion.

On Monday, Lee said during a virtual appearance at the conference that a bank in that delegation had since backed the Development Bank of Kazakhstan with US$785 million in financing.

World.title: Hong Kong emerges as leading Asian study destination for Kazakhstani students
World.content:
Kazakhstan has recorded the largest student population and fastest enrolment growth at Hong Kong’s public universities among Central Asian countries in recent years, according to official data, while students from the country said the city was the most preferred regional higher education destination in Asia among their peers.

Among Hong Kong’s tertiary education institutions, City University (CityU) enrolled the largest share of Kazakhstani students.

CityU council chairman Michael Ngai Ming-tak told the South China Morning Post that students from Kazakhstan were among the university’s top-performing undergraduates and that the country’s government was committed to educating its young people.

According to University Grants Committee (UGC) figures, Kazakhstan accounts for the largest number of students studying at Hong Kong’s publicly funded universities among the five countries that make up Central Asia.

The number of Kazakhstani students at the universities rose from 97 in the 2017-18 academic year to 493 in 2025-26, an increase of 408 per cent – the highest growth rate among Central Asian countries.

CityU enrolled 203 Kazakhstani undergraduates this year, a record 49 per cent rise from 135 the previous academic year.

World.title: Hong Kong aviation success today means more than just adding routes
World.content:
When Cathay Pacific Airways announced direct flights to Almaty starting next January, the significance went beyond adding another destination. The service will be Cathay Pacific’s first to Central Asia and the only non-stop passenger connection between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan.

Another announcement pointed to Hong Kong’s growing aviation reach from a different direction. Qatar Airways Cargo relocated its regional office to Hong Kong and agreed with the Airport Authority to increase frequencies and develop new routes through the city. The airline already operates around 56 cargo flights a week via Hong Kong.

Taken together, these developments offer an interesting glimpse of how Hong Kong’s aviation map is evolving.

As Cathay celebrates its 80th anniversary this year, Hong Kong also finds itself entering a new era for its airport. The three-runway system and Skytopia development signal ambitions that extend well beyond aviation. Hong Kong International Airport is no longer being positioned simply as one of the world’s best to arrive at or for transit, but as an integrated destination for tourism, business and entertainment.

In this year’s budget, the government reaffirmed the Airport City development as a strategic economic initiative. Hong Kong’s airport handled some 63 million passengers in the year ended March 31, nearly 15 per cent more than in the previous year, while remaining the world’s busiest cargo airport.

Yet these developments also pose an important question. If Hong Kong’s ambitions for its airport have evolved, has our thinking about what makes a successful aviation hub kept pace?

World.title: AI, chip firms among bidders for flagship Northern Metropolis tech hub at border
World.content:
Hong Kong’s flagship tech hub at the border with mainland China received bids from firms specialising in cutting-edge fields such as chips, artificial intelligence and quantum technology, the South China Morning Post has learned.

The government last week said that it received an “enthusiastic response” to the tender for four land parcels in the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park (HSITP), with a better-than-expected six bids submitted

The sites are earmarked for laboratories and talent accommodation, with a combined gross floor area exceeding 76,000 square metres.

“The Loop Hong Kong Park Company is considering advancing the announcement of the tender results, as it aims to speed up the hardware developments of the park to draw crowds and build up popularity,” a government insider said on Monday.

According to the source, five companies submitted six bids. Of these, three specialise in cutting-edge technologies including chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology.

The remaining two are conglomerates with AI, data and medical research departments or subsidiaries.

World.title: Foreign, mainland students flock to Hong Kong, sparking property demand in education sector
World.content:
Hong Kong’s bid to become a global education hub is likely to transform the sector as a sustainable source of property demand, with the city tipped to see around 200,000 non-local students by 2035, according to CBRE.

The city’s international schools are estimated to require enormous additional real estate to accommodate nearly 30,000 to 40,000 non-local students, as the institutions would need to set up 40 to 50 new school campuses.

This could mean up to an extra 1.11 million square metres (12 million square feet) of gross floor area, a study released by the consultancy on Monday showed.

At the tertiary level, with a projected inflow of 150,000 students, universities were likely to expand their academic space by 1.39 million to 2.14 million square metres (15 million to 23 million square feet). Currently, Hong Kong’s 12 institutions that award degrees occupy around 4 million square metres of gross floor area.

Moreover, the student accommodation segment would also need more than 70,000 additional beds to provide living space for these students in about a decade.

“Hong Kong’s education sector is undergoing a structural transformation,” said Marcos Chan, executive director and head of research at CBRE Hong Kong.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018996/When China’s Star Intellectuals Fly Too Close to the Sun
World.title: When China’s Star Intellectuals Fly Too Close to the Sun
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018996/When China’s Star Intellectuals Fly Too Close to the Sun
World.content:
In Classical Greek mythology, few things are more dangerous than hubris. In one of the most renowned examples, Icarus, fleeing the island of Crete, flew too close to the sun until the heat melted the wax on his wings, plunging him into the sea. It was a tragedy, and also a reminder of the seductive peril of overreach, especially for aspiring young people.

Recent years have seen plenty of writers, academics, and artists take Icarian falls of their own. The latest is Zhuge Yiyang, the 29-year-old political philosophy Ph.D. candidate at Boston College and founder of the wildly popular Chinese-language podcast “Monologues of a Committed Observer.” In the weeks since her August interview with director Christopher Nolan made her a global star, Zhuge, who also goes by the alias Zhong Shu, has seen her reputation in China collapse, as critics accuse her of serial plagiarism in both her writing and podcast scripts.

Zhuge has denied the allegations, but the backlash has already taken a toll on her career, with multiple public events where she was due to appear being canceled without explanation.

Prior to her viral Nolan interview, Zhuge had built an idol-like fandom among young Chinese, attracting over 970,000 subscribers to her podcast. Her fans praised her confident, assertive tone and unapologetic approach to being a young female intellectual. They were also drawn to her seemingly boundless knowledge, ranging from Greek philosophy to the modern history of the Middle East, as well as her astonishingly prolific output — in addition to her Ph.D. studies, she managed to release podcast episodes roughly every three days and publish six translated books in the span of a year, all while writing regular columns and maintaining an active presence on social media and at public events.

Zhuge is something of an extreme case, but her profile is representative of China’s new generation of public intellectuals. It’s no longer enough to be a good writer, translator, or speaker. Fans and employers alike demand all-around excellence and near-constant output. The rewards are handsome, but it’s no coincidence that all the industries Zhuge has dabbled in, including academia, media, and publishing, are struggling financially and no longer offer secure employment.

Take academia, for example. A July report on the extent of recent layoffs in British higher education — nearly 4,000 cuts in a single year, according to the Guardian — drew attention on Chinese social media, where young scholars shared their own stories of the deteriorating academic job market and the dim prospects of surviving the harsh “up or out” tenure system.

Faced with a lack of opportunities inside the ivory tower, a number of Chinese Ph.D. students in the social sciences and humanities have turned to social media. Some start podcasts or other ambitious projects; many more use their profiles to advertise tutoring and proofreading services: a side hustle to subsidize tuition fees and living costs or cushion themselves against post-graduation unemployment.

Likewise, fearing they are fighting a losing war against social media and short-form videos, news outlets are increasingly gambling on “stars” rather than subject-matter experts. Newsrooms across China now incentivize journalists to build their own “personal IP” — a euphemism for becoming online influencers.

In many cases, this means doing research, voiceover, video editing, and social media operations all by themselves or with the support of a small team. It also involves creating renshe, or “persona,” which gives the journalist a memorable public image — such as being “funny,” “knowledgeable,” or “resilient” — a strategy borrowed from the wider community of online celebrities.

For cultural workers, the distinction between being a beloved influencer or a mere expert can make a material difference. When a guest on her podcast noted that rates for Chinese translators of academic books are typically lower than 0.1 yuan ($0.015) per Chinese character, without royalties, Zhuge appeared surprised, saying that her book deal was quite different.

Indeed, publishing houses often offer more to celebrity translators with big fanbases, even if they do not deliver the finest translations. This is especially true in niche markets such as the humanities and social sciences, where the benchmark for a best-seller can be as low as 10,000 copies a year.

This influencer model ultimately shifts industry-wide crises and responsibilities onto individuals. Although intellectuals have always been entangled in market dynamics, their role as salespeople has never been more prominent than it is today. As far as industry or academia are concerned, scholars, journalists, translators, and countless others in the cultural industry who struggle financially have only themselves to blame for lacking an appealing online persona.

Many find themselves trapped in an inherently volatile situation. The race for ever more impressive public images pushes ambitious young writers, journalists, and academics to prioritize performative work, incentivizing plagiarism, polarizing content, and exaggeration of their credentials. Original work gets depreciated: doctoral research, investigative journalism, and book projects that take years of painstaking effort continue to be undervalued.

The unbalanced distribution of resources, wealth, and responsibilities eventually drains cultural institutions’ ability to attract the best talent. It also damages their most valuable asset: trust.

This is particularly frustrating for those who draw inspiration from success stories like Zhuge, including women denied the right to speak assertively under patriarchal culture; ethnic minority scholars sidelined in Western academic discourse, especially in disciplines such as Classics that have been reserved for white elites; and people eager to access knowledge that’s been paywalled by academic journals or expensive degree programs.

In Chinese fandom, an idol doesn’t fall from the sky; rather, their house collapses around them. Known as tafang, the word describes the world-ending despair fans feel when their favorite celebrity lets them down.

The recent controversies surrounding her work may not end Zhuge’s career, but they offer a useful example of what happens when intellectualism is rebuilt around the ideal of superhuman output. The cultivation of over-inflated personas has enriched a few and demoralized the rest. Addressing the challenges facing cultural institutions and workers requires sustained investment and broad-based public support. Hinging everything on individual effort, no matter how Herculean, will only speed their collapse.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018990/China Moves to Address Self-Driving Cars in National Law
World.title: China Moves to Address Self-Driving Cars in National Law
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018990/China Moves to Address Self-Driving Cars in National Law
World.content:
China has proposed adding autonomous driving to its national traffic law, marking the first time the new technology has been addressed at the national legal level.

The draft, submitted to the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress for its first reading on Aug. 25, introduces a legal framework for when self-driving vehicles can use public roads, which party is responsible when such vehicles violate traffic rules, and how insurance liability should be handled.

China’s autonomous-driving rules have largely remained at the level of national standards, regulations, and local legislation, leading to inconsistencies when assigning responsibility in traffic accidents involving self-driving cars. The lack of a national law has also made it difficult to enforce regulations regarding self-driving cars on public roads.

In 2021, China introduced a new national standard that established a driving automation classification system, which allowed vehicles to be categorized into six levels based on their degree of automation, but did not legally address autonomous driving. Cities including Beijing and the southern tech hub Shenzhen have introduced local rules for autonomous driving, which state that autonomous driving is permitted in limited locations.

The proposed amendment is based on a basic distinction between autonomous driving vehicles and cars with driver-assistance functions.

The draft law states that autonomous vehicles can continuously perform all driving tasks without a driver. If a violation occurs when an autonomous-driving function is active, the manufacturer or importer is thus legally responsible. If the manufacturer or importer argues that a violation was unrelated to autonomous-driving functions, it would have to provide evidence to support that claim.

Driver-assistance functions, by contrast, only provide help during select maneuvers. Under the new amendment, a vehicle operating in driver-assistance mode is therefore still treated as a conventional vehicle.

Legal scholar Zheng Fei, a professor at the Institute of Evidence Law and Forensic Science at China University of Political Science and Law and a government advisor on the autonomous driving provisions, told Sixth Tone that the amendment is the first time the country has addressed responsibility in accidents involving autonomous vehicles.

Zheng said the amendment considers whether autonomous driving functions are active at the time of an accident, not just whether a vehicle has the capacity for autonomous driving. He said the distinction is intended to address problems with the country’s existing traffic law, which was written under the assumption that a human driver is always in control of a vehicle.

For consumers, Zheng said, such a distinction can also protect consumer rights and interests, allowing them to clearly judge the vehicle’s capabilities and clarify their own responsibility.

The draft amendment also addresses insurance liability for autonomous driving accidents, proposing that autonomous vehicles be subject to China’s compulsory motor vehicle traffic accident liability insurance system. It also encourages manufacturers, importers, and owners of autonomous vehicles to purchase commercial insurance.

To prevent consumers from confusing driver assistance with autonomous driving, the amendment also requires manufacturers and importers to clearly define self-driving and driver-assistance functions.

The move comes in response to previous disputes in which carmakers were accused of equating the term “intelligent driving,” or zhineng jiashi, to autonomous driving as a marketing tactic. Critics say such claims have led consumers to overtrust these systems’ capabilities, contributing to serious accidents.

However, Zheng said that the provisions do not fully address civil compensation, product liability or criminal liability. He pointed to the unresolved issue of liability during “handover” — the period when a person takes the wheel after full self-driving mode, and vice versa.

He also cautioned that autonomous driving systems can be deactivated by automakers, and could be tampered with by automakers in cases of accidents to avoid liability. Rules regarding data storage duration and anti-tampering also need clarification, he said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Vectorstock/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018966/Did AI Find Murakami’s Voice? Student’s $2 Experiment Divides China’s Literati
World.title: Did AI Find Murakami’s Voice? Student’s $2 Experiment Divides China’s Literati
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018966/Did AI Find Murakami’s Voice? Student’s $2 Experiment Divides China’s Literati
World.content:
Chinese readers of Haruki Murakami used to wait over a year for a faithful Mandarin translation of his latest book after its official release in Japanese. Not this time.

An unlicensed, high-fidelity digital version of the author’s new novel, “The Tale of KAHO,” was available to download in Chinese just hours after it went on sale in Tokyo on July 3.

There were no lengthy negotiations over rights, no translators straining to make a deadline, no pondering on how to capture Murakami’s distinct voice. Instead, it was accomplished in a relative flash for less than $2 using an AI-based tool developed by a 21-year-old university student.

“The Tale of KAHO,” a novel about a picture book illustrator who slips between dream and reality, was the first real test for Wenyi, a coding project that instructs large-language-model artificial intelligence on literary translation. Its designer, who asked to be identified by the pseudonym Ping Ming for privacy reasons, says he wanted to know whether AI could handle not only simple text but also glossary management, polishing, and rounds of spontaneous self-reviews.

What he discovered could fundamentally alter how novels are translated.

Wenyi’s unlicensed translation of the novel quickly began circulating on Chinese social media and the resale platform Xianyu, as well as the free online archive Z-Library.

Anecdotal evidence suggests readers are impressed. On China’s interest-oriented networking platform Douban, the most-liked review of the novel reads, “If this is purely AI translation, the quality is astonishing! … If AI can already do this much, what’s the point of having human translators?”

Readers might be happy, but publishing industry insiders feel AI still has a long way to go before it can replace humans — while legal experts warn that copyright holders could lose out either way.

Staying faithful

Nanshan Youlu, a part-time Japanese-to-Chinese translator who asked to use his online alias, worked with a friend on a manual translation of “The Tale of KAHO,” which they also began sharing bit by bit on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, on July 3.

Their first post received more than 2,000 likes, with many users expressing gratitude and complimenting the quality of their translation. Yet shortly after completing the final chapter, the duo wiped their version from the internet, citing that Wenyi’s translation was just too good — virtually 100% faithful to the original Japanese text.

“When human translators work on a novel, they will read the whole book first, and therefore will build their own interpretation and create their own ‘context.’ It’s basically impossible for them to achieve 100% wording fidelity,” Nanshan Youlu, a 30-something working at a tech company in Beijing, tells Sixth Tone. “They don’t translate mechanically — every sentence they translate serves the context they build.”

Wenyi works differently. Ping explains that his program started by dividing the book into chunks of fewer than 2,000 words, which it then sent one by one to the Chinese AI model DeepSeek for translation. To maintain continuity, each chunk overlapped by six paragraphs. “If you feed AI tens of thousands of words all at once, there’s a risk of AI hallucination, which can result in lots of mistakes,” he says.

The program also asked AI to extract important terms and proper nouns from the material so it can continuously update a glossary of keywords to ensure consistency. Once finished, the system reviews the entire book — again, chunk by chunk — to check for problems.

Not a single human had read the Chinese translation before Ping uploaded it to Z-Library just four hours after the official version of the novel was released in Japan. The project had cost him just 13 yuan ($1.90) in DeepSeek tokens.

However, once online, he soon began noticing mistakes. Some nouns, such as the various nicknames for the protagonist Kaho, hadn’t been extracted for the glossary and were inconsistent, while some wording was unnatural, more machine-like.

He decided to translate it again, this time refining his code to instruct the AI to be more meticulous about names, and requesting a complete polish of the text. This second version was better, he says, although it took longer.

Ping, a literature major at Nanjing Normal University in the eastern Jiangsu province, taught himself to code using the Python programming language two years ago. To train Wenyi, he used English-language literature including works by the 19th-century American writer Edgar Allan Poe and Scottish novelist Ian McEwan.

“When I was a child, I always found hackers in the movies so cool, and I wanted to have those skills,” Ping tells Sixth Tone, adding that in more recent years he has been attracted by the rapid developments in AI technology.

The idea for Wenyi partially stemmed from his passion for literature. As a fan of Murakami, Ping always wanted to read the author’s books as soon as they were released, but he can’t read Japanese. He recalls attempting to digest an unlicensed Mandarin version of Murakami’s novel “The City and Its Uncertain Walls” produced using the free DeepL online translation tool in 2023, “but it was unacceptably bad — the grammar, pronouns, proper nouns, all were a mess.” He had to wait another year for the official Chinese version, translated by the prominent literary scholar Shi Xiaowei.

Machine translation has been around a while, but conventional tools have never been considered good enough for literary works.

“Someone needs to step forward and explore how good AI translation can be,” says Ping. “If it were not me, it would be someone else. … The original AI models set the lower limit (of translation), while Wenyi sets the upper limit.”

However, not everyone is impressed. Lin Shaohua, who translated Murakami’s earlier works, including the best-sellers “Kafka on the Shore” and “Norwegian Wood,” told China Newsweek that while Wenyi’s translation was technically fluent, it had failed to capture the author’s true voice.

“AI translation has achieved ‘grammatically coherent and reads smoothly’ — but that’s all,” he’s quoted as saying. “AI is still not quite capable of conveying subtle nuances of language and stylistic nuances. … The story itself is not literature. Only its particular tone makes it literature. Literature is the art of language.”

However, over the years, Lin has faced criticism from readers over alleged mistakes in his translations that might have changed what the original author intended to convey.

Nanshan Youlu believes this is hard to avoid and sees translation as a continuation of the creative process. While some translators aim to follow an author’s style to the letter, for him, the core of the job is to convey the feelings in a text, rather than reproduce the exact wording. Sometimes, after working for hours on a draft, he will review it and find areas that aren’t exactly faithful to the source novel — though revising them might disrupt the structure and context that he’s already built.

“If you read the AI translation closely, you’ll find it’s quite fragmented when it comes to context,” he says. “There’s a certain disharmony to it, a sense that the whole thing was pieced together.”

However, for Ping, fidelity to the original is essential. “If a translation doesn’t match, I’d simply call it a mistake — that’s non-negotiable,” he says. “No matter how good your education and cultural literacy, or how beautiful and fluent your translations are, if you’re not faithful to the original, there’s nothing to talk about.”

There be pirates

Of course, without a licensing agreement, both Ping Ming and Nanshan Youlu risk accusations of copyright infringement for releasing their translations online, regardless of whether they profited financially.

Under China’s Copyright Law, using published works for personal study, research, or appreciation is considered fair use. However, this doesn’t apply if the use is seen as harmful to the copyright holder’s rights and interests — for example, negatively affecting sales of Murakami’s books in China.

“The nonprofit nature of their conduct does not constitute grounds for exemption from liability,” Zhang Jie, an attorney from Shanghai-based law firm Zhihe Partners with experience handling intellectual property (IP) disputes, tells Sixth Tone. “The law’s control over acts such as reproduction, adaptation, translation, and dissemination via information networks naturally extends to the use of AI. Whether infringement has occurred has little to do with whether a work was created by a human or with AI assistance.”

She adds that China legally protects the IP rights of overseas authors under the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works and other international treaties.

While this initial breakthrough in AI literary translation may have skirted the law, it does demonstrate the technology’s potential legitimate use by publishing houses. However, industry insiders suggest the overwhelming preference is still for human translators, especially when handling more complex projects.

Liu Chengxu, an editor at Guangdong People’s Publishing House, says, “If the original book is straightforward to understand, I’d choose AI translation. Frankly speaking, in those cases, there isn’t much difference between the work of a seasoned human translator and that of an AI translator. But if the original is more complex, like if it’s hard sci-fi or a thought experiment, I would choose a human translator.”

Compared with the lightning speed of DeepSeek, a professional translator will need about six months to complete a 350-page book like “The Tale of KAHO.” Then come editorial reviews, proofreading, publication, and distribution, with the book finally hitting shelves after about a year. Meanwhile, translators earn 100 to 120 yuan per 1,000 characters — not a high rate, but still far more than the current cost of AI.

Despite the obvious benefits, Puzhao, an editor at the Shanghai Translation Publishing House who goes by a pen name, feels that using AI to translate fiction still isn’t a viable option. “I prefer collaborating with humans,” he says. “When it comes to literary books, we need humans to translate them in their own words.”

He cites Emily Wilson’s acclaimed 2017 version of Homer’s epic “The Odyssey” as an example that a new translation of a classical or even modern text has the power to spark widespread discussion. This, he says, demonstrates that translation is not merely a mechanical transfer of words but a way to use contemporary language to introduce stories to new audiences.

On an ethical level, Puzhao concedes that he dislikes AI translation because it “deprives humans of job opportunities,” adding that people “put so much time and effort into creating original content, only for some tech monopoly to feed it into AI training. All we can do is make some small acts of resistance. My position is non-cooperation.”

In the summer of 2023, China introduced the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, requiring tech companies to carry out training activities only with data from lawful sources and to guard against IP infringement.

Whether Ping’s experiment will fundamentally change the future of literary translation is yet to be seen — but it’s certainly got people reading into the consequences.

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from Westend61, Shijue, and iStock/VCG, reedited by Ding Yining/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018985/Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.title: Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018985/Can VR Capture the Power of China’s Ancient Caves?
World.content:
Under the blazing July sun, Zhang, a high school teacher from northern China, stood outside the Digital Exhibition Center of the Mogao Grottoes, a modern building designed to resemble the surrounding dunes. A shuttle bus would soon take him and other tourists to the foot of Mingsha Mountain, where they would see the original Mogao Grottoes: 492 caves containing Buddhist murals and painted sculptures spanning more than a thousand years, now strictly protected as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Zhang had just watched two introductory films at the center, “A Thousand Years of Mogao Caves” and “The Splendor of Buddha’s Palace,” the latter screened in its dome theater. His eyes sparkled with excitement. “It is so spectacular that I am speechless! I hope other heritage sites in China can be presented like this.”

The Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang, northwestern China’s Gansu province, are the product of more than a millennium of cultural exchange between East and West along the historic Silk Road. Renowned for the extraordinary aesthetic and cultural value of their cave art, they attract large numbers of tourists. Yet the grottoes are intrinsically fragile, threatened by both the surrounding desert and the carbon dioxide and humidity generated by visitors.

To reduce pressure on the caves and ensure their long-term preservation, the Dunhuang Academy, which manages and researches the site, has been developing the Digital Dunhuang project since the late 1980s. More than 200 caves have been documented through photography, image stitching, and laser scanning, with the material transformed into online and on-site experiences spanning films, virtual and augmented reality, and museum exhibitions. These digital experiences have become an increasingly prominent part of visiting Mogao.

Putting “cultural heritage” and “digital technology” together creates an immediate tension. Heritage looks backward, toward the past and the old; technology looks forward, toward the future and the new. When the two are brought together, digital representations exist alongside the physical heritage itself, raising questions such as: what qualities of the original are irreplaceable, and to what extent can they be reproduced or conveyed digitally?

I conducted a year of fieldwork at the Mogao Grottoes between 2024 and 2025, spending long periods in both the physical caves and digital exhibitions and talking with visitors. While physical and digital exhibitions at heritage sites can tell separate stories, at Mogao they are closely intertwined. The tension between heritage and technology highlights both their differences and how they complement each other, as visitors often observed.

Among the visitors I spoke with was a middle-aged British artist traveling with her partner. The two had sharply contrasting reactions. She was fascinated by the distinctive smell inside the caves, a mixture of dust, moisture, and history that would be difficult to reproduce digitally. Her partner, by contrast, was perfectly content with the digital exhibitions. “I really got my fix! I could just go with the digital,” he said. He drew parallels with Lascaux Cave in France, where replicas receive visitors while the original, closed to the public since 1963, is preserved.

For some caves, digital representations are the only way visitors can experience their fragile artworks. Cave 285, built during the Western Wei period and containing inscriptions dated to 538 and 539, is one of Mogao’s most important early caves, renowned for its rich murals and diverse artistic styles. It is currently closed to the public for conservation, but a virtual reality exhibition immerses visitors in the stories depicted on the murals and even lets them use handheld controllers as drumsticks to play music alongside mythological beings.

Wang, visiting from the southern city of Shenzhen with her young child, told me: “I like it very much, and it is also child-friendly. The VR shows real scenes from the cave while telling the stories in detail. It even surpasses the real cave!”

For visitors like Wang, VR not only reproduces the physical cave but creates a space of its own, allowing them to experience it in a playful, multisensory way impossible inside the original. “I am so touched that I almost cried,” another visitor told me. “I know Cave 285 is not open to the public, so I am very grateful for the opportunity to see it up close.”

For caves that remain open, experiencing both their physical and digital versions can offer a more nuanced perspective on the art. Cave 61 contains the largest surviving Buddhist historical landscape painting at Mogao. Based on the geography of the Tang dynasty (618–907), the mural depicts pilgrimage routes leading to the sacred Mount Wutai, over 2,000 kilometers east of the caves. It is also featured in “The Splendor of Buddha’s Palace” in the center’s 360-degree dome theater.

Later, on a poplar-shaded path, a college student, Xiaoyang, reflected on the contrast. “When I saw the mural from Cave 61 on the big screen, it was so bright. It really looked real, but I knew it wasn’t. I couldn’t feel the traces of time. But when I actually stood inside the cave and faced the mural, I began wondering how ancient cartographers had trudged through Mount Wutai and how painters had depicted the scene on the wall.”

Her response points to what digital reproductions can lose even as they make the art more visible. On-screen, details are easier to see, but this digital representation weakens the power of age and decay that connect viewers to the mural and the people who created it centuries ago. The digital image shows what can be difficult to see inside the cave, while the physical mural confronts visitors with the passage of time. Together, they encourage visitors to consider both the image and the history behind it.

Another crucial component of Digital Dunhuang is the digital repatriation of manuscripts and artifacts now held overseas. In the early 20th century, the discovery of more than 70,000 manuscripts, paintings, and other objects in the Library Cave, or Cave 17, opened a new chapter in Mogao’s history. Most were removed amid the era’s turmoil. Now dispersed around the world, they are being brought together digitally through collaborations between the Dunhuang Academy and international institutions.

Adjacent to Caves 16 and 17 is a museum housing the exhibition “Treasure in Caves,” which recounts the artifacts’ dispersal and virtual reunification. Replicas of objects now scattered among collections worldwide stand side by side in rows of glass cases.

Visiting the caves and exhibition offers complementary experiences, making this place marked by loss feel slightly more complete. A woman in her 50s discussing Cave 17, a memorial cave containing a statue of the Tang-dynasty monk Hong Bian, said: “Cave 17 is a physical place that has endured these historical events. The exhibition tells their story and shows the artifacts, so I can hear the echoes of history and finally breathe a sigh of relief.”

Like these visitors, I have found my own answers to questions about the authenticity. Now writing about Dunhuang from afar, I often revisit photographs from my fieldwork. Yet when I close my eyes, I can still recall the original caves: their warmth, their solemnity, and their sense of history.

The tension between the digital and physical does not necessarily have to be resolved in favor of one or the other. Digital representations can make inaccessible caves available, reveal otherwise difficult-to-see details, and reunite objects that have been physically dispersed. But they can also erase the traces of time and distance that give the originals much of their power. At Mogao, the two forms are most effective not when one substitutes for the other but when they work in tandem to deepen the experience.

By presenting the grottoes from multiple perspectives while carefully controlling access to the physical caves, the Dunhuang Academy shows how digitization can expand our understanding of authenticity rather than simply imitate the original. Perhaps another thousand years from now, the Mogao Grottoes will still move us, both through their carefully preserved physical form and through the digital versions that capture, interpret, and transmit them.

According to research guidelines, all names in this article are pseudonyms.



Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018986/China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.title: China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018986/China Gives Schools More Flexibility as Enrollment Shrinks
World.content:
Amid falling primary school enrollment, multiple regions in China are combining primary and secondary school levels, encouraging primary school teachers to transfer to higher grades, and creating schools with flexible enrollment.

Starting this September, several newly built schools designed to allow more flexible enrollment in Yiwu, in the eastern Zhejiang province, as well as the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, have opened and welcomed their first classes of students.

The change comes amid decreasing numbers of new students enrolling in primary school. In 2025, 14.6 million students were reported to have enrolled in primary schools nationwide, down nearly 10% from the year before and 22% from the enrollment peak in 2023. The number of junior high school students is also expected to peak this year, according to the Ministry of Education.

Previously, primary schools have generally acted as independent institutions with relatively fixed sizes and facilities. But as student numbers decline, some regions are launching schools that adjust capacity according to fluctuating enrollment, known as “tidal,” or chaoxi, schools.

Two of the first such schools opened this fall in Yiwu. Of them, the New Silk Road School’s Choucheng campus accepts students from primary school through junior high school, and features facilities that can be “dynamically allocated to different grades,” according to the local government. The other, Suxi Middle School — which hosts both junior and senior high school students — has implemented a flexible enrollment policy that accommodates classes of different sizes depending on the year.

Huli Innovation Experimental School in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen also expanded from a nine-year to a 12-year school this year, cutting its primary and junior high classes to make room for 30 senior high school classes.

Another school in Xiamen, Lianhua Middle School’s Longshan campus, originally intended to be a primary school, was converted into a 36-class junior high school this fall.

In March, authorities in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province, announced plans to build the city’s first tidal school, with construction set to be completed in 2028. Over the next three years, four more such schools are planned for the city’s Xiaoshan District, with a total investment of over 1.5 billion yuan ($223 million). In addition to space for 8,100 junior and senior high school students, local education authorities estimate that the model could save 18.7 hectares of land and nearly 900 million yuan in public funds.

Since June, several regions, including the eastern Fujian, Anhui, and Jiangxi provinces, have also released announcements recruiting junior high school teachers from primary and senior high schools. A teacher transfer training program was also recently launched in Shanghai, helping teachers make the move from kindergartens to primary schools and from primary schools to junior high schools.

On social media, users claiming to be primary school teachers said they had been asked to transfer to other grades. Data shows that the number of full-time primary school teachers in China fell by 131,900 in 2025.

The topic has received more than 14 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many users expressing concerns about the quality of teaching, arguing that teachers accustomed to teaching primary school may struggle to adapt to the curriculum and student needs at the junior or senior high school level.

Some teachers who have transferred to other educational levels face issues such as lower pay and inadequate training, Chen Chunyong, a researcher at the National Academy of Educational Sciences, wrote in an online commentary.

Chen called for national and provincial authorities to establish certification standards for teachers transferring between educational levels, including clear requirements for academic qualifications, assessments, and training.

Xiong Bingqi, deputy director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute in Beijing, also said the new reforms may undermine the country’s recent promotion of small-class teaching.

“Many regions still use traditional class size to calculate teacher staffing allocations, leading to the conclusion that there is a ‘surplus of primary school teachers and they need to be transferred to other levels to reduce excess,’’ he said. “This kind of traditional logic hampers the implementation of small-class reforms and affects the long-term distribution of teaching resources.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Students on their first day of school in Kunshan, Jiangsu province, Aug. 30, 2022. VCG)
