World.title: Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018983/Two Filmmakers, 1,100 Villages, and a Race to Record Rural China
World.content:
SHAANXI, Northwest China — “You have gone off route. Recalculating.” For the fourth time that day, Zhao Yushun and his wife, Yuan Zhenzhen, ignored the GPS. By then, jujube trees, signs advertising local specialties, and a view of distant mountains had already pulled them off course.

Now it was a farmer sorting pears beneath a black sunshade by the roadside in Dali County, northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.

“What kind of pear is this? I’ve never seen it before,” Zhao asks after they pull over. “How’s the harvest this year? Have people here been growing pears longer, or jujubes?”

“Jujubes,” the farmer says with a wry smile. His family has grown them since he was a child, but over the past decade more and more people have started planting them, and the returns are no longer what they once were. “Things are worth more when they’re scarce.”

As he speaks, Yuan raises her camera and starts recording, keeping it around waist height to make it less conspicuous.

The farmer soon moves beyond pears, telling Zhao about his years as a migrant worker in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen and his eventual return home to care for his children and aging parents. With jujube profits falling, he has also begun growing pears, hoping for a better return.

Thirty minutes later, Zhao and Yuan are back on the road. The encounter becomes the closing scene of the fifth episode of their “Yellow River” series.

Since 2021, Zhao and Yuan have traveled through more than 1,100 villages and towns, turning roadside conversations and unplanned stops into short documentaries about rural China. Their account, Yuzhenjishi, or “Encountering Reality,” has more than 530,000 followers on Bilibili, one of China’s largest video platforms.

Many of the people Zhao and Yuan film are farmers in their 60s or older who grew up working the land, spent years as migrant workers in cities, then returned home after being aged out of many urban jobs. They now farm through falling crop prices, increasing mechanization, extreme weather, and the departure of younger generations.

Since July, Zhao and Yuan have been traveling along the Yellow River, one of China’s longest and most historically important waterways, filming a six-episode series on the farms and pastures along its banks. Sixth Tone joined them for three days as they traveled through Henan, Shanxi, and Shaanxi provinces.

Down to earth

For Zhao and Yuan, leaving rural China had once seemed the obvious measure of success. Both grew up largely in the care of older relatives while their parents worked in cities, part of a rural generation known in China as “left-behind children.”

When Zhao did well in school growing up in a village in central China’s Hunan province, villagers would tell him: “Your hands aren’t meant to hold a hoe. They’re meant to hold a pen. You have to get out and go to the big city.”

He studied journalism; Yuan, who grew up in a small town in the southern Guangdong province, studied Chinese literature. Both made it to university, but neither found the stable urban life that education had seemed to promise.

As graduates of second-tier universities, they moved between media jobs in Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and other cities, rarely earning enough to feel settled.

“We moved so many times,” Zhao said. “Every time we moved, we wondered whether we should hire a medium-sized truck, only to find that our stuff filled barely half of a small one. After we left, there wouldn’t be any trace of us in the city.”

By 2021, Zhao and Yuan were both 27 and living in a rented apartment in Beijing. Zhao spent about three hours a day commuting by bus and subway. He came to recognize the passengers who got on and off at particular stops without ever knowing who they were.

The routine made him feel like “a cog in the machine.” Yuan described herself as “someone stuck in a corner.”

One night in 2021, they decided to start their own video account. They named it Yuzhenjishi, combining one character from each of their names with the slogan: “Let the overlooked be seen.”

Their first post was an edit of news footage about a herd of elephants that had wandered north from their habitat in the southwestern Yunnan province. At the end, they added a caption: “A herd of elephants drifting north, just like us leaving home to make a living.”

The couple soon moved to Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, where they continued working in media while filming in their spare time. At first, they focused largely on small cities around the province. But after making a video about left-behind children in a mountainous area, they found themselves increasingly drawn to villages and towns.

Within a year, Yuan proposed a more drastic move: quitting their jobs and making videos full time. After spending much of their childhoods trying to study their way out of rural China, Zhao and Yuan began returning to it with cameras.

For Zhao, the change brought a sense of connection he had rarely felt while covering new skyscrapers and suburban redevelopment in cities. The rural stories were “things I genuinely care about,” he said. “I finally felt grounded.”

As they began filming rural communities, viewers increasingly responded with stories of their own. Some left comments 400 or 500 words long.

One viewer from Hunan described growing up in a mountainous area where families had little land to farm and few ways to save money. “We all ended up taking the same path: leaving home to find work,” the viewer wrote. “It was all just to make a living.”

An agricultural university student wrote that after drought destroyed an experimental crop, they began searching for coverage of similar losses and were struck by how little they found. “Farmers and real rural communities barely have a voice of their own,” the student wrote.

The responses became important enough that Zhao and Yuan later printed a selection in a leaflet accompanying their first book, an anthology adapted from the written narratives of their videos. They came to see their videos as only half the story; viewers supplied the other half.

“We’re like a little public square,” Zhao said. “I pick up a loudspeaker and shout, ‘If anyone has something they want to say, come over.’ And then people really do come and tell their stories.”

On record

In practice, Zhao’s “loudspeaker” is usually just a question.

In a cornfield, he picked up an ear the harvester had missed and called to a farmer gleaning nearby: “Do you still want this?” Soon, the man was telling him about a nearby reservoir he had helped repair years earlier.

On the banks of the Yellow River, Zhao approached two men overseeing repairs to an embankment. “We’re from the south and have never seen this kind of embankment,” he said. “Could you explain it to us?”

Few turn him away. And once they begin talking, Yuan watches for the moment to start filming.

After filming a group of peach farmers packing nectarines for delivery to a foreign trade company, Zhao and Yuan were offered some fruit. When they asked how much they owed, one farmer waved them off.

“No need to pay,” he said. “Just put this in your video.”

Zhao remembered another farmer telling him much the same thing: “Little brother, there’s no money in farming these days. Look how hard life is for us farmers. Film this and put it on people’s phones. I’ll give you a like.”

“Farmers actually really want to talk,” Zhao said after returning to the car. “They just don’t have a channel to do so. So we bring the microphone to their doorstep.”

Zhao and Yuan describe these farmers as “standing at the crossroads of an era,” perhaps the last generation shaped primarily by traditional small-scale farming.

Their conversations often return to money and work, from falling crop prices and thin margins to years of physical labor and pensions that leave many older rural residents with little to live on.

Zhao argues that rural life is often viewed from outside in one of two ways. “People tend to imagine the countryside either as an idyllic retreat or as a place of poverty and hardship,” he said. “But both are ways of looking in from the outside.”

“We’re part of this world ourselves,” Zhao said. “What we do is document it from within and then communicate it outward.”

One of their most watched videos underscored the point more directly. Released in 2022 under the title “China’s 760 Million Farmers Don’t Need Praise,” it has nearly 5 million views.

“Since primary school, textbooks have taught us to praise farmers and applaud their hard work, but they never taught us to truly understand them,” the video said. “For farmers, mountains and rivers are not poetic, and rural life is no pastoral idyll. Farming is about survival.”

They have also tried posting on YouTube, with limited success. Zhao believes many of their stories require too much background knowledge for overseas audiences.

“After all, we are not Li Ziqi,” he said, referring to the hugely popular Chinese creator known internationally for idealized videos of rural life. “We are not making a pastoral fantasy.”

Still rolling

This spring, Zhao and Yuan hoped to film elderly porters who haul oranges out of the mountainous Three Gorges region along the Yangtze River.

But by the time they went looking for them, drones had taken over most of the work. Only a handful of porters still do it today, mainly on plots with too few orange trees to meet the minimum charge for drone transport.

“And of course, that’s a good thing. It’s a sign of progress that people no longer have to do such grueling work,” Zhao said. “But what that generation of porters went through, the lives they lived, and the labor they endured, was never recorded.”

They have encountered the same problem while trying to document people who built reservoirs, canals, and other water projects more than half a century ago.

Yuan’s grandmother had helped build an irrigation canal when she was young. Before she died, Zhao and Yuan took her back to see it. “Canal, reservoir — I’ve come to see you with my walking stick,” she said.

Children were playing nearby. Yuan’s grandmother tried to strike up a conversation with a gray-haired man in his 60s. “Did you help build the canal?” she asked. “It was such hard work back then.”

“How could I have?” he replied. “Anyone who worked on it would be at least 80 or 90 by now.”

Yuan’s grandmother smiled and said nothing more.

Many of the projects were built more than 60 years ago, and Zhao said it is increasingly hard to find surviving workers who can still tell their stories.

During the Yellow River trip, they met a man who had worked on one such project. Later, Zhao repeated a line the man had uttered in his local accent: “Once it was finished, it had nothing more to do with us.”

“If we don’t film these stories now, in another 10 years, there’ll be no one left who remembers them,” Yuan said.

The couple says they plan to spend 10 years documenting rural China. They are not worried about running out of stories, because many of the questions they pursue — about farming, migration, aging, and the changes reshaping villages — have no simple answer.

For Zhao, putting those questions on camera is a necessary first step. “First it has to be seen,” he said. “Once it is seen, people can start paying attention.”

Keeping that space open also costs money. After quitting their jobs in 2022, Zhao and Yuan burned through their savings and accumulated more than 250,000 yuan ($37,000) in debt.

They bought their camera, drone, and car on installments and took on outside commercial projects to support their documentary work. Even now, they sometimes sleep in the car while filming and get a hotel only when they need to do laundry.

It was not until 2025, the year they married, that they felt for the first time that they had actually made some money. After paying down debts and heading out to film again, much of it was soon gone.

“We were constantly moving money around just to keep things afloat,” Yuan said. “At the beginning of the year, we landed some other commercial deals, and it barely made us feel alive again. It’s like dying and coming back to life, then dying and coming back again.”

The two have nevertheless settled into a division of labor that requires little discussion. Zhao does most of the interviewing, appears on camera and narrates; Yuan films and edits. On the road, they often know without speaking when Zhao should deliver a piece to camera, when Yuan needs another shot, or when they should stop and try again.

But they differ over what they expect the work to achieve.

For years, Yuan wrote the same sentence on every résumé she sent to prospective employers: “Images have the power to change the world.” Zhao often repeated it too.

She is less certain now.

“I’m just going through a bit of a period of uncertainty,” Yuan said. “Change is difficult. Video may not necessarily change the world, but it can record the world.”

“I want to change things; he wants to record them,” she added. “I’m the more radical one.”

For Zhao, the record itself is reason enough to continue. “These are precious historical records,” he said. “A hundred years from now, someone may look through our videos to understand what this generation of farmers was thinking.”

Along the Yellow River, Zhao and Yuan collected water in plastic bottles at different points on their journey. At the river’s estuary in the eastern Shandong province, they opened the bottles one by one and poured the water back in.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Zhao Yushun (left) and Yuan Zhenzhen film a flooded field in Baise, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, October 2025. Courtesy of Zhao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018971/Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.title: Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018971/Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.content:
Photographer He Xu first passed through the China-Nepal border at Gyirong Port in 2010. He remembers that it was just a row of rustic, clay-colored bungalows.

Over the past 16 years, he has revisited at least 100 times, witnessing the area’s steady growth, with those bungalows eventually replaced by a grand, imposing building.

Yet that progress came to a violent halt on the morning of Aug. 26, when a flash flood caused by a mountain glacier ripped through the port in Shigatse, in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. As of Sept. 2, the disaster had killed at least 1,204 in Nepal and 21 in China, according to Xinhua News Agency. Almost 5,000 people remain missing, including 546 in Gyirong.

He, who runs a photo studio in the regional capital, Lhasa, was in Beijing when he heard the news. Over the years, he had gotten to know more than 20 people working at the port, including customs and immigration officials, firefighters, and disease-control workers. He began hurriedly searching through his phone contacts.

“Are you safe? Please reply when you see this. I’m really worried,” he texted them. Most of his messages went unanswered.

Nestled in a deep, winding valley at the foot of the Himalayas, about 100 kilometers from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, China’s Gyirong County is referred to as “the back garden of Mount Qomolangma” — or Mount Everest, as it’s known in the West. The land port there is historically among the largest for trade between China and Nepal. After opening for bilateral customs clearance in 2014, the volume of goods passing through has increased rapidly.

“On one side of the port was a huge parking lot, where vehicles from both countries waited for inspection,” He recalls. “Next to the lot were several white buildings, four or five floors each, where the on-duty staff lived.”

Across from the lot was a police station and a row of small stores including a supermarket run by a middle-aged couple from the neighboring Sichuan province, a souvenir shop run by a Nepalese merchant, and three restaurants.

“Most visitors were tourists who took a quick photo at the border gate and left,” says the 50-year-old photographer. “There wasn’t much demand for a bustling commercial street. But the port staff stayed year-round, and these outlets were their only options for shopping and dining.”

Many of these border officials are among the missing.

With the flash flood destroying about three kilometers of the highway leading to Gyirong, it took two days for the first rescue teams from Xizang and Sichuan to reach the disaster zone. The highway was reportedly reopened on Sept. 2, allowing access to more rescuers, emergency supplies, and heavy machinery.

A warm welcome

The first reply that He received was from a Tibetan friend working at the port’s disease-control station. He had requested the day off on Aug. 26 and gone into town, narrowly escaping the massive torrent of rock, ice, and water that had wiped out his workplace.

The photographer offered to transfer some money so that his friend could purchase food and emergency supplies and bring them to the port, but he declined. “All the roads over there are blocked,” he replied. “The rescue teams are still using bulldozers and excavators to clear a path, moving forward inch by inch.”

After two sleepless nights, He set off from Beijing for Gyirong on the morning of Aug. 28. He had no idea how he would help — he just knew he had to go.

Since the disaster, the Gyirong Entry-Exit Border Inspection Station’s official channel on the WeChat messaging platform has been inundated with messages from well-wishers.

Many staff at the port are in their early 30s and hail from various parts of China. Far from their families, most live quiet, monotonous lives.

He Xu once wandered into the staff dormitories and noted the austerity of the rooms, with just two beds, a desk, and simple storage cabinets. The housing complex had a recreation room with table tennis and other sports facilities, but he’d never seen anyone using them. “The most typical thing I saw staff doing after work was calling their families,” he says.

The workers rarely ventured far, He says, leaving them little opportunity to appreciate the valley scenery — so he decided his lens would be their “eyes.” One person wanted to see a kiang, an indigenous wild ass; another, the splendor of Ngari prefecture, a 15-hour drive west; another, the view from a 4,500-meter platform in the Himalayas just an hour away. Each time, He would capture what they asked for and share the pictures on WeChat.

The customs staff rotated every three or four days. Off-duty workers are accommodated in the county seat, about 90 minutes away by bus, where they can enjoy more variety in terms of meals, shopping, and entertainment.

Those who have passed through Gyirong Port often speak of the “pleasant, helpful” nature of the customs and security personnel there.

Wen Lili from China’s northwestern Shaanxi province visited in early August. She remembers a young police officer who helped suggest the best places to take photos — the checkpoint, boundary marker, and the Friendship Bridge over the border — and where to exchange Chinese renminbi for Nepalese rupees. “It’s such a tiny place, and he told me everything there was to see,” she says.

He Xu says that, one time, his pickup truck was dangerously low on fuel, and a police officer drove more than 40 kilometers to the nearest gas station to bring him a full jerry can.

Two years ago, He joined a customs officer named Dorje and some of his friends for a meal in town. Dorje came from Maizhokunggar County, more than 800 kilometers from Gyirong, and was 10 years from retirement. With a beaming smile, he had talked of his three children, who had all gone to work in major cities.

With the savings he had accumulated, Dorje had planned to return to his hometown, buy some cattle and sheep, and spend his days tending them with his wife. It was his ideal life, he’d said.

Two-way street

Ma Baoxiang, who runs a general store in Gyirong, would often drive the 20 kilometers to the port to shoot videos for his social media channel.

Having made countless trips, he had become familiar with its rhythms: mornings were busiest, as tourists and truck drivers rushed to cross the border before lunch, although crowds could also swell in the afternoon, with vehicles sometimes lining the road. Most were trucks bearing Nepalese license plates, but Ma says that in recent years he has noticed an increase in travelers crossing the border in private cars.

The Bangxing Logistics Park, a 40-minute drive from the port, is the initial destination for most goods arriving from across the border. The facility gets so busy that drivers can be stuck waiting for up to two days to load or unload their cargo.

Nepalese residents near the border with exit-entry permits would also regularly pass through the port to stock up on clothes, daily necessities, and food from the stores in Gyirong.

“You often see Nepalese merchants buying wholesale goods in town,” says Ma, who every few months goes the other way to buy copperware, handicrafts, tea, and other specialty products, which he ships home to sell to tourists.

Trade at Gyirong Port once largely consisted of small businesses run by local residents. In April 2015, when an earthquake in Nepal damaged facilities at the larger Zhangmu Port, Gyirong became the primary China-Nepal border crossing. It was expanded into an international port in 2017.

By 2024, the value of imports and exports passing through Gyirong reached 4.24 billion yuan ($632 million), the highest among all the ports in Xizang.

Ma Qi, the local branch manager of Musa International Logistics, says his company had at least a dozen trucks en route to the port when the disaster struck on Aug. 26. He immediately told the drivers to pull over and wait, and then contacted nearby warehouses to arrange 6,000 square meters of emergency storage for their cargo.

“Gyirong is the best port,” says Ma Qi, who has worked in cross-border export logistics for 13 years. His company exports 400 to 500 cubic meters of goods a day, including clothing, hardware, small household appliances, construction machinery for bridge and tunnel projects, and electric vehicles. He describes the port as a “lifeline.”

The growth in tourists has also helped turn Gyirong into an economic hub, bringing many restaurants and hotels.

“After the mudslide, Gyirong suddenly emptied out,” says Lin Tian, who has owned a store in the county seat selling Nepalese specialty goods for the past five years. “The only people here are residents and the people working or running shops.”

Locals are no strangers to floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters. It has become an inevitable part of life.

When a mudslide triggered flooding on both sides of the border in July last year, Gyirong Port was closed for nearly six months, forcing logistics companies to shift operations to smaller ports.

“These past few days, the government has been coordinating with us to register and report the cargo stranded at the port. They will arrange for it to be shipped out through the Zhangmu and Lizi ports instead,” says Ma Qi. In the meantime, he is mobilizing resources and coordinating with relief organizations in Lhasa and Shigatse to help transport emergency supplies to the disaster zone.

In late 2024, Gyirong was hit by landslides, leaving many port workers stranded in town with no power for more than a week. The mud in some places was shin-deep.

He Xu recalls asking several port staff whether they feared natural disasters. One simply smiled and replied, “I’m not worried. We’ve always made it through before.”

This time, He wasn’t so sure. In the early hours of Aug. 28, he finally received another message from a contact at the port, this time from a police officer. “I’m in downtown Shigatse. I’m fine,” it said.

Reading it, he felt his anxiety ease a little. Yet many others have remained silent.

(Due to privacy concerns, Wen Lili, Dorje, and Lin Tian are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Shuyuan, Zhang Lingyun, and Wang Qian.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Search and rescue personnel look for survivors in Gyirong Port, Xizang Autonomous Region, Sept. 2, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.title: Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.content:
Content creators are falling victim to scammers lodging mass fabricated reports of platform violations in China, some of whom boast making over 50,000 yuan ($7,400) per month from their services.

Sellers are offering “account-striking,” including “software-based mass reporting” and “precision strikes,” on domestic secondhand trading platforms, according to an investigation published Tuesday by domestic media outlet The Beijing News. One such service was priced at 25 yuan for 500 platform complaints or 60 yuan for 5,000 complaints.

Account striking, or dahao, became widespread this summer, according to the investigation. This may in part be because it can take advantage of social media platforms’ increasing use of AI to review account-violation complaints.

One 19-year-old creator who posts short videos of herself painting told The Beijing News that one of her accounts, boasting nearly 60,000 followers, had been banned, while a second featuring 260,000 followers saw numerous videos taken down. Both incidents occurred after the same striker reported the accounts to their respective platforms.

The striker then privately messaged her, demanding a ransom of 1,000 yuan to withdraw the complaints. After she transferred the money, the complaints were withdrawn, and her videos were restored.

Jia Bojun, a vlogger who posts videos debunking claims about sports supplements and diets, was also targeted. On Aug. 14, eight of his videos were taken down in under an hour for “portrait rights infringement,” despite the videos featuring no other people.

According to interviews with content creators affected by account strikes, The Beijing News found that teams of strikers often submit complaints simultaneously through a platform’s official reporting channel and by email, doubling success rates.

“To avoid liability, the platform will take down the video as long as there is even a slight possibility (of a violation), regardless of whether the complaint is real or not,” an anonymous account striker told The Beijing News.

Another long-time operator said that many of the attacks stem from brand-to-brand mutual reporting, a commonplace tactic in today’s e-commerce-driven marketplace.

Some strikers go on to recruit apprentices, teaching them step-by-step takedown tactics and providing complaint scripts tailored to each platform, all for an additional fee. The most enterprising even establish their own online account-striking “schools.”

Multiple short-video vloggers were quoted saying that appealing complaints requires significant time and effort, as well as submitting extensive personal information and evidence that they have not violated platform rules — and even then, a successful appeal is not guaranteed.

A cybersecurity expert who works with multiple short-video platforms said that although AI moderation offers platforms a “low-cost, high-efficiency solution” to complaints, it tends to take accounts and videos down first and review later. The cost then falls entirely on creators. “The right to report is a public governance tool provided to users by platforms,” the expert said. “It should not be turned into a priced commodity.”

The expert urged platforms to employ real people to review high-risk reports and flag suspicious accounts, as well as to protect creators’ rights. Platforms should also be required to share malicious-reporting data with police, they said.

Wang Hongmei, a lawyer at Hebei Sanhe Shidai Law Firm, called fabricating complaints and exploiting platform loopholes to maliciously take down videos or ban accounts for illicit gain a form of online “soft violence.” According to Wang, such behavior potentially violates China’s Public Security Administration Punishment Law and is therefore punishable by fines or detention.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iStock Vectors/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Centuries in the making: Singsons’ unrivaled power in Ilocos Sur
World.content:
The clan has built an empire in Ilocos Sur and has 16 members currently holding seats in government

The Singson clan’s rise to power was built over centuries of carefully planned moves that entrenched the family in politics.

From the Spanish colonial period, where the family marks its origins, until today, the Singsons have controlled the province of Ilocos Sur.

They trace their beginnings to the marriage of a Chinese merchant, Joaquin Ayco, and a local from Vigan named Rosa Songnio. It was during the 19th century that the family began its ascent to power through wealth. They held gobernadorcillo positions for five terms and their influence continued over the American and Japanese occupations.

In 1945, the region turned to tobacco as a means of economic recovery, which boomed and led to the conflict between the Singsons and the Crisologo family, then closely intertwined — family patriarch, former Ilocos Sur governor Luis “Chavit” Singson is the nephew of then-congressman Floro Crisologo. Both families became fierce competitors over the tobacco trade.

Floro was assassinated inside a church on October 18, 1970, and the case remains unsolved. The political leadership of the Crisologos ended a year later when the Singson brothers were elected — Chavit became governor and his elder brother Evaristo “Titong” II became Vigan mayor. The family won through Chavit’s promise of streamlining tobacco production.

The clan’s power in the province remains unmatched despite alleged involvement in plunder and graft charges. Only a few have tried to defeat the Singsons and they ultimately failed.

In May 2026, Chavit claimed that 5,500 flood control projects in the country were non-existent. This challenged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s announcement at his 2024 State of the Nation Address that 5,500 projects were completed nationwide.

He was charged with a private cyber libel complaint in June but was granted bail. Afterwards, Chavit proclaimed during a press conference that he would not be stopped and doubled down on his exposé of the anomalous flood control corruption scandal.

PATRIARCH. Former Ilocos Sur governor Luis ‘Chavit’ Singson holds a press conference on the flood control controversy on September 19, 2025. Photo by Errol Almario/Rappler

No arrest, case, or political pressure will stop him from revealing the truth, he asserted.

This is not uncharted territory for him. With his family’s decades-long grip on power, he knows exactly how to play the long game.

An obese political dynasty

The Singsons are one of the biggest and oldest political families. They hold numerous seats in the Ilocos Region.

Research by the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism revealed that in the 2025 elections, Chavit had 23 relatives running for office.

Rappler’s research shows that 16 current officials are members of the Singson clan:

Ronald Singson – 1st District Representative (Ilocos Sur) Richelle Singson Michael – Partylist Representative Jeremias “Jerry” Crisologo Singson – Governor (Ilocos Sur) Ryan Luis Singson – Vice Governor (Ilocos Sur) Ericson Singson – 2nd District Board Member (Ilocos Sur) Janina Medina-Fariñas – 1st District Board Member (Ilocos Sur) Fayinna Zaragoza – 2nd District Board Member (Ilocos Sur) Eric Singson – Mayor (City of Candon) Randolf “Randy” Singson – Mayor (City of Vigan) Goulart Germelina Singson – Mayor (Caoayan) Kristelle Gocho Singson – Vice Mayor (City of Candon) Juan Paolo Singson Ancheta – Vice Mayor (Caoayan) Evaristo “Bobit” Singson III – Councilor (City of Vigan) Jaime “Jimboy” Singson – Councilor (City of Candon) & Philippine Councilors League President – Ilocos Sur Chapter Luis Charles Singson – Councilor (Narvacan) Eric “Owen” Singson Jr. – Councilor (City of Candon)

The Singson Dynasty A timeline mapping the notable rotation and overlap of local government positions held by the Singson family across three decades.



Scroll or swipe right to see the dynasty’s full timeline. Tap or hover a bar for details, including family ties and each member’s years in power. Source: Comelec, public records

Attempts to challenge the family have failed. In 2019, Chavit beat long-time rival Edgardo Zaragoza for mayor. In 2023, Chavit then filed graft charges against Zaragoza and his relatives over the alleged misuse of P81 million in tobacco excise tax funds.

When Chavit backed out of his reelection bid for governor in 2013, his son, Ryan Luis, replaced him. He was challenged by former ally and aide of Chavit, Roque Verzosa Jr. Verzosa filed a case against Ryan Luis for vote-buying after he supposedly gave out at least P20,000 during a fiesta event. Yet the elections ended with the same result: the Singsons still dominated the region.

FATHER-SON. Ryan Luis Singson with his father Luis ‘Chavit’ Singson in 2013. Photo courtesy of Ryan Luis Singson’s official facebook page

In 2011, Ronald, Chavit’s other son, resigned as congressman after pleading guilty to drug trafficking in Hong Kong and was detained by authorities for 11 months. Ryan Luis, who was vice mayor of Vigan at the time, defeated Liberal Party candidate lawyer Beltrand Baterina in a special congressional election.

Then-councilor Lourdes Baquiran replaced Ryan Luis for the vice mayoral seat after his win.

The family also operates as a politicontractor. Their construction firm, Satrap Construction, secured P2.1 billion in infrastructure projects in Ilocos Sur from 2016 to 2025. They have ties, too, to DITO Telecommunity Corporation and entered the transportation sector to produce electric vehicles.

Playing ‘chess’

The family’s power did not just rely on politics. It required money and carefully thought-out moves that favored them. When the Singsons took control of the region in the 1970s, the family divided power.

Titong II replaced his brother Chavit as governor. Another brother of theirs, Jerry, became a councilor and eventually a provincial board member.

Chavit’s niece, Eva Marie Singson-Medina, became a provincial board member in 1992 and Vigan mayor from 1995 to 2004. The patriarch’s son, Randolf, became councilor for multiple terms. The influence extended to their cousins, who won seats in other towns.

Chavit also fulfilled his promise of passing Republic Act No. 7171, which mandates the allocation of excise tax on locally manufactured cigarettes for the benefit of local government units (LGUs) and tobacco farmers. This became a regular revenue for the region.

But his biggest political move happened in 2000.

Chavit’s friendship with then-president Erap Estrada fell apart after Estrada gave a gambling license to Chavit’s cousin and rival, Eric. In a press conference, Chavit exposed Estrada’s link to jueteng, accusing him of taking P130 million from the tobacco excise tax share of Ilocos Sur.

This sparked a chain of events that culminated in Estrada’s ouster during EDSA II.

In the 2010 elections, Chavit left the Lakas-Christian Muslim Democrats for the Nacionalista Party to endorse former senator Manny Villar.

The clan was also careful with its political alliances. Though Chavit joined the Uniteam tandem before, he joined the September 21, 2025 protest and called on students to skip classes and go against the government.

A group claiming to be former Marcos loyalists also pushed for a possible tandem between Vice President Sara Duterte and Chavit in the 2028 national elections.

On September 6, Chavit was also seen arriving at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court at the time Duterte posted bail for three counts of grave threats. However, he said he was only there to allegedly check on the progress of his case and not support the Vice President.

Switching sides and alliances through every election and political rift had just become second nature to the Singson family. And they have thrived. – Rappler.com

World.title: Impeachment court issues new calendar for Sara Duterte trial
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) Senators will work 'double time' to end the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte before the end of the year while allotting enough time for deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget

MANILA, Philippines – Amid the ongoing Senate budget deliberations and the passage of the upper chamber’s legislative agenda, the Senate impeachment court on Tuesday, September 8, issued a new schedule for the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Senators earlier agreed on adjustments in their work schedule primarily to achieve two goals: complete deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget on time and finish the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte before the end of the year.

They also agreed to suspend the Senate rules and allow the finance committee to hold budget hearings while the plenary session is ongoing. Under this, senators who are in budget hearings during the plenary session will still be marked present during the roll call.

Impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero announced the latest calendar for the trial as follows:

September 14 to 30 (Monday to Wednesday)

10 am to 2:30 pm: Impeachment trial

3 pm onwards: Plenary sessions, budget hearings, and committee hearings for the legislative agenda

October 1 to 15 (all weekdays)

10 am to early evening

October 16 to November 8 (all weekdays)

No trial to give way to budget deliberations and preparation of Senate version of the proposed 2027 budget

November 18

Trial resumes at 10 am to 2:30 pm (but may also be held earlier than November 18)

November 23

10 am to 2:30 pm: Impeachment trial

3 pm onwards: Plenary sessions, budget hearings, and committee hearings for the legislative agenda

The senators earlier held a caucus on September 3, the same day that Senator Migz Zubiri raised the need for senators to agree on a work schedule adjustments that would allow them to allot time for budget deliberations alongside the impeachment trial and their normal work.

Zubiri said that without this schedule, it would not be possible for the Senate to finish deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget on time. It was also during his September 3 manifestation when he made a viral remark about the 12-hour workday of senators since the trial began, as sessions were being held after the trial ends in the afternoon.

“Sa totoo lang, Mr. President, pagod na pagod na ako. Twelve hours per day po tayo na nandito. From 9-9 nandito tayo,” he said, a remark that drew backlash online, with some netizens saying they, too, were tired from the grueling and low-wage realities faced by ordinary Filipino workers.

(Truth be told, Mr. President, I am very tired. We’re here 12 hours per day, from 9 am to 9 pm.)

In response to criticism of his remark, Zubiri later told reporters that he was just being “candid” and “honest.”

“Binanggit ko lang ang aking present condition at that time kasi napakahirap i-juggle ng tatlong napakalahagaang activities in Senate. It’s the first time na nangyari na nagkaroon ng impeachment, budget hearings, at legislative agenda,” he added.

(I just described my present condition at that time because it’s so difficult to juggle three important activities at the Senate. It’s the first time that we were holding the impeachment, budget hearings, and hearings for the legislative agenda simultaneously.)

The Senate is currently handling three major tasks: deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, the ongoing impeachment trial of Duterte, and the passage of its legislative agenda. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Post offering cash, livelihood aid under Bong Go’s name is fake
World.content:
The post claims to offer P29,000 in livelihood aid from Senator Bong Go, but its registration link redirects users to an unrelated website listing job vacancies

Claim: People in need of livelihood assistance can receive P29,000 from Senator Bong Go by registering online.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact checked this: An anonymous Facebook account posted the graphic in the “DSWD Cash Assistance Update PayOut” group on August 31. The group has 602,100 members as of writing.

The graphic claims that people who have no source of livelihood can receive P29,000 from Senator Bong Go by registering online. The post uses Go’s name and photo alongside the logos of government agencies, including the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).

It also includes supposed registration links for the alleged livelihood assistance program.

The facts: The post is fake. There is no indication that the supposed P29,000 cash assistance advertised in the graphic is offered through an official government program.

In a Facebook post on September 5, Go warned the public against social media posts offering livelihood or investment assistance in his name.

“Huwag maniwala sa mga social media post na nangangako na magbibigay ng puhunan o pangkabuhayan na tulong sa pangalan ni Senator Bong Go. Walang Palista Program si Senator Bong Go,” the post read.

(Do not believe social media posts that promise Senator Bong Go will give business capital or livelihood assistance. Senator Bong Go does not have such a program.)

The senator also reminded the public not to provide their personal information through dubious links or social media posts.

Fake link: The supposed registration link included in the post redirects users to a website containing local and international job listings. Clicking “Apply Now” on the website redirects users to a job search website.

The job listings have no apparent connection to the P29,000 cash assistance promised in the Facebook post.

This is not the first time Go’s name has been used in a false cash assistance offer. In May 2025, Go debunked a Facebook post bearing his photo and the Senate logo that falsely claimed he was offering P5,000 in cash assistance to people who messaged a Facebook page. He warned the public against clicking suspicious links that ask for personal information, saying these could expose users to potential scams. (READ: Phishing 101: How to spot and avoid phishing)

Not offered by DSWD: The DSWD does not have a program that provides the P29,000 cash assistance advertised in the post, particularly one distributed through or associated with a specific politician. The department instead provides assistance through established programs such as the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS), which offers financial and other forms of aid to qualified individuals based on their circumstances and after assessment by DSWD social workers.

To apply for aid under AICS, applicants are required to submit a valid identification card and supporting documents appropriate to the type of assistance being requested to the nearest DSWD field office, Social Welfare and Development Office, or satellite office.

The DSWD has also repeatedly warned the public about fraudulent social media posts and messages promising cash assistance. In February 2026, the agency warned against scammers offering supposed DSWD cash aid in exchange for personal information. The DSWD said these offers were not authorized by any of its offices.

In April 2026, the agency again clarified that it does not ask for personal information through text messages or private social media messages in exchange for financial assistance. It also warned against posts asking people to pay a fee to receive cash aid, emphasizing that DSWD does not charge any amount to receive financial assistance.

The agency has likewise clarified that applications for its programs are not processed through private social media accounts, personal messages, or unauthorized intermediaries, and that there is no “backer system” for obtaining or expediting assistance. – Mark David Silencio/Rappler.com

Mark David Silencio is an Information Technology student at Bulacan State University in Plaridel, Bulacan. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, he is also the managing editor for Administration of Pacesetter.

World.title: Teodoro hits China at Seoul forum: ‘Maging disente naman kayo’
World.content:
'I will keep this paper as a memento of how desperate China is and how ineffective its position is in the face of a real audience,' quips the defense chief

MANILA, Philippines — At a dialogue attended by defense and military officials, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. criticized Beijing for “disrespecting” international law and the crowd at the Seoul Defense Dialogue after he was slipped a note apparently outlining China’s position and rejection of the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award.

In a video clip posted by the Department of National Defense on Tuesday, September 8, Teodoro, a sitting Cabinet official sanctioned by China, is interrupted mid-answer as someone hands him a note on a piece of paper.

“I have a note here. I think this is from China,” said Teodoro, among the loudest voices in the Philippines against Beijing’s actions in maritime, domestic, and even diplomatic spaces. Teodoro spoke during the first plenary session of the forum, titled “Collaborative Architecture for International Stability.”

Teodoro went on to comment on China’s stand on the landmark ruling, which affirmed the Philippines’ 200-nautical mile exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea that it calls the West Philippine Sea. The same award found China’s historical claim of the vast waterway without basis, and said Beijing’s island building activities damaged the fragile marine ecosystem.

China has refused to recognize the award and calls it “illegal, null, and void” even if it ought to be binding under United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), of which Beijing is a signatory to.

Play Video

After criticizing Beijing’s stand line by line, Teodoro said: “How can you deal with a country in an international forum — beyond the question asked to me — disrespecting the organizers of this forum? How do you expect to deal with it civily?”

“Is this the right paper to post to me when I’m asked a question on the floor? And how will you treat this kind of behavior? If this is a Chinese position sent to me, it not only disrespects international law — throwing UNCLOS to the floor and trampling upon it — but it also disepresects the basic decency that should be accorded to our most gracious host, the Republic of Korea and the audience here. Perhaps basic decency and behavior is what China needs to do,” said Teodoro.

The audience at the dialogue erupted into a strong, albeit initially hesistant, round of applause.

He added: “In Filipino, maging disente lang kayo ng kaunti, mahiya naman kayo ng kaunti (Try to show some shame and decency).”

Teodoro said the note was proof of “actual coercion, bullying, and aggression.”

“We need to coalesce,” he said.

The plenary session that Teodoro was a part of was centered on how “norms and multilateral institutions… [are] once again being tested by today’s international security environment.”

The conference note for the session reads: “Discussions will focus on restoring strategic trust, preventing crises and managing conflicts, strengthening the effectiveness of multilateral institutions, enhancing the roles of international organizations and regional security frameworks, and designing governance mechanisms that encompass security, economic, and technological domains.”

“I will keep this paper as a memento of how desperate China, is and how ineffective its position is in the face of a real audience. Thank you very much to the person who gave me this piece of paper. You have just done your country a great favor and I hope you don’t suffer in a gulag for it,” said Teodoro, eliciting another round of applause.

This is not the first — and is unlikely to be the last — time Teodoro has taken China to task at an international forum. At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, the region’s premier defense forum, Teodoro has twice openly lambasted Beijing over its actions in the South China Sea and beyond.

At the 2026 edition of the forum, Teodoro warned against trusting Beijing as Southeast Asian countries and China seek to conclude negotiations on a code of conduct for the South China Sea.

Shortly after those remarks in Singapore, Beijing imposed sanctions on Teodoro, his wife, and son. He is the first sitting Cabinet member of the Marcos administration to be sanctioned by China.

Bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing have been strained in recent years, as the Philippines under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has taken a stronger stance on the West Philippine Sea and in implementing the 2016 Arbitral Award.

Manila’s assertion of both its entitlements and claims has meant tense confrontations between Philippine and Chinese maritime forces in flashpoints in the South China Sea. — Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Ara Mina quote card criticizing Dutertes is fabricated
World.content:
A Facebook page attributed a strong anti-Duterte statement to actress Ara Mina, but there is no credible evidence that she allegedly made this statement

Claim: Actress Ara Mina made a statement criticizing the Dutertes, saying it was “obvious” that they had stolen money but had not been jailed. She also called them out for aspiring to run for office in 2028.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post attributed a strongly worded statement against the Duterte family to actress Ara Mina. The post also refers to Vice President Sara Duterte’s plans to run for president in 2028.

The Philippine Daily Inquiry Facebook page garnered 279 reactions on its August 25 post. It was also reposted by other Facebook pages, including Bayan ng Pangako, where it received 2,500 reactions, 2,600 comments, and 81 shares, and the page Tiger 99, where it garnered 788 reactions and 21 shares as of this writing.

The quote card shows the actress allegedly saying, “Nagtataka talaga ako kung saan nanggagaling ang kapal ng mga mukha ng mga hay*p na yan! Halata namang nagnakaw ‘yang mga Duterte na yan tapos hindi pa nakukulong? Tapos gusto pa tumakbo sa 2028? Ang kapal ng mukha!”

(I really wonder where these people get the nerve. It’s obvious that the Dutertes stole money, yet they haven’t even been jailed? And now they still want to run in 2028? The audacity!)

The facts: The statement attributed to the actress is fabricated. No interview, official statement, social media post, or news report could be found showing that the actress allegedly made the remarks against the Duterte family.

The claim appears to have originated from the Philippine Daily Inquiry page, which appears to mimic the name and design of the legitimate news outlet Philippine Daily Inquirer. Versions of the claim, using the same quote card, were reposted by other Facebook pages, including Bayan ng Pangako and Tiger 99.

While the misleading post contains several factual details — such as Vice President Sara Duterte’s announcement of her 2028 presidential bid and the allegations concerning her use of confidential funds which are under investigation — these separate facts do not authenticate the quote attributed to the actress.

Corruption allegations vs Dutertes: Duterte is currently facing an impeachment trial over questions involving the alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, which she previously led. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte)

She also faces allegations of unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (LIST: The 4 articles of impeachment vs VP Sara Duterte)

Debunked: The PH Daily Inquiry page has also previously been flagged for posting another fabricated quote attributed to Senator Pia Cayetano on recent class suspensions and a fake quote from actress Bianca Gonzalez supposedly criticizing the Dutertes. – Vic Albert Bagaan/Rappler.com

Vic Albert Bagaan is a petroleum engineering student at Palawan State University in Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. The editor-in-chief of Pioneer Publication, he is an Aries Rufo Fellow for 2026.

World.title: PNP logs 41.77% drop in PH crime rates in August 2026
World.content:
Philippine National Police headquarters in Camp Crame. File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) has recorded a drop in focus crimes across the country, down from 3,584 incidents in 2025 to 2,087 in 2026 — or a 41.77 percent drop.

In a statement on Tuesday, the PNP said the data referred to focus crimes recorded from January to August 2026, compared with data for the same period in 2025.

Focus crimes refer to carnapping, rape, physical injuries, theft, robbery, and homicide.

Article continues after this 

“The figures reflect the value of sustained police presence and prevention efforts, while emphasizing that every remaining incident still calls for attention,” PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in a statement.

“The PNP remains committed to sustaining the positive gains while addressing persistent concerns through responsive and responsible policing,” he added.

READ: PNP: Crime rate drops by 19.96% in February 2026

The PNP detailed that carnapping of motor vehicles declined by 67.74 percent in August 2026 compared to the same month in 2025, while rape cases declined by 58.65 percent and carnapping of motorcycles by 53.64 percent.

The national police force further noted that physical injury cases also decreased by 46.83 percent; theft by 41.67 percent; robbery by 33.16 percent; and homicide by 3.33 percent. /mcm

World.title: Abaca school bag production pushed in Leyte
World.content:
School bags made out of abaca fiber were shown during a training in Southern Leyte on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo from PhilFIDA Eastern Visayas)

TACLOBAN CITY — The Philippine Fiber Industry Development Authority (PhilFIDA) regional office here is pushing for abaca bag making as an alternative livelihood in Leyte provinces.

This is part of an effort to revitalize fiber-based handicrafts.

PhilFIDA Eastern Visayas Regional Director Joseph Salas said in a phone interview on Monday that they have completed a training of trainers in Southern Leyte for school bag making on Sept. 1 to 4.

Article continues after this 

They are scheduled to roll out the training in Leyte on Sept. 8 to 11.

“The capacity-building activity aimed not only to develop participants’ skills in producing abaca-based products, but also to establish a pool of trainers capable of sharing these skills with communities across Leyte provinces and other parts of Eastern Visayas,” Salas said.

The agency tapped experts from Antique for the 25 trainers to learn more about various stages of abaca school bag production, including design, assembly, finishing and quality control.

They completed the required outputs and produced durable and functional school bags using locally produced abaca twine.

The newly trained participants now form an additional pool of abaca handicraft trainers who can help bring skills development closer to fiber-producing communities.

Article continues after this 

The agency will roll out that training with the support of local government units.

Southern Leyte is the top producer of abaca in Eastern Visayas.

Article continues after this 

In 2024, the province logged a 1,457 metric tons (MT) yield.

Leyte ranks third with 606.16 MT output.

World.title: 2,320 Bukidnon scholars to get ‘finisher fund’ worth P46.4M
World.content:
Bukidnon. INQUIRER FILES

MANILA, Philippines — Some 2,320 graduating college students in Bukidnon are set to receive P46.4 million in financial assistance from the Office of the President (OP), Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a statement on Tuesday.

Malacañang referred to the assistance as a “finisher fund,” with each student receiving P20,000 under the OP’s Socio-Civic Projects Fund.

The money may be used for tuition balances, transportation, learning materials and other school-related expenses.

Article continues after this 

READ: LIVE UPDATES: Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 8, 2026

According to Malacañang, Recto discussed the program during a meeting with the 155 Presidential Scholars from Quezon town last Sept. 4, after inspecting the ongoing construction of the Bukidnon Airport.

The 155 scholars come from the municipality’s 31 barangays, with five students selected from each barangay. They are among the 2,320 beneficiaries identified across Bukidnon.

Recto said the assistance would help students who face financial difficulties during the final stage of their college education.

“Hindi dapat mapurnada ang ilang taong pagsisikap dahil lamang kapos ang pamilya sa panghuling gastos,” Recto explained in a statement.

Article continues after this 

(Years’ worth of hard work should not be foiled just because a family runs short of the last expenses they need.)

The Bukidnon beneficiaries are part of a nationwide program expected to assist more than 200,000 graduating college students from over 42,000 barangays.

Article continues after this

World.title: PNP seeks P1.5B for infrastructure under proposed 2027 budget
World.content:
Philippine National Police headquarters in Camp Crame. — File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) is seeking nearly P1.5 billion for infrastructure projects under its proposed P242.53-billion budget for 2027, as it continues assessing police stations and other facilities for repairs and improvements, the agency said Tuesday.

In a statement, the PNP said the proposed budget is about P16 billion higher than the P226.55 billion appropriated for the agency in 2026.

Of the proposed 2027 budget, P1.499 billion is earmarked for infrastructure projects, while P2 billion is allocated for the Capability Enhancement Program, covering mobility, communications, firepower and anti-terrorism equipment.

Article continues after this 

READ: PNP eyeing 2,000 new recruits in 2027

Another P3.12 billion is proposed for information and communications technology.

PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said the assessment of police stations and other facilities is ongoing, particularly those affected by tropical cyclones and heavy rains in recent weeks.

The assessment will help determine which facilities need to be constructed, repaired or improved, according to the PNP.

Nartatez said the PNP would ensure that funds allocated for infrastructure projects are used properly to improve police services.

Article continues after this 

“Police stations serve as the frontline of PNP services to the Filipino people, and we are committed to ensuring that all our facilities are accessible and presentable at all times,” Nartatez said.

The infrastructure allocation, Nartatez added, would also help provide police personnel with facilities that better support their duties.

Article continues after this 

The proposed budget remains subject to congressional deliberations and approval. — Rendell Ivan Manuel, INQUIRER.net trainee /das

World.title: Nueva Ecija student found strangled with blanket; relative arrested
World.content:
Wesleyan University -Philippines (WU-P), one of the largest campuses in Cabanatuan City, denounced the murder on Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026, of one of their scholars at her home in the Nueva Ecija town of San Antonio. INQUIRER FILES

CABANATUAN CITY – Wesleyan University -Philippines (WU-P), one of the largest campuses in Cabanatuan City, denounced the murder on Sunday of one of their scholars at her home in the Nueva Ecija town of San Antonio.

Another student, who reportedly discovered the lifeless remains of 21-year-old nursing student Ann Pauline Fajardo, was later apprehended and had confessed to killing her, police said.

The suspect initially claimed that Fajardo had committed suicide at her residence in Barangay Sto. Cristo at 10:30 a.m. on Sunday. “Upon arrival, the responding officers found the victim already lifeless, with the blanket still tied around her neck,” the police reported.

Article continues after this 

READ: Student found dead in University of Makati campus

Fajardo’s mobile phone, a P66,990.00 iPhone Plus, was missing. But using the phone’s tracking feature, the unit traced it back to the student who reported to the police regarding Fajardo’s death.

The suspect eventually admitted to killing Fajardo, who was her relative, after she allegedly refused to lend him P5,000 at that same morning.

“We condemn this heinous and unspeakable act in the strongest possible terms. Violence against any member of our community is an outrage to our shared humanity, and we grieve deeply for a bright future cut short so cruelly,” the WU-P said in a statement issued on Monday.

WU-P described Fajardo as “a dedicated student, a cherished friend, and a promising future nurse whose passion, hard work, and kindness touched everyone around her.”/coa

World.title: Romualdez ordered to appear in Sandiganbayan on Sept. 10
World.content:
Former House Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez was served a warrant for his arrest by the CIDG at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Monday night, Sept. 7, 2026. — INQUIRER.net photo by Jason Sigales

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered former House Speaker Martin Romualdez to appear before the anti-graft court on Thursday, Sept. 10, for the hearing of his motion for continued hospital confinement.

Romualdez, who faces a non-bailable plunder case, has yet to appear before the anti-graft court as he remains hospitalized at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.

READ: Romualdez arrested in hospital for plunder

Article continues after this 

“Accused Romualdez is directed to appear before the court should his condition permit,” the court order stated.

The court emphasized that custody of Romualdez already belongs to the court.

“If there are concerns regarding the accused’s medical condition, it is only this court that can determine whether such condition affects the implementation of the warrant, the confinement of the accused at a hospital, or his commitment to a jail facility,” the order further stated.

The Third Division also issued subpoenas ad testificandum to Romualdez’s doctors Rody Sy, Rogelio Libarres, Kurt Allen Sibayan, and Rosalio Torres.

The Philippine National Police on Tuesday returned Romualdez’s warrant of arrest for plunder, after he did not appear in court as he filed an Urgent Motion ad Cautelam for Continued Hospital Confinement with the Third Division in a bid to extend his hospital confinement.

Article continues after this 

Police served Romualdez’s arrest warrant, and the lawmaker also underwent booking procedures while in confinement.

READ: PNP returns Romualdez arrest warrant to Sandiganbayan

Article continues after this 

In his motion, Romualdez said he is suffering from Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism, and other illnesses.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co, and two others hours after the Office of the Ombudsman filed the information containing the formal charges against the accused.

According to the information containing the formal charges filed by prosecutors before the anti-graft court, Romualdez and Co were charged with “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least 15 occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.

The amount allegedly came from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025, according to the information.

World.title: Experts Say Kazakhstan’s Youth Advantage Won’t Last Without Action
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has one of the relatively young population structures globally, with people under 18 accounting for 34.2% of the population in 2025 and placing the country 80th among 163 countries and territories. Experts say the large share of children gives Kazakhstan a potential demographic dividend, but realizing that opportunity will depend on education, healthcare, employment and long-term planning.

According to data from the UN Population Division Data Portal, Kazakhstan ranks between countries with substantially older population structures and the world’s youngest societies. The Central African Republic has the highest share of people under 18 at 56.2%, followed by Niger at 53.3%, Somalia at 53.0%, Mali at 52.9% and Chad at 52.7%.

At the other end of the ranking, children account for just 12.9% of South Korea’s population, while Japan, Taiwan and Singapore also have shares below 15%.

The contrast highlights two very different demographic challenges. Countries with large youth populations need to create enough schools, healthcare services and eventually jobs for growing generations. Countries with very small younger generations face a shrinking future workforce and increasing pressure from population aging.

For Kazakhstan, experts say the current age structure creates a window of opportunity, but one that is time-limited.

A young population is a potential dividend, not a guarantee

Independent financial analyst Andrei Chebotaryov said Kazakhstan’s relatively young population should be viewed as an economic opportunity rather than an automatic source of prosperity.

“A large number of children is by no means automatically wealth. It is a potential demographic dividend,” he wrote on his Telegram channel.

According to Chebotaryov, that dividend materializes only if a country provides younger generations with quality education, healthcare, skills and opportunities to find employment. If those conditions are met, a large youth cohort can eventually become a substantial workforce, a larger group of taxpayers and consumers, and a source of entrepreneurship and domestic demand.

“Kazakhstan is in an interesting position. Our population is noticeably younger. This means that Kazakhstan currently has a very valuable window of opportunity: the young generation is already here. Now the main thing is to use it correctly,” Chebotaryov wrote.

The demographic gap of the 1990s is still being felt

Kazakhstan’s current age structure, however, is also shaped by demographic disruptions that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union. Demography researcher and PaperLab Making New Experts graduate Darina Dauletbek, speaking on the Zhiza podcast on YouTube, said the country’s demographic situation cannot be understood without considering the sharp decline in births during the 1990s.

She described this as a demographic “pit” – a significant drop in the number of births that later moves through the population structure in waves. In the late 1980s, around 400,000 children were born in Kazakhstan, according to figures Dauletbek discussed. By 1999, the number had fallen to just over 200,000.

The decline coincided with the economic crisis following the collapse of the Soviet Union, as well as significant migration out of Kazakhstan. The effects are now visible in the size of the generation reaching adulthood.

People born in the late 1990s and early 2000s are now roughly in their late 20s and 30s — the age when many people marry, have children, and establish careers and businesses. Because relatively few people were born during that period, fewer people are reaching these life stages.

“This demographic pit creates the noise we are seeing today: falling birth rates and a decline in the number of marriages,” Dauletbek said in an interview with the Zhiza podcast.

Fertility matters, but so does the size of each generation

Dauletbek also highlighted the importance of the total fertility rate: the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her reproductive years. In Kazakhstan, the total fertility rate fell to about 1.8 in 1999, compared with approximately 3.5 during the Soviet period, according to figures cited in the interview.

A fertility rate of around 2.1 is generally associated with replacement-level fertility under stable mortality and migration assumptions. When fertility remains below that level over a prolonged period, population growth becomes increasingly difficult to maintain without other demographic factors.

Kazakhstan subsequently experienced a recovery in fertility, but the demographic effects of the 1990s did not disappear. They moved through the age structure and are now affecting the number of potential parents. This illustrates why demographic trends are difficult to reverse quickly. A smaller generation today means fewer potential parents tomorrow, regardless of whether those people individually want larger families.

Kazakhstan has a window, but it will not last indefinitely

The global comparison makes Kazakhstan’s position particularly notable. Africa dominates the countries with the largest shares of children: 28 of the top 30 countries in the ranking are African, with Afghanistan and Yemen the only exceptions. Higher fertility rates have contributed to these youthful population structures.

But a young population becomes an economic advantage only when institutions and infrastructure can absorb the coming generations. East Asian economies illustrate the opposite challenge. South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Singapore all have child shares below 15%, meaning substantially smaller generations are entering the future workforce.

Kazakhstan sits between these two demographic models. Its 34.2% share of people under 18 gives it a relatively young population and a potentially favorable labor-force trajectory, while the demographic consequences of the 1990s and the prospect of population aging create longer-term constraints.

As Chebotaryov put it, the demographic bonus cannot simply be postponed. The children who represent potential future workers, entrepreneurs and taxpayers will eventually become those people, and the policies adopted today will influence how large an economic dividend Kazakhstan ultimately receives.

World.title: Joint Statement by Ministers of Foreign Affairs of States Parties on Occasion of 20th Anniversary of Signing of CANWFZ Treaty
World.content:
We, the Foreign Ministers of the States Parties to the Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia (hereinafter referred to as the “CANWFZ Treaty”), on the occasion of the 20th anniversary of the signing of the CANWFZ Treaty in Semipalatinsk

reaffirming our commitment to humanity’s common goal of achieving a world free of nuclear weapons, and recognizing the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of any use or testing of nuclear weapons,

emphasizing that the establishment of nuclear-weapon-free zones is one of the most powerful universal tools for preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons and strengthening the global disarmament process,

noting the importance of the Treaty between the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Republic of Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the Republic of Uzbekistan on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation for Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century in strengthening peace and security in the region,

recalling that the idea of establishing a nuclear-weapon-free zone in Central Asia was first proposed by the Republic of Uzbekistan in September 1993 at the 48th session of the UN General Assembly,

convinced that the establishment of a nuclear-weapon-free zone in Central Asia represents a successful example of the consolidation of efforts by the countries of the region, and emphasizing that this was an important step toward strengthening the nuclear nonproliferation regime and the process of nuclear disarmament, regional and international peace and security, as well as the development of cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and the environmental rehabilitation of areas affected by radioactive contamination,

welcoming the thirty-fifth anniversary of the closure of the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site and the thirtieth anniversary of the opening for signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, and paying tribute to the memory of the numerous victims of nuclear explosions and their consequences in all regions of the world,

we hereby declare the following:

1. We reaffirm our commitment to the historically significant CANWFZ Treaty, signed by the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Republic of Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and the Republic of Uzbekistan on 8 September 2006, in Semipalatinsk. As the result of collective efforts of all five Central Asian states in their aspiration to ensure security, stability and peace in the region, and as it remains the first and only such zone located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and directly bordering two nuclear-weapon States, the Semipalatinsk Treaty continues to play an important role in strengthening the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime and serves as a symbolic example of Central Asia’s transformation from a region where nuclear weapons were once actively tested and deployed into one of the leaders of global efforts toward nuclear disarmament.

2. We reaffirm the key role of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) as the cornerstone of international efforts to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons and, ultimately, to achieve their complete elimination. In this regard, we regret that the Eleventh Review Conference of the States Parties to the NPT concluded without adopting substantive outcomes, reflecting continuing differences and a lack of trust in the field of nuclear disarmament and nonproliferation. We call on all NPT parties to continue negotiations in good faith on the effective implementation of obligations under all three interrelated and mutually reinforcing pillars – nuclear disarmament, nonproliferation, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

3. In light of the urgent and unprecedented challenges threatening global security and stability, we express serious concern over the lack of substantial progress in the field of nuclear disarmament in accordance with Article 6 of the NPT, as well as the cessation of key arms control agreements, coupled with an alarming trend toward the modernization of nuclear arsenals. At the same time, we note the special responsibility of nuclear-weapon States to engage in negotiations on nuclear disarmament and call for the urgent development of new, verifiable arms control mechanisms to prevent a nuclear arms race.

4. We affirm our unwavering support for the activities of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in implementing the provisions of the NPT, promoting cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, and applying safeguards and monitoring of nuclear programs in the Agency’s member states.

5. We firmly advocate for the necessity of the earliest entry-into-force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) which will mark exactly thirty years since its opening for signature on 24 September 2026. In this regard, we emphasize the need to preserve and further strengthen the international norm against nuclear testing and call for refraining from any actions that could undermine this norm.

We emphasize the important role of raising awareness on disarmament and non-proliferation in fostering a culture of peace, trust and responsibility, and note the particular importance of involving the youth in discussions on disarmament and international security. We support the continued promotion of the International Day for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Awareness, initiated by the Kyrgyz Republic and symbolically observed annually on 5 March – the date the NPT entered into force – as well as related regional educational initiatives.

In this regard, we note the relevance of the recommendations contained in the UN Study on Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Education, as well as the UN Secretary-General’s Agenda for Disarmament, “Securing Our Common Future: An Agenda for Disarmament.”

6. We welcome the signing on 6 May 2014 by the nuclear-weapon States of the Protocol on Negative Security Assurances to the Treaty on the Central Asian Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone and its ratification by four nuclear-weapon states, and we express our hope for the earliest completion of the ratification process for the Protocol by the United States of America.

7. We express our interest in the institutional development of the CANWFZ Treaty and in expanding further partnerships with existing nuclear-weapon-free zones with the aim of strengthening the global nuclear non-proliferation regime and uniting international efforts to ensure peace and security. In this context, we welcome the signing of Memoranda of Understanding with the African Commission on Atomic Energy (AFCONE) and the Organization for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean (OPANAL), as well as the holding in Astana on August 28–29, 2024, under Kazakhstan’s chairmanship, of the second meeting of representatives of all existing nuclear-weapon-free zones.

8. We note the great importance of strengthening regional security as a key factor for sustainable development and stability in Central Asia, and we reaffirm our intention to continue to cooperate closely in addressing common challenges and threats.

9. We support efforts to establish new nuclear-weapon-free zones in regions where they do not currently exist, including in the Middle East.

10. We welcome the adoption of the resolution “Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia” at the 79th session of the UN General Assembly as well as the holding, of an anniversary meeting of the Treaty’s participating States in Ashgabat on 5 December 2024, under Turkmenistan’s chairmanship, with the participation of representatives of other existing nuclear-weapon-free zones and international organizations.

World.title: US Lawmaker Urges End to Cold War-Era Trade Restrictions on Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA — The United States should establish permanent normal trade relations with Kazakhstan and offer greater economic opportunities rather than pressure the country to choose between Washington, Moscow and Beijing, Congressman Jimmy Panetta said during a Hudson Institute discussion on Sept. 2, as Washington weighs how to deepen its economic and strategic engagement with Central Asia.

Panetta, a California Democrat and a member of the House Ways and Means Committee, said repealing the Jackson-Vanik amendment would send an important signal of Washington’s commitment as it seeks new critical-mineral suppliers and greater influence in Central Asia.
