He noted that closer engagement would serve U.S. interests at a time when securing diversified critical-mineral supply chains has become a growing priority in Washington. His remarks followed a House Ways and Means Committee hearing in which lawmakers considered legislation granting Kazakhstan permanent normal trade relations.

Jackson-Vanik is holding back U.S.-Kazakhstan ties

At the center of that conversation was the decades-old Jackson-Vanik amendment, which Panetta described bluntly as a “Cold War relic.” The Jackson-Vanik amendment, adopted in 1974 to pressure the Soviet Union over restrictions on emigration, links normal U.S. trade relations to freedom of movement. Kazakhstan has met its requirements for decades but remains formally covered by the law.

Panetta framed the continued application of Jackson-Vanik as a contradiction in U.S. policy: Washington is seeking closer economic ties with Kazakhstan while retaining a trade mechanism created during the Cold War.

Panetta called the repeal a “huge step to take to demonstrate symbolically our commitment at a very low cost to the future of not just Kazakh-U.S. relations,” while also noting that it would benefit the U.S. by helping diversify supplies of rare-earth and other critical minerals.

Kazakhstan’s reforms

Yet the significance of Jackson-Vanik in this debate goes beyond economics, because the case being made in Washington is also about how the U.S. assesses Kazakhstan politically and whether it recognizes the context in which the country is pursuing domestic change. Panetta pointed specifically to reforms under President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. He cited Kazakhstan’s single seven-year presidential term as evidence of political reform, while acknowledging that “more can be done.”

“These are big steps that President Tokayev is taking in the face of a very tough history of this country in order to show that it is willing to make the types of changes that are needed to enhance its democracy and uphold its democratic values. I think it is a major reform not just for Kazakhstan, but for the region, because I guarantee you, Kazakhstan’s biggest neighbors, China and Russia, didn’t like to hear that,” Panetta said.

Panetta described Kazakhstan as a country with exceptionally deep ties to both Russia and China and said that expecting Astana to sever those relationships would be strategically unrealistic.

During the discussion, the possibility was also raised that Kazakhstan’s participation in both U.S.-backed Pax Silica and a Chinese AI initiative could create pressure for Astana to choose one technological ecosystem over the other. Panetta rejected that approach.

“I do not think that is the right strategy to have, and we have to continue to give them the options to choose America,” he said.

The U.S. should compete, not pressure

American engagement should be strong enough that countries choose the U.S. because doing so serves their interests, rather than because Washington has successfully compelled them to choose, he added.

For Kazakhstan, the argument is particularly relevant because the discussion does not present its balanced foreign policy as an obstacle to closer U.S. engagement, but rather as a reality Washington needs to understand and, potentially, use to its advantage.

As Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, noted, Kazakhstan’s multi-vector approach may actually benefit the U.S., because Kazakhstan’s geography and economic position make close ties with China and Russia unavoidable, while its relationship with Washington provides another channel for influence. Panetta agreed, emphasizing that Kazakhstan’s position makes such a strategy understandable and that the U.S. should seek to become part of that balancing act rather than demand it abandon it.

This approach also rests on a practical calculation. The discussion repeatedly returned to Kazakhstan’s potential importance for U.S. critical-mineral supply chains, and therefore to the broader question of whether Washington is prepared to translate its renewed strategic interest in Central Asia into the kind of sustained economic engagement that could compete with the relationships China and Russia have already built.

Panetta noted that Washington is only beginning to move in that direction, pointing to the bipartisan support for Jackson-Vanik repeal and the lengthy effort required to bring the issue before the Ways and Means Committee.

“Passing legislation in Congress, one, it is a marathon. Two, it takes a lot of luck. Three, it takes a lot of timing,” he said, adding that the process is beginning to move in the right direction.

Trump visit could send a strong signal

When asked about a possible visit by President Donald Trump, Panetta declined to say whether one was likely but said a presidential trip would signal that Washington intended to remain engaged in a region where China and Russia maintain a strong diplomatic presence.

As leaders gathered in Bishkek recently for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, including Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, Narendra Modi, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistan’s leadership, Panetta pointed to the gathering as evidence of how quickly geopolitical space can be occupied when Washington is absent.

Panetta’s argument was that Washington does not need Kazakhstan to abandon its relationships with Moscow and Beijing; it needs to ensure that the U.S. is sufficiently useful, credible and economically attractive to become another indispensable partner.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Tourism Sector Enters New Growth Phase As Investment And Visitor Numbers Rise
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s tourism sector is entering a new stage of development as investment, visitor numbers and transport connectivity expand, with the industry increasingly positioned as a contributor to economic growth rather than simply a recreational sector.

The sector’s total contribution to Kazakhstan’s economy reached 5 trillion tenge (US$9.26 billion) in 2025, while employment exceeded 600,000 people, according to the government.

Investment is also accelerating. Capital spending in tourism rose from 787.3 billion tenge (US$1.46 billion) in 2023 to 947.5 billion tenge (US$1.75 billion) in 2024 and 1.25 trillion tenge (US$2.31 billion) in 2025, an increase of 32.6% in one year.

More than 328 investment projects worth around 1.3 trillion tenge (US$2.41 billion) are currently being implemented across the country. They are expected to create about 10,000 permanent jobs and include 25 new international-standard hotels, including projects involving Hilton and Mandarin Oriental, as well as the expansion of the Oi-Qaragai mountain resort.

Growing visitor numbers create new economic opportunities

Infrastructure expansion is being accompanied by stronger tourism demand. Kazakhstan received 15.7 million foreign visitors in 2025, compared with 9.2 million in 2023. Of these, 11.1 million were classified as tourists, and foreign visitors spent $2.9 billion in Kazakhstan.

China has emerged as a key driver of growth. The number of visitors from China increased by 46.8% in 2025, exceeding 960,000. In the first half of 2026, Kazakhstan received 7 million foreign tourists, with Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Russia accounting for the largest shares.

Domestic tourism is also expanding. The number of Kazakh citizens traveling within the country increased from 7.1 million in 2023 to 8.7 million in 2025.

The figures suggest that Kazakhstan’s tourism market is benefiting from two parallel trends: increasing international interest and a growing domestic travel market. Together, they provide a more stable basis for investment in accommodation, transport and attractions.

Infrastructure remains critical to further growth

One of the main constraints on tourism development is access to destinations outside major cities. Air connectivity is also being expanded. New regional tourist airports are being developed in Katon-Karagai, Zaysan and Kenderli, while airports in Arkalyk and Balkhash have resumed operations and the terminal in Urzhar is being modernized.

For the summer season, 45 subsidized flights a week have been arranged to destinations including Alakol, Balkhash, Turkistan, Burabai and the Caspian coast. Expanding transport infrastructure matters because Kazakhstan’s tourism potential is geographically dispersed. Its mountain, steppe, lake and Caspian destinations cannot generate significant visitor flows if reaching them remains expensive or time-consuming.

Events and nature tourism broaden the offer

Kazakhstan is also using major cultural and sporting events to attract international visitors. The Fifth World Nomad Games in Astana brought 12,400 foreign visitors, while international concerts have generated significant tourist spending. A Jennifer Lopez concert in Almaty, for example, attracted 7,000 foreign visitors from 35 countries, according to the government. Spanish singer Enrique Iglesias performed in Astana on Sept. 3, followed by a concert in Almaty on Sept. 5, drawing fans from Kazakhstan and abroad.

Earlier, the three-day Park Live Almaty festival, held Aug. 21–23, brought together around 60,000 spectators, according to local media reports. The festival featured international headliners including Jack White, Gorillaz and The Offspring, with Gorillaz’s Aug. 22 performance attracting tens of thousands of people.

The country is simultaneously developing nature-based tourism. Visits to national parks increased from 2.4 million in 2023 to 3.7 million in 2025. As of 2026, 179 tourist routes and 42 ecological trails operate in protected areas.

This diversification is important for Kazakhstan because tourism growth does not have to depend on a single type of destination. Mountain resorts, cultural tourism, national parks, events, road trips and coastal destinations can attract different groups of visitors and extend the tourism season.

The next challenge is turning growth into a sustainable industry

The government has introduced several measures to stimulate further development, including subsidies for tour operators bringing foreign visitors, support for tourist transport and infrastructure, the Kids Go Free program, and incentives for roadside services and ski resorts.

A tourism coordination council has also been established, while new rules have formalized the status of visitor centers and strengthened regulation of guides, tour operators and instructors.

These measures address some of the practical barriers to tourism growth. But the scale of investment and rising visitor numbers also raise a broader question: whether Kazakhstan can convert increasing tourist flows into lasting economic value.

That will depend on more than the number of hotels or visitors. Higher-quality services, reliable transport, skilled workers, diverse tourism products and effective management of natural destinations will determine how much tourists spend, how long they stay and whether they return.

Kazakhstan’s current tourism expansion therefore represents a shift from building individual attractions toward creating a broader tourism ecosystem. With investment and millions of domestic and international visitors, the sector is becoming increasingly significant to the national economy.

World.title: Next Opportunity in Central Asian Wealth Management: Singapore-AIFC Corridor
World.content:
For much of the past three decades, the international wealth-management conversation has centred on a relatively small number of financial centres: Switzerland, Singapore, Hong Kong, London and until Donald Trump’s special military operation against Iran, Dubai. Central Asia has rarely featured prominently in that discussion. That may be beginning to change.

Kazakhstan’s Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) has developed into a credible financial jurisdiction connecting Kazakhstan and Central Asia with international capital markets. The introduction of a dedicated Family Offices Framework in 2024 was another important step in that development.

For international multi-family offices, wealth managers and private banks, the more interesting question is therefore no longer simply whether Kazakhstan can develop a family-office industry. The question is whether AIFC could eventually become the family-office and private-wealth gateway for Central Asia and eventually for the world.

Kazakhstan has experienced an extraordinary economic transformation since independence in 1991. Natural resources played a central role. Kazakhstan possesses substantial reserves of oil, natural gas, uranium, copper and other strategic commodities. But private wealth has also been created through banking, telecommunications, construction, consumer businesses, technology and financial services.

This matters because Kazakhstan is gradually entering a new stage of wealth development. The first generation of successful entrepreneurs increasingly faces questions that are familiar across every mature private-wealth market: How should wealth be preserved? How should a family’s assets be diversified internationally? How should ownership pass from one generation to the next? How should family members participate in investment decisions? And how can a family protect its wealth while simultaneously creating opportunities for future generations?

These are precisely the problems that family offices were created to address.

The Astana Financial Services Authority introduced the AIFC Family Offices Framework effective July 1, 2024. Importantly, the framework currently focuses specifically on Single Family Offices (SFOs). It allows SFOs to establish SFO Funds and provides streamlined regulatory provisions appropriate to structures managing the wealth of a single family.

That distinction is important. A Single Family Office exists primarily to serve one family. A Multi-Family Office, by contrast, provides professional services to several unrelated families and can therefore potentially undertake regulated activities including investment management, investment advice, fund management or arranging investments.

The existing framework should consequently be regarded as an important beginning rather than the final destination for the development of a broader AIFC private-wealth ecosystem. For AIFC, the next opportunity may be the development of an environment in which independent multi-family offices can flourish alongside SFOs, investment managers, private banks, lawyers, trustees, custodians and other professional advisers.

Family offices require more than favourable legislation. They need a functioning financial ecosystem. Here AIFC’s recent development is encouraging.

According to the Astana Financial Services Authority, assets under management within AIFC’s asset and fund-management sector exceeded $5.4 billion in 2025 when collective investment schemes and Managing Investments activities are considered together. By the end of 2025, the jurisdiction had 71 fund managers overseeing 177 investment funds, compared with 57 managers and 101 funds only one year earlier.

Collective investment scheme assets reached approximately $4.3 billion, while assets associated with firms conducting Managing Investments activities increased from approximately $314 million to $1.1 billion. These are still modest numbers compared with Singapore, Switzerland or the major Gulf financial centres. But the direction of travel is significant. AIFC is moving from being primarily an ambitious financial-centre project toward becoming an increasingly substantive investment-management ecosystem.

This creates an interesting opening for international MFOs. The opportunity is not necessarily to convince wealthy Kazakh families to move all their assets from Switzerland, Singapore, Dubai or London back to Kazakhstan. That would misunderstand how international private wealth operates.

A family might have custody relationships in Switzerland, an investment company in Singapore, property in London or Dubai, operating businesses in Kazakhstan and private-market investments across several jurisdictions. The modern family office sits above these individual relationships. It acts as the family’s financial architect and coordinator.

This suggests a potentially powerful role for an AIFC-based MFO: becoming the bridge between Central Asian families and the global financial system.

Rather than attempting to replicate established financial centres, AIFC could complement them. A wealthy Central Asian family might maintain assets with several international private banks while using an AIFC-based family office for strategic asset allocation, investment oversight, consolidated reporting, family governance and access to regional opportunities.

A private bank naturally provides custody, investment products, financing and portfolio management. But the family office can occupy a different position: it represents the family. An independent MFO can evaluate different banks, managers, funds and investment strategies while helping the family determine how much capital should be allocated to each.

For Central Asian entrepreneurs accustomed to dealing with multiple banks and jurisdictions, this independent Chief Investment Officer function could become increasingly valuable. The opportunity therefore extends considerably beyond portfolio management.

Perhaps the biggest strategic opportunity is geographic. AIFC should not think only about Kazakhstan. Central Asia is experiencing significant economic change. Uzbekistan is opening its economy, attracting foreign investment and developing its capital markets. The Kyrgyz Republic continues to develop its financial system. Across the wider Eurasian region, entrepreneurial wealth is expanding.

This creates the possibility of AIFC becoming a regional centre serving families from Kazakhstan and neighbouring markets. The proposition could eventually extend toward wealthy entrepreneurs and families from Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and selected neighbouring Eurasian markets. The potential addressable market would consequently become much larger than Kazakhstan alone.

AIFC’s Development Strategy for 2026-2028 reinforces this opportunity. The strategy emphasises deeper integration with international capital markets, expansion of asset management, growth in the number of licensed financial companies and development of alternative investment products.

AIFC is targeting $23 billion of structured investments by 2028 and $30 billion by 2030. It is also seeking to develop areas including exchange-traded products, sustainable finance, Islamic finance, digital assets and asset tokenisation. These initiatives matter to family offices because sophisticated private investors increasingly allocate capital beyond conventional listed equities and bonds.

For international MFOs, one particularly interesting model could be a Singapore-AIFC corridor. Singapore already possesses the mature side of the equation: international banks, global custody, fund management, professional services, sophisticated family-office infrastructure and access to Asian and global investment markets.

AIFC offers something different: proximity to Central Asian wealth, local relationships, regional investment opportunities and an increasingly sophisticated financial jurisdiction. Singapore could function as the international portfolio and wealth-management hub. AIFC could function as the Central Asian relationship, investment-origination and regional advisory hub. The two centres therefore need not compete. They can complement each other.

The opportunity should nevertheless be viewed realistically. AIFC remains a young financial centre. It cannot replicate overnight the private-banking infrastructure, professional networks, investment expertise and institutional trust accumulated over generations in Switzerland or over several decades in Singapore.

Family-office development also requires more than regulation. It requires experienced investment professionals, lawyers, tax advisers, trustees, accountants, consolidated-reporting systems, global custody relationships and – most importantly – confidence. Private wealth is based fundamentally on trust.

For multi-family offices, regulatory structuring also requires careful consideration. The streamlined AIFC regime introduced in 2024 specifically addresses Single Family Offices. An MFO serving unrelated families may require appropriate AFSA authorisation depending upon the financial services it conducts.

For global MFOs prepared to take a long-term view, the period between 2026 and 2030 could therefore represent an unusually attractive window in which to establish relationships, build local credibility and participate in the institutionalization of Central Asian private wealth.

The author is Rainer Michael Preiss, a partner and a portfolio strategist, DAS family Office, Singapore.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: S&P Sees Stronger Bank Oversight in Kazakhstan as Credit Growth Slows
World.content:
ASTANA – S&P Global Ratings improved its assessment of Kazakhstan’s banking industry risk and upgraded or raised the outlooks on several financial institutions, citing stronger supervision as credit growth and banking-sector profits slowed in the first seven months of 2026.

In its Sept. 4 release, S&P said stronger supervision, banks’ capital buffers and Kazakhstan’s sovereign strength should help preserve financial stability during economic downturns. The agency raised Bank CenterCredit’s long-term issuer credit rating to BB+ from BB and assigned positive outlooks to Halyk Bank, Nurbank, Freedom Holding Corp. and four of its core subsidiaries. It also raised national-scale ratings on Nurbank, Freedom Finance and Freedom Bank Kazakhstan.

S&P improved its assessment of Kazakhstan’s banking industry risk to 6 from 7 under its Banking Industry Country Risk Assessment, or BICRA, framework. The economic-risk score remained at 7, while the starting point S&P used to rate Kazakh banks remained unchanged at BB. Scores range from one to 10, with one representing the lowest risk.

The revision, according to the agency, reflects the “number of initiatives undertaken by the Kazakh regulator to enhance supervision of the financial institutions in Kazakhstan over recent years.”

Among the highlighted improvements are regular systemwide asset-quality reviews, the adoption of the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process, or SREP, and measures to curb banks’ risk appetite, particularly in the rapidly expanding retail lending segment.

The agency also said stronger oversight should help banks withstand periods of heightened uncertainty stemming from geopolitical risks and their potential effects on commodity prices, supply chains, economic activity and credit conditions.

S&P also revised the trend for Kazakhstan’s economic risk assessment to positive while leaving its score unchanged at 7. The change indicates that the score could improve if inflationary pressures ease and banks’ asset quality strengthens.

“This reflects our expectation of a resilient macroeconomic perspective with solid GDP growth over the next couple of years and reducing risks for the banking system,” S&P said.

The agency said an improvement would require evidence that economic imbalances, particularly elevated inflation, are putting less pressure on banks and nonbank financial institutions. Any improvement would also depend on stronger asset-quality indicators, which it considers a weakness of Kazakhstan’s banking sector, supported by more effective regulatory oversight.

S&P said Kazakhstan’s banks could benefit as inflation slows and the National Bank gradually cuts interest rates. Annual inflation declined from 10.2% in July to 9.8% in August, while the National Bank has lowered its base rate by a total of 1.25 percentage points since the beginning of the year.

The agency expects inflation to ease to 7-9% in 2027 and 2028, and slower price growth could leave households with more disposable income and make it easier for borrowers to repay their loans, reducing risks for banks.

S&P pointed to closer coordination between monetary, fiscal and macroprudential policies. However, it expects the tenge to weaken gradually in the second half of 2026, particularly if the central bank continues cutting rates.

Credit growth slows

The latest sector data present a mixed picture: banks accumulated more assets and deposits, but lending growth slowed. According to the Halyk Finance analytical center, banks’ assets, loan portfolios and deposits increased in July. However, growth in corporate and retail lending since the beginning of 2026 was slower than in the same period last year.

Banking-sector assets rose 6.9% from the beginning of the year to 75.6 trillion tenge (US$166.2 billion) in July. Liquid assets accounted for 35.4% of total assets, up from 34.1% a year earlier.

The total loan portfolio expanded 5.2% in the first seven months of 2026 to 45.5 trillion tenge (US$100 billion), compared with 10.5% during the same period last year. Corporate lending fell 0.7% in July but remained 4.7% higher than at the beginning of the year.

Retail lending grew 5.5%, roughly half the 11.2% increase recorded in January-July 2025. Consumer lending grew 4.6%, compared with 13.8% in January-July 2025.

In terms of business lending, loans to large companies, which accounted for 36.1% of the total volume of business lending, fell 5.9% from the beginning of the year, while lending to small and medium-sized businesses rose 11.9%. Deputy National Bank Governor Akylzhan Baimagambetov said the composition of lending was becoming more balanced as banks directed more financing toward businesses rather than household consumption.

“The share of SMEs and individual entrepreneurs in corporate lending reached 69%. For the past 12 months, 22 trillion tenge [US$48.4 billion] in loans have been issued to businesses, which is 16.8% more than the previous year,” said Baimagambetov.

“Thus, the lending structure gradually becomes more balanced: business lending outpaces consumer lending. This reflects the impact of previously adopted prudential measures and signifies reallocation of credit resources from consumption toward financing of the production activities, rather than a reduction in the overall availability of borrowed funds,” he said.

Deposit trends

Deposit data also indicated stronger demand for tenge-denominated savings. According to Halyk Finance, banks’ total deposit portfolio increased 1.5% in July and 6% from the beginning of the year to 50.9 trillion tenge (US$111.9 billion). That marked faster growth than the 2.7% recorded in the first seven months of 2025.

The growth was concentrated in tenge-denominated deposits, which increased 2.3% in July and 8.7% from the beginning of the year. Foreign-currency deposits fell 1.5% for the month and 3.9% since the start of 2026. Dollarization fell to 19.1% from 22.2% in July 2025.

Overall corporate deposits rose 3.1% from the beginning of 2026 to 22.5 trillion tenge (US$49.5 billion), compared with a 0.9% decline a year earlier. Corporate tenge deposits increased 2.8% in July and 4.9% from the start of the year, reaching 17.2 trillion tenge (US$37.8 billion).

Retail deposits grew 8.5% from the beginning of the year, accelerating from 5.7% in January-July 2025. Tenge-denominated retail deposits rose 1.9% in July and 11.6% from the start of the year, while foreign-currency deposits fell 2.1% for the month and 5.6% over the seven-month period.

Profits decline but remain strong

The banking sector reported net profit of 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.1 billion) in January-July, down 14.9% from the same period in 2025, according to the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market.

S&P said Kazakh banks have “demonstrated their capacity to generate earnings.”

“This could help create a buffer against risks in an external operating environment that remains uncertain and volatile,” said the agency.

“We expect the sector will demonstrate a similar magnitude of earnings generation in 2026-2027, with an average net interest margin fluctuating at about 6% and return on average equity of 20%-25%. This is on the back of slower but continued solid loan growth, operating efficiencies, and cyclically low loan losses,” said the agency.

The bank rating actions followed S&P’s August upgrade of Kazakhstan’s sovereign rating to BBB from BBB-, with a stable outlook.

World.title: World Nomad Games: Where Sport Meets Spirit of Steppe
World.content:
ASTANA – The sixth World Nomad Games (WNG) came to a close in the Kyrgyz Republic on Sept. 6, leaving a lasting impression on athletes, visitors, volunteers and everyone who helped bring the event to life.

For six days, the games were filled with color, energy and the competitive spirit of athletes determined to win, while upholding one of the most important values of sport – respect for their opponents. Beyond the medals and victories, the event offered a powerful reminder that nomadic culture is not simply a chapter of the past. It remains an important part of the region’s identity, roots and living heritage.

From the horse races and wrestling arenas to eagle hunting and kok boru, the games brought centuries-old traditions into the present, giving thousands of participants and visitors a chance to experience the spirit of the steppe firsthand.

Kazakhstan finished the WNG with 74 medals, including 32 gold, 20 silver and 22 bronze, reported the Kazakh Ministry of Culture and Sports.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated Kazakhstan’s national team on its performance, saying the results reflected the athletes’ dedication, hard work and determination.

Tokayev expressed gratitude to the medalists, coaches and specialists who contributed to Kazakhstan’s strong showing and helped strengthen the country’s international standing as a center for the development of traditional sports.

Experiencing the spirit of the games

Beyond the sporting results, the games also offered visitors and participants an opportunity to experience nomadic culture and traditional sports.

For Kazakh volunteer Miras Yauda, the games were an unforgettable experience.

“Every day, we were at the heart of the events, watching teams compete across various sports. We felt the spirit of nomadic culture, saw the genuine interest of foreign visitors and shared in victories that left no one indifferent,” Yauda told The Astana Times.

He also highlighted the high level of preparation and skill demonstrated by the athletes.

Among the events he watched were eagle hunting and archery, where Kazakh athletes competed for the top honors.

“It was spectacular. I got goosebumps when I heard that our athletes had won gold. It is important to showcase our nomadic heritage and draw attention to our traditional sports,” he said.

World-famous Japanese blogger Yuji Beleza also attended the games and paid particular attention to kok boru (a martial equestrian art of the Kyrgyz people) matches.

Speaking to local media, Beleza said the competition in the Kyrgyz Republic appeared more intense than what he had seen previously, while describing it as entertaining and energetic.

Beleza had previously watched kok boru at the fifth WNG in Astana in 2024, but this was his first time attending the event in the Kyrgyz Republic.

He said he enjoyed the local atmosphere and the energy of the fans and strongly recommended experiencing kok boru live at least once.

The U.S. kok boru players attending the games also highlighted the welcoming atmosphere, strong fan support and significance of the event.

“This is my first time here, and I can see how strong these athletes are. For me, lifting a goat is difficult, yet even children here can do it using the proper technique. I am learning from everyone and am grateful for this experience,” said U.S. athlete Jason Speta.

Held in the Kyrgyz Republic from Aug. 31 to Sept. 6, the games brought together about 3,000 athletes from 113 countries, making the 2026 edition the largest in the history of the competition.

World.title: Kazakhstan Looks For New Deposits as Expert Points to Investment Challenge Beyond Exploration
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan plans to increase exploration drilling over the next three years, with up to 200 exploration and appraisal wells expected to be drilled by 2028. While the expansion could help replenish the country’s resource base, experts say the real challenge will be turning geological discoveries into economically viable projects.

Speaking at the KAZDRILLING conference in Atyrau, Vice Minister of Energy Yerlan Akbarov said exploration and appraisal drilling could reach around 80 wells in 2026 and increase to up to 120 wells annually in 2027–2028, reported the Ministry of Energy on Sept. 7.

The government sees higher drilling activity as necessary to identify new deposits and replenish Kazakhstan’s hydrocarbon resource base. The plans come as Kazakhstan seeks to increase geological exploration while also developing the domestic drilling and oilfield services sector.

More drilling targets underexplored basins

Particular attention is being given to relatively underexplored sedimentary basins that are considered to have significant oil and gas potential. The government has also simplified the process for allocating such areas. Following submission of an application, the Ministry of Energy is to hold an auction within 10 working days.

The work programs for selected areas require seismic surveys covering at least 30% of the relevant block during the first three years, followed by the drilling of exploration wells. This approach is intended to accelerate the movement from identifying prospective areas to obtaining more concrete geological data.

However, the number of wells drilled will not by itself determine whether the programme succeeds.

Discovery is only the beginning

For investors, the key distinction is between identifying a resource and establishing that it can support a commercially viable project.

“Much work is being done by companies to find these resources, but this is only the beginning of the journey,” said Nurlan Saurambayev, the managing partner of Aurin Capital, an investment and strategic advisory firm focused on mining and natural resources in Kazakhstan.

For a discovered resource to become a developed project, reserves need to be confirmed, appropriate extraction and processing technologies identified, and infrastructure requirements addressed to establish whether the project is feasible. He stressed that this process requires more than geological expertise.

“Mining projects are long-term and capital-intensive, so they need to be implemented sequentially: geological exploration, resource assessment, technological studies, engineering, financing and construction,” Saurambayev said.

Skipping stages in this chain can lead to incorrect investment decisions, capital losses and other risks, according to the expert.

The point is particularly relevant as Kazakhstan increases exploration activity. A larger number of discoveries can strengthen the country’s resource base, but it does not necessarily translate into a proportional increase in production, exports or government revenues.

The economic value of a discovery ultimately depends on whether companies can demonstrate that the resource can be extracted and processed at a competitive cost and supported by the necessary infrastructure and financing.

Domestic drilling industry expected to benefit

Alongside exploration, the government is seeking to increase the share of domestic companies and equipment in the drilling industry. Kazakhstan already has manufacturing capabilities in the sector. The Atyrau-based Zhigermunaıservis plant, for example, produces drill bits, stabilizers and other drilling equipment.

The development of local suppliers could allow the expected increase in drilling activity to generate benefits beyond the discovery of new reserves, including demand for domestic equipment, services and skilled workers.

“Our task is to create a sustainable and competitive market for drilling services,” Akbarov said. “The result should be new geological discoveries, replenishment of reserves, development of domestic production, creation of qualified jobs and increased tax revenues.”

The extent to which those benefits materialize will depend partly on whether domestic companies can develop capabilities that remain competitive as exploration and production projects become more technically demanding.

Critical minerals add another dimension

The exploration push also has implications beyond oil and gas. Kazakhstan is seeking to expand exploration for critical and rare-earth minerals as global demand for materials used in energy, technology and advanced manufacturing increases. Saurambayev said the country has an opportunity to strengthen its position in global value chains, but stressed that geological resources alone are insufficient.

“It is possible, but the presence of resources alone is not enough,” he said. “It is necessary to develop processing and move up the value chain where economically justified.”

That would require technologies, capital, infrastructure and experienced project teams, he said.

Kazakhstan’s expanded drilling programme could provide the geological foundation for future production, but there is a considerable distance between a promising well and a functioning industrial project.

For hydrocarbons, this means establishing commercial reserves and production potential. For critical minerals, the challenge can be even broader, extending from exploration and resource assessment to beneficiation, processing and access to markets.

World.title: Former Georgian prosecutor general becomes commander of Russian military unit
World.content:
Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who now lives in Russia and is known as Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, will lead an international military unit formed to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Russia’s state-run news agency TASS reported this on 7 September, citing Partskhaladze himself.

In Georgia, Otar Partskhaladze has been charged in absentia with organising a murder and placed on an international wanted list.

Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, known in Russia as Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze. The photograph was shared by Partskhaladze’s friend Mamuka Pipia.

TASS describes Partskhaladze as a “veteran of the special military operation”. In an interview with the agency, he linked the creation of the unit to the Second World War and relations between the Russian and Georgian peoples.

“It was Russian Mikhail Yegorov and Georgian Meliton Kantaria who raised the Victory Banner over the Reichstag in 1945. One in four of my compatriots fought for freedom. I am certain that, as then, the symbol of the enemy’s defeat will once again be raised by a Russian and a Georgian.

“Our like-minded supporters, who advocate uniting our peoples and countries and defending traditional family values, have formed the international ‘St George’ unit,” the former prosecutor told TASS.

Partskhaladze explained that the unit’s name refers to the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk, which he says played an important role in the history of the Georgian people. The treaty brought the eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti under the protection of the Russian Empire.

Partskhaladze also says the new unit’s main task is “to finish the fight against the evil that threatens not only us, but the whole world”.

The former prosecutor says he decided to fight on Russia’s side and has helped Russian troops and people in the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic, as well as in Russia’s Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod regions, with his team since the start of the “special military operation”.

“Today, as Russia fights Western pressure to preserve its identity, traditions, language and culture, I am ready to help my homeland achieve all the goals set by its leader,” TASS quoted Otar Partskhaladze as saying.

Who is Otar Partskhaladze?

Otar Partskhaladze became Georgia’s prosecutor general in November 2013, after the current ruling Georgian Dream party came to power. But he remained in the post for just 47 days and resigned on 30 December that year.

His resignation followed a scandal over his criminal conviction for theft in Germany. Partskhaladze confirmed that he had been convicted, but claimed that the case concerned resisting police rather than theft.

After leaving the prosecutor general’s office, Partskhaladze moved into business. For many years, however, he was considered an influential figure close to the inner circle of ruling party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili. Ivanishvili himself has said that Partskhaladze is a close friend of his son, Bera Ivanishvili. Bera Ivanishvili is the godfather of Partskhaladze’s grandson.

In 2017, Partskhaladze was accused of assaulting Lasha Tordia, who was then head of Georgia’s State Audit Office. Tordia linked the attack to an investigation by the Audit Office into ties between Tbilisi City Hall and a company owned by Partskhaladze. In 2021, the Tbilisi City Court acquitted Partskhaladze in the case.

Partskhaladze later obtained Russian citizenship and has lived in Russia in recent years.

He subsequently changed his surname to Partskhaladze-Romanov. According to information JAMnews obtained from open sources, he also has business interests in Russia.

In September 2023, the US imposed sanctions on Partskhaladze. According to the US State Department, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) worked with Partskhaladze to influence Georgian society and politics in favour of Russia. The State Department says Partskhaladze worked with FSB officer Alexander Onishchenko, who also helped him obtain Russian citizenship.

After the sanctions were imposed, Georgian banks initially froze Partskhaladze’s accounts. However, after Georgian Dream leaders criticised the decision, the National Bank of Georgia changed its rules on implementing sanctions and restored Partskhaladze’s access to his accounts.

In October 2023, then-Georgian President Salome Zourabichvili stripped Partskhaladze of his Georgian citizenship.

In 2025, the UK also sanctioned Partskhaladze for supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Partskhaladze is currently a defendant in a criminal case in Georgia. In December 2025, the Interior Ministry named him as the organiser of the killing of businessman Levan Dzhangveladze. According to the ministry’s account, Partskhaladze led an organised criminal group and ordered the murder of Dzhangveladze. He was charged in absentia and placed on an international wanted list.

As it turns out, none of this has stopped Russia’s state-run news agency from interviewing him.



Otar Partskhaladze to lead a military unit

World.title: Armenian and Turkish business leaders call for borders to reopen. Is it likely to happen?
World.content:
Armenian-Turkish business forum in Yerevan

Against the backdrop of a two-day business forum held in Yerevan with the participation of business representatives from Armenia and Turkey, debate over normalising Armenian-Turkish relations and reopening the border between the two countries has intensified in Armenian society.

Following the forum, the Union of Manufacturers and Businessmen of Armenia and the Van Chamber of Commerce and Industry issued a joint statement. The two countries’ business leaders called for the borders to reopen, border crossing points to resume operations and procedures for crossing the border to be simplified for both sides.

“Reopening the border crossing points would not only boost trade, but also mark an important step towards normalising relations. It would strengthen contacts, promote economic cooperation and build mutual trust between the peoples of the two countries. Opening the borders is crucial to unlocking the region’s economic potential in trade, investment, tourism and cultural exchange,” the statement said.

In an interview with JAMnews, political analyst Robert Ghevondyan said: “Under normal circumstances, developing economic and trade ties would have a significant impact on the process of reopening the borders. But our situation is not normal.” He was referring in particular to Azerbaijan’s enormous influence over Turkey through various means, including economic leverage.

“Yes, such initiatives provide a positive boost, at least at a psychological level. But for substantial changes to take place, the political issues must first be resolved. Above all, we need to focus on resolving relations with Azerbaijan,” Ghevondyan said.

From increasing trade to reopening the border: business leaders issue joint statement

Eighty representatives of the Van Chamber of Commerce and Industry travelled to Yerevan to attend the business forum. The two sides discussed opportunities for trade and investment, and explored prospects for closer cooperation between their business communities.

Business representatives described the forum as a “significant step” towards normalising relations and developing economic cooperation between Turkey and Armenia:

“The business community can make a significant contribution to building relations based on mutual understanding, trust and shared economic interests, regardless of borders and political differences. We believe that stronger economic and trade ties between Turkey and Armenia would contribute significantly to the economic and social development not only of the two countries’ business communities, but also of border regions, as well as Van and Yerevan.”

They said reopening the border would be crucial not only to boosting trade but also as an important step towards normalising relations:

“Van could become a natural trade and logistics bridge between Turkey and the Caucasus. Strengthening economic ties between Van and Yerevan could help develop regional trade and build greater understanding between the two peoples.”

On 3-4 September, Yerevan hosted a two-day business forum attended by representatives of the Armenian and Turkish business communities. The forum took place as part of the EU programme “Supporting the normalisation of Armenian-Turkish relations: strengthening cross-border ties”. Its aim was to bring together business and government representatives from the two countries to explore new forms of cooperation and build trust.

Comment

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan says that despite the lack of diplomatic relations between Armenia and Turkey, trade ties between the two countries have long been established. However, these ties exist at the business level rather than between the governments.

He says there is now active work under way to normalise relations, which is also helping to develop economic ties further:

“Reopening the border could provide a major boost to further progress in this direction. We hope the border will open soon and that we will see the results.”

Ghevondyan notes that Turkey has already lifted its ban on direct exports to Armenia:

“Turkish companies can now file customs declarations directly for exports to Armenia and sell their goods there. As a result, Armenian and Turkish businesses no longer need intermediaries.”

At the same time, Ghevondyan points out that goods are transported through Georgia. Transit costs will therefore remain in place until the Armenian-Turkish border opens.

According to the political analyst, the next step is to reopen the border. This could lead to a major increase in economic ties.

Robert Ghevondyan says he cannot predict exactly when the border will open. But he hopes it will happen “as soon as possible”. He also stresses that reopening the border depends on the normalisation of Armenian-Azerbaijani relations:

“Azerbaijan sees the closed border with Turkey as a lever for putting pressure on Armenia. Once Azerbaijan decides that it no longer needs this leverage, the Turkish border will most likely open.”

As for whether the signing of an Armenia-Azerbaijan peace agreement could influence the process, Ghevondyan is not convinced that this would be the decisive factor:

“There is a possibility that even if a peace agreement is signed, Azerbaijan could ask its Turkish partners not to open the border. In that case, the border will remain closed.

“But there is also a possibility that no peace agreement will be signed, but Azerbaijan will no longer ask its Turkish partners to keep the border closed. In that case, the border will open.”

Speaking about Azerbaijan’s influence over Turkey, the expert listed the following factors:

Baku’s investments worth billions of dollars in Turkey;

the personal ties between Aliyev and Erdogan;

perceptions among Azerbaijani and Turkish societies.

“When Turkey opened the border for 10 days to allow humanitarian aid from Armenia to reach Syria, there was discontent in Azerbaijani society. This affected the decision-making circles in Turkey,” he said.

At the same time, Ghevondyan says Turkey does not even try to hide the extent of Azerbaijan’s influence:

“At meetings at different levels, Turkish partners say directly: ‘We have no problem with opening the border, but our Azerbaijani partners must not object.’”

Context

Turkey officially recognised the Republic of Armenia in 1991. But the two countries still have no diplomatic relations. In 1993, Turkey unilaterally closed its air and land borders with Armenia. The air border reopened in 1995, according to the Armenian Foreign Ministry website, “under pressure from the international community”.

Talks on normalising Armenian-Turkish relations intensified after the second Karabakh war. Although the normalisation process is taking place on a bilateral basis, Turkey coordinates the negotiating agenda with Azerbaijan.

In December 2021, Yerevan and Ankara said they were ready to take steps towards normalising relations. The two countries appointed special representatives to begin negotiations.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the border between Armenia and Turkey would open on 1 February to citizens of third countries and holders of diplomatic passports. The two countries’ special representatives had agreed on this in July 2022. However, the agreement has still not been implemented.

The Margara checkpoint on the Armenian side has been ready for operation since December 2023. Despite the agreements reached, however, the border remains closed.

At the same time, there have been occasional signs of limited progress. Since 1 January 2026, for example, Armenia and Turkey have simplified the visa process for citizens of the two countries who hold diplomatic, special or service passports. Those staying in the neighbouring country for no more than 21 days can obtain an electronic visa (e-visa) free of charge.

Armenian-Turkish business forum in Yerevan

World.title: Armenia is building AI factory with Nvidia chips: what has been implemented for Azerbaijan under Washington agreement?
World.content:
What did the Washington agreement give Azerbaijan?

The US made Armenia’s access to advanced Nvidia processors one of the economic incentives offered during the peace talks. The project is already under way in Yerevan. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, received a strategic partnership document from Washington, the suspension of Section 907 and a number of pledges of cooperation. However, the road to Nakhchivan has yet to open.

Armenia will not manufacture Nvidia chips. But with a US export licence, the country is using them to build one of the region’s largest computing centres for artificial intelligence.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Washington used access to advanced Nvidia processors as one of the incentives intended to speed up a preliminary peace agreement between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

The Armenian government describes the project not as a reason for reaching the agreement, but as a “peace dividend” for the country. However, the launch of the Firebird project raises another question:

What concrete dividends has Azerbaijan received since the Washington agreement of 8 August 2025?

Armenia is already benefiting

The WSJ reports that US officials believed Nikol Pashinyan needed tangible economic gains from the peace process to offset the domestic political costs of an agreement with Azerbaijan.

As part of this effort, a US export licence for advanced Nvidia processors for the Firebird project in Armenia was included in the negotiations. The project was initially licensed to receive around 6,000 processors. Following the Washington agreement, the US authorised the export of another 41,000 Nvidia GB300 processors.

In August 2026, the first phase of the centre was launched near Hrazdan. According to the Armenian government, $500 million was invested in the first phase, more than 6,000 Nvidia Blackwell processors were installed and computing infrastructure with a capacity of 18 megawatts was built.

The investment is expected to exceed $4 billion in the next phases. By the end of 2027, the number of processors is expected to rise to more than 100,000, while infrastructure capacity is planned to exceed 400 megawatts.

The US did not provide Armenia with the chips free of charge. Investors are financing their purchase and the development of the infrastructure. The main advantage Washington provided was the export licence. Because access to the most powerful AI processors is subject to US national security controls, securing such a licence provides an economic advantage while also signalling political trust.

What did the US promise Azerbaijan?

On 8 August, Azerbaijan signed a memorandum with the US to establish a working group to prepare a Charter on Strategic Partnership.

The document outlined three areas of cooperation: regional connectivity, including energy, trade and transit; investment, including in artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure; and security cooperation, including defence supplies and counterterrorism.

However, the memorandum contained no legally binding commitments or funding guarantees. The two sides were expected to prepare a broader Charter on Strategic Partnership within six months.

The document was signed in February 2026 during US Vice-President JD Vance’s visit to Baku. The charter refers to the creation of AI data centres in Azerbaijan, defence supplies, energy projects, cybersecurity, demining and investment opportunities along the Middle Corridor.

Unlike the Armenian project, however, it does not name specific companies, investment amounts, the quantity of equipment or launch dates for the projects. Although the document says the two sides should agree on a list of projects and roadmaps for their implementation within three months, the full list has not been made public.

In June, the creation of a data centre in Azerbaijan was also discussed only as “potential cooperation” during a meeting between Azerbaijani Minister of Digital Development and Transport Rashad Nabiyev and a US delegation. The ministry’s statement did not name a specific investor, budget or construction schedule.

Section 907 suspended, but not repealed

One of the most concrete outcomes for Azerbaijan from the Washington meeting was the latest suspension of Section 907, which restricts direct US assistance to the country.

A decision by Donald Trump on 8 August 2025 temporarily removed restrictions on US security cooperation with Azerbaijan and the provision of US government assistance.

However, this does not mean that Section 907 has been repealed. It remains part of US law, while the president can only suspend its application. Ilham Aliyev has also said he expects Congress to repeal the provision completely.

During his visit to Baku, Vance also said the US would provide Azerbaijan with new boats to help protect its territorial waters. However, the statement did not specify their number, models, cost or delivery dates. There is also no publicly available evidence that the boats have so far been delivered to Azerbaijan.

Minsk Process closed: the main political gain for Baku

The most significant political outcome for Azerbaijan was the closure of the OSCE Minsk Process and related structures. This had long been one of Baku’s key demands.

The foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan signed a joint appeal on the issue in Washington. On 1 September 2025, the OSCE decided to close the Minsk Process, and the administrative procedures were completed on 30 November that year.

The previous international mediation mechanism for the Karabakh conflict was therefore formally abolished. The move has no direct economic impact, but it is important in terms of international recognition of the political reality that emerged after the war and was consolidated by Baku.

The road to Nakhchivan remains closed

One of the most widely discussed elements of the Washington agreement for Azerbaijan is the TRIPP project, which is intended to establish a connection between the country’s main territory and Nakhchivan.

However, the 8 August Joint Declaration does not give Azerbaijan an established right to transit. It only sets out the goal of creating “unimpeded connectivity” and says Armenia will work with the US to develop the framework for implementing the TRIPP project.

In January 2026, the Armenian government said that routes still had to be determined, a TRIPP company established, land-use issues resolved and construction permits issued. On 31 August, Aliyev and Pashinyan also discussed the “next practical steps” towards implementing the project.

Azerbaijan still has no operational road or rail link to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The route has not opened, transport operations have not begun, and the tariff and customs arrangements have yet to be tested in practice.

Two different “peace dividends”

It would be wrong to say that Azerbaijan received nothing from Washington. The application of Section 907 has been suspended, the Minsk Process has been closed, a strategic partnership with the US has been established, and new channels for defence and technology cooperation have been opened.

However, most of these outcomes are political in nature or remain commitments to future cooperation. Armenia’s benefit has already taken concrete and measurable form: an export licence has been granted, thousands of Nvidia processors have been installed and the first phase of a $500 million project has been launched.

Baku says it did not need economic incentives to reach an agreement with Washington. Hikmet Hajiyev, an aide to the Azerbaijani president, told the WSJ:

“We won the war and also wanted to achieve peace.”

This position may explain why the US offered a more concrete economic incentive to Yerevan. But the outcome remains the same: the Armenian part of the Washington package has already taken tangible form in a data centre, while a significant share of the commitments concerning Azerbaijan remains a promise for the future.

What did the Washington agreement give Azerbaijan?

World.title: Azerbaijan is building drone fleet on Caspian sea: what will SALVO and KAYRA change?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s drone fleet in the Caspian

Azerbaijan has launched local production of armed naval drones and loitering maritime drones based on Turkish technology. The new systems are designed for a range of missions, from protecting energy infrastructure in the Caspian Sea and carrying out reconnaissance to attacking ships. However, the number of drones being produced, the cost of the programme and the share of manufacturing actually carried out in Azerbaijan have not been disclosed.

On 6 September, President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Azerbaijani Navy.

The visit was intended to showcase two unmanned naval platforms: the SALVO armed uncrewed surface vessel and the KAYRA maritime kamikaze drone.

According to Azerbaijan’s presidential website, the drones are being produced by a joint venture between MİRAS, a defence industry company operating under Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Defence, and Turkish shipbuilder DEARSAN. Aliyev was briefed on the drones’ technical specifications before the systems underwent live demonstrations.

The official statement did not disclose production volumes, the cost of the project or when the first batch would be delivered to the Azerbaijani Navy.

They have been showcased before

SALVO and KAYRA are not being shown in Azerbaijan for the first time. SALVO was unveiled in August 2025 during military exercises focused on “the protection and defence of maritime energy infrastructure”.

KAYRA was presented in November that year at a military parade in Baku.

The significance of the 6 September presentation, therefore, is not the introduction of the systems themselves. The key change is that they are now being produced at a joint facility in Azerbaijan, and the production process was officially demonstrated to the country’s leadership for the first time.

This suggests that Azerbaijan wants to move beyond simply buying finished military equipment from Turkey towards domestic production, maintenance and potentially technology transfer. However, the official information does not make clear how much of the hulls, engines, electronics, communications and control systems is actually produced in Azerbaijan.

What is the difference between SALVO and KAYRA?

SALVO is a larger, multi-purpose platform designed for repeated use. KAYRA, by contrast, is a smaller kamikaze drone designed to rapidly approach and destroy its target.

Specification SALVO KAYRA Length 14.79 metres 7,6 metres Maximum speed More than 35 knots, around 65 km/h More than 60 knots, around 111 km/h Maximum range Up to 400 nautical miles, around 740 km 300 nautical miles, around 555 km Hull Aluminium Composite material Main role Patrolling, surveillance and armed operations One-way attack and target destruction

According to DEARSAN, SALVO can be used to patrol coastlines and borders, conduct reconnaissance, combat smuggling, carry out search-and-rescue operations and engage surface targets.

During tests conducted by the company in 2022, SALVO launched a Cirit missile made by Turkish defence company Roketsan, hitting a moving target. A stabilised 12.7mm machine-gun mount produced by ASELSAN was then tested. The platform can be controlled from a mobile station on shore, a command centre or another military vessel.

It is not known what weapons will be fitted to the SALVO platforms intended for Azerbaijan.

The missions listed for KAYRA are primarily offensive. According to its manufacturer, the drone is designed to strike enemy ships and patrol boats, naval bases, ports, coastal infrastructure and logistics routes.

The type and amount of explosive carried by KAYRA, its guidance system and its ability to operate autonomously if communications are lost have not been publicly disclosed.

Why are these systems needed in the Caspian?

One of the main tasks of the Azerbaijani Navy is to protect oil and gas infrastructure in the Caspian Sea, as well as ports, pipelines and the country’s maritime borders.

According to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Defence, during naval exercises in 2025, ships patrolled and monitored areas where oil and gas pipelines run. They also practised responding to attacks by a simulated enemy, countering underwater sabotage groups and dealing with the threat of mines.

SALVO-type systems can carry out some of these tasks without putting ship crews at risk. They can conduct surveillance for extended periods, track suspicious vessels and, when armed, use force if necessary.

KAYRA, by contrast, is more of an offensive and deterrent weapon than a defensive one. Their small size and high speed could create additional challenges for the defences of warships. Using several such drones simultaneously from different directions could force a larger vessel to devote more resources to self-defence.

At the same time, drones do not replace a conventional navy. Their effectiveness depends on the quality of intelligence, the resilience of communications, operator training and their integration with other vessels into a unified command system. Electronic warfare, GPS jamming and loss of communications are considered key vulnerabilities of such systems.

Lessons from the war in Ukraine

The war in Ukraine has significantly changed perceptions of the role of naval drones in modern warfare. Ukraine, which does not have a large conventional navy, has used relatively cheap uncrewed boats to limit the capabilities of the Black Sea Fleet of Russia.

The experience has shown that smaller states can develop a maritime deterrent without having to build up large warships on a comparable scale. However, Russia has also strengthened its defences, port barriers and drone detection systems over time. This shows that the advantage provided by such technologies is not permanent.

The fact that Azerbaijan is producing KAYRA alongside SALVO, with KAYRA designed for one-way attacks, suggests that Baku is embracing this new model of naval warfare.

Will the military balance in the Caspian change?

The Caspian littoral states are Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan. The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, calls on the parties to develop their military capabilities within “reasonable sufficiency”, maintain a balance of arms and ensure transparency. The convention also bans the presence of armed forces from non-littoral states in the Caspian.

Producing equipment in Azerbaijan based on technology from a Turkish company does not violate this ban. It involves technological and industrial cooperation rather than the deployment of foreign armed forces in the Caspian.

The emergence of two new platforms does not, by itself, alter the regional military balance. Assessing their impact would require knowing how many systems will be produced, what weapons they will carry and how they will be integrated with the rest of the navy.

There is also no public evidence that Azerbaijan is developing these systems specifically against Russia or Iran. Baku conducts joint exercises in the Caspian with Iran and Kazakhstan. Nevertheless, amid rapid rearmament and the spread of military technologies, neighbouring states are likely to take every new strike capability into account when planning their defences.

Key questions remain unanswered

The president’s visit officially confirmed that the naval drones are being produced in Azerbaijan. However, key information needed to assess the scale of the project remains undisclosed:

How many SALVO and KAYRA systems are planned for production?

How much will the contract and the production facility cost?

What share of the components will be manufactured in Azerbaijan?

What weapons and control systems will the Azerbaijani versions carry?

Have the systems already entered operational service, or are they still undergoing testing?

Who will decide when and under what procedures the kamikaze drones can be used?

SALVO could expand Azerbaijan’s surveillance and armed patrol capabilities in the Caspian, while KAYRA could provide a new asymmetric strike capability. Local production could also make maintenance easier and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers to some extent.

However, the actual capabilities of this “drone fleet” will depend on production volumes, how well the systems are integrated into a unified combat command network, and the financial terms of the project, which have not yet been disclosed.

Azerbaijan’s drone fleet in the Caspian

World.title: Azerbaijani activist living in France: ‘My father in Baku and I have received threats’
World.content:
Threats against Azerbaijani activist living abroad

Azerbaijani civic activist Ramazan Tagiyev, who lives in France, says he continues to receive threats over posts criticising the authorities on social media. He says the latest messages have also targeted his father, who lives in Baku.

“He said he knows where my father is in Baku”

Tagiyev says that on 3 September, a man named Rashad, who goes by the nickname “Roma”, contacted him again, threatening to beat and kill him. He also said he was currently in the French city of Toulouse and intended to track him down.

Tagiyev says that this time the threats also targeted his father, who lives in Baku:

“Rashad wrote that he knows where my father is in Baku and that he would make sure people found and beat him. The threat against my father is particularly worrying. It shows that the threats are no longer directed only at me but are now extending to my family.”

Threats began in March

The civic activist says the threats began in March 2026 after he started posting material on social media criticising the Azerbaijani government, state projects and prominent public figures.

At the time, he received calls from different unknown numbers as well as threatening messages.

Tagiyev says the situation escalated further in May after he published a critical post about Azerbaijani meykhana performer Rashad Dagly, who is currently serving a prison sentence for murder.

He says people living in Toulouse who, he claims, have links to criminal circles threatened to track him down and “deal with” him.

Fearing for his safety, Tagiyev left Toulouse soon afterwards.

Facebook account blocked after mass complaints

Tagiyev says that in August, following a series of posts about the Cavan TV project and bloggers, his Facebook page was hit by a wave of complaints, after which the account was blocked.

Tagiyev links the attacks on his social media accounts and the threats he received around the same time to his civic activism.

“What is Cavan TV and why did Tagiyev criticise it?”

Cavan TV is a media project run by the CAVAN Youth Movement, a public association targeting a young audience and receiving state support. Some of the movement’s projects receive financial and organisational support from the Youth Foundation of Azerbaijan and the Ministry of Youth and Sports.

Cavan TV is known for covering socially significant events using manipulative techniques. During high-profile events, such as the flooding of Baku after heavy rains, the platform has published material that shifts attention away from the responsibility of state institutions, eases public discontent and redirects the discussion towards secondary issues.

This was the focus of Ramazan Tagiyev’s criticism of Cavan TV.

Claims of links to criminal circles

Tagiyev says he learned about the past of the man who threatened him, Rashad, and his alleged links to criminal circles from Rashad himself.

The activist says Rashad told him that he had served two prison sentences in France and had links to criminal circles.

Tagiyev also claims that Rashad told him that some of the people accused of involvement in an attempted attack on Azerbaijani blogger Mohammed Mirzali, who lives in France, had stayed at his home.

According to the activist, Rashad also told him that he had come to Toulouse after an incident in Germany in which a man was stabbed, and threatened Tagiyev with “the same fate”.

Reported the threats to French police

Ramazan Tagiyev says he reported the threats to the French police. According to him, French law enforcement launched an investigation and located the man who had threatened him.

Jamnews was unable to independently verify Tagiyev’s claims with French law enforcement. The man named in the allegations has not been contacted for comment.

Threats against Azerbaijani activist living abroad

World.title: What do Abkhaz residents expect from Tbilisi? A video discussion with Abkhaz experts
World.content:
De-isolation of Abkhazia

Abkhaz journalist and editor of Chegemskaya Pravda, Inal Khashig, and civic activist Adgur Lagvilava discussed the key challenges facing Abkhazia’s foreign relations, as well as its ties with Georgia’s official authorities in Tbilisi.

Key points and arguments:

Fuel crisis and relations with Georgia: Resolving the gasoline shortage in part through purchases in Georgia sparked absurd accusations from the Georgian opposition regarding supplies to the Russian military.

Resolving the gasoline shortage in part through purchases in Georgia sparked absurd accusations from the Georgian opposition regarding supplies to the Russian military. Distorted perception of Abkhazia in Georgian society: A historically inaccurate narrative prevails in Georgia alleging that Abkhaz are an “alien people,” which is used to justify Georgian claims. Abkhazia has become a political simulacrum for Tbilisi, and ignoring Abkhaz agency hinders dialogue.

A historically inaccurate narrative prevails in Georgia alleging that Abkhaz are an “alien people,” which is used to justify Georgian claims. Abkhazia has become a political simulacrum for Tbilisi, and ignoring Abkhaz agency hinders dialogue. Politicization of history in Georgia: Georgian authorities pragmatically rewrite history and rehabilitate historical figures (such as King Heraclius II) to justify their current political course and rapprochement with Moscow. The speakers view this approach as a dangerous manipulation of the past for the sake of short-term gain.
