World.title: President Ilham Aliyev sends congratulatory letter to President of North Macedonia
World.content:
Photo: Press service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev has sent a congratulatory letter to Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, President of the Republic of North Macedonia.

The text of the letter was published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Dear Madame President,

On my own behalf and on behalf of the people of Azerbaijan, I extend my sincerest congratulations to you and, through you, to your entire people on the occasion of the 35th anniversary of the Independence of the Republic of North Macedonia.

The strengthening of interstate relations and partnership between Azerbaijan and North Macedonia, built on good traditions and enriched with new content year after year, is a source of satisfaction.

Today, there are good opportunities for expanding our partnership. I am confident that we will successfully continue our joint efforts to enhance relations between Azerbaijan and North Macedonia and further expand our bilateral and multilateral cooperation in line with the interests of our friendly peoples.

On such a remarkable day, I convey my best wishes to you and wish your friendly people everlasting peace and prosperity," the letter reads.

World.title: Azerbaijan highlights cases of mine re-contamination of cleared areas during floods
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Cases of re-contamination of demined areas with mines during floods and mudslides have been observed in Azerbaijan, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Azerbaijan National Agency for Mine Action (ANAMA), Vugar Suleymanov, said during a high-level roundtable on "Advantages and Challenges of AI-integration to the Multi-hazard Early Warning Systems" within the framework of the 4th Baku Climate Action Week (BCAW), Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

Suleymanov noted that the impact of climate change is also felt in mine clearance activities.

"Considering the specifics of our activities, we cannot work on rainy days for safety reasons. Recently, the increase in rainfall in recent years has undoubtedly had a negative impact on our activities," he pointed out.

He also noted that cases of re-contamination of cleared areas with mines during floods and mudslides have been observed several times.

"River waters, during floods, mines are brought to low-lying areas with river waters. Of course, this is an alarm for us. We are already paying attention to these issues and are additionally inspecting areas after floods and mudslides," the ANAMA chairman emphasized.

Suleymanov noted that since November 2020, more than 300 thousand hectares of land in Azerbaijan have been cleared of mines and unexploded ordnance. According to him, as a result of these clearance operations, about 262,000 mines and unexploded ordnance were discovered and neutralized.

Will be updated

World.title: Uzbekistan hosts SOCEA, CANSO summits to advance air navigation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Uzbekistan is hosting two major international events focused on air navigation and air traffic management for the first time, bringing together aviation authorities, air navigation service providers and international organizations from Europe and Asia.

This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Transport of Uzbekistan.

The 3rd Annual General Meeting of the Regional Coordination Platform for Europe and Asia (SOCEA AGM/3) opened in Tashkent, gathering representatives of European and Asian air navigation service providers and international aviation organizations, according to the statement.

The meeting’s agenda includes SOCEA’s activities and results, aviation safety, cooperation among air navigation service providers and priorities for the platform’s further development.

SOCEA serves as a regional platform for coordinating air navigation between Europe and Asia, supporting cooperation in air traffic management and aviation safety while facilitating the exchange of information, expertise and best practices.

“The organization of these international events in Tashkent marks an important step in strengthening cooperation between air navigation service providers and expanding Uzbekistan’s role in regional aviation coordination,” the organizers said.

The second major event, the CANSO Eurasia ANSPs Summit, is scheduled to take place in Tashkent on September 9.

The summit will focus on the development of air traffic management (ATM) systems and communications, navigation and surveillance (CNS) technologies. Participants are also expected to discuss the use of artificial intelligence in aviation, Green ATM initiatives, air traffic flow management (ATFM), efficient use of airspace and cross-border coordination among air navigation service providers.

The back-to-back events are expected to provide a platform for aviation industry representatives from across Europe and Asia to exchange experience and discuss technological and operational solutions for managing increasingly complex airspace.

The focus on artificial intelligence, greener air traffic management and cross-border coordination reflects broader efforts to modernize aviation infrastructure while improving safety, efficiency and the use of available airspace.

For Uzbekistan, hosting the meetings provides an opportunity to strengthen international aviation partnerships and increase cooperation with regional and global air navigation organizations.

World.title: Azerbaijan suggests applying artificial intelligence in flood risk prediction
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Artificial intelligence (AI) can be applied to predict flood risks in Azerbaijan, First Deputy Chairman of the Azerbaijan State Water Resources Agency Khayyam Mammadov said during a high-level roundtable on "Advantages and Challenges of AI-integration to the Multi-hazard Early Warning Systems" within the framework of the 4th Baku Climate Action Week (BCAW), Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

He noted that the significant increase in flood events in Azerbaijan in recent years necessitates the wider use of AI and early warning systems to predict these risks in advance and take preventive measures.

According to him, if previously flood events were observed in the country about 10-20 times a year, in recent years this indicator has increased by 10-15 times.

"These indicators show that only the development of infrastructure and operational response to events isn't enough, and require us to switch to a more proactive approach. We need to monitor the processes taking place in the atmosphere and river basins in real time, predict what will happen in the next stage in advance, and take necessary preventive measures by identifying possible threats in advance," said Mammadov.

He pointed out that climate change is increasing both the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world.

"Longer droughts, more severe flood and flood events, and intensive precipitation have serious impacts on various sectors of the economy, including agriculture, urban infrastructure, and the well-being of the population," emphasized the first deputy chairman of the agency.

According to Mammadov, Azerbaijan is also a country sensitive to climate change in terms of the water sector, and the implementation of adaptation measures is of particular relevance.

He said that Azerbaijan is highly dependent on transboundary rivers. Fluctuations in the level of the Caspian Sea, the reduction of the region's snow reserves, the shrinking area and volume of glaciers, and changes in precipitation regimes create additional pressure on the formation of water resources.

The official also said that currently, 84 hydrological stations operate across the country to assess water flows in rivers.

"40 of them use automated measuring devices, and 44 use traditional gauges," he noted.

Mammadov further noted that one of the main goals within the framework of the "National strategy for ensuring the efficient use of water resources" is to expand and modernize the observation network, form a more flexible, accurate and operational database.

According to him, these steps can allow for the prediction of water consumption and water levels in rivers, earlier identification of flood and drought risks, detection of risky areas, and preliminary assessment of possible impact zones.

"In the next stage, analysis with the support of artificial intelligence, taking into account historical hydrological data, meteorological observations, satellite data, GIS maps and climate scenarios, may allow for the identification of climate risks at an early stage," added Mammadov.

Mammadov noted that a number of strategic steps are being taken in Azerbaijan to manage the emerging flood waters.

According to him, the "State program on the improvement of water supply, rainwater and wastewater systems in Baku city and the Absheron peninsula for 2026-2035" was adopted at the initiative of President Ilham Aliyev.

The program envisages the construction of 12 new sewage collectors with a total length of 346 kilometers and the repair and rehabilitation of existing infrastructure, as well as the separation of rainwater and wastewater systems from each other.

He noted that the construction and reconstruction works carried out at the Sugovushan, Khachinchay, Zabukhchay and Kondalanchay reservoir complexes located in the Karabakh and East Zangezur economic regions, as well as the construction of the Yengija reservoir in the Gabala district, Alijanchay reservoir in the Oghuz and Shaki districts, will be of great importance in the fight against floods, in addition to improving water supply.

Mammadov noted that work on the construction of the Aghsuchay, Zayamchay, Hakarichay and Bargushadchay reservoirs is also ongoing.

He stressed that the water resources of the rivers of the East Zangezur and Karabakh economic regions, which amount to 2.35 million cubic meters, constitute 24% of the country's internal water resources.

"Their use is of great importance in solving the problem of water shortage in the country and combating floods," the official said.

He added that President Ilham Aliyev's decree No. 1016 dated April 28, 2026, instructed to ensure the continuity of the work done to combat the dangerous and harmful effects of floods and landslides and to implement appropriate measures to prevent similar situations from recurring in the future.

The First Deputy Chairman of ADSEA noted that the application of artificial intelligence systems requires a large amount of high-quality information, computing capabilities, technical expertise and financial resources.

He said that in this regard, international cooperation should be aimed not only at technology transfer, but also at the development of national potential and human resources.

"Strong regional cooperation is especially important between countries that share river basins and climate-related risks. Because the establishment of an early warning system within one country alone cannot fully provide the expected effect," Kh. Mammadov emphasized.

According to him, dangerous hydrometeorological events are the result of broad regional atmospheric and hydrological processes and are not limited to state borders.

Mammadov added that joint cooperation and coordinated information exchange can have a positive impact on forecasting river flows, identifying periods of water scarcity, optimizing reservoir management, and assessing the impacts of climate change on water resources.

"The combination of all these factors can allow us to predict climate events earlier, manage water resources more effectively, protect communities, and strengthen climate resilience," he added.

World.title: Kazakhstan PM orders launch of National Profession Transformation Center by year-end
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Kazakhstan’s Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov has instructed the Ministries of Science and Higher Education and Labor and Social Protection of the Population to ensure the full launch of the National Profession Transformation Center by the end of 2026, the government press service said.

He made the instructions during the government meeting.

The center is to be established jointly with leading companies under a public-private partnership model, according to the government’s press service.

Bektenov also instructed the government to take measures to increase the attractiveness of colleges and ensure that vocational education programs are aligned with labor market needs.

“Training programs need to be constantly modernized based on demand from the labor market and the population. Short-term modular programs should be opened to provide in-demand micro-qualifications. A college should become a place that people consciously choose in order to acquire professional knowledge and skills,” Bektenov said.

The Prime Minister also drew attention to the condition of technical and vocational education infrastructure. More than 70% of existing technical and vocational education institutions were built more than 40 years ago.

“Within this task, the Head of State has approved approaches to the construction and comprehensive modernization of colleges,” Bektenov said.

The Ministry of Education, together with relevant government bodies and regional akimats, was instructed to submit to the government by November 1 a Program for the Development of Modern Technical and Vocational Education Infrastructure for 2027-2030.

Bektenov also ordered the creation of sectoral training and independent personnel certification clusters in each region, taking into account the needs of priority sectors of the economy.

“To more effectively train personnel for the specific needs of regions and new high-tech industries, it is necessary to determine the exact number of jobs in order to form the state order for colleges,” he said.

The Ministries of Labor, Education, and Science and Higher Education, together with regional akimats, were instructed to establish a system for annually forecasting the types and number of jobs at production facilities.

The forecasts are to be regularly updated and posted on the Enbek.kz information system, ensuring a direct link between personnel training and the actual needs of the economy. Overall coordination of the work has been assigned to First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlybek Naliyev.

World.title: Azerbaijan weighs digital FIATA Bill of Lading rollout
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Azerbaijan is studying the possibility of introducing the FIATA Bill of Lading (FBL), a multimodal transport document, in digital form, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Kamran Habibov, chairman of the Freight Forwarders Association of Azerbaijan (FFAA), said this at the 5th International Forum on Freight Transportation in the Black and Caspian Regions — 2026, being held in Baku.

According to him, the FIATA Bill of Lading is a multimodal document that allows cargo to be transported under a single document regardless of the number of changes in modes of transport.

“At present, our association and the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport of Azerbaijan are holding consultations and studying the issue of introducing this document in the country,” he said.

Habibov noted that introducing the document only in Azerbaijan would not be sufficient.

“Once we launch this process in our country, we will likely initiate its introduction in other countries as well, demonstrate the advantages of this document and bring corridor participants that are not yet involved into the process,” he added.

According to him, documents are gradually being converted into electronic formats, and FIATA is also working on digitizing the FBL.

“Work in this direction is ongoing. Perhaps we will be able to present the first results by the end of the year,” Habibov said.

World.title: Azerbaijan chairs UNEP Permanent Representatives Committee's meeting in Nairobi (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. The 13th annual subcommittee meeting of the Committee of Permanent Representatives of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) began its work in Nairobi under Azerbaijan's chairmanship on September 7.

The Permanent Mission of Azerbaijan to the UN in Nairobi reported that this meeting, held once a year, is the main intersessional meeting of the UN Environment Assembly (UNEA). The 5-day meeting, which will be attended by more than 150 member states and civil society organizations, will discuss the general agenda of UNEP activities, the implementation of the strategic plan for 2026-2029, as well as the results of multilateral activities on environmental protection and climate change, and future plans.

Permanent Representative of Azerbaijan to the UN Office in Nairobi, Sultan Hajiyev, has been the Chairman of the Bureau of the UNEP Committee of Permanent Representatives for 2025-2027 since June last year.

During the meeting, it was noted that within the framework of this chairmanship, Azerbaijan is contributing to related processes together with the current President of UNEA, Jamaican Minister for Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda.

The meeting emphasized the role of Azerbaijan in the global climate agenda within the framework of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Climate Week and COP29 Baku Climate Action Week 2026, currently being held in Baku. The contributions of the UNEP World Environment Day hosted by Azerbaijan in May of this year and the 3rd Shamakhi Meeting of the Chairs of the UNFCCC negotiating groups held in July were also noted. On the first day of the event, Azerbaijan and Jamaica organized a joint official reception for participants of the 13th annual subcommittee meeting.

World.title: Azerbaijan to develop roadmap for reducing methane emissions in agriculture - CCAC
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Azerbaijan is set to develop a national roadmap aimed at reducing methane emissions in the agricultural sector, the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) and UN Environment Programme (UNEP) representative Amina Akhmetzhanova said, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

She made the remarks on the second day of Baku Climate Action Week 2026 (BCAW 2026).

She said that CCAC supports countries in addressing short-lived climate pollutants, including methane, black carbon, hydrofluorocarbons and tropospheric ozone. “Methane is particularly important because it is a powerful but relatively short-lived climate pollutant. This means that reducing methane emissions can help slow the pace of global warming within a relatively short period of time,” Akhmetzhanova said.

She noted that discussions on reducing methane emissions in agriculture should focus not only on emissions cuts, but also on the benefits these measures can bring to farmers and production efficiency. “Reducing methane emissions can support farmers, increase productivity, improve the efficiency of agricultural resource use and create investment opportunities,” she said.

According to Akhmetzhanova, improving the quality and optimization of animal feed can help livestock use feed more efficiently, increase milk and meat production, while reducing methane emissions.

She added that improving animal health, breeding practices and herd management can also contribute to higher productivity and more efficient use of resources. “Better manure management can reduce methane emissions while also creating additional value. In some agricultural systems, manure can be used as a source of biogas and energy. Therefore, it should not be viewed only as waste,” Akhmetzhanova said.

She noted that Azerbaijan already has an important foundation for advancing this work. Azerbaijan became a government partner of CCAC in 2024 and has also joined the Global Methane Pledge. “As a participant in the Global Methane Pledge, Azerbaijan contributes to the collective goal of countries to reduce methane emissions by 30% by 2030 compared with 2020 levels,” she said.

Akhmetzhanova added that the modernization of Azerbaijan’s agricultural development program provides an important opportunity to link climate action with the modernization of the livestock sector, increased productivity and improved resilience. “Within this framework, we are pleased to announce cooperation between the Ministry of Agriculture and CCAC. We have launched a project to develop a National Roadmap for reducing methane emissions in agriculture, with a focus on the livestock sector,” she said.

According to her, the main objective of the roadmap is to develop a practical action plan aligned with Azerbaijan’s national circumstances and priorities.

Akhmetzhanova said the roadmap will first identify the main sources of emissions. The assessment will examine methane emissions in Azerbaijan’s livestock sector, production systems, animal digestion processes and manure management practices. “The second key question is which solutions are most suitable for Azerbaijan’s livestock sector. The roadmap will assess priority measures tailored to the country’s agricultural sector, including improved feeding practices, animal health development and manure management,” she added.

World.title: Breaking: Child dead, six others injured in crash west of Melbourne
World.content:
A school aged child has died and six others have been taken to hospital with injuries after a single vehicle crash in Parwan, west of Melbourne, this afternoon.

Emergency services received reports of a crash near the Nerowie and Parwan-Exford road intersections just before 4pm.

Victorian Police said one child died at the scene while six others were injured.

"Despite CPR being performed, one school-aged child died at the scene," a spokesperson said.

"A second child was airlifted with critical injuries. Five more children were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

"One woman was taken to hospital for observation."

Ambulance Victoria said its specialist crews were responding to the incident.

"Two specialist Air Ambulance Victoria helicopter crews, two Mobile Intensive Care Ambulance paramedic crews and five Advanced Life Support paramedic crews are currently on scene," a spokesperson said.

"Their priority is with their patients."

An investigation into the crash is ongoing.

World.title: Smokers should face tougher penalties over illicit tobacco, police chief suggests
World.content:
South Australia's police commissioner has again raised the possibility of tougher illicit tobacco laws that would crack down on those who purchase — rather than just those who sell or traffic — the black market product.

Speaking to 891 ABC Adelaide this morning, Grant Stevens said the matter of penalising people caught buying illegal cigarettes was one that "needs to be considered".

"There is an opportunity for people to avoid significant costs by purchasing illicit tobacco, and I think that there are questions that need to be asked about how we can kill off the market," the commissioner said.

"Why are there no sanctions for people who are, essentially, creating the market for organised crime?

"It's illegal to sell it [illegal tobacco], it's illegal to import it — it's not illegal to buy it and use it."

Has tobacco tax gone too far? The Liberals and One Nation have a simple solution to end Australia's tobacco black market. But Labor says there's no easy fix.

Tobacco laws are enforced jointly by federal, state and territory authorities.

The commissioner, who issued a similar call two years ago, said while the problem was not "not anywhere near as bad" as what it had become in the eastern states, it had nevertheless led to significant criminal activity in SA.

"We certainly have a problem with illicit tobacco distributors being the target of criminal offending, including arsons; we've had some drive-by shootings, we've had assaults," he said.

"This is because there is this illicit market that has crept into South Australia.

"We have a dedicated taskforce that are investigating the criminal offending associated with the illicit tobacco market, and this illicit market that is being exploited by organised crime exists because the market has been able to flourish."

His comments coincide with the seizure of more than one million illegal cigarettes and vapes in a series of raids throughout Western Australia and the Northern Territory, as well as national debate about ways to curb the illegal trade.

The federal opposition last week announced that a future Coalition government would take steps including slashing the tobacco excise by 80 per cent and legalising and taxing vapes and nicotine pouches.

Last month, One Nation unveiled a plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent.

But Labor has argued there is no evidence a dramatic cut would end the illicit trade and said slashing the excise would "kill people".

"If we drop the excise, in the way that is being suggested by the Coalition, that's a guarantee we will see smoking and vaping rates in this country increase. That will lead to deaths," Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said earlier this month.

The SA government has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Hundreds face homelessness within weeks amid government funding stand-off
World.content:
Darwin's largest homeless shelter is on track to close within weeks despite an offer from the Commonwealth to split the cost of buying the facility to keep it open.

The imminent closure of the YiSSA centre has left more than 230 residents living there fearing the prospect of homelessness as early as next month.

They include 85 children, people undergoing renal dialysis and facing serious health problems, and families escaping domestic violence.

The facility's closure would also mean more than 300 people currently on a waitlist to live there would be left with nowhere to live.

What's happened so far?

Two months ago, the Northern Territory government announced YiSSA would close in October after its offer of $3 million for the buildings was rejected by the owner Ausco Modular, which is seeking $6.5 million.

Robyn Cahill first announced the closure of YiiSSA in July. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

In August, Federal Senator Malarndirri McCarthy wrote to NT Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill offering to split the cost of purchasing YiSSA between the NT and federal governments to keep it open.

"I am prepared to consider a Commonwealth contribution of up to $3.5 million," she wrote.

However, negotiations appeared to reach a stalemate last week, with Ms Cahill criticising the terms of the federal government's proposal, and arguing the facility was ageing and not fit-for-purpose beyond another two to three years.

Hundreds face homelessness as accommodation set to close Hundreds of residents fear they could be left homeless after the Northern Territory government announced it will shut a Darwin short-stay accommodation centre in less than 90 days.

The conditions of the Commonwealth offer include allowing Yilli Rreung Housing Aboriginal Corporation to continue running YiSSA for at least another five years, taking on operational costs and remediating the site when it eventually closes.

Yesterday, Senator McCarthy criticised the NT government on social media over its refusal to negotiate, saying YiSSA residents "deserve answers".

She also questioned why the Territory government had not yet announced a transition plan or explained how it would meet the need for short-stay accommodation once YiSSA closed.

The ABC has contacted the NT government about whether it is continuing to negotiate a deal, but has not received a response.

The Territory government has repeatedly promised to find accommodation for all those living in the facility, but today many residents said they were fearing the worst and voiced concerns about being kept in the dark about where they would be going.

Rose Laynba says residents are worried about where they will end up. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

"We are worried. We are sad. We are thinking, 'What's our next movement? Where will we go?'" long-term YiSSA resident Rose Laynba said.

She said she was angered by the governments "arguing over money".

"Instead of arguing, just throw it in and pay for it, stop making excuses," she said.

"First Nation people here are struggling and they're arguing who's going to pay, who's going to buy it — it's just plain stupid.

"We are becoming refugees, refugees in our own backyard."

Ausco has confirmed it is seeking $6.5 million for the infrastructure. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

For fellow resident Christine Martin, YiSSA has been a lifeline, after she spent more than six months staying in hotels, unable to find a home in Darwin.

While she has been told she is on a list for a house, she said the lack of information had left her feeling uncertain.

"They're telling us not to worry, but it's like telling water not to be wet," she said.

"Maybe this place will close before I even get a place.

"There's a lot of people here that have nowhere to go … and they're going to have to be on the streets, because if they can't return [to their community] there's no other place."

She said with just a few weeks left until closure, people were increasingly feeling desperate.

"Most of the people I talk to, they're like, 'Where are you going?'" she said.

"We all don't know what's going on."

Grandmother Francis Gaykamangu said she was one of the lucky residents who had been offered a priority house to live in, but she said she was sad to be leaving her home.

Francis Gaykamangu and her granddaughter Shana are among the lucky residents who have somewhere to go. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

Aboriginal services call on NT government to negotiate

A group of NT Aboriginal service providers, including the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency and Danila Dilba Health Service, are calling on the Territory government to prevent YiSSA from closing and to negotiate with the Commonwealth.

Residents at homeless shelter plead for help to save their homes Hundreds of residents living at Darwin's largest homeless shelter have been told they need to be out by October.

The NT already has the highest rate of homelessness in the country — more than 12 times the national average — but the organisations say the closure of YiSSA would risk even more people sleeping rough in parks, shopping precincts and on beaches.

Danila Dilba Health Service chief executive Rob McPhee said the closure would also put a strain on emergency departments and other frontline support agencies.

"If YiSSA closes, our teams will spend far more time trying to locate clients across multiple locations, making it harder to provide consistent care and increasing the likelihood that people will end up presenting to emergency departments," he said.

"This will place even greater pressure on hospitals and emergency services that are already operating under significant strain."

The service providers also said allowing YiSSA to close would contradict the NT government's own homelessness strategy, which aims to prevent homelessness and deliver culturally safe services.

The NT government has previously said YiSSA will close on October 11.

World.title: Inquest to begin into Russell Island house fire that killed father and five boys
World.content:
An inquest is set to probe whether domestic violence had anything to do with a house fire that killed a man and his five sons in south-east Queensland, after triple-zero callers claimed the boys' parents fought often and that they believed "one day they would kill these kids".

In August 2023, 34-year-old Wayne Godinet Jr, 11-year-old Zackary, 10-year-old Harrison, four-year-old twins Kyza and Koah and three-year-old Nickolas died of smoke inhalation inside their Russell Island home after it caught alight in the early morning.

The children's mother Samantha Stephenson and her sister managed to escape the blaze unharmed.

All six deaths will be the subject of a coronial inquiry which has been set down for November in Brisbane.

The charred remains of the home on Russell Island. (ABC News: George Roberts)

On Tuesday, counsel assisting the coroner Corinne Leach told a preliminary hearing Ms Stephenson lived at the home with the boys and her sister at the time, and Mr Godinet Jr would stay with them occasionally.

"As he worked on the mainland during the week and he and Samantha's relationship was on and off," she said.

'Real heartbreak is outliving children': Loved ones gather to mourn loss of five boys, father on Russell Island Five boys and their father were killed in the blaze, the state's worst house fire tragedy since 2011.

The court heard Ms Stephenson had told investigators her and Mr Godinet Jr had both been underneath the house in a makeshift entertainment area the night before the fire broke out.

Ms Stephenson told investigators she recalled the pair smoked cigarettes and fell asleep cuddling on the couch, before she woke up some hours later and saw black smoke everywhere.

She recalled watching Mr Godinet Jr run up an internal staircase, which was partially on fire, and then seeing flames near a generator and a work bench downstairs where she was.

Ms Stephenson said she then ran outside and saw the external stairs were also on fire, and then heard her sister and Mr Godinet Jr screaming from inside the upper level.

She also told investigators she later saw her sister on the verandah and she told her to jump, which she did, and she expected Mr Godinet Jr and the children to follow, but they did not emerge.

Triple Zero callers make DV claims

The court heard 20 calls were made to the Queensland Fire Department (QFD), with some people reporting they had heard frequent fighting and screaming coming from the home in the past.

One person reported hearing arguing from about 5am that morning before the fire started, while another claimed "there was domestic violence in there all the time".

Another caller told operators, "we knew that one day they would kill these kids, but nobody has done anything" and "the house is f***ing horrid I've called the police a number of times."

Ms Leach told the court these people would be called to give evidence.

"Whether the domestic and family violence reported contributed to the fire that caused the deaths is an issue that will be explored at inquest," she said.

A preliminary hearing heard Ms Stephenson lived at the home with the boys and her sister, and Mr Godinet Junior would stay with them occasionally. (Supplied)

The court heard a fire investigation report was completed by QFD which found it was probable the blaze had developed in the ground floor area.

However, the court heard the exact point of origin was unable to be determined and human initiated ignition could not be categorically ruled out.

Whether the source of the fire was an electrical issue was also unable to be eliminated due to the extensive damage to the property. This will be another issue for the coroner.

The court heard the house, which was a raised Queenslander, had been relocated to Russell Island in 2012, and was renovated the following year.

Underneath the home was not built in, and the court heard it had been converted by Ms Stephenson and Mr Godinet Jr recently as a place to watch television.

The court heard the pair used blankets to cordon it off, and to power the area they used a five-point power board, which was plugged into an extension cord leading from a room upstairs.

Ms Leach told the court the power points in the house were described as "bad, hanging out, and with exposed wires".

"The power point from which the extension lead was plugged was known to short out and did not sit properly in the wall," she said.

A 61-year-old woman was fined for failing to have compliant smoke alarms installed. (ABC News)

The lack of compliant smoke alarms installed in the home will also form part of the inquest.

In the months after the blaze, the homeowner pleaded guilty to breaching the Fire Services Act and was fined but no conviction was recorded.

The emergency response will also be considered at the inquest, including whether Russell Island has sufficient resources to deal with house fires.

Sixteen witnesses including fire experts, police, and Ms Stephenson are expected to be called to testify at a 10-day hearing.

World.title: Crook elbows and big dreams propelling unheralded Knights for NRL finals
World.content:
Newcastle forward Francis Manuleleua might be less than two weeks off dislocating his right elbow but at the end of an interview he'll still shake your hand and shake it hard.

"Nah, let's go for it G," Manuleleua said when offered the chance to forgo a handshake, just in case.

"It's gotta be strong."

The 22-year-old's right arm bent in a way that right arms are not supposed to bend in the Knights loss to the Warriors a fortnight back.

Manuleleua suffered a dislocated elbow against New Zealand two weeks ago. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

It looked gruesome — Manuleleua was straight on the green whistle and phrases like "bony deformity" were used in analysis of the video.

But with Newcastle already without key men Dylan Lucas, Trey Mooney and Jacob Saifiti due to injury and suspension ahead of Friday's sudden-death semifinal against South Sydney and after being cleared of a fracture, Manuleleua will push to play.

He was named on Tuesday for what would be his NRL finals debut and is one of an unheralded mix of youngsters and journeymen in the Knights forwards who will be tasked with taking down the Rabbitohs.

In terms of star power it's a no-contest. Every player in the South Sydney starting pack has played either Test or Origin football except for Tallis Duncan, who might not have to wait long to join them.

Duncan pushing for maiden World Cup berth Australia are facing a shortage of backrowers for this year's Rugby League World Cup but South Sydney tyro Tallis Duncan could prove to be the answer.

Manuleleua has a mere 11 NRL matches to his credit and fellow second rower Jermaine McEwen is wrapping up his first full season as an every week player.

The baby of the side is starting prop Cody Hopwood, still just 20, although at 196cm and 105kgs that's a damn big baby.

He's great mates with eight-gamer Lachlan Crouch, who received his first Knights cap from Paul Harragon himself upon his NRL debut earlier this year.

Both the rookies played their juniors in Maitland, as did the more seasoned Thomas Cant and Pasami Saulo who both fit the image of the honest toiler.

Cant has played almost 40 NRL matches since his debut in 2023 and is yet to score a try but that pales compared to Saulo — he's about to finish his ninth season in the league without a single four-pointer to show for it.

Injuries have ripped through the Knights pack in recent weeks. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Newcastle will lean heavily on the experience of 300-gamer Tyson Frizell and the underrated Matt Croker at lock as they match it with a South Sydney pack that is both fully loaded and battle-hardened.

Cameron Murray, Junior Tatola, David Fifita and Keaon Koloamatangi all have 150 NRL games or more to their credit and all but Fifita have been through multiple finals campaigns.

Even Duncan, by far their least experienced starting forward, has made more first grade appearances than Manuleleua, Crouch, Hopwood and McEwen combined.

Given he's marking up on the reborn Fifita, Manuleleua might be facing the biggest task of all and certainly the hardest test of an NRL career that began just a few months ago. He can't wait for it.

"He's a big, powerful boy and there's a job to do. But I'm keen for the challenge," said Manuleleua.

"They've got a lot of strengths on their edge with Fifita, Latrell Mitchell and Jack Wighton and a great ball-player in Cody Walker, so it's a good challenge for us edges.

"But that's the kind of footy we want to play anyway. We want to go after that challenge, go after them and see what happens."

Despite making his NRL debut in Round 3, a steady start is leading to a big finish for Manuleleua.

It wasn't until Round 20 that he became a regular starter following Lucas going down with an ankle injury.

But with six line breaks, two tries, five try assists and 23 tackle busts in the six games since, Manuleleua has proven to be one of the finds of the season.

He's a big, explosive man who can do big, explosive things and has it in him to be a wrecking machine but he's also fresh enough that so much of this is still new.

The match against the Warriors, for example, was the first time the Papatoetoe junior got to play back in New Zealand and over 25 family members and countless friends packed out the stands to see him.

Manuleleua scored a try on his return to New Zealand last week. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

"It's pretty surreal. I still can't believe it. I didn't think I'd be playing finals footy this early in my career," said Manuleleua.

"It was gun, that game against the Warriors. They (my family) were loud as hell, Warriors had 25,000 fans but I could still hear my family and it was the first time I played an NRL game in front of them at home.

"It was bittersweet because we couldn't win the game but they were just happy I scored a try."

Manuleleua's clash with Fifita might be the most difficult job but it's not the biggest — that belongs to Hopwood, who will start at prop.

He did the same in the club's most recent clash with South Sydney in Round 19, when Hopwood and Crouch got in the mix with the Rabbitohs amid a torrid physical battle.

The two Maitland boys are popular members of the Knights squad given they have a special brand of front-row charm, as Manuleleua explains.

"They're intentionally funny. They'll do something weird but it'll be funny," said Manuleleua.

"When it comes to the game they look like monsters but they're kind at heart, they're good people."

Hopwood doesn't have time to think about what Manuleleua is talking about given he's about to play the biggest game of his life.

Hopwood will start in the front row for an NRL final at just 20 years of age. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

"I have no idea what that means. I don't think I want to know either," said Hopwood.

"Whenever you're out and about people are wishing you luck for Friday night, the town's flying and we're all excited.

"I'm really confident, I'm in a good spot mentally and physically. Attack it front on, that's probably the best way to go. Just go hard and try to go for longer."

Hopwood was a highly rated junior, representing New South Wales Under 19s twice, but despite making his NRL debut in the final round of last season he never thought he'd play as much first grade in 2026 as he has.

"Not at all, but I've had some really good people around me that have helped with the transition," said Hopwood.

"I thought I might only play two or three games this year, so it's all come pretty quick.

"I'm feeling really supported and I don't want to let anyone down, I want to repay that faith."

Hopwood did not expect to play more than one or two NRL games this year. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar )

Hopwood's done a fine job with it so far, starting seven of his 14 games this season, and seems the type who never learned to take a backward step.

Whether that will be enough against players like Koloamatangi and Murray remains to be seen but Hopwood isn't thinking about the odds stacked against him or his side.

Like any good Novocastrian, he has dreamed of making a difference for the Knights his whole life and was there as a 17-year old in the crowd for their last finals win three years ago.

Dom Young roaring down the sideline for a length-of-the-field try is a memory that will never leave him and now all he wants is to give Knights fans another moment that lasts forever.

"I remember thinking how much I'd love to be a part of something like that and I get to live it on Friday night," said Hopwood.

"How good is that?"

World.title: Gigantic mechanical 'esky lid' is Brisbane's newest defence against flooding
World.content:
Engineers have completed an 80-tonne mechanical contraption named "The Esky Lid" designed to protect Brisbane's new underground tunnels from flooding.

The Esky Lid was unveiled today at Albert Street Station, which will be part of Brisbane's Cross River Rail underground train network.

Loading...

The 22-metre by 10-metre barrier will be able to descend from the ceiling over the station's main entrance, sealing it shut from floodwaters.

Sliding panels allow the barrier's modules to click into place, blending in with the station ceiling when not in use.

During intense flooding, shutters will also close off the entrance to the northern side of Albert Street Station.

Albert Street Station will be the most important line of defence, since it will be the deepest point of the 10-kilometre Cross River Rail network.

The station itself is in a low-lying, flood-prone area of Brisbane's CBD.

The lid will keep the station flood-proof up to about 10.3 metres above street level, which is rated as a 1-in-10,000-year probability.

Cross River Rail Delivery Authority program director Jeremy Kruger said they called it The Esky Lid because it could close like the lid of an esky.

Jeremy Kruger says it is unlikely that the company Esky will try to sue them over the name. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Mr Kruger said passengers would be evacuated before the esky lid came down in the event of an extreme flood.

However, Mr Kruger said there was a good chance that people alive today would never see this "ingenious" feat of engineering in action.

"This will be a nice, open amenity 99.999 per cent of the time," Mr Kruger said.

"For that 0.001 per cent flood, it can come down, seal, deploy, and protect the station."

A history of blowouts

Mr Kruger said construction work would finish in early 2027, with safety tests to follow afterwards.

However, he said passenger services were not due to begin until 2029.

Cross River Rail was originally due to open in 2024 at a budget of $5.4 billion, but the project has suffered repeated blowouts over the years.

Mr Kruger said the project was now expected to cost around $19 billion, almost four times the original estimate.

It will be Queensland's single largest and most expensive infrastructure project in history.

World.title: Australia records worst-ever maths and reading scores in global test
World.content:
Australian high school students' scores in maths and reading have hit their lowest point on record, according to a major international test.

While the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) exams showed a slight improvement in science results since the last test in 2022, Australia's long-term learning decline continued overall.

The 2025 test results released today showed Australia continued to perform above the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average, with Australian students ranking 10th in science and reading, and 16th in mathematics among the 91 countries and economies that sat the test.

"What the data shows us is that we see long-term declines in reading and in mathematics. We were able to stabilise our scores in science," Jonas Berling from the Australian Council for Educational Research (ACER), which administers the test, said.

According to the OECD, 20 points on a test score is roughly equivalent to one year of learning for the average student.

Those declines mean science students today are almost one year of learning behind students who sat the exam in 2006.

In reading, students last year were roughly two years behind where they were in 2000. In mathematics, they were a little over two years behind the 2003 results.

"What PISA shows is that we see a decline in especially reading and mathematics where we haven't caught up with the levels from 10 or 20 years ago, when Pisa started," Mr Berling said.

"While we see some declines in the long run, we're still a very strong country," Mr Berling said.

Jonas Bertling says Australia is still performing well overall in the PISA testing. (ABC News: Scott Jewell)

Blaise Joseph from the Centre for Independent Studies think tank said the long-term picture was "troubling".

"We also have fewer high performers and more low performers across all three subjects," Mr Joseph said.

Australian students reported improved discipline in classrooms compared to earlier findings, but remained among the lowest countries in the world on that measure, ranking 69th out of 80.

The disciplinary climate is measured by surveying science students, and 21 per cent reported they could not work well in most or all lessons compared to the OECD average of 19 per cent.

Forty-one per cent of Australian students reported there was noise and disorder in their classrooms compared to the OECD average of 31 per cent, echoing a report released last week that found one-third of lesson time was being lost to misbehaviour.

"Disruption remains a challenge in our Australian classrooms," Mr Burling said.

"I think it's important that we see disruption in the larger context of the Australian system and see what resources are needed in the classroom to improve on this."

Mr Joseph blamed the high rates of misbehaviour for Australia's lack of learning growth.

"Students cannot learn effectively when classrooms are regularly disrupted. Schools need clear expectations, explicitly taught routines and consistent approaches to behaviour so teachers can teach and students can learn," he said.

Fifteen-year-olds in Australia have sat the PISA exams every three years since 2000. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Australian students also skipped school at almost twice the OECD average, with 44 per cent of students reporting skipping a day of school in the two weeks before testing compared to the OECD average of 24 per cent.

Federal Education Minister Jason Clare said the results showed the importance of reforms the government introduced to classroom teaching practice and increased public school funding.

He said the United Kingdom introduced similar reforms 20 years ago, and in this year's PISA testing, rose three places in reading, four places in maths and seven places in science.

"This shows why the reforms we are rolling out are so important. The UK results are impressive. It's also hard-earned. It's something almost 20 years in the making," Mr Clare said.

"In Australian schools that have been doing this for a while, we can see the same thing that has happened in the UK. But we have to keep going and roll it out everywhere."

Mr Clare said too much screen time might be a problem in Australian schools.

"This doesn't mean there is no place for tech in schools. Students need to learn digital skills. That includes how to use, and how not to use AI," Mr Clare said.

" But it does point to the need to wind back the amount of screen time in schools. "

Australian students perform strongest in new domain

One big positive from the latest results was Australia's performance in the "learning in the digital world" category, designed to measure a student's ability to learn in technology-rich environments.

Australian students achieved a mean score of 532 points compared to the OECD average of 500 points, with 75 per cent of Australian students reaching the national proficient standard.

James Casey, a Year 10 student at Gymea Technology High School, a public school in Sydney's outer south, took the test last year.

James Casey took the new "learning in the digital world" test last year. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

"This was more simply a test of just pure logic and reason and ability to think," James said.

School principal Katherine Edwards said the learning in the digital world results would help equip students for the jobs of the future.

Katherine Edwards says STEM skills are becoming increasingly important to have. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

She said the school had a strong focus on science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM).

"It's an area that our students, as they're moving into the workforce, need more and more, and the jobs that they're moving into are relying on those STEM skills and are increasingly needing them," Ms Edwards said.

World.title: Court bolter tackled by police wanted to kiss partner goodbye
World.content:
A man who escaped police custody wanted to kiss his partner goodbye, a court in Burnie has heard.

Stephen Keith Edwards, 29, appeared in the Burnie Magistrates Court via video link on Tuesday for sentencing after pleading guilty to one count of escape, two counts of assaulting police and several other charges.

Edwards also pleaded guilty and was sentenced for several unrelated offences, including stealing, burglary, common assault, resisting police, breaching bail conditions, and possessing drug paraphernalia.

Magistrate Jackie Hartnett said body cam footage played to the court was evidence of a "significant struggle", and that Edwards did not stop resisting police.

Ms Hartnett said instances of escape were always taken seriously, and that she viewed the assault of police officers as "particularly serious".

"Fortunately, they did not have any long-lasting physical injuries," Ms Hartnett said.

Defence lawyer Lizzie Arnold told the court Edwards wanted to say goodbye to his partner and "panicked".

Following the sentencing hearing on Monday, Edwards was remanded in custody and again asked the court if he could say goodbye to his partner, who was outside the courtroom at the time, and give her and their baby a hug.

His request was again denied, and Edwards led himself to the dock and was taken into custody.

'Quit being stupid', police tell escapee

The court heard Edwards was taken into police custody on December 6, and taken to the Burnie courthouse for an after-hours session.

After he was remanded in custody, the court heard Edwards wanted to kiss his partner goodbye but was denied, which Magistrate Hartnett described as "entirely appropriate".

Edwards then pushed open the door to the dock, ran past two police officers in the courtroom, and ran towards the exit.

CCTV footage played in court showed Edwards exit the courtroom and run through the courthouse foyer towards the front entrance as the police officers chased after him.

Prosecutor Sam Reid said Edwards damaged a sliding glass door at the courthouse entrance as he was attempting to leave the building and was caught by police.

In body cam footage played to the court, police officers and court security guards could be seen struggling with Edwards, who thrashed around for several minutes as police attempted to restrain and handcuff him.

The prosecution told the court Edwards struck both police officers in the face during the altercation, and a court security guard was pushed.

Ms Arnold told the court the escape was "short-lived" and that Edwards was "embarrassed by his actions".

"He was in a very poor headspace, and essentially he panicked," she said.

A second body cam video from outside the courthouse showed Edwards continuing to resist police as they attempted to put him in a police van.

Throughout the footage played to the court, police could be heard yelling at Edwards and telling him to stop resisting.

"Stephen, what are you doing? You're going in either way, mate, just give up," one of the officers said.

" Quit being stupid and get in the van. "

'I love you darl, so sorry', escapee tells partner

After a prolonged struggle, police administered pepper spray and eventually shut the van door with Edwards inside.

In addition to the escape incident on December 6, 2025, Magistrate Hartnett also sentenced Edwards for a range of offences including stealing, burglary, common assault, resisting police, breaching bail conditions, and possessing drug paraphernalia.

Edwards was sentenced to 14 months' imprisonment, backdated to November 7, 2025, accounting for time already served.

After Magistrate Hartnett handed down the sentence, Edwards's partner yelled "I love you" from the courtroom, and Edwards replied over video link, saying: "I love you darl, so sorry."

World.title: Audit office to take a look after Labor accused of ‘sports rorts’ pork-barrelling
World.content:
The auditor-general will consider probing a $560 million Commonwealth grants program after revelations that almost three-quarters of taxpayer funding went to Labor-held electorates, putting the distribution of public money under fresh scrutiny. The Australian National Audit Office will also examine whether to audit a $170 million Albanese government program supporting multicultural communities, where about 85 per cent of funding went to government-held seats. A golf course in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate was a beneficiary of the grant. AP The decision comes after revelations about the distribution of grants sparked fresh scrutiny of Labor’s handling of Commonwealth funding and raised comparisons with the Morrison government’s controversial “sports rorts” scheme. Auditor-General Caralee McLiesh wrote to the Coalition on Tuesday confirming both programs would be included in an initial assessment before determining whether to proceed to a full audit.



The Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program was an invitation-only scheme established before the 2025 election to fund projects including upgrades to sporting facilities, parks, playgrounds and swimming pools. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ An analysis released by the Centre for Public Integrity found $409.1 million, or 73.2 per cent of the program’s funding, went to safe Labor seats and marginal electorates. Coalition-held seats received $126.3 million, or 22.6 per cent. The centre found the disparity was greater when the political competitiveness of electorates was taken into account. Labor-competitive marginal seats received $66.5 million more than a proportional distribution would have suggested, while seats where Labor was not competitive and safe or fairly safe non-Labor seats received $116.6 million less. Labor argues the grant programs are above board because they relate to election promises, not competitive grants.



Last month this masthead reported that the Coalition also accused the government of exploiting a $171 million multicultural fund to bankroll its own seats and entrench “ghettoisation” of migrant communities. The Supporting Multicultural Communities program flowed at about 85 per cent to Labor seats. The Centre for Public Integrity’s research strategy director, Professor Gabrielle Appleby, said the government had not adequately explained how those organisations were chosen, despite repeated questions in parliament. Professor Gabrielle Appleby, the research strategy director of the Centre for Public Integrity. “When questions were raised about who was invited and why, they were never sufficiently answered by the government,” she said. “Now analysis shows us where the money went, and the pattern raises serious questions that need to be answered.” The analysis found the funding was geographically concentrated, with Victoria alone receiving approximately $205.9 million.



Adjusted for electors, Tasmania received 9.1 per cent of funds despite holding only 2.3 per cent of electors, while Queensland received just 9.2 per cent despite holding 20.7 per cent of electors. NSW and Queensland collectively received $104.6 million less than would be expected under a proportional distribution. Opposition’s assistant infrastructure spokesman Ben Small said Labor ministers had “failed the standard they set in opposition”. “Now the question is whether they have breached their own Commonwealth grant standards in doing so,” he said. But Infrastructure Minister Catherine King said the program was consistent with longstanding government practice and Commonwealth grants rules.



She said ministers did not make funding decisions on applications in their own electorates, while successful projects were assessed against criteria including value for money, community amenity and economic benefits. “What we’ve done very carefully is make sure that there’s a process by which we test, is the election commitment value for money? Is it deliverable? ” she told the ABC. “Ministers don’t make decisions. I don’t sign off on election commitments in my own seat. We’ve got a pretty clear process, and it’s a closed program.” But the closed nature of the program has become a central point of attack with allegations of blatant pork-barrelling. Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen Independent MP Helen Haines, whose electorate of Indi was among 45 divisions not invited to participate, said community organisations had been denied the chance to compete for funding. She said the issue was highlighted by the contrasting treatment of golf clubs.



Marrickville Golf Club, in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler, received $6 million for upgrades, while the Rutherglen Golf Club in Indi was not given an opportunity to apply. Haines questioned why the Marrickville club was selected when sporting organisations across the country were seeking infrastructure funding. “This isn’t about whether these projects are worthwhile, it’s about whether every community gets a fair shot at funding for projects that matter locally,” she said. “Taxpayers shouldn’t have to wonder whether their local sporting club, community organisation or council misses out because their electorate wasn’t politically useful.” Marrickville Golf Course has received $6 million for upgrades from the federal government in a controversial “invite-only” grants program. Janie Barrett Naomi Beattie, the secretary of Rutherglen’s Barkly Park Precinct committee of management, said the town’s facilities were dilapidated and dangerous.



She said the town had lost its Australian rules women’s team because they had no change rooms while opposition netball teams had threatened not to play there because of the bad surface. “As someone who has voted Labor in the past it’s upsetting to hear we are not being considered when we really need some help,” she said. In 2020, the Australian National Audit Office found evidence of distribution bias in the scheme and that the then-sports minister, Bridget McKenzie, had departed from Sport Australia’s recommendations in some funding decisions. McKenzie ultimately resigned after failing to declare her honorary membership of a gun club that received a $36,000 grant. Senator Bridget McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman. Alex Ellinghausen



Labor spent years attacking the Coalition over sports rorts and demanding greater transparency in the distribution of taxpayer-funded grants. McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman, turned the comparison back on the Albanese government, arguing the current program was even more opaque because it was not subject to a competitive application process. She has questioned who selected the projects and whether adequate conflict-of-interest safeguards were applied, including in relation to the Marrickville grant. “Delivering on election promises is an important part of trust in a democracy. However, I think it is concerning that this is a closed program where there were no other invitees other than those who were selected by, it seems, the Labor Party,” she told the ABC.
