World.title: Graya’s co-founder on how to tackle the city’s housing crisis
World.content:
Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, Graya co-founder and managing director Rob Gray tells us how he thinks the city should tackle the housing crisis, what Brisbane 2032 will mean for construction prices, and the suburbs Graya has its eye on. We meet Gray at Teneriffe ferry stop, just a short walk from his head office. He’s immediately recognisable in a Graya branded T-shirt. As we cruise along the Brisbane River, we spot multiple Graya-branded signs at prime real estate spots in the city’s most affluent areas. Developer Rob Gray says as Graya grows, he feels more responsibility to the Brisbane community to do a good job. William Davis What’s your controversial Brisbane opinion? I think, personally, we have a little bit of a housing crisis at the moment. Houses are really expensive; rents are really expensive. What would really help would be going up and not out. Potentially lifting some height limits in the busy areas would really help everybody.



In a perfect world, if money wasn’t an object and you could do whatever you want, what would be your dream Brisbane project? This is going to sound corny, but I think the dream Brisbane projects I’m already doing. You know, from riverfront developments in Saint Lucia, to restaurants and retail developments in Racecourse Road and James Street, it’s things that I’ve always wanted to do. Maybe the next thing I really want to be part of is the Brisbane skyline. What inspired you to get into development? From a very young age, I always wanted to get into property development. I just really loved doing things with my hands. I loved creating something. I like the fulfillment, seeing something come out of the ground and be able to experience the hard work.



There are whole areas in Brisbane that Graya is really reshaping. Do you feel it’s a big responsibility, and how have you dealt with that? Related Article City council Dining lane to link huge new tower to James Street precinct I think as Graya has matured as a business, I am starting to feel more responsibility to the Brisbane community that we need to do a really good job. Especially now, because we’ve moved out of individual homes and now we’re doing what we like to call lifestyle developments. We like to bring in the retail and fashion and restaurants. It’s putting a huge responsibility on us to make our city great. You’ve had an enormous amount of success in quite a short period of time in what’s very famously a hugely cutthroat industry. What’s the secret behind your success and your rapid growth?



It might look like it’s quite quick from the outside in, but for us, it’s been quite slow. But we’ve been really determined from the outset to do a really good product, so we really focused on that for a long period of time. Related Article Perspective

City life What ‘the James Street effect’ says about our city And you look back over a decade and a half, and you really have done a lot of things. Graya’s got a really distinctive aesthetic and style. How did that come about? Is there a building in Brisbane you’re particularly proud of? I think we’re really fortunate in Brisbane, we’ve got such a good climate – it’s not too cold, it’s not too hot – so we can do this really subtropical architecture.



We really like to put greenery within our buildings, and something that I’m really, really proud of is a New Farm building called Mason. It’s on the corner of Moray Street, and it has this draping greenery. Every year it ages, it just gets better and better. Graya’s obviously got its detractors, and you’ve got under the skin of some other developers, among others. Why do you think that is, and how have you dealt with that? I think as we grow as a business, we’re moving into more prominent areas, and in those areas, there’s been a lot of long-standing owners that have, and like it, run a certain way. As we move into these areas, we just need to be really mindful of that previous history and try not to step on too many toes, and respect other people’s opinions and do the best job we can. Loading



Is there an upcoming project you’re particularly excited about? We have heaps of upcoming projects that I’m like crazy excited about. There’s one particularly, on James Street, that’s under construction right now called James Place, which is just a phenomenal development. What it will do to Brisbane and James Street is going to be next level, much like what the Calile did to James Street when it was first developed. Are there any suburbs that you’re moving into, or any suburbs that Graya’s really eyeing as future growth areas? Graya has really taken a shine to the Saint Lucia pocket. It’s something that we’ve always known about because we grew up in Indooroopilly and the Chapel Hill area. In the very early days, we spent a lot of time developing the New Farm, inner-city area, but we’ve really highlighted Saint Lucia as somewhere we want to do more and more apartments.



With your knowledge of development in Brisbane specifically, how do you see the years leading up to the Olympics and beyond playing out? How do you think Brisbane’s going to change in that time? Related Article City life The material this design influencer wants Brisbane to build its identity around I’m really excited for seeing what’s going to happen in Brisbane leading up to the Olympics. I think everyone can already see the value that’s been added with that. I think it’s probably one of the safest investments in the world right now. I think the construction market is going to get awfully busy. I feel like that will push up construction prices, which is probably not a good thing but it’s just always a temporary thing that everyone just needs to be mindful of. If someone wants to do some construction, you probably should get going pretty soon. It’s probably a dream for some people and a nightmare for others, but what’s it like working with your brother every day?



Oh, it’s definitely a nightmare some days, but no, I’m really fortunate, like just having someone you’ve grown up with as your ally next to you that you trust implicitly. We’re just really lucky to be working together. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: We’ve been naive. To beat the tobacco mafia, we need to think like the mafia
World.content:
PoliticsFederalTobacco Opinion We’ve been naive. To beat the tobacco mafia, we need to think like the mafia Tom Hird Economist September 8, 2026 — 6:00pm

September 8, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Six years ago, the Commonwealth collected $16.3 billion in tobacco excise. That figure will have collapsed to $4.1 billion this year, Treasury estimates, and by the end of the decade it’ll be just $2 billion. Meanwhile, investigations of wastewater by the Australian Bureau of Statistics suggest that since 2017 nicotine consumption (including from illegal vapes) has increased by 40 per cent. Let’s face it: the mafia has won the tobacco wars. The Commonwealth now faces competitors in the form of black market shops on every second suburban strip. Those competitors have 80 per cent market share to the Commonwealth’s 20 per cent. The Commonwealth is a bit player now with the main field of competition between the black market suppliers – and that is why we have seen more than 200 firebombed tobacco shops in Victoria alone. Billions of dollars of revenue are going up in smoke while the crime bosses are cashing in. Marija Ercegovac Let’s be clear about who we are dealing with. Organised crime is run like a business. It has suppliers, logistics, retail outlets and market share estimates. Its product costs a couple of dollars to make and sells for $15 to $20 against a legal price of $40 to $50, of which about $30 is tax. It responds to margins as any firm would, and uses arson the way a legit business uses advertising.



Imagine an organised crime business watching its revenues fall from $16 billion to $4 billion. It would not have watched. It would have organised itself so that the leak was noticed early and made sure that people who could stop it were rewarded for stopping it. If you are going to fight the mafia, you need to think like the mafia. That means thinking like a business, and thinking about incentives. Ours are wrong. The Commonwealth sets the tax and collects every dollar. The states run the police, the inspectors, the licensing schemes and the courts that actually determine whether the tax gets paid. The states bear all the costs of closing down the mafia but get none of the revenue. Preventing an illegal sale sends $30 to Canberra of which the state governments in Spring and Macquarie Street get nothing. What Spring/Macquarie Street do get is the costs of enforcement: a police taskforce, a licensing bureaucracy, more cops on the beat, more time taken up in courts and space taken up in remand/prison. The revenue they would protect belongs to somebody else. Nobody should be surprised at what has happened. The Commonwealth kept lifting the tax rate implicitly assuming the states would “do their job” of enforcement without giving them any incentive to do so. The states treated illicit tobacco as somebody else’s problem until the arson made it theirs. The Commonwealth’s answer has been grants, around $98 million so far to fund enforcement costs against a black market worth billions a year. A grant changes a state’s budget but not its incentive. Unless strings are attached, a grant arrives whether or not the enforcement works. Police footage of an alleged firebombing attack in Melbourne’s west last week. Victoria Police No crime boss would run a territory this way. A boss who set the price but relied on local crews to collect it would make sure they kept some of the proceeds. Each crew gets a cut of its own turf, so that every dollar of leakage is felt where it can be stopped. Legitimate business does the same with its branches. The Australian manager of Toyota is incentivised by Tokyo to sell Toyotas – they don’t just assume the Australian manager will do his best, they monitor and reward them based on performance.



Related Article Analysis

Tobacco The tobacco tax is a disaster playing out on our streets and in our budget The same should have been done, and should still be done, with tobacco. Give each state a share of the excise attributable to legal sales in its territory. Even a quarter share makes every illegal packet a state shuts down worth $7.50 to its own budget. The police taskforce stops being a cost centre and becomes a revenue driver. Both governments would be looking at the same ledger, which is where the mafia has been looking all along. Would this have prevented the rise of the black market? Not entirely; a $30 tax on a $2 product invites evasion under any regime. But the black market would have been smaller, noticed earlier and fought by the governments able to fight it, instead of Canberra blaming enforcement while the states blame the excise. So, should the excise be cut? That depends on what we are trying to achieve. If the only objective is to destroy the illegal market, then yes: slash the tax. Liberal leader Angus Taylor’s proposed 80 per cent cut (taking the tax on a packet from about $30 to $6) would probably do it. The black market would not vanish, but with legal packets selling under $20 the mafia’s margin shrinks from irresistible to barely worth the arson. Under this strategy we beat the mafia by matching its prices. That works, but it surrenders the health policy objective – which needs a high price. The excise alone cannot deliver the health policy objective because smokers don’t have to pay the legal price, they can choose the lower price on the street. The federal excise sets the price of a legal packet. Enforcement by the states sets the price of an illegal one. Ideally, it raises the mafia’s costs of illegally importing, warehousing and retailing tobacco until the discount they offer isn’t enough for the consumer to risk buying products from a criminal. A high excise with weak enforcement doesn’t make cigarettes expensive; it just lets the mafia collect the tax. So a serious anti-smoking policy needs both: a high excise, and enforcement strong enough to keep the street price close behind it. And the most efficient way to fund that enforcement is to give the states a cut of the excise – and skin in the game.



Dr Tom Hird is an economist and the founder of CEG Asia-Pacific. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Our tower of learning is leaning. Improving results is difficult but possible
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Editorial Our tower of learning is leaning. Improving results is difficult but possible The Herald's View Editorial September 8, 2026 — 6:00pm

September 8, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Spare a thought for Australia’s 15-year-olds. Life can be hard enough without representing the nation in international maths, science and reading tests, and then falling short of the 15-year-olds who attended school at the turn of the millennium by two and a half years. In the latest OPEC Programme for International Assessment, the current cohort of high school students recorded their worst results in reading and mathematics. Science results across the country have flatlined. Australia owes its children a high-quality education that equips them for an uncertain future. iStock Australia now ranks 11th in the world for reading and science and 17th for mathematics. The country was outperformed by Singapore, Poland and the United Kingdom in mathematics, and New Zealand, Ireland and Estonia in reading.



Related Article Education Australian students’ reading and maths results plunge in global rankings The decline in NSW’s results was not as severe as that in other states and territories. The world’s largest international assessment of student learning, PISA, measures how well 15-year-old students who are nearing the end of their formal education can apply their knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science. This year, more than 760,000 students from 91 countries and economies, including 15,000 Australians, took part. PISA’s testing has always been controversial. Many argue, fairly, that a country’s education systems shouldn’t be judged on the results produced by a sample of 15-year-olds (an age group notoriously unenthusiastic about exams, especially when they don’t see their results) and that international rankings are inherently flawed. Nevertheless, the Australian 15-year-olds chosen from all school systems to sit the first PISA tests in 2000 did exceptionally well. Results have been declining or treading water since, as other countries in the OECD improved.



For Australia, the most telling comparison is between its own 15-year-olds. The fact that the latest cohort was two and a half years behind the cohort of 2000, and a year and a half behind the cohort of 2018, should give us pause. Since the turn of the century, the diminution has ridden side by side with radical changes in the school experience. Schools have had to navigate the arrival of mobile phones, laptops in class and artificial intelligence, coupled with what many consider to be higher rates of classroom inattention and noise, creating a tsunami of distractions. Little wonder, then, that the impact continues to wreak damage. Australian students recorded more disruptive classrooms than 68 countries. The PISA results are a reason to remain concerned about whether Australian education can turn around the persistent decline, particularly as the latest results in NAPLAN – a more valid measurement than PISA – show a third of NSW’s year 3 students were failing to meet expected numeracy benchmarks. Similar countries have managed to turn their results around. The standout success story in this year’s results was the United Kingdom, which leaped three places in reading, four places in mathematics and seven places in science.



A safe and relatively wealthy country, Australia owes its children a high-quality education that equips them for an uncertain future. Improving results is a slow process, but the United Kingdom has shown it can be done. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Strike by Arts Centre workers threatens to disrupt Macy Gray concert
World.content:
Workers at Arts Centre Melbourne are threatening to disrupt a concert by Grammy Award-winning American singer Macy Gray as part of a 24-hour strike over pay.

Staff at the centre – which includes the Arts Centre building and Hamer Hall and is Australia’s largest performing arts complex – say they will walk off the job for 24 hours on Friday as part of a campaign of industrial action.

Arts Centre Melbourne with its famous spire and Hamer Hall next door. Mark Gambino

Gray is scheduled to perform at Hamer Hall on Friday night. Other performances that could be affected in the Arts Centre buildings on the same night include the play Grimm in the Fairfax Studio and Burn the Floor: Luminous at the Playhouse.

Several hundred workers who are part of the Community and Public Sector Union and the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance voted to go on strike after rejecting a pay offer of 3 per cent, which they say is below inflation.

World.title: Classroom screen time quietly driving down Victorian student results
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaHigh school Classroom screen time quietly driving down Victorian student results Alex Crowe September 8, 2026 — 5:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a quarter of Victoria’s 15-year-olds lack the foundational maths skills needed for further education or work and one in five is falling short in reading as Australia records its worst results in both subjects since international testing began. The results, released today as part of the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment 2025, show East Asian countries surged ahead of the rest of the world in maths, reading and science with researchers warning that digital devices in classrooms were disrupting learning. Almost 15,000 students from 766 Australian schools participated in the assessment. Louie Douvis OECD Director for Education and Skills Andreas Schleicher said Australia’s biggest fall since the previous PISA test in 2022 after maths was reading, amid evidence students read “faster but less accurately” on digital devices. “Declining levels of reading for enjoyment and a rapid shift to digital reading…they may have compromised the ability of young people to engage with more complex information,” Schleicher said.



“In Australia [and] in New Zealand students spend quite a bit of time on devices in schools for learning, and also quite a bit of time for leisure [during] school.” Almost 15,000 students from 766 Australian schools participated in the assessment, a key component of the National Assessment Program, which includes NAPLAN and the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study, and provides insight on progress towards the goals of the Alice Springs education declaration (Education Council, 2019). Ninety-one countries or economies participated in PISA 2025, although in some countries the assessment was only conducted in select regions. The assessment focused on science but also measured how 15-year-olds apply their knowledge in reading and maths, with computational problem-solving or “learning in the digital world” included for the first time.



Students completed a two-hour computer-based assessment and a 45-minute questionnaire on their background and beliefs. Principals and science teachers also completed a 45-minute questionnaire about their schools and teaching. In Victoria, 26 per cent of students were classified as “low performers” in maths, 21 per cent in reading and 17 per cent in science. Low performers typically “have not yet developed the foundational competencies required for full participation in further learning, the workforce, and civic life in the 21st century,” according to a report by the Australian Council for Educational Research, which managed the test nationally. “In science, this means they struggle to interpret simple data or identify evidence in a graph,” Schleicher wrote in his report.



“In reading, they will find it hard to understand simple texts, while in maths they could have trouble deciphering the relationship between units and price - the kind of tasks embedded in everyday life, from grocery shopping to reading a utility bill.” Australian students’ performance in science remained stable between 2022, when the test was last run, and 2025, with 60 per cent attaining the National Proficiency Standard. Nationally, students’ results declined in reading, with 55 per cent attaining the national benchmark - down from 2022. A similar trend was observed in maths, with 49 per cent attaining the national benchmark, also down from 2022. Independent schools outperformed Catholic schools nationally and both sectors outperformed government schools. However, private schools did not perform better when student performance was adjusted for students’ socioeconomic backgrounds.



The results show a worrying long-term trend for Australian students, with performance declining across all three disciplines from when they were first the focus of the tests, which researchers say is the most accurate comparison. This was 2000 for reading, 2003 for maths and 2006 for science. Since those respective starting points, science has declined 18 points, reading 37 points and maths 46 points. “And to give you a sense of that, 20 points are roughly equivalent to what 15-year-olds would learn in a year,” Schleicher said. ACER report co-author Eveline Gebhardt said Australia started well above the OECD average in all three disciplines, and while performance has declined nationally, it has not declined as sharply as the OECD average.



Gebhardt said the proportion of Australian students who reported being distracted by digital devices was much higher than the OECD average, despite 85 per cent of students attending schools that had banned mobile phones. “So this distraction is unlikely to be caused by phones, more by the use of laptops or tablets in the classroom. Maybe students play games, or they look things up on the internet, or text each other,” she said. “What is different in Australia than in other countries is that in Australia, digital distraction was not associated with performance. In other countries, when students report more disruption they usually show lower achievement, and that relationship was not found in Australia.” In the global rankings, Australia moved up one place in reading from 2022 to 11th, remained 17th in math and slipped one place to 11th in science. The four participating jurisdictions of China - Beijing, Jiangsu, Shanghai, and Zhejiang - topped the rankings in science and mathematics, followed by Singapore. Singapore outranked the Chinese provinces in reading and topped the global rankings.



The United Kingdom, which PISA considers a comparable country, jumped three places in reading, four places in maths and seven places in science. Education Minister Jason Clare said the UK’s results showed what was possible and why the reforms Australia is currently rolling out - the sort of reforms England rolled out almost 20 years ago - were so important. Under Clare, Australia rolled out Year 1 phonics checks at all public schools this year. NSW and South Australia rolled out Year 1 numeracy tests at all public schools this year, and pilots are underway in Victoria and most other jurisdictions. Clare has also tied $20 billion in funding for public schools to states implementing evidence-based teaching practices and more individualised support, including small-group tutoring. Education ministers will be presented with recommended changes to the maths curriculum at their next meeting in October, with decisions about the next stage of the reforms expected then.

World.title: World of Warcraft gaming meeting ended in alleged rape
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts World of Warcraft gaming meeting ended in alleged rape Tom Wark September 8, 2026 — 5:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A night out to socialise with online role-playing gamers ended with an alleged sexual assault in a couple’s hotel room, a jury has heard. Victorian man Taylor Johnson pleaded not guilty to the alleged assault of a fellow gamer during a World of Warcraft social weekend in Sydney. His trial began on Tuesday in Sydney’s Downing Centre District Court with his barrister telling the jury the pair did have sex and it was entirely consensual. Taylor Johnson (left) arrives at court on Tuesday. AAPIMAGE The alleged victim, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, is expected to say the 33-year-old had sex with her while she was asleep, heavily intoxicated and not willing to have sex with him.



“She was asleep or unconscious at the time the sexual intercourse commenced,” prosecutor Daniel Rainey told the jury. “She was so affected by alcohol that she was incapable of consenting.” Johnson’s barrister told the jury the alleged victim, who had also travelled from Victoria, was a willing participant. “The complainant, despite the alcohol she had consumed ... did and could consent to this sex,” Harriet Skinner said. Johnson, his partner and the complainant were all members of the same “guild” in the online game, and its leader had organised for members to meet in Sydney in March 2025, Mr Rainey said.



The name of the guild was “Brave and Crazy” and they would conduct twice-weekly raids in the game, agreed facts in the case state. After arriving in Sydney separately, the trio met for the first time in person at the Fortress gaming venue in the city centre to participate in a raid for their guild, the jury heard. Over the course of the night, the three consumed copious amounts of alcohol, the jury heard. An expert is expected to say the alleged victim consumed 18 standard drinks during the night, Mr Rainey said. In the early hours of the morning, Johnson started to kiss and sexually touch the intoxicated complainant at a nightclub, the jury heard.



The three took an Uber back to Johnson and his partner’s hotel where the complainant could no longer stand or walk on her own. Having wheeled out a trundle bed for the alleged victim to sleep on, Johnson got in the room’s main bed with his partner, the court heard. But about 4:30am, the alleged victim woke to Johnson having sex with her while groping her breast, Mr Rainey said. His partner was still asleep, the prosecutor said. Ms Skinner disputed the complainant’s account, saying the sex was “completely and entirely consensual”.



Later that week, the complainant texted Johnson looking for answers about the sex in the hotel, Mr Rainey said. “It was very much mutual until we both were like ‘what the f***’,” Johnson is said to have replied. “Please don’t reply, I’m having my world crumble at the moment and I’m trying to salvage what I can.” The trial continues. World.title: Audit office to take a look after Labor accused of ‘sports rorts’ pork-barrelling
World.content:
The auditor-general will consider probing a $560 million Commonwealth grants program after revelations that almost three-quarters of taxpayer funding went to Labor-held electorates, putting the distribution of public money under fresh scrutiny. The Australian National Audit Office will also examine whether to audit a $170 million Albanese government program supporting multicultural communities, where about 85 per cent of funding went to government-held seats. A golf course in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate was a beneficiary of the grant. AP The decision comes after revelations about the distribution of grants sparked fresh scrutiny of Labor’s handling of Commonwealth funding and raised comparisons with the Morrison government’s controversial “sports rorts” scheme. Auditor-General Caralee McLiesh wrote to the Coalition on Tuesday confirming both programs would be included in an initial assessment before determining whether to proceed to a full audit.



The Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program was an invitation-only scheme established before the 2025 election to fund projects including upgrades to sporting facilities, parks, playgrounds and swimming pools. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ An analysis released by the Centre for Public Integrity found $409.1 million, or 73.2 per cent of the program’s funding, went to safe Labor seats and marginal electorates. Coalition-held seats received $126.3 million, or 22.6 per cent. The centre found the disparity was greater when the political competitiveness of electorates was taken into account. Labor-competitive marginal seats received $66.5 million more than a proportional distribution would have suggested, while seats where Labor was not competitive and safe or fairly safe non-Labor seats received $116.6 million less. Labor argues the grant programs are above board because they relate to election promises, not competitive grants.



Last month this masthead reported that the Coalition also accused the government of exploiting a $171 million multicultural fund to bankroll its own seats and entrench “ghettoisation” of migrant communities. The Supporting Multicultural Communities program flowed at about 85 per cent to Labor seats. The Centre for Public Integrity’s research strategy director, Professor Gabrielle Appleby, said the government had not adequately explained how those organisations were chosen, despite repeated questions in parliament. Professor Gabrielle Appleby, the research strategy director of the Centre for Public Integrity. “When questions were raised about who was invited and why, they were never sufficiently answered by the government,” she said. “Now analysis shows us where the money went, and the pattern raises serious questions that need to be answered.” The analysis found the funding was geographically concentrated, with Victoria alone receiving approximately $205.9 million.



Adjusted for electors, Tasmania received 9.1 per cent of funds despite holding only 2.3 per cent of electors, while Queensland received just 9.2 per cent despite holding 20.7 per cent of electors. NSW and Queensland collectively received $104.6 million less than would be expected under a proportional distribution. Opposition’s assistant infrastructure spokesman Ben Small said Labor ministers had “failed the standard they set in opposition”. “Now the question is whether they have breached their own Commonwealth grant standards in doing so,” he said. But Infrastructure Minister Catherine King said the program was consistent with longstanding government practice and Commonwealth grants rules.



She said ministers did not make funding decisions on applications in their own electorates, while successful projects were assessed against criteria including value for money, community amenity and economic benefits. “What we’ve done very carefully is make sure that there’s a process by which we test, is the election commitment value for money? Is it deliverable? ” she told the ABC. “Ministers don’t make decisions. I don’t sign off on election commitments in my own seat. We’ve got a pretty clear process, and it’s a closed program.” But the closed nature of the program has become a central point of attack with allegations of blatant pork-barrelling. Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen Independent MP Helen Haines, whose electorate of Indi was among 45 divisions not invited to participate, said community organisations had been denied the chance to compete for funding. She said the issue was highlighted by the contrasting treatment of golf clubs.



Marrickville Golf Club, in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler, received $6 million for upgrades, while the Rutherglen Golf Club in Indi was not given an opportunity to apply. Haines questioned why the Marrickville club was selected when sporting organisations across the country were seeking infrastructure funding. “This isn’t about whether these projects are worthwhile, it’s about whether every community gets a fair shot at funding for projects that matter locally,” she said. “Taxpayers shouldn’t have to wonder whether their local sporting club, community organisation or council misses out because their electorate wasn’t politically useful.” Marrickville Golf Course has received $6 million for upgrades from the federal government in a controversial “invite-only” grants program. Janie Barrett Naomi Beattie, the secretary of Rutherglen’s Barkly Park Precinct committee of management, said the town’s facilities were dilapidated and dangerous.



She said the town had lost its Australian rules women’s team because they had no change rooms while opposition netball teams had threatened not to play there because of the bad surface. “As someone who has voted Labor in the past it’s upsetting to hear we are not being considered when we really need some help,” she said. In 2020, the Australian National Audit Office found evidence of distribution bias in the scheme and that the then-sports minister, Bridget McKenzie, had departed from Sport Australia’s recommendations in some funding decisions. McKenzie ultimately resigned after failing to declare her honorary membership of a gun club that received a $36,000 grant. Senator Bridget McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman. Alex Ellinghausen



Labor spent years attacking the Coalition over sports rorts and demanding greater transparency in the distribution of taxpayer-funded grants. McKenzie, the Coalition’s infrastructure spokeswoman, turned the comparison back on the Albanese government, arguing the current program was even more opaque because it was not subject to a competitive application process. She has questioned who selected the projects and whether adequate conflict-of-interest safeguards were applied, including in relation to the Marrickville grant. “Delivering on election promises is an important part of trust in a democracy. However, I think it is concerning that this is a closed program where there were no other invitees other than those who were selected by, it seems, the Labor Party,” she told the ABC. World.title: Graya’s co-founder on how to tackle the city’s housing crisis
World.content:
Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, Graya co-founder and managing director Rob Gray tells us how he thinks the city should tackle the housing crisis, what Brisbane 2032 will mean for construction prices, and the suburbs Graya has its eye on. We meet Gray at Teneriffe ferry stop, just a short walk from his head office. He’s immediately recognisable in a Graya branded T-shirt. As we cruise along the Brisbane River, we spot multiple Graya-branded signs at prime real estate spots in the city’s most affluent areas. Developer Rob Gray says as Graya grows, he feels more responsibility to the Brisbane community to do a good job. William Davis What’s your controversial Brisbane opinion? I think, personally, we have a little bit of a housing crisis at the moment. Houses are really expensive; rents are really expensive. What would really help would be going up and not out. Potentially lifting some height limits in the busy areas would really help everybody.



In a perfect world, if money wasn’t an object and you could do whatever you want, what would be your dream Brisbane project? This is going to sound corny, but I think the dream Brisbane projects I’m already doing. You know, from riverfront developments in Saint Lucia, to restaurants and retail developments in Racecourse Road and James Street, it’s things that I’ve always wanted to do. Maybe the next thing I really want to be part of is the Brisbane skyline. What inspired you to get into development? From a very young age, I always wanted to get into property development. I just really loved doing things with my hands. I loved creating something. I like the fulfillment, seeing something come out of the ground and be able to experience the hard work.



There are whole areas in Brisbane that Graya is really reshaping. Do you feel it’s a big responsibility, and how have you dealt with that? Related Article City council Dining lane to link huge new tower to James Street precinct I think as Graya has matured as a business, I am starting to feel more responsibility to the Brisbane community that we need to do a really good job. Especially now, because we’ve moved out of individual homes and now we’re doing what we like to call lifestyle developments. We like to bring in the retail and fashion and restaurants. It’s putting a huge responsibility on us to make our city great. You’ve had an enormous amount of success in quite a short period of time in what’s very famously a hugely cutthroat industry. What’s the secret behind your success and your rapid growth?



It might look like it’s quite quick from the outside in, but for us, it’s been quite slow. But we’ve been really determined from the outset to do a really good product, so we really focused on that for a long period of time. Related Article Perspective

City life What ‘the James Street effect’ says about our city And you look back over a decade and a half, and you really have done a lot of things. Graya’s got a really distinctive aesthetic and style. How did that come about? Is there a building in Brisbane you’re particularly proud of? I think we’re really fortunate in Brisbane, we’ve got such a good climate – it’s not too cold, it’s not too hot – so we can do this really subtropical architecture.



We really like to put greenery within our buildings, and something that I’m really, really proud of is a New Farm building called Mason. It’s on the corner of Moray Street, and it has this draping greenery. Every year it ages, it just gets better and better. Graya’s obviously got its detractors, and you’ve got under the skin of some other developers, among others. Why do you think that is, and how have you dealt with that? I think as we grow as a business, we’re moving into more prominent areas, and in those areas, there’s been a lot of long-standing owners that have, and like it, run a certain way. As we move into these areas, we just need to be really mindful of that previous history and try not to step on too many toes, and respect other people’s opinions and do the best job we can. Loading



Is there an upcoming project you’re particularly excited about? We have heaps of upcoming projects that I’m like crazy excited about. There’s one particularly, on James Street, that’s under construction right now called James Place, which is just a phenomenal development. What it will do to Brisbane and James Street is going to be next level, much like what the Calile did to James Street when it was first developed. Are there any suburbs that you’re moving into, or any suburbs that Graya’s really eyeing as future growth areas? Graya has really taken a shine to the Saint Lucia pocket. It’s something that we’ve always known about because we grew up in Indooroopilly and the Chapel Hill area. In the very early days, we spent a lot of time developing the New Farm, inner-city area, but we’ve really highlighted Saint Lucia as somewhere we want to do more and more apartments.



With your knowledge of development in Brisbane specifically, how do you see the years leading up to the Olympics and beyond playing out? How do you think Brisbane’s going to change in that time? Related Article City life The material this design influencer wants Brisbane to build its identity around I’m really excited for seeing what’s going to happen in Brisbane leading up to the Olympics. I think everyone can already see the value that’s been added with that. I think it’s probably one of the safest investments in the world right now. I think the construction market is going to get awfully busy. I feel like that will push up construction prices, which is probably not a good thing but it’s just always a temporary thing that everyone just needs to be mindful of. If someone wants to do some construction, you probably should get going pretty soon. It’s probably a dream for some people and a nightmare for others, but what’s it like working with your brother every day?



Oh, it’s definitely a nightmare some days, but no, I’m really fortunate, like just having someone you’ve grown up with as your ally next to you that you trust implicitly. We’re just really lucky to be working together. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: We’ve been naive. To beat the tobacco mafia, we need to think like the mafia
World.content:
PoliticsFederalTobacco Opinion We’ve been naive. To beat the tobacco mafia, we need to think like the mafia Tom Hird Economist September 8, 2026 — 6:00pm

September 8, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Six years ago, the Commonwealth collected $16.3 billion in tobacco excise. That figure will have collapsed to $4.1 billion this year, Treasury estimates, and by the end of the decade it’ll be just $2 billion. Meanwhile, investigations of wastewater by the Australian Bureau of Statistics suggest that since 2017 nicotine consumption (including from illegal vapes) has increased by 40 per cent. Let’s face it: the mafia has won the tobacco wars. The Commonwealth now faces competitors in the form of black market shops on every second suburban strip. Those competitors have 80 per cent market share to the Commonwealth’s 20 per cent. The Commonwealth is a bit player now with the main field of competition between the black market suppliers – and that is why we have seen more than 200 firebombed tobacco shops in Victoria alone. Billions of dollars of revenue are going up in smoke while the crime bosses are cashing in. Marija Ercegovac Let’s be clear about who we are dealing with. Organised crime is run like a business. It has suppliers, logistics, retail outlets and market share estimates. Its product costs a couple of dollars to make and sells for $15 to $20 against a legal price of $40 to $50, of which about $30 is tax. It responds to margins as any firm would, and uses arson the way a legit business uses advertising.



Imagine an organised crime business watching its revenues fall from $16 billion to $4 billion. It would not have watched. It would have organised itself so that the leak was noticed early and made sure that people who could stop it were rewarded for stopping it. If you are going to fight the mafia, you need to think like the mafia. That means thinking like a business, and thinking about incentives. Ours are wrong. The Commonwealth sets the tax and collects every dollar. The states run the police, the inspectors, the licensing schemes and the courts that actually determine whether the tax gets paid. The states bear all the costs of closing down the mafia but get none of the revenue. Preventing an illegal sale sends $30 to Canberra of which the state governments in Spring and Macquarie Street get nothing. What Spring/Macquarie Street do get is the costs of enforcement: a police taskforce, a licensing bureaucracy, more cops on the beat, more time taken up in courts and space taken up in remand/prison. The revenue they would protect belongs to somebody else. Nobody should be surprised at what has happened. The Commonwealth kept lifting the tax rate implicitly assuming the states would “do their job” of enforcement without giving them any incentive to do so. The states treated illicit tobacco as somebody else’s problem until the arson made it theirs. The Commonwealth’s answer has been grants, around $98 million so far to fund enforcement costs against a black market worth billions a year. A grant changes a state’s budget but not its incentive. Unless strings are attached, a grant arrives whether or not the enforcement works. Police footage of an alleged firebombing attack in Melbourne’s west last week. Victoria Police No crime boss would run a territory this way. A boss who set the price but relied on local crews to collect it would make sure they kept some of the proceeds. Each crew gets a cut of its own turf, so that every dollar of leakage is felt where it can be stopped. Legitimate business does the same with its branches. The Australian manager of Toyota is incentivised by Tokyo to sell Toyotas – they don’t just assume the Australian manager will do his best, they monitor and reward them based on performance.



Related Article Analysis

Tobacco The tobacco tax is a disaster playing out on our streets and in our budget The same should have been done, and should still be done, with tobacco. Give each state a share of the excise attributable to legal sales in its territory. Even a quarter share makes every illegal packet a state shuts down worth $7.50 to its own budget. The police taskforce stops being a cost centre and becomes a revenue driver. Both governments would be looking at the same ledger, which is where the mafia has been looking all along. Would this have prevented the rise of the black market? Not entirely; a $30 tax on a $2 product invites evasion under any regime. But the black market would have been smaller, noticed earlier and fought by the governments able to fight it, instead of Canberra blaming enforcement while the states blame the excise. So, should the excise be cut? That depends on what we are trying to achieve. If the only objective is to destroy the illegal market, then yes: slash the tax. Liberal leader Angus Taylor’s proposed 80 per cent cut (taking the tax on a packet from about $30 to $6) would probably do it. The black market would not vanish, but with legal packets selling under $20 the mafia’s margin shrinks from irresistible to barely worth the arson. Under this strategy we beat the mafia by matching its prices. That works, but it surrenders the health policy objective – which needs a high price. The excise alone cannot deliver the health policy objective because smokers don’t have to pay the legal price, they can choose the lower price on the street. The federal excise sets the price of a legal packet. Enforcement by the states sets the price of an illegal one. Ideally, it raises the mafia’s costs of illegally importing, warehousing and retailing tobacco until the discount they offer isn’t enough for the consumer to risk buying products from a criminal. A high excise with weak enforcement doesn’t make cigarettes expensive; it just lets the mafia collect the tax. So a serious anti-smoking policy needs both: a high excise, and enforcement strong enough to keep the street price close behind it. And the most efficient way to fund that enforcement is to give the states a cut of the excise – and skin in the game.



Dr Tom Hird is an economist and the founder of CEG Asia-Pacific. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Strike by Arts Centre workers threatens to disrupt Macy Gray concert
World.content:
Workers at Arts Centre Melbourne are threatening to disrupt a concert by Grammy Award-winning American singer Macy Gray as part of a 24-hour strike over pay.

Staff at the centre – which includes the Arts Centre building and Hamer Hall and is Australia’s largest performing arts complex – say they will walk off the job for 24 hours on Friday as part of a campaign of industrial action.

Arts Centre Melbourne with its famous spire and Hamer Hall next door. Mark Gambino

Gray is scheduled to perform at Hamer Hall on Friday night. Other performances that could be affected in the Arts Centre buildings on the same night include the play Grimm in the Fairfax Studio and Burn the Floor: Luminous at the Playhouse.

Several hundred workers who are part of the Community and Public Sector Union and the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance voted to go on strike after rejecting a pay offer of 3 per cent, which they say is below inflation.

His trial began on Tuesday in Sydney’s Downing Centre District Court with his barrister telling the jury the pair did have sex and it was entirely consensual. Taylor Johnson (left) arrives at court on Tuesday. AAPIMAGE The alleged victim, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, is expected to say the 33-year-old had sex with her while she was asleep, heavily intoxicated and not willing to have sex with him.



“She was asleep or unconscious at the time the sexual intercourse commenced,” prosecutor Daniel Rainey told the jury. “She was so affected by alcohol that she was incapable of consenting.” Johnson’s barrister told the jury the alleged victim, who had also travelled from Victoria, was a willing participant. “The complainant, despite the alcohol she had consumed ... did and could consent to this sex,” Harriet Skinner said. Johnson, his partner and the complainant were all members of the same “guild” in the online game, and its leader had organised for members to meet in Sydney in March 2025, Mr Rainey said.



The name of the guild was “Brave and Crazy” and they would conduct twice-weekly raids in the game, agreed facts in the case state. After arriving in Sydney separately, the trio met for the first time in person at the Fortress gaming venue in the city centre to participate in a raid for their guild, the jury heard. Over the course of the night, the three consumed copious amounts of alcohol, the jury heard. An expert is expected to say the alleged victim consumed 18 standard drinks during the night, Mr Rainey said. In the early hours of the morning, Johnson started to kiss and sexually touch the intoxicated complainant at a nightclub, the jury heard.



The three took an Uber back to Johnson and his partner’s hotel where the complainant could no longer stand or walk on her own. Having wheeled out a trundle bed for the alleged victim to sleep on, Johnson got in the room’s main bed with his partner, the court heard. But about 4:30am, the alleged victim woke to Johnson having sex with her while groping her breast, Mr Rainey said. His partner was still asleep, the prosecutor said. Ms Skinner disputed the complainant’s account, saying the sex was “completely and entirely consensual”.



Later that week, the complainant texted Johnson looking for answers about the sex in the hotel, Mr Rainey said. “It was very much mutual until we both were like ‘what the f***’,” Johnson is said to have replied. “Please don’t reply, I’m having my world crumble at the moment and I’m trying to salvage what I can.” The trial continues. World.title: Albanese’s fix for your social media feed has one big flaw
World.content:
Analysis TechnologySocial media Albanese’s fix for your social media feed has one big flaw David Swan September 8, 2026 — 5:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthony Albanese has a good line for his United Nations speech in New York this month: Australians get to switch off the algorithm. Like the teen social media ban, it is a popular idea that fits in one sentence, and the prime minister will take it to the UN as a model for others. It’ll win votes back home in Australia. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as he presented his new social media rules at Parliament House in Canberra on Tuesday. Alex Ellinghausen The trouble is what the switch does once you flick it – and what it doesn’t do. The algorithm uses swaths of data to guess what you’ll buy and what will keep you scrolling. It’s the system that has made social media so addictive, and so destructive.



Turn it off under the model Communications Minister Anika Wells announced on Tuesday, and you’ll just see the accounts you already follow. Consent campaigner Chanel Contos has spent the past nine months warning us of the issues with social media algorithms: the 16-year-old boy who has spent a year marinating in gym content, then hustle culture, then the online sludge that tells him women are the reason his life is hard. He follows 40 of those accounts now. Consent campaigner Chanel Contos has called for laws to give Australians more control over what they see on social media. Alex Ellinghausen Under the government’s new “My Feed, My Way” initiative, he opts out – and still sees 40 manosphere accounts in a row. That’s because the algorithm has already won before he’s seen the off switch.



This masthead ran the experiment last week: a fake profile for a 17-year-old boy was served manosphere content on TikTok within 13 minutes. Related Article Breaking

Social media Australia to opt out of social media algorithms, Albanese confirms This is the flaw at the centre of an otherwise serious and commendable bill, and it is why Contos has spent nine months arguing for the opposite. Contos is proposing an “opt in” model that would return the default feed to something closer to 2016: chronological posts from accounts a user actually chooses to follow. She calls it affirmative consent applied to a screen. The dangers of doing nothing are real: men who hold the attitudes manosphere content promotes are 17 times more likely to have hit a partner, according to research she cited at the National Press Club.



She has warned it would be “too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform”. Contos is right to be cynical. The likes of Meta and TikTok will probably opt for malicious compliance, burying the switch under five sub-menus or making the chronological feed so clunky that users give up and opt straight back in to getting whatever the algorithm feeds them. Social media giants like Meta are likely to look for ways to bypass the new rules. AP In fact, this is exactly what Meta did three years ago when Europe mandated an opt-out feed: it buried the option deep in its menus and reset to the algorithmic feed every time a user closed the app. That behaviour drew a lawsuit in the Netherlands and an investigation by Ireland’s tech regulator. Then there is the glaring blind spot: advertising.



Recommendation and ad targeting are separate systems. Opt out of a personalised feed, and you can still be profiled and sold to advertisers because the bill as it stands says nothing about how paid content is ranked or targeted. Europe went further three years ago, barring personalised advertising to users aged 13 to 17. Australia’s draft doesn’t deal with that issue at all. To be fair, this is difficult work, and the government is having a crack at US behemoths that until recently seemed untouchable. It threatens fines of up to $109.2 million, hefty unless you are Meta, which just settled US child safety claims for $25 billion. Communications Minister Anika Wells faces an uphill battle beyond the inevitable teeth gnashing from the tech giants. Alex Ellinghausen And if the government’s plan works, it will be a paradigm shift, moving the obligation from cleaning up after harm to preventing it. It also extends beyond social media to games, apps and chatbots. Approved researchers and the eSafety commissioner will be able to use false identities to audit what children are served online. These are helpful moves. The fix, in my eyes at least, is relatively straightforward. Flip the default for new accounts only, so a 16-year-old opening Instagram for the first time starts with the people they choose to follow, and has to ask for the algorithm if they want it. Ban profiling-based ads to under-18s, as Europe does.



Meta declined to comment on Wells’ announcement, but said there was no one single “algorithm” that could simply be switched off. The company argues that its ranking systems are useful for detecting abuse and demoting low-quality content, and points to Instagram’s “Following” and “Favourites” feeds, which already show posts chronologically. Related Article Opinion

Social media I posed as a 17-year-old boy on social media. It took 13 minutes to be shown the manosphere Amber Schultz Reporter The minister faces an uphill battle beyond the inevitable teeth gnashing from the tech giants. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and One Nation have raised free-speech objections, though Wells’ opposite number, Sarah Henderson, says nothing should be off the table, including a permanent opt-out. The Greens want the algorithm off by default. If Albanese and Wells get their way, you will be able to switch off the algorithm. You just won’t be able to switch off what it already did. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter. Sign up to receive it every Friday.

World.title: Two people arrested after hours long stand-off with Nelson police
World.content:
Two people have been arrested after an hours long stand-off with police in Nelson.

Senior Sergeant Mark Surman said police were at an address in Toi Toi regarding an unrelated incident when a man became enraged, threatened police, then locked himself inside a residence and refused to leave.

Armed police were at the scene as a precaution and cordons were put in place along Emano Street from Murphy Street to Toi Toi Street.

A neighbour who entered the property during the stand-off was also arrested.

Both were taken into custody about 6.25pm and cordons were lifted at 7pm.

Police want to reassure the public that there was no threat to public safety.

World.title: NZ science and maths students turn around 20 years of decline in international tests
World.content:
New Zealand's science and maths scores in the international Pisa tests for 15-year-olds have improved or stabilised after more than 20 years of decline.

This country's average score in science improved from 504 to 509 points, and in maths by a single point to 480.

In reading, New Zealand reached a new low of 497, a small drop of four points caused by a fall in boys' scores.

The changes were considered statistically insignificant, but the science and maths results would be regarded as good news following successive declines that left reading 32 points adrift of a high recorded in the early-2000s, maths down 43 points, and science 23 points.

The OECD said 20 points were equivalent to a year of learning.

Supplied

Other countries' scores also declined in that period and especially since Covid, meaning New Zealand maintained its position around the top 10 in reading and science and above the OECD average in maths.

However, New Zealand's scores might be inflated by as much as 15 points because the students who sat the test were not an entirely representative sample of the country's 15-year-olds.

"The analysis showed slightly more high achieving students participated. This means the results will likely show New Zealand in a more positive light than if we had an unbiased sample, potentially by about 10-15 PISA points," an Education Ministry report on New Zealand's results said.

"It is important to note that the bias may not affect trend or country comparisons to its full extent, because a similar (although, likely, smaller) bias may also affect past results and the results of other countries and economies."

A similar problem affected the previous 2022 test results for New Zealand.

Singapore, Macao, Taiwan and China (where Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang, participated) topped the tables.

Singapore had the highest score in reading (535) followed by China and Taiwan. China was top in maths (612) and in science (597) followed by Singapore, Macao and Taiwan.

Estonia was the highest-scoring nation outside of Asia in science with 527 points and in maths (508), and in reading it scored 499, fractionally behind Ireland with 500.

A report on New Zealand's results said the science result had not changed significantly since 2012, and the reading score was considered similar to results going back to 2015.

However, the gap between the highest and lowest performers in reading had grown to 302 points, similar to the gap recorded in Australia and the USA but above the OECD average of 264 points.

Nearly a quarter (23 percent) of New Zealand students were considered poor readers, slightly more than in 2022 and well above the 14 percent recorded in 2000.

Just 14 percent were top-scorers in reading.

In science, 19 percent of New Zealand students were low achievers, and 13 percent were high achievers.

In maths, 29 percent of New Zealand teens were low performers, nearly double the figure recorded in 2003-9, while 11 percent were top performers, about half the figure in 2003-9.

World.title: 'Golden visa' migrant investments soon to include build-to-rent housing developments
World.content:
Migrants on the so-called golden visa will soon be allowed to invest in funds that support long-term rental housing developments.

The Active Investor Plus visa 'growth' category requires a minimum investment of $5 million.

From December, applicants will be able to include build-to-rent housing developments as part of their overall investment in New Zealand.

As it stands they can make direct investments, invest in managed funds, or make donations (which cannot exceed 20 percent of the total amount invested).

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford said it would help people make a meaningful contribution to the economy.

"The growth category is particularly focused on investment that supports business growth, innovation and productivity," she said.

"Adding Build to Rent gives investors another option, while keeping that focus through the managed funds model."

Chris Bishop. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Housing Minister Chris Bishop said it would help boost the country's housing stock.

"Build to Rent can add to rental supply over time, while the managed funds model provides clear safeguards around who manages the investment and how developments are delivered," he said.

Direct investment in build-to-rent developments would not be accepted.

In April 2025 the government updated the Active Investor Plus visa settings to create two categories: growth (at least $5 million investment for at least three years) and balanced (at least $10 million investment for at least five years).

Since then, there had been $5 billion invested across more than 900 applications, the government said.

World.title: Neighbour 'in shock' after woman and two children killed in Rotorua home
World.content:
A man who lives across the road from where a woman and two children were killed in Rotorua says he's in shock after the last night's events.

Police earlier said they arrived at a property on High Street in Glenholme shortly before 10.30pm on Monday, where they found two dead children and a woman with life-threatening injuries. The woman died at the scene.

Police said a man was assisting police with their inquiries.

A 79-year-old man who had lived on the street his whole life, said he heard some noise across the road last night, and got out of bed to look out the window.

He said he was in shock since learning what happened.

The people living in the house seemed to have recently moved in, he said and he'd seen new children around the street.

* Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Police at the scene this morning. NZME

Another man living next to the scene said he heard police last night.

Jason said he heard the sounds of doors slamming and thought someone might be trying to take his car.

He rushed outside and saw four or five police cars parked next door.

Jason said he knew something bad had happened, but didn't realise how bad until he read the news this morning.

On Tuesday, a man aged in his early 20s appeared in the Rotorua District Court charged with assaulting a person in a family relationship.

The court heard that court documents named three victims. The man, who appeared via audio-visual link, was wearing white coveralls.

The man, and the victims, were granted interim name suppression.

The man was remanded in custody until 2 October.

A relative of the man declined to comment when approached by RNZ.

Google Maps

Family members have been seen hugging and crying at the Rotorua home where a woman and two young children were killed.

The family embraced each other outside the Glenholme house.

A hearse arrived at the house this evening, and police continue to stand guard into the night.

Earlier, Bay of Plenty acting district commander Inspector Logan Marsh said it was an "incredibly traumatic incident for all those involved".

"Our focus now is on supporting the family, our first responders and getting answers to what occurred last night," Marsh said.

"We know this event will be felt widely in the community and people will want answers. We are methodically working through the scene, including a detailed forensic examination."

He said this could take several days and there would be a police presence in the area.

"We know people will be understandably shaken following this incident and police will be carrying out additional reassurance patrols over the coming days and nights in Glenholme and the wider community.

"Out of respect for the victims and their family, we ask that people refrain from speculation or conjecture. Our focus remains on establishing exactly what occurred and providing answers for those affected."

World.title: Police officers made 'split second tactical decisions' in fatal shooting of Kaoss Price, High Court told
World.content:
Lawyers for the Crown have told the High Court in Wellington officers involved in the fatal shooting of Kaoss Price in 2022 made "split second tactical decisions".

Counsel are testifying on the second day of proceedings in a Judicial Review of the Independent Police Conduct Authority's decision not to charge the officer who fired the fatal shot.

The IPCA's investigation found the officer who fired the fatal shot used excessive force, but did not recommend prosecuting the officer.

Split second decisions

Crown Counsel Peter Gunn said three and a half minutes elapsed between officers attempting to pull over a car driving ahead of Price, his accelerating away and side swiping a police dog van before being shot while trying to hi-jack another car.

Price had been released from prison earlier that year and Gunn told the court a prior search of a vehicle linked to Price had recovered four firearms - including a loaded shotgun.

"Mr Price had been well known to police. He had numerous criminal convictions which included theft, car conversion, assault and driving offences," Gunn said.

Officers armed at the beginning of their shift

On the night of the incident the two officers involved had chosen to wear their Glock pistols at the beginning of their shift which they put down to their awareness of a warrant for Price and concerns over two other individuals in the area.

At about 9.30pm on 16 April, Price's VW Golf was seen driving closely behind another BMW vehicle.

"They both knew that Mr Price was a repeat offender, was known to carry firearms and knives and was also the subject of an arrest warrant," Gunn told the court.

Gunn told the court when the officers signalled to pull the BMW over the VW Price was driving then turned off its head lights and accelerated away.

He said the VW turned and drove towards the officers' vehicle at high speed and on the wrong side of the road.

In interviews Officer A said he felt Price was "hunting" the officers.

"I thought I was going to die. I thought my name was going to be on the plaque at the police college," the officer said.

The officers described feeling their vehicle (a dog van) shudder as the VW narrowly passed and turned in front of oncoming traffic before heading back.

"Both officers felt the vehicle collide with the dog van and scrape along the vehicle. During the Collision Officer A drew his pistol and fired two shots through the open window at the passing vehicle," Gunn said.

The officers heard the VW's engine revving and gears grinding and feared the VW would be put into reverse.

Price climbed out of the VW and ran away from the officers, down the road, trying the handles of vehicles as he went while Officer A fired more shots.

Price then forced his way into an occupied Hyundai and struggled with the driver to gain control of the vehicle.

Gunn said Officer A told interviewing officers he had only moments to decide his course of action.

"I needed to help those two people [occupants of the vehicle]. There was no time to sit back and discuss what I was going to do. I had to make a decision," the officer told investigators.

Officer A arrived at the car and ordered Price to get out of the car, he did not comply, and the officer shot Price in the chest through the window.

A second officer then tasered Price and he was removed from the car and given first aid. He died at the scene.

Lawyers argue investigation failed Bill of Right's obligations

Yesterday, lawyer for Price's family, Max Harris, said the IPCA's investigation had failed in its obligations under the Bill of Rights to be independent, impartial, prompt, thorough and transparent - and the process had undermined the effectiveness and the credibility of the investigation.

Gunn said it was inaccurate for lawyers for Price's family to suggest to suggest that the IPCA was not acting independently of police.

"If a police investigation misfires then the Section 8 [Bill of Rights] obligation may be made by the IPCA. [Here] we have an IPCA investigation report which has not been challenged," Gunn said.

He said police had drawn investigating officers from other parts of the country and delays in interviewing the officer were related to public holidays near the incident and police's commitment to head the investigation with staff not close to the officers involved.

In response to the family's lawyers' criticism of the IPCA - stemming from the authority's handling of disgraced former Police Commissioner Jevon McSkimmings - Gunn told the court the investigation into Price's shooting showed no similar evidence of collusion or influence from police to conceal the nature of the events.

Gunn also took aim at criticism of the police interviews and said officers who called Officer A "mate" fourteen times during his nearly seven hour interview were "building rapport" with the officer.

"What they are attempting to do is find common ground. When you show empathy people open up," Gunn said.

Gunn said that police actions following the shooting demonstrated they were aware a charge of homicide was a real possibility.

"[The officer] was tested for firearm residue, performed a drug and alcohol test and his uniform was seized before he was allowed to go home," Gunn said.

Gunn told the court that a senior officer cautioned Officer A as to his rights as was necessary when a person was detained, or questioned as a suspect.

"At the time, in the absence of an explanation and the circumstances - as I understood them to be - I thought there was a strong possibility of a homicide charge and a Bill of Rights caution was appropriate," The officer told investigators.

Gunn said the police's actions towards the officers involved highlighted seriousness with which they approached the incident and their "open mind" towards the potential prosecution of the officers involved.

Police letter to family 'unhelpful' - Justice Heine

Counsel for the Crown, Peter Marshall defended the letter sent to Price's family informing them of the circumstances of his death, police intelligence regarding his offending and a single sentence as to why his shooting would not be prosecuted which read:

"Based on an assessment of the circumstance and the law relating [to] self defence and the defence of another (Section 48 of the Crimes Act), police has determined there is insufficient evidence to support criminal prosecution of the officers involved in this incident."

"Decisions are made by public prosecutors in the public interest. They are not ever made in the interest of victims," Marshall said.

Justice Victoria Heine said the language used to convey the decision was "economical" and "not particularly helpful" to the family.

But Marshall said it was not up to prosecutors to "evaluate the evidence" for the benefit of the family.

He went on to tell the court that a homicide charge against Officer A could be defended on the grounds that the officers actions arose from the belief that Price intended to kill the officers or harm others.

"It's not whether [Price] intended to do that but whether you could prove the officer did not hold that belief," Marshall said.

'There was time to make a tactical assessment to disengage'

In summing up, lawyer for the family Christopher Stevenson contrasted Price with the case concerning Stephen Wallace, who was shot as he advanced on officers with a weapon in 2000.

"By the time Mr Price had climbed out of the vehicle he'd been shot at twice, he was then running away and Officer A made that choice to follow him to the vehicle [where he was shot].

"There was time to make a tactical assessment to disengage but that didn't happen," Stevenson said.

He said the officer had conceded that he had seen Price's empty hands as he attempted to enter nearby vehicles.

He said because the ICPA could not instigate prosecution it could not cure the deficiencies in the police investigation.

He argued that Counsel for the Crown's point that Officer A being cautioned as to his rights could be seen as an indication that police saw a real potential for charges being laid against the officer but said that wasn't reflected in a decision to treat the officer as a witness.

"The unarmed man fleeing police - and then he was shot - that does require [the officer] to be treated as a suspect," Stevenson said.

World.title: Warriors welcome back Jackson Ford for NRL finals campaign
World.content:
For the first time since June, Warriors coach Andrew Webster can call on "one of the best players in the competition" for Saturday's qualifying final against the Dolphins at a sold-out Mt Smart Stadium.

Front-rower Jackson Ford returns to the team after suffering a pectoral injury in round 16. He is set to make his comeback on the bench.

Before he was injured and missed the last 10 matches of the regular season Ford had played in evey game this season for the Warriors and Webster thought he had been unlucky to miss out on State of Origin duty.

"It's a good headache to have players returning, some experience, one of the best players in the competition - he was the best player at the time in the competition," Webster said of Ford.

Ford has been named in the 17 jersey in a squad which also sees centre Leka Halasima, second rower Kurt Capewell and hooker Wayde Egan back on deck after missing last week's final regular season match against the Sea Eagles.

While they return, winger Dallin Watene-Zelezniak isn't yet available after breaking his right clavicle in the round 25 game against South Sydney last month.

With Watene-Zelezniak still sidelined, Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad will again line up on the right wing for what will be his 150th career appearance, his 84th for the Warriors.

While Nicoll-Klokstad marks his 150-game milestone, Halasima, still only 20 years old, becomes the second of the club's young guns to make 50 appearances for the Warriors.

Loose forward Erin Clark will stretch his run of consecutive appearances for the club to 50 since returning home last season and 74 all up counting the 24 unbroken games he played for thew Titans in 2024; the last time he missed a game was at the end of the 2023 season.

There are a lot of factors outside of Webster's control ahead of the game against the Dolphins and he is wary of "over coaching" at this end of the season.

"You can try and fix every little detail, you only need to worry about the biggest ticket items, the items that matter most don't worry about what you can't control.

"Just lean into the fact that we've got a lot of experience, a lot of confidence, a lot of players that we believe in, just bring your best football and the rest takes care of it."

Warriors coach Andrew Webster has had to make some tough calls ahead of qualifying final. RNZ/Nick Munro

Heading into their first game of finals, Webster does not want to stray from what got the team there.

"I'll repeat myself 100 times, [it's] making sure we don't turn up on game day and start trying to be something we're not.

"We know what our footy looks like, we don't mind if someone else knows, if the opposition knows what we look like, we bring our best and do it our way, we're confident."

Webster has similar advice for the fans who will fill Mt Smart.

"Don't change, just be yourselves, because they've done a great job. They're fun, they're intimidating, they're loud, they're enjoyable ... we need you, we love you and don't change just keep it rolling."

The Warriors and Dolphins met twice this year with only two points separating the sides each time, the Warriors prevailing 20-18 in round eight on Anzac Day in Wellington before the Dolphins stole a 26-24 victory with a late try in the round 17 meeting at Suncorp Stadium.

Throughout their rivalry, the clubs have shared results each season.

In 2023 the Warriors won 30-8 at Go Media Stadium and lost 10-34 at Suncorp Stadium while in 2024 they prevailed 24-20 at home and lost 32-34 in Brisbane. Last year they won 16-12 at Suncorp Stadium then lost 18-20 in Auckland.

Warriors team for qualifying final:

1. Taine Tuaupiki, 2. Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad, 3. Ali Leiataua, 4. Leka Halasima, 5. Alofiana Khan-Pereira, 6. Chanel Harris-Tavita, 7. Te Maire Martin, 8. James Fisher-Harris, 9. Wayde Egan, 10. Mitchell Barnett, 11. Kurt Capewell, 12. Jacob Laban, 13. Erin Clark

World.title: 'Dodgy' QR codes now also being  found on Auckland Transport parking meters
World.content:
Scam QR codes on parking machines appear in Auckland Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

"Dodgy" parking QR codes have found their way to Auckland as the city's transport agency warns people to avoid them entirely.

Auckland Transport said it had found a "handful of scam QR code stickers" on parking meters in the city centre last week.

This comes after both Wellington and Christchurch city councils raised the alarm over similar fake QR stickers on meters across each city.

AT's Head of Transport and Parking Compliance Rick Bidgood told Checkpoint AT does not use QR codes on any of its parking meters or machines and the public should be vigilant.

"We only picked up a very very small handful so they were dodgily placed on top of where the payment methodology should be on the payment machine"

He said the codes were "not broadly spread" and only found in the lower city towards the viaduct.

"I do believe it takes you to a payment gateway so please don't scan it.'

AT said in a Facebook post the QR codes directed people to a website that appeared legitimate, asking for details like parking duration and licence plate information before wanting them to pay.
