Bidgood said there have been no reports yet from the public of any scams.

He said the AT team had done a sweep of the city's parking meters as part of their regular checks, but they have also alerted police.

Police were urging caution about where people provide their credit card details, saying it's often an offshore scam.

Detective senior sergeant Craig Bolton said people should use official apps or parking machines wherever possible.

"Pay close attention when you're paying for parking. If you are scanning one of these dodgy QR codes, there's a high chance the website you're being directed to is being run by an offshore scam centre.

"From there, the scammers will use your credit card details to wreak havoc and attempt to fraudulently use your money."

Bolton said if a person does enter their details into a "dodgy website", acting fast was key.

"The sooner you act, the less chance scammers have to do any damage."

This is not the first time fake QR codes have been spotted around the country.

Last week Wellington City Council said parking staff had removed about a dozen fake stickers from parking meters around the city over the past couple of days.

In July, Christchurch City Council also found fake QR code stickers on several council-owned and privately-owned parking meters.

Bidgood said using debit or credit cards on the AT parking app or at parking machines was the safe option.

World.title: Birds flocking back after possums eliminated from Otago Peninsula
World.content:
Otago Peninsula celebrating being possum free Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The Otago Peninsula is cementing its reputation as a birdwatcher's delight, after it was officially declared possum free in March.

The milestone marked more than 15 years of hard mahi championed by community members, who said they were already reaping the rewards.

When Dunedin mayor Sophie Barker was growing up in Larnach Castle, it seemed like possums haunted the place.

They would shriek and growl in the cabbage trees outside her bedroom window.

"They would come into the castle at night time so I would perhaps be watching a little bit of TV, sitting on the sofa, and then lo and behold a possum appears, walking towards me and I stood on the sofa and screamed," she said.

Dunedin mayor Sophie Barker said possums would growl and shriek outside her window when she lived at Larnach Castle. Tess Brunton/RNZ

"And then I realised I actually needed to do something about this possum so I locked it in the bathroom and called my dad who had a gun, so he took care of it."

They would eat everything - her mum's roses were a prized treat, and native bird life suffered too.

Decades on, she was delighted the peninsula had been officially possum free for about six months.

"It's been incredibly inspiring. We've always been worrying about that one possum that's getting away, but the change on the peninsula's just been incredible," she said.

"I love that all of the communities worked together and become so excited and dedicated at making it possum free."

She would love to see the peninsula eventually revegetated in native bush, but for now, she's welcoming the return of more birds including tui.

Hereweka-Harbour Cone on the Peninsula. Tess Brunton/RNZ

"I didn't grow up with tui so one time I was up the top of the tower recently and there was a tui on top of a very tall tree, singing away and that was just magic."

Closer to Taiaroa Head, Edward Ellison - Ūpoko of Te Rūnanga ō Ōtakou - has lived on the family property near the marae since 1950.

"You would hear them sliding down roofs with their claws out, calling at night and just generally leaving their evidence in their spoutings and even at our doors," he said.

"So they were a very noticeable problem."

Ūpoko of Te Rūnanga ō Ōtakou Edward Ellison hoped to see more kereru return to the marae now possums have been eliminated. Tess Brunton/RNZ

But he had not noticed signs of possums near his home in a few years and, now, he was seeing more birds.

He would like to see kereru at Ōtākou Marae.

"Back in the days when the first Europeans arrived, they talk about the skies going dark with the birds, with the kereru flying overhead and the sound of them was deafening and yet I'd never seen one until actually last year, he said.

It had taken remarkable dedication, perseverance and collaboration to get the peninsula free of possums, Ellison said.

"It is really exciting and a real testament to what we can go on and do further in terms of restoring biodiversity here on the peninsula."

When freelance journalist Rob Tipa and his partner Stella first moved onto their property on the Peninsula 30 years ago, they were greeted by tangles of bramble, ivy and banana passionfruit, and chest-high grass.

They spent years clearing it, planting a mix of natives and non natives, creating a refuge for native birds.

Stella McDonald, Rob Tipa and their dog Tío Tess Brunton/RNZ

But Tipa noticed it was not just the birds enjoying the garden - possums were nibbling at his orchard and the banana passionfruit in the nearby gully.

"Every day you would walk down and you would see fruit had been stripped off the trees, most of it had been eaten out, so we figure that we probably had a much bigger possum problem than we knew about," he said.

By the time he started trapping possums about five years ago, he said they were mostly gone from the area.

He was astonished how quickly native birds have bounced back.

"We seem to see more breeding birds, younger birds, young tuis, getting to learning how to use a feeder and seeing adult tuis with their young birds is just a thrill," Tipa said.

Native bush was resilient if you gave it a chance and conservation efforts could start in your own backyard, he said.

"It's a real lesson to us what we've seen, the speed of the regrowth here, that you can create a piece of native bush out of nothing, out of a slip site," he said.

World.title: Popovic knocked back four-year Socceroos contract extension
World.content:
Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

Popovic instead signed a six-month extension during the World Cup to take the team through to the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia, which begins in January.

"It was my choice to go until the Asian Cup. Although I was offered a four-year deal, I decided to go to the Asian Cup," Popovic told journalists on Tuesday.

"And I think that is something that I think is good.

"It gives the FA the opportunity if they want to go in a different decision they can, and I'm very comfortable with the decision that's been made."

FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' Football's major governing bodies continue to fight over the failed plan by FIFA president Gianni Infantino to sell off the rights for the World Cup, with the global governing body accusing European body UEFA of a "smear campaign" against the president.

Popovic led the Socceroos to the round of 32 knockout stage of the World Cup in the United States, where the team lost to Egypt in a penalty shoot-out heartbreaker.

His side won its opening match against Türkiye, lost to the United States and drew with Paraguay before the fateful match against Egypt ended the Socceroos' dream run.

He led the youngest side at the World Cup of all 48 nations with an average of 25 years and 155 days.

Some of the Socceroos stars of the tournament have since signed transfer contracts worth up to $33 million, including Lucas Herrington (Hull City), Nestory Irankunda (Sporting Lisbon), Alessandro Circati (Benfica), Patrick Beach (Troyes) and Paul Okon-Engstler (Köln).

When asked directly whether he wanted to continue coaching the Socceroos, Popovic declined to give a direct answer, instead elaborating on his focus on fostering young talent.

"I love coaching the Socceroos," he said.

"When we qualified there was obviously 12 months before the World Cup.

"I ended up signing [his six-month contract] the last week before the first [World Cup] match, and we started this evolution of the team for 12 months without knowing whether I'd be there or not.

"I've never shied away from the expectation of results.

"But I've always had an eye on the future, and I think that was reflected in the squad we chose, the players we played and how much the team changed in 12 months."

Socceroos' World Cup story ends in heartbreak The Socceroos exited the World Cup in the cruellest possible manner, on penalties to Egypt. But the roots of the defeat could be found in the 120 minutes of play, which clearly showed where Australia must improve.

He said he was happy to make those decisions without the security of a long-term contract.

"I had no concerns about whether I signed or not and if I hadn't signed I would have been happy with what I had done and what I have left behind," he said.

"The same will be after the Asian Cup.

"I know the legacy that I will leave behind.

"And if it's someone else that takes it forward, that's fine; if it's me, great, if we agree to do this together," he said.

Popovic's decision to not take up the four-year contract offer gives him the option of pursuing a club contract now that he's been able to shop his talents through the World Cup window.

In his first press conference since returning from the World Cup, Popovic reflected on the decisions he made at the tournament and said there was little he would change.

He drew criticism from commentators for the goalkeeper substitution minutes before the penalty shoot-out against Egypt, which the Socceroos ultimately lost 4-2 when Harry Souttar and Lucas Herrington missed penalties.

Popovic introduced captain Matt Ryan, who hadn't played a minute in the World Cup, for Patrick Beach, who had been outstanding, conceding just three goals in four matches.

He said he would make the same decision again.

"There are many reasons why Matty came in," he said.

"Matty has experience; Matty saved two penalties for us in the qualifiers; Matty saved penalties for [his Spanish club team] Levante.

"Patrick Beach has not saved one penalty in any shoot-out, pretty much.

"In that moment it was very clear to me that Matty should come in.

"And like I said the next day I would have done the same thing."

The Socceroos play their first Asian Cup match against Singapore on January 9, where Popovic said he would continue his youth policy.

There will be a lot of young players probably at the Asian Cup, and that will be done without losing any expectation that I believe that we should be challenging for the Asian Cup," he said.

"Once you're there, you want to win it.

"I think that should happen for Australia."

The team has two friendlies later this month against the might of five-time world champions Brazil in Townsville and Brisbane.

Popovic said the team would have a chance to play another round of matches during the November friendly window, most likely in the Middle East.

World.title: Cricket Australia agrees to bring private investment to Big Bash
World.content:
Cricket Australia has agreed to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

The Cricket Australia (CA) board made the announcement on Tuesday, with the sale process of the Renegades to be the first venture into bringing private investment into the franchise T20 league.

Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation The Big Bash League is set to look like it never has before as Cricket Australia prepares to welcome private ownership to the competition.

CA is hoping the Renegades will play under new ownership for the 2027/28 Big Bash season.

Depending on the success of the Renegades sale, CA said in a statement on Tuesday that it would "consider taking other clubs to market under a self-determination model that gives each State member the ability to assess the optimal pathway for its own club and community".

CA chair Mike Baird said the decision was a major moment for cricket in Australia.

"Beginning the sales process for the Renegades allows us to take the first step in a self-determination model for our members and represents a defining moment for the game," he said.

"Importantly, CA and its members will maintain control over the most significant aspects of Australian Cricket operations, including international scheduling, player availability, the Big Bash Leagues' salary caps, branding proposals as well as the reserve price for a licence to operate that must be achieved, and approval of investors."

The move to bring private investment into the Big Bash Leagues has been debated for months.

CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said in May that private investment was "inevitable", and privatisation was thrust into the spotlight when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Renegades in June.

Baird said inviting private investment would allow cricket to grow at every level of the game.

"Cricket Australia and its state members are united in our commitment to investing in and growing the BBL and WBBL, and to advancing the interests of cricket at every level," he said.

"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash Leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game, accelerate growth and ensuring we can keep investing in community cricket and grassroots participation, domestic and international pathways and the elite level.

"This is a significant decision that has involved an enormous amount of analysis, discussion and collaboration over many months. I'd like to thank all involved as we move to what we believe is the best way to secure cricket's future in this country, strengthen the Big Bash and protect our standing on the global stage."

World.title: Lion turns down monster, premiership Bulldog call time
World.content:
Brisbane Lions premiership hero Zac Bailey has re-signed with the reigning premiers, ending a long-running saga about whether he would move to Adelaide.

In an added subplot to this Saturday night's semifinal between the Lions and the Crows at the Gabba, Bailey has turned down a monster offer from Adelaide.

The restricted free agent has penned a new eight-year deal to remain with the Lions until the end of 2034.

A two-time All-Australian, Bailey has enjoyed another outstanding season with 31 goals and averaged a career-high 21.7 disposals.

The 26-year-old's call comes as the Lions prepare to farewell star veteran Lachie Neale, who is expected to move to Collingwood during the trade period.

Bailey's signature comes just three days after the Lions were unexpectedly smashed by Sydney in the qualifying final at the SCG.

Western Bulldogs AFL premiership hero Tom Liberatore retires

Western Bulldogs stalwart and premiership hero Tom Liberatore has retired, drawing a stellar AFL career to a close.

Liberatore, 34, has been a heart-and-soul player for the Bulldogs since he was drafted as a father-son selection in 2010, including playing a pivotal role in the breakthrough 2016 premiership.

Loading Instagram content

But the son of club great and Brownlow medallist Tony Liberatore battled with injury and concussion in recent years, playing just 11 AFL matches this year.

Liberatore retires with 268 AFL games, 93 goals, a premiership and a Charles Sutton Medal as the Bulldogs' 2014 best and fairest to his name.

"This club and its community have been such a huge part of my life," Liberatore said in a club statement.

"I'm so fortunate to have lived out my dream for 16 years, from watching my old man play for the club to being part of a premiership that meant so much to all of our fans and to the western suburbs, it's been a real privilege.

"I still love being here and competing each week but it's time for me to step aside, spend more time with my family and friends and support this great club from the stands.

"I've built lifelong friendships with many teammates through the years, that's what means the most to me.

"I'm really proud of where the club is going and excited about what the group is capable of moving forward. I'm looking forward to watching on with a beer in hand."

Liberatore's retirement means captain Marcus Bontempelli is the only surviving Bulldog from the 2016 premiership team.

Marshall demands trade from Saints, Duursma wants to leave Roos

Meanwhile, Rowan Marshall is demanding a trade from St Kilda, a year after Geelong tried to lure the experienced ruckman.

Rowan Marshall wants to be traded away from St Kilda. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

Marshall is contracted at the Saints until the end of next season, with the Cats and Essendon his strongest suitors.

He tried to leave for Geelong at the end of last season but has not yet nominated his preferred new club.

Cats coach Chris Scott was tight-lipped on his club's prospects of signing the 30-year-old.

"If I was [interested], I wouldn't tell you," Scott told reporters on Tuesday.

"It's an unfortunate situation. I think everyone would like us all to be a bit more open, but I think it's got to the stage now [where] the communication should be driven by the players themselves.

"I don't think it's our place to sort of speak on their behalf, so it's probably a question better directed at him."

Scott said the fact Marshall remained contracted at the Saints complicated matters.

Marshall played 21 games this season for the Saints, who opted for ex-Carlton recruit Tom de Koning as the club's first-choice ruck.

St Kilda said it would consider its options ahead of the trade period, which opens on October 5.

"Marshall has not nominated a preferred destination at this stage, with the club making clear that any trade will need to be in the best interests of the St Kilda Football Club," the statement said.

Meanwhile, the fourth pick from the 2023 draft, Zane Duursma, has told North Melbourne he wants to move to Melbourne.

Loading...

The Demons have long been linked to the 21-year-old, who has played 38 games for the Kangaroos in three seasons.

Duursma has resisted signing a fresh three-year contract offer from the Roos, who last week sacked veteran coach Alastair Clarkson.

The Demons are understood to have separately told former captain Jack Viney that he is welcome to explore a trade after an injury-cruelled season.

Viney, 32, played only one game — in Melbourne's wildcard finals loss to Carlton — after having pre-season Achilles surgery and then suffering back and toe injuries.

Viney, a premiership player in 2021, is contracted until the end of 2028.

AAP

World.title: Dutchman who knocked de Minaur out of US Open stages epic comeback
World.content:
Dutch tennis player Botic van de Zandschulp saved match point to avoid losing in straight sets, before staging a huge comeback to advance to the US Open quarterfinals.

The 30-year-old, who downed Australian Alex de Minaur in a second-round upset at Flushing Meadows, was on the brink of defeat against Frenchman Arthur Gea but recovered to make it to a grand slam quarterfinal for the second time in his career.

Gea, who got into the main draw tournament when 2022 runner-up Casper Ruud pulled out with a back injury, was trying to become the first lucky loser to make a men's singles grand slam quarterfinal.

After winning the opening two sets, Gea had match point in the third-set tiebreaker, but van de Zandschulp saved that, then staged his comeback to claim a 3-6, 6-7(0), 7-6(7), 7-6(3), 6-4 victory in 5 hours, 13 minutes.

It was the fourth-longest match in US Open history.

"I think this is probably better than the first quarterfinal I made here," van de Zandschulp said, referring to his other US Open quarterfinal appearance in 2021.

"It hasn't sunk in yet, but I think tomorrow it's going to be a great feeling."

Zverev through to quarterfinals in straight sets

Men's top seed Alexander Zverev has marched into the quarterfinals at Flushing Meadows with a 6-2 6-2 7-6(3) straight-sets win over Italian Luciano Darderi.

Germany's Alexander Zverev defeated Italy's Luciano Darderi in their round of 16 match at the US Open. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

It is a second consecutive straight-sets win for the German, after opening his grand slam with back-to-back five-setters in New York.

Zverev, who claimed his maiden grand slam title at this year's French Open, was expecting a much later night in New York, but was able to wrap up his victory before midnight, local time.

"I think after 10 hours on court, I just maybe found my rhythm a little bit better, which is helpful because the first two matches were really not great level," Zverev said.

"I think I'm going in the right direction, moving forward in the right direction."

Zverev will face van de Zandschulp in the quarterfinals.

Number 28 seed Alexander Blockx beat 24th seed Francisco Cerundolo 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5 to become the first man from Belgium to reach the US Open quarterfinals, where he will play Karen Khachanov.

Khachanov also needed five sets to advance to the quarterfinal stage, downing American 14th seed Learner Tien 7-5, 4-6, 6-7(6), 6-1, 6-4.

ABC/AP/Reuters

World.title: Aussie Maya Joint caught up in handshake snub at US Open
World.content:
Maya Joint's US Open has come to an end with defeat in the third round of the women's doubles in New York, but the Aussie's exit came with an unexpected controversy.

Joint and partner Hao-Ching Chan, who eliminated Serena and Venus Williams in the opening round of the grand slam, lost their third round match in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4, to Su-wei Hsieh and Jelena Ostapenko.

But the controversy came after match point, when Chan and Hsieh, both from Taiwan, did not shake hands at the end.

When match point was won, Ostapenko screamed towards Chan's coaching box before celebrating with her teammate. Despite Ostapenko's boisterous and vocal act following the victory, Chan had no issue shaking her hand at the net.

But once that was done, Chan walked off the court without looking at Hsieh.

The pair reportedly have a decade-long feud that stems from Hsieh claiming the Chinese Taipei Tennis Association gave greater resources and funding to Chan.

The loss brings an end to an eventful grand slam for Joint.

She advanced to the second round of the women's singles draw after defeating Liudmila Samsonova in the first round, but fell to ninth-seeded Ukrainian Elina Svitolina in a competitive three-set match.

In the women's doubles, Joint and Chan staged a huge comeback in a 10-point tiebreaker to defeat the Williams sisters in front of a packed crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Joint and Chan would then defeat the team of Tamara Korpatsch and Nicole Fossa Huergo in the second round.

Mixed emotions as Andreeva embraces injured idol after US Open win

US Open fans have witnessed a display of sportsmanship as Mirra Andreeva tended to and consoled an injured Anastasia Potapova as the fifth seed won their fourth-round match.

Potapova jarred her knee as she lost the first point of what turned out to be their final game on Louis Armstrong Stadium, prompting Andreeva to rush to the other end of the court to check on her.

She helped the 24th seed up and Potapova was able to limp to her bench, where Andreeva asked if someone could bring her ice.

The French Open champion finished off the next three points for a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 victory that sent her to the quarterfinals in Flushing Meadows for the first time, jogging around the net again for a warm embrace.

"It's not the perfect end to the match," 19-year-old Andreeva said.

Potapova appeared to be tearing up as Andreeva came around the net for a long embrace after the final point.

Potapova represents Austria but was born in Russia and still played under that flag when she won the junior Wimbledon championship in 2016.

"For me, Nastya, she was always like a prodigy," Andreeva said of her 25-year-old opponent.

"She came on tour early. She also had a lot of wins. I also remember we were all watching and cheering for her when she won juniors Wimbledon title. I remember watching that match.

"For me, she was always, like, a little star that I was kind of always looking at."

Potapova (right) appeared to be tearing up as the pair embraced after match point. (Getty Images: Pete Staples/USTA)

Potapova won their first meeting on tour in 2022 but Andreeva has won the past four, preventing Potapova from reaching her first grand slam quarterfinal.

"First, she just beat me. So after, I just kind of knew that she's a tough player to play, but at the same time, she was so nice," Andreeva said.

"Then since then we would practice together, and just like that, the more you see each other, the more you spend time together, then you just talk about everything, discuss everything. Then, just like that, I feel like we have a good connection off the court."

Elsewhere, Qinwen Zheng mounted another extraordinary fightback to upset six-time major winner Iga Świątek and reach the quarterfinals.

Qinwen Zheng is the first qualifier since 2021 to make it this far in the women's draw. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng has become Flushing ‌Meadows' most entertaining escape artist this year, coming back from a 0-5 deficit in the deciding set against third-round foe Madison Keys.

She let the first five games slip through her fingers in 20 minutes against 2022 champion Świątek before digging in, and she collapsed to the court with her hands ⁠in her face after sealing the win on the fourth match ‌point.

China's Olympic champion is the first qualifier ​since Emma Raducanu in 2021 ‌to reach the quarterfinals of the women's draw, as she battles back from a chronic elbow injury that had stunted her career.

Two-time winner Naomi Osaka was summarily swept aside by second seed Elena Rybakina, who won 6-1, 6-4 in just over an hour.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 champion, beat 18-year-old Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 in an ​all-American clash to decide the final women's quarterfinalist.

Gauff will face Andreeva, and Rybakina will take on Zheng. On the other side of the draw, third seed Jessica Pegula faces Emma Navarro, while world number one Aryna Sabalenka is up against Wimbledon champions Linda Noskova.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Everything you need to know ahead of NFL Melbourne
World.content:
American Football will roll into the MCG for a regular-season NFL match for the first time on Friday.

The San Francisco 49ers will take on the Los Angeles Rams, who are the nominal home team for the game.

This will be the first regular-season NFL game ever hosted in Australia, although American Football matches have taken place in the country before.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the game?

Davante Adams (left) will look to continue his excellent form into the new year. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The game takes place on Friday morning AEST, with kick-off at 10:35am.

That is what time kick-off will be in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, that is a 10:05am kick-off. In Western Australia, kick-off will be 8:35am.

This is to cater for the Thursday night television audience in the United States, with a New York kick-off time of 8:35pm, while in LA the game will get underway at 5:35pm.

If you are going to the game, the gates open at 7am local time, with access to the Yarra Park precinct, which the NFL has dubbed the NFL Stadium Campus.

There will be food, entertainment, sponsor activations and fan activities to keep punters busy once they get inside.

Who is playing?

The 49ers and the Rams will meet in their season opener. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers are the two teams who are set to play in this historic clash.

The Rams are the home team and come into the season as one of the favourites for this year's Super Bowl, with a stacked offence and miserly defence.

If you think the Rams sound familiar but the LA bit is confusing you, that's because the team has moved around a bit.

The team was formed in 1936 as the Cleveland Rams, moved to LA in 1946, but then shifted to St Louis in 1995, where they stayed for 20 years.

In 2015, the Rams moved back to Los Angeles.

You don't need a hat like this, but I'm sure it will help. (Getty Images: MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Keith Birmingham)

They are two-time Super Bowl Champions, winning their most recent in 2021. They play at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.

The 49ers have always expected to reach the play-offs at an absolute minimum and will think they can do so again, despite a season beset by injuries last year.

Formed in 1944, the 49ers have always been based in the Bay area, although they currently play outside San Francisco at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.

They have won five Super Bowls, but have not won one since 1994, despite appearing in three Super Bowls since then, most recently in 2023.

How can I watch?

The game will be available to watch in Australia on Fox Sports/Kayo or on free-to-air on Channel Seven or 7Plus.

Coverage starts from 10am AEST.

Are tickets still available?

Want to join the Rams fans? There's still time. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Greg Fiore)

If you'd rather watch the game live, as of Monday, there are still tickets available, both standing and seated, for the game at the MCG.

You can purchase the tickets via Ticketmaster.

Why is the NFL playing in Australia?

Heading into the 2026 season, there have been 62 regular-season NFL games played away from the USA.

Starting in 2005 with Mexico City, the NFL has gradually expanded its global reach, with games in nine different cities so far, with two more added in 2026.

Melbourne, Paris and Rio de Janeiro join London, Mexico City, Toronto, Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich, São Paulo and Madrid in hosting regular-season matches.

The idea is to spread the gospel and increase the global presence of a league that has no international competition outside of America.

MCG joins illustrious list

The MCG adds itself to an exclusive list of stadiums. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Morgan Hancock)

Here's a pub quiz stat for you — the MCG will become the fifth stadium to host an NFL game and the opening/closing ceremony of an Olympic Games.

The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum (1932, 1984), Berlin's Olympiastadion (1936), London's Wembley (1940) and the Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro (2016) have all hosted an Olympic Games opening ceremony, as did the MCG in 1956.

The Stade de France (closing ceremony at Paris 2024) will join it on that list when it hosts its first game later in the season.

Given the Rams are the home team, they will now have hosted matches at two different Olympic stadiums, having played at the Coliseum between 1946-1979 and 2016-2019.

Perhaps less surprisingly, the MCG is the first stadium to have hosted a Cricket World Cup final and an NFL regular-season game, so there is that.

At 100,022, the stadium has the largest capacity of any that will be used by the league this season.

Players to watch: Rams

Matthew Stafford had a career-best year in 2025. (Getty Images: Kevin Sabitus)

Quarterback Matt Stafford led the league with 4,707 passing yards and 46 passing touchdowns last season, with just eight interceptions.

That was one reason why the Rams' offence was the best in the entire league, averaging 30.5 points per game last season.

He has two elite wide receivers in his armory in Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, who was rated as the fourth-best player in the entire league by the NFL cohort.

The potential issue is that Stafford is now 38 years old and has historically struggled to back up productive passing seasons in the past.

Defensively, Myles Garrett was recently polled as the number one player in the NFL by his peers, and it's easy to see why.

According to the NFL players, Myles Garrett is the best player around. (Getty Images: Ric Tapia)

The 30-year-old defensive end led the league in sacks (23) and tackles for loss (33) last season for the Browns and his acquisition fills a gaping hole that was ruthlessly exposed as the Rams struggled down the stretch in 2025.

It's not just Garrett who has come in, though. The Rams have recruited two elite cornerbacks in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson.

They will also welcome back Super Bowl-winning defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who has come out of retirement to lead the defensive line one last time.

Players to watch: 49ers

Two of the 49ers best players either side of the ball; defensive end Nick Bosa and tight end George Kittle, are coming off serious injuries from last season, so all eyes will be on how they front up when they suit back up this year.

Brock Purdy will want to iron out his interceptions this season. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

On the defensive side, the 49ers pass rush is a genuine concern, especially if Bosa can't return from the ACL injury that ended his season, which means former Dallas Cowboy Osa Odighizuwa may need to really up his game from defensive tackle

Offensively, Brock Purdy will be desperate to stay fit for long enough to really get into a rhythm this season.

Last year the young quarterback started just nine games and managed a TD/INT ratio of 20/10. That's too many interceptions for an elite quarterback and, given the addition of quality wide receivers Mike Evans and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling, the Niners fans will hope he can find his accuracy.

Given all those new toys for Purdy to play with, running back Christian McCaffrey shouldn't need to be thrown to as many times as he was last year.

Christian McCaffrey got through a mountain of work in 2025. (Getty Images: Ezra Shaw)

The running back had an astonishing 102 receptions — the sixth most of any player in the league — for 924 yards and seven touchdowns last season.

That's in addition to his day job of running with the ball, where he had 1,202 yards from 311 rushes for 10 touchdowns, the eighth most rushing yards of anyone in the league.

His backup is likely to be Kaelon Black, so keep an eye on him as to whether he can carry some of that running load this season.

World.title: Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
World.content:
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.

Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.

The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.

BBL privatisation 'inevitable': CA Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg says private investment in the Big Bash League is "inevitable" and waiting for too long could mean "we've missed the boat" as more competitions pop up around the world.

It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.

However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.

The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.

The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.

This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.

Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.

BBL privatisation became more of a reality when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades franchise earlier this year. (AAP Image: James Ross)

But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.

South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.

New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.

Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.

Cricket Australia believes the privatisation will allow the BBL to keep up with other domestic T20 competitions around the world, such as India's IPL. (AP)

In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.

Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.

It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.

In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.

Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

World.title: V'landys accuses NRL players of 'not telling truth' on rule confusion
World.content:
Peter V'landys has accused players of "not telling the truth" about set-restart confusion, as a survey of finals captains revealed ongoing uncertainty around the ruck.

The topic of set restarts is set to dominate the NRL finals, after Melbourne star Harry Grant claimed widespread frustration from players at the weekend.

The Melbourne captain declared most no longer knew what constituted a fast or slow play-the-ball, and the NRL needed to decide between being rugby league or touch football.

An AAP survey of captains and representatives at Monday's finals launch backed up Grant's claims, with six of the sides indicating they were still not entirely clear on what ruck speed referees wanted.

According to V'landys, Storm skipper Harry Grant (pictured) has 'got it wrong' when it comes to set-restarts. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Also raised by players was the fact there is no chance to ask for clarification, given the game rolls on quickly with a set restart.

But V'landys disagreed, pointing to the fact there are only two reasons for set restarts and players had become more compliant for offside ones.

"I don't buy that," ARL Commission chairman V'landys said.

"The wrestling's got to go. The fans did not like the wrestling, they didn't like people slowing down the ruck speed. And we've accommodated that.

"The players know when they're trying to control the ruck speed.

" I think that they're not telling the truth if they believe when they're giving a six again, they didn't know what it was for. I mean, I think it's pretty obvious. "

Set restarts increased dramatically over the first half of the season, before dropping off through the State of Origin period and rising again in recent weeks.

The rise at the start of the year coincided with the NRL expanding the area in which they can be awarded to from 60 metres of the field to 80.

V'landys indicated they would not be repealed next season, rejecting Grant's claims there was confusion this year.

"I have the ultimate respect for Harry, and Harry's an absolute ornament of the game, but he's got this one wrong," V'landys said.

"When you look at the facts, the ruck speed is still the same as it was last year. It's around 3.5 seconds, and it remains that way.

Sharks co-captain Cameron McInnes (pictured) backed up Grant's viewpoint over the players' confusion. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Some teams try to take advantage of the ruck and slow the ruck down … we make no apology that we're going to keep the ruck speed the same for both teams.

"The raw numbers don't back up what Harry is saying."

The majority of club representatives surveyed on Monday did not blame referees, but suggested there was still some grey area around ruck interpretation.

"With some of the six agains, who knows what they are for," Cronulla co-captain Cameron McInnes said.

"I just think about a fan watching at home … you just see them and think 'what was that for? It was like the tackle before'.

"That's a problem."

Warriors captain Roger Tuivasa-Sheck (pictured) is concerned that a faster game will lead to more injuries for the players. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Asked if he shared the same confusion, McInnes suggested he did.

"I get the clear as day ones where guys are taking the piss … but then there are flops and re-grips that don't get called as well," he said.

"I don't know what their mindset is, but there will be some at the start of the game that is given a six again, and others that are not."

Some players at the NRL finals launch also raised concerns around whether a faster game had prompted an increased injury toll.

"I feel like it's not a clear understanding [of the interpretation]," injured Warriors veteran Roger Tuivasa-Sheck said.

"As players we understand they want a faster and more entertaining game, but they're risking that with the number of injuries every team has.

"That's what they have to weigh up.

"Yes we're building a very entertaining game and people love the product. But at the same time you lose all these big players out."

AAP

Tech.title: Xiaomi’s wide foldable promises more power than Samsung’s
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Xiaomi is the latest manufacturer to release a short, wide foldable phone, in the week Apple is expected to do the same. I got to try the 18 Fold behind closed doors at IFA last week, and while it looks and feels similar enough to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, superior specs make it feel like the phone I wish Samsung had made.

The 18 Fold is Xiaomi’s first book-style foldable since 2024’s Mix Fold 4, but the company has followed Huawei and Samsung in moving to a short, squat design. Xiaomi’s phone goes further though: it’s both shorter and wider than Samsung’s, with a roughly 1.4:1 aspect ratio on both the 7.58-inch inner and 5.38-inch outer screens — almost an exact match for both international paper sizes and IMAX screens, meaning this may be the one phone capable of playing The Odyssey without letterboxing.

The 5.38-inch has generously rounded corners. Both screens have almost the same aspect ratio. It makes the Z Fold 8 look positively tall and slender.

In practice, this still feels similar to the Z Fold 8 though. It’s compact and pocketable when closed and the cover screen is comfortable to use single-handed — though I expect it too will have issues with some apps running awkwardly on the short screen. When open this is a natural form factor for watching movies or reading ebooks, if perhaps slightly less well suited to multitasking work, though Xiaomi still includes both split-screen apps and floating windows with multitasking in mind.

Where Samsung may have the edge is build quality. The 18 Fold looks great, available in black, white, or this striking red, plus a pink ceramic special edition that the company is only making 1,500 of. But it’s slightly heavier and thicker than the Z Fold 8, and Xiaomi hasn’t announced any IP rating for it at all. There’s also the crease, which to my eye feels more obvious than on this year’s Samsung foldables. Oppo remains the only company to have all-but eliminated the foldable crease, in its Find N6 foldable, and I’ll be fascinated to see how close Apple gets to matching that this week.

I do love this deep red finish. The triple camera is welcome, even if its specs still lag behind Xiaomi’s slab flagships. This is a little thicker than the Z Fold 8, but still fairly slender. Xiaomi hasn’t shown off any foldable software flourishes you won’t find elsewhere.

While my brief time with the 18 Fold was focused on getting to grips with the form factor, the phone arguably stands out more for its specs. For one, this is the first Xiaomi phone powered by its own Xring O3 chipset, which promises Snapdragon 8 Elite-level performance. It includes the debut of Arm’s Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU, which brings with it mobile-first support for Arm’s DLSS-style graphics acceleration on Android.

It’s not just the chip though. The 6,000mAh silicon-carbon battery is substantially larger than the Samsung phone’s 4,800mAh, with support for 67W wired charging and 50W wireless. The two OLED displays deliver up to 4,000 nits of peak brightness. Most importantly there’s a triple rear camera bolstered by Xiaomi’s long-running Leica partnership, with a 200-megapixel main camera using a 1/1.56-inch-type sensor, a 50-megapixel 3.5x periscope telephoto, and a 50-megapixel ultrawide.

I really loved the Galaxy Z Fold 8 when I reviewed it, surprising myself with how quickly I adapted to the new design. My biggest hesitation was that it lacked the triple camera I’d expect from any phone approaching $2,000 in price. By fixing that, while improving on the battery and displays, Xiaomi has made what could become my pick of the foldables on the market right now — though the lack of IP rating does give me pause.

We don’t yet know if the 18 Fold will ever launch outside China.

Of course, that foldable market is about to change dramatically if Apple announces the foldable iPhone we’re all expecting it to tomorrow. In the meantime, Xiaomi has laid down the gauntlet — at least in China. The 18 Fold is available to preorder there from ¥10,999 (about $1,600), with official sales on September 10th, but Xiaomi hasn’t yet confirmed whether or not the phone will ever see an international launch.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Tech.title: First Xiaomi, then the world: why Arm might give phone gaming a huge graphics boost
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

China is getting first crack at a British technology that might change how mobile games are made and played. Today, the Xiaomi 18 Fold launches in mainland China with an Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX graphics processor inside its custom Xring O3 chip. What’s so special about that? After five years of development, Arm now has an AI gaming graphics accelerator inside its GPU.

By following Nvidia’s playbook, Arm-powered phones are about to have PC-like technologies to make games run faster, at higher resolution, with advanced lighting techniques, all without using more power than they do today. The jagged edges you see in the mobile versions of popular games might begin to go away.

And these advancements won’t just be locked to Chinese phones. The chips, devices, and games are already inbound.

“You will be able to buy it; you will be able to get it in phones next year, you will be able to get it in other types of larger screen devices, whether that be tablets or Chromebooks,” Arm’s Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI, tells The Verge in an interview.

While he can’t say which other devices will contain the Mali G2-Ultra NX, he hints that some of Google’s upcoming Googlebooks might use this graphics tech as well.

“We think it’s going to be huge,” Bergey tells me.

DLSS for Android

There are two ways to look at Arm’s new Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX. One is that it’s stronger than prior mobile GPUs, period, with an alleged 85-percent performance increase over the GPU that Xiaomi was using previously, and a 14 percent increase over Arm’s previous flagship in “non-AI gaming.”

But the other, more important way is that it enables a suite of hardware-accelerated graphical techniques that sound very similar to Nvidia’s DLSS, including AI upscaling (where it imagines a higher-resolution image), frame generation (where it generates new “fake” frames between existing ones), and even ray reconstruction like Nvidia’s DLSS 4.5.

“This really is about bringing Tensor-like capabilities into the GPU shader,” Bergey tells us. Image: Arm

Arm is calling all of these techniques “neural graphics,” but it doesn’t mean quite the same thing as when Nvidia uses that term — we’re not talking about enhancing faces by reimagining how light and shadow work, at least not just yet.

Note: Games won’t necessarily feel four times faster even if they look that way. Image: Arm

Instead, these improvements are about speed, offering what Arm claims is up to four times the framerate when “Neural Super Sampling,” “Neural Frame Rate Upscaling” and “Neural Denoising” are all applied simultaneously, because each technique lets the system do less work rendering actual pixels and frames, counting on AI to fill in the rest.

Note that games likely won’t feel four times faster, though, even if they look that way. Half of the boost is because your phone will imagine new frames between existing ones — and when Nvidia, AMD, and Intel do “frame generation,” it typically comes with the cost of additional latency.

Regardless, these techniques won’t all arrive immediately. “The first titles will largely be super sampling,” says Bergey, with frame gen coming in early 2027 and denoising “soon after that.”

But when you put them together, he says a phone can now genuinely play an experience like this Neural Dawn technology demo, below — and without draining your battery fast. “It might be like, hey, you can now play 1080p, 60 frames per second for three hours,” Bergey tells me. “In the past, it was 30 minutes.”

With the Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, which pairs Arm’s GPU with a larger battery, screen, and surface area for cooling, may offer even more performance. The Chinese company is showing off 3.2K resolution at 120 frames per second.

Bergey says that an entire phone with these chips will consume no more than 2.5 watts, with only 1.5 watts allotted to the GPU. “That’s basically what you want for real sustained gaming where it’s not getting warm in your phone, you’re not like ‘Oh, where’s my charger,’ that kind of thing,” says Bergey.

Or, he says, device and chipset makers can run this GPU at lower wattage to last longer. It’s not just for gaming phones: “This is not overclocking, this is mainstream,” he says. “This is about AI replacing traditional rendering; anywhere you can use it, you will use it,” he says.

Xiaomi claims its flagship Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, with the same Xring O3 chip, can play games at 3.2K resolution and 120fps. Image: Xiaomi

It’s not just for premium phones and tablets, either: “While Mali G2-Ultra NX targets flagship smartphones, neural graphics will also be available across the Premium and Pro configurations, bringing the technology to a broader range of mobile segments and tiers.”

Arm isn’t the only one attempting to push these speed-boosting PC technologies into the mobile realm. The developers of the graphically intensive Stellar Blade, for example, recently revealed they’re making their game run at 60fps on the Nintendo Switch 2 by using both Nvidia’s DLSS and a version of AMD’s frame generation technique. The Switch 2 has an Arm-based mobile chip too, though it contains a custom Nvidia GPU.

Like with the most advanced versions of Nvidia, AMD, and Intel’s techniques, game developers will need to integrate Arm’s features into their games, though participating game engines like Unreal Engine and Unity can help. Bergey doesn’t think it’s a switch gamers will be able to flip for just any game they like.

Arm’s partners. Image: Arm

Where Winds Meet, Infinity Nikki and Arena Breakout: Infinite are the first three games confirmed to take advantage of Arm’s new graphics accelerator, and Bergey tells us more games are on the way. Some will be announced in the coming weeks, he says — he’s just not allowed to reveal them quite yet.

Tech.title: Audi’s new A2 E-tron is its most affordable and efficient EV yet
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When shopping for an electric vehicle, affordability is becoming a more common trait. But affordable and energy efficient is truly a rare breed. Often you have to sacrifice one for the other. Want something affordable? Great, here’s a range loser. Want something that goes the distance? Be ready to pay the price.

Surprisingly, here comes Audi to split the difference. The German automaker’s new A2 E-tron compact crossover is inexpensive, starting at just £32,200 (about $45,000). And it absolutely impresses with an ultra low drag coefficient and a range of battery and drivetrain options that, when configured correctly, can produce a range of up to 401 miles.

Unfortunately for us Yanks, this rear-wheel drive compact car is just for the European market for now. But perhaps Audi will eventually see the error of its ways, or Americans will get their heads out of their tailpipes long enough to see the real advantages of a highly efficient, compact EV with an Audi badge.

Previous Next









1 / 6

Efficient is often synonymous with aerodynamic, and the A2 E-tron certainly confirms that. Flush door handles, cool air intakes, a fully enclosed underbody, and gap reducers around the wheel arches help reduce the drag coefficient down to 0.24, a first for Audi. Another first is bidirectional charging, which will help support vehicle-t0-load via an outlet in the trunk, or vehicle-to-home with the right compatible DC wall box.

With the right motor and battery setup, the A2 E-tron consumes just 12.8 kWh per 62 miles (100 km), while the real mile-eater of the lineup manages up to 401 miles (645 km) on the European WLTP cycle. Inside, the A2 E-tron features a standard curved MMI panoramic display that combines an 11.9 inch digital gauge cluster with a 12.8 inch center touch screen.

Previous Next











1 / 7

There’s also plenty of clever storage thanks to a Fidlock magnetic fastening system that allows owners to click things like cupholders and charging cable bags into dedicated points around the cabin and trunk. Cyclists may be familiar with the tech that can keep their water bottles attached to their bike without a cage, but Audi says this is the first time it’s making an appearance in a production car.

While Audi gave up on its EVs-or-bust pledge last year, the automaker is leaving the door open for a mix of gas, hybrid, and electrification. The A2 may not be appearing alongside its brethren like the impressive S6 Sportback E-tron at the dealership anytime soon, but nothing is set in stone.

Images by Audi

Tech.title: Six years later, Sony revisits its legendary XM4 headphones
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Six years ago Sony and Bose were in the middle of a noise-canceling battle, with each new model of headphones better than the last. In the fall of 2020, Sony released the WH-1000XM4 headphones to wide acclaim. They sat atop best headphones lists for years, thanks to their great sound, competitive ANC, and compact size, until they went out of stock. Now Sony has brought them back, with minor improvements, as the WH-1000XM4C.

The XM4C look identical to the original XM4 (although they now have a lavender option), with the same hinge design and ability to fold up. It’s a compact design that Sony moved away from when it released the XM5 in 2022, and then returned to (although not quite as compact) with the XM6. But it’s not just the look that’s returned. The XM4C still use the same QN1 processing chip and four microphones for ANC. That design is showing its age: The XM5 still used the QN1, but had eight mics. Last year’s XM6 have 12, plus the new QN3 chip.

In addition to the standard white and black, the XM4C will be available in lavender. Image: Sony

Sony did update the XM4C’s sound profile to bring it in line with current models, and the headphones have a 10-band EQ in the Headphones app, instead of the 5-band on the XM4, plus a gaming preset. The XM4C also support Bluetooth 6 instead of 5. Surprisingly, the battery performance on the new headphones is slightly worse. Sony claims the XM4C get up to 27 hours of use with ANC on as opposed to 30 hours previously. Not a huge difference, and still more than enough for a cross-country trip.

The XM4C will be available later this fall for $300, which is $50 cheaper than the XM4 when they first came out (and $100 cheaper than the XM6 are now), but more than they could be found for before being discontinued.

I have loved the Sony XM4 since they came out, and still have my pair hanging on the side of my desk. Beyond nostalgia, though, I’m confused why they’re coming back. A review sample of the XM4C arrived at my door while I was writing this, so some deeper investigation will be coming soon. But the headphones industry has moved forward in the past six years, and I’m not sure there’s a need to go back. And the XM5, while they don’t fold up as nicely as the XM4C, are excellent headphones and currently available for $200 (though that price may be an effort to clear out inventory ahead of the XM4C).

Alongside the XM4C, Sony released the next generation of two of its less-expensive midrange and entry-level headphone lines: the WH-CH730N and WH-CH530. They both get the same 10-band EQ upgrade and gaming EQ preset as the XM4C, and the CH730N will now fold up into a more compact form.

The entry-level CH530 come in six different colors. Image: Sony The $180 CH730N offer ANC with battery life up to 50 hours. Image: Sony

The two headphones also get a boost to battery life according to Sony: The CH730N get up to 50 hours with ANC, and the CH530 get up to 55 hours (there’s no ANC on the CH530). A new safe mode in the app allows a user to limit the max volume output of the headphones. It’s a nice addition for parents looking to protect their kids’ hearing, although there’s no way to lock the limit once it’s been set.

The WH-CH530 come in black, cobalt, mint green, white, pink, and coral and cost $70. For $180, you can get the WH-CN730N in black, blue, oat, white, or pink. Both headphones are available now.

The Hello Kitty headphones will be available in pink, of course. Image: Sony

Sony is also doing a partnership with Hello Kitty. Bundles include headphones — the WH-1000XM6, WH-CH730N, or WH-CH530 available in black or pink — a Hello Kitty-shaped carrying pouch, and Hello Kitty-branded bag. The bundles will be available in limited supply later this year on the Sony website only.

Tech.title: EcoFlow makes the miniature power station even smaller
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you’re in the market for a tiny power station that punches well above its size and weight then have a look at EcoFlow’s new fourth-generation River series.

The River 260 Gen4 features a 256Wh capacity battery while the 520 Gen4 packs in 512Wh — storing about 2.5x and 5x the energy of the largest airline-approved power banks, respectively. Better yet, the batteries are built using longer-lasting LFP chemistry that’s far less volatile. The River 260 Gen4 features four USB ports, and 300W of max continuous output delivered out its lone AC jack. The River 500 Gen4 features the same USB port selection but offers a pair of AC jacks good for 500W of continuous output.

Both of EcoFlow’s Gen4 power stations feature class-leading energy density that cuts both the weight and size, making these power stations lighter and more compact than similarly-specced competition. That makes them ideal for an overnight camping trip or photo shoot in the literal field. The EcoFlow 520 Gen4 is powerful enough to keep a standard US fridge running for about 4 hours during a blackout.

EcoFlow’s River 520 Gen4 can power a fridge much larger than the one pictured. Image: EcoFlow EcoFlow’s River 260 Gen4 has just one AC outlet with only 300W out, but all the same USB ports. Image: EcoFlow

Here’s a quick comparison to show just how much energy these remarkably small power stations are packing, starting with the River 520 Gen4:

Power Station Capacity (Wh) Dimensions (W × D × H) Volume (Liters) Weight Volumetric Energy Density (Wh/L) EcoFlow RIVER 520 Gen4 512 Wh 13.9 × 17.7 × 22.9 cm 5.63 L 4.6 kg (10.1 lbs) 90.9 Wh/L EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max 512 Wh 27.0 × 26.0 × 19.6 cm 13.76 L 6.1 kg (13.4 lbs) 37.2 Wh/L Anker 535 512 Wh 29.2 × 18.8 × 25.1 cm 13.78 L 7.6 kg (16.8 lbs) 37.2 Wh/L Bluetti AC50B 448 Wh 28.0 × 20.0 × 22.0 cm 12.32 L 6.7 kg (14.8 lbs) 36.4 Wh/L

And here’s how the River 260 Gen4 compares to some of the main competition:

Power Station Capacity (Wh) Dimensions (W × D × H) Volume (Liters) Weight Volumetric Energy Density (Wh/L) EcoFlow RIVER 260 Gen4 256 Wh 13.9 × 17.7 × 17.5 cm 4.30 L 3.0 kg (6.6 lbs) 59.5 Wh/L EcoFlow RIVER 2 256 Wh 24.5 × 21.4 × 14.2 cm 7.44 L 3.5 kg (7.7 lbs) 34.4 Wh/L Anker Solix C300 288 Wh 16.4 × 16.1 × 24.0 cm 6.34 L 4.1 kg (9.1 lbs) 45.4 Wh/L Bluetti EB3A 268.8 Wh 25.5 × 18.0 × 18.3 cm 8.40 L 4.6 kg (10.1 lbs) 32.0 Wh/L

Both models can serve as a UPS for your computer, with a cutover time of less than 10ms, and feature one state-of-the-art 140W USB-C PD3.1 port that’s bidirectional. That little trick lets these power stations eschew charging bricks in favor of direct DC charging from a 140W USB-C wall charger you might already own, or a portable USB-C solar panel EcoFlow will happily sell you.

EcoFlow has also addressed a common problem with all power stations that causes them to eventually die if left idling too long. By minimizing the energy spent converting stored DC to AC output, more watt-hours remain to charge your drone, bike computer, and phone, or to power your Starlink Mini and compact fridge.

The River 260 Gen4 will be available in Europe from Q4 2026, while the River 520 Gen4 will follow sometimes in Q1 2027. Pricing for both will be announced as we get closer to their global release dates.

Tech.title: The real reason your phone is getting more expensive
Tech.content:
When Apple debuts the next generation of iPhones this week, they’re likely to come with an unwanted change: a higher price tag. A price hike from the supply-chain powerhouse would be the clearest sign yet that soaring memory costs have become unavoidable — with no end to the memory crunch in sight.

Call it “chipflation” or “RAMageddon.” The shortage is reversing a decades-long decline in memory costs that helped make consumer electronics more powerful without making them dramatically more expensive. The terms “memory prices” and “memory shortage” appeared in 473 company transcripts last quarter, according to data provided by AlphaSense. The entire industry is seemingly working on the problem. And yet, we’re years away from seeing it fixed.

The common wisdom is that AI is at fault: The technology isn’t just contributing to higher energy prices and layoffs; it’s also helping drive up the cost of everything from smartphones to game consoles.

But the shortage was brewing well before ChatGPT took off — and was then amplified by AI’s unending hunger for RAM. The current market is the product of a complicated and very profitable reshuffling of the memory industry within a system that was already failing to keep up.

“We need to build more wafer capacity,” Manish Bhatia, president and COO of Micron — one of the three largest memory manufacturers — told The Verge. “[It’s] a very different challenge for the industry than it had been for many years before, where technology alone was able to keep up with the demand.”

Samsung HBM chips on a wafer at the Nano Korea expo, July 8th, 2026. Photo: SeongJoon Cho / Bloomberg via Getty Images

For years, memory manufacturers could increase production by fitting more chips onto each wafer. But those gains were shrinking and taking longer to achieve. In 2021, even as pandemic-era electronics demand surged, Micron concluded that the problem was more fundamental: Technological advances alone would no longer create enough capacity to keep pace with long-term demand. Manufacturers would have to process more wafers — and build enormous new facilities to do it.

Then the memory business collapsed. Pandemic-era purchases of computers, tablets, and phones had pulled demand forward; consumer spending weakened, and manufacturers were left with excess inventory. They lost money and slowed their expansion plans.

By the time the market began recovering, generative AI had unleashed a wave of demand far larger and more memory-intensive than manufacturers had ever anticipated.

The memory business is also extraordinarily concentrated. Three manufacturers account for about 90 percent of the market, according to Counterpoint, leaving the world dependent on a handful of companies to divide limited capacity between AI infrastructure and consumer devices. Counterpoint estimates that Samsung controlled 39 percent of the memory market in the second quarter of 2026, followed by SK Hynix at 26 percent and Micron at 25 percent.

The memory inside your phone or computer broadly falls into two buckets. DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory, temporarily holds the information a device needs while opening apps, loading webpages, or running software. NAND flash memory provides longer-term storage for things like photos and files.

“It’s not as simple as saying data centers are consuming RAM. The RAM is not the same.”

Inside AI data centers, specialized processors rely heavily on a form of DRAM called high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.

“It’s not as simple as saying data centers are consuming RAM,” David Naranjo, associate director at Counterpoint, told The Verge. “The RAM is not the same.”

By stacking memory chips together and using advanced connections and packaging, HBM can move enormous quantities of data to and from those processors much faster and more efficiently.

It’s more difficult to produce, but also more lucrative to sell. Deep-pocketed AI chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD and tech giants like Meta and Microsoft have an insatiable need for it to power their AI systems — and are more than happy to pay.

HBM also consumes significantly more manufacturing capacity than conventional DRAM. Memory chips are made many at a time on large, circular silicon wafers. Because a finished HBM product stacks multiple, larger chips together, it requires considerably more silicon. Micron estimates that producing a given amount of HBM requires roughly three times as many wafers as producing the same amount of conventional DRAM.

The incentives increasingly favor AI. Rather than guessing how many phones or laptops will sell a year from now, memory makers can lock in multiyear commitments from some of the world’s richest companies.

“We have been engaging in discussions with customers, prioritizing those who can guarantee committed future captive demand,” Jaejune Kim, Samsung’s executive vice president of memory, said on the company’s last earnings call.

AI is also increasing demand for conventional DRAM. Phone and PC makers want to run smaller AI models directly on their devices, requiring more sophisticated conventional memory — and more of it. Future models may need substantially more memory than their predecessors to support those capabilities.

“The three big memory guys, they’re just basically allocating the capacity that they have to these companies.”

“As AI spreads across various services such as search, coding, and productivity tools, the scope of demand is widening from a memory perspective,” said Song Hyun-jong, president of SK Hynix, another of the big three memory manufacturers, on the company’s most recent earnings call. “We are witnessing a structural shift in demand where both AI memory and conventional memory are growing together.”

Samsung and Micron have both said they remain committed to conventional DRAM. Micron’s Bhatia told The Verge that it still accounts for most of the company’s wafer capacity. But limited supply, surging demand, and AI customers willing to make long-term commitments have made it extraordinarily lucrative to cede space to HBM.

SK Hynix posted a record 76 percent operating margin last quarter, up from 41 percent a year earlier, while Micron’s adjusted gross margin hit a record 85 percent. Samsung’s semiconductor profits, meanwhile, jumped roughly 250-fold from a year earlier.

“It’s more profitable,” Naranjo said. “The three big memory guys, they’re just basically allocating the capacity that they have to these companies.”

Counterpoint estimates that DRAM prices for smartphones increased roughly 56 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to a quarter earlier, and grew around 83 percent in the second quarter. For 16GB of DRAM for a smartphone, Counterpoint estimates that it cost roughly $42 in the second quarter of 2025 and about $181 a year later — an increase of more than 300 percent.

Those aren’t necessarily Apple’s prices — few companies have more leverage with suppliers — but the figures show how dramatically the component costs of building a high-end phone have changed.

Micron held a groundbreaking ceremony for its upcoming facility in Clay, New York, on January 16th. Photo: Heather Ainsworth / Bloomberg via Getty Images

The obvious solution is to make more memory. The problem is that it takes years to accomplish — even if you’re working fast.

Micron is currently demonstrating just how much work “more” entails.

In July, the company poured the first concrete for its planned manufacturing complex near Syracuse in upstate New York. Once completed, the site will contain 2.4 million square feet of cleanroom space, making it the largest semiconductor manufacturing site in US history by that measure — and Micron’s largest facility anywhere in the world.

Those cleanrooms where the chips are made will occupy only a fraction of the entire build, which is roughly the size of 350 football fields.

“By the time we’re done, we’ll have built probably 15 to 20 million actual square feet of building space to support the 2.4 million square feet of cleanroom,” Bhatia told The Verge. In one of Micron’s fab designs, the cleanroom occupies just one floor of a five-story building.

Micron doesn’t expect meaningful output until 2030

The remaining space will house a vast network of water-treatment, power, air-handling, and utility-distribution systems needed to keep it running.

Even though Micron reached the concrete pour ahead of schedule, it still took more than two years. The company began permitting after its CHIPS Act grant for New York was confirmed in March 2024, broke ground in January 2026, and poured concrete about six months later.

The physical construction unfolds in three broad stages. Preparing the ground can take six to nine months, Bhatia said. Building the concrete structure and facade can require another 18 months. But the most complicated stage comes after the building is standing: installing the vast network of mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and piping systems required to operate a semiconductor fab.

Those systems must turn an enormous industrial building into an environment where a single microscopic particle doesn’t land in the wrong place and ruin a chip.

Bhatia offered a sense of the precision required:

“Imagine trying to build all of New York state and not have any ants anywhere in the entire state,” he said. “That’s what we’re trying to do on every one of these wafers, and we do it over and over again.”

Completing the building still doesn’t produce memory. Micron expects to activate and test essential systems like power, water, and ventilation at the end of 2028, then spend 2029 moving in manufacturing equipment and beginning pilot production. The company doesn’t expect meaningful output until 2030. Even on an accelerated timeline, the journey from permitting to production will have taken roughly six years.

The company’s new Idaho fab is further along and is expected to begin wafer output in mid-2027.

Micron is spending enormous amounts to move the process along more quickly, roughly doubling its capital expenditure from a year earlier to exceed $25 billion this year.

Even with that investment, Micron can’t identify a clear point at which supply will catch up because demand continues to grow almost as quickly as manufacturers can expand.

“We’ve said that right now it’ll be beyond 2027, and we don’t see when it closes just because demand continues to grow so fast,” Bhatia said.

Counterpoint doesn’t expect capacity to catch up with demand until late 2027 or early 2028 in the best-case scenario. The market data firm IDC similarly expects the shortage to last through 2027 and well into early 2028 before there is meaningful relief.

An iPhone 17 using AI-powered notification alerts. Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

PC and smartphone makers can’t absorb component costs that have multiplied several times over indefinitely. They can raise prices. They can make fewer devices. They can put less memory in them. Or they can focus on more expensive devices with enough profit margin to absorb the added cost.

Citing soaring memory costs, Microsoft recently raised Xbox prices by another $100 to $150, leaving some models as much as $300 more expensive than at launch. Microsoft also raised the price of some Surface Pro laptops and tablets by $500 over their original starting price. Meta, meanwhile, added $100 to the cost of its Quest 3 headset.

Apple is perhaps the most revealing test case because it should be among the companies best equipped to withstand the shortage. Its scale gives it extraordinary leverage with suppliers, and its customers have historically proved willing to pay premium prices. Yet Apple has already raised prices across its lineup of Macs and iPads.

Now attention is turning to the iPhone.

Rather than releasing its full lineup at once this fall, Apple is expected to introduce the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max alongside its first foldable iPhone, while holding the standard iPhone 18 and refreshed Air until spring 2027, according to Bloomberg.

Tim Cook described memory pricing as a “100-year flood”

That leaves Apple’s fall lineup concentrated heavily at the most expensive end of the market — exactly where it has the most room to protect its margins. Counterpoint’s supply-chain tracking shows Apple preparing roughly 10 percent more iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max units for September through December than it allocated to the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max during the same period last year.

On Apple’s last earnings call, the company forecast slower growth due partly to worsening supply constraints, including for memory chips, and said higher memory costs had directly reduced its gross margin. Then-CEO Tim Cook described memory pricing as a “100-year flood,” citing “exponential increases” that had caused Apple to raise prices.

The iPhone 18 Pro could start at $1,299, according to The Wall Street Journal’s calculation based on estimates from TechInsights that factor in component costs and attempt to minimize margin reductions. That would be $200 more than the iPhone 17 Pro. Samsung and Google have each raised the starting prices of some new phones by $100 this year, though several also come with more storage.

Apple may be better positioned than most companies to pull off higher prices. Its installed base, tightly integrated ecosystem, and loyal customers make its phones behave more like luxury goods than interchangeable electronics. The company has already gained market share by keeping its prices steady while lower-end competitors raised theirs. In places like China, the world’s largest smartphone market, it almost became common sense to opt for a premium iPhone when lower-cost alternatives were selling for nearly as much.

For other manufacturers, the options are worse.

Counterpoint and IDC are already seeing smartphone companies reduce expected shipments while shifting toward more expensive models. If they can’t sell as many phones, they can at least try to extract more revenue from each one.

That means more OLED displays, AI features, larger memory configurations, and other upgrades that can justify higher prices. As a result, revenue for PCs and smartphones could actually remain flat or even rise as unit sales decline.

In other words, AI isn’t just making electronics cost more. The memory shortage is changing which electronics companies bother making in the first place.

A silicon wafer being sorted inside Micron’s Boise, Idaho, plant on June 10th, 2024. Photo: Kyle Green / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Eventually, more supply should arrive.

Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron are all investing heavily in additional manufacturing. But because new facilities take years to build, that spending won’t bring immediate relief.

SK Hynix is investing 600 trillion won in its Yongin Semiconductor Cluster, a massive complex south of Seoul first announced in 2019, and has accelerated its target for completion from 2045 to 2033. The company says it will double its capacity within five years but still expects demand to outpace supply through 2030.

Samsung and SK Hynix also plan to invest a combined 800 trillion won, or about $588 billion, in four new memory-chip factories in southwestern South Korea, according to The Wall Street Journal. Micron’s New York and Idaho projects are part of the more than $250 billion it says it will spend on US manufacturing and research through 2035.

A potentially important fourth player is also emerging in China. CXMT is building additional fabs, though its technology isn’t yet considered as advanced as that of Samsung, SK Hynix, or Micron. Apple is currently testing CXMT chips but would need approval from the Trump administration to do business with the company.

The other possibility is that supply won’t have to catch up because demand will collapse first. If the AI investment bubble bursts, memory manufacturers could suddenly find themselves facing very different economics.

For now, that remains hypothetical. The long-term contracts AI companies have signed with memory suppliers make the immediate future easier to predict.

“2027 is pretty locked and loaded,” Naranjo said.

Counterpoint and IDC expect price increases to slow from the breathtaking pace of the past year to single or low double digits. But slower increases aren’t the same as falling prices.

“Not to say prices will come down to 2025 levels, but the price increases will stabilize at a new normal,” Nabila Popal, a senior director at IDC, told The Verge. That new normal is “at least triple what they used to be.”
